State regulations define "hours worked" as follows:
Hours worked--The term includes time during which an employee is required by the employer to be on the
premises of the employer, to be on duty or to be at the prescribed work place, time spent in traveling as part of
the duties of the employee during normal working hours and time during which an employee is employed or
permitted to work; provided, however, that time allowed for meals shall be excluded unless the employee is
required or permitted to work during that time, and provided further, that time spent on the premises of the
employer for the convenience of the employee shall be excluded.
34 Pa. Code § 231.1(b) (emphasis added). Because we determine that walking time falls within the PMWA's
definition of "hours worked," we grant Mr. Davis's motion for partial summary judgment and deny Target's motion.
1. The Pennsylvania Supreme Court's decision in Heimbach controls our analysis.
According to [**12] Mr. Davis, Heimbach demands an expansive reading of the PMWA [*195] under which
walking time constitutes "hours worked" because it is time during which an employee is required to be on the
premises. DI 59 at 11-16. Target argues that Heimbach — and any definition by the Pennsylvania Supreme Court
of "hours worked" under the PMWA — is distinguishable and non-dispositive. DI 64 at 7-9; DI 60-1 at 13-15.
It helps to put the issue at hand in the context of past interpretations of both the Pennsylvania labor law and the
much older, federal version: the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 (FLSA). With the FLSA, Congress created the
right to a minimum wage and to "time-anda- half" overtime pay for employees working over forty hours a week. 29
U.S.C. § 201 et seq. At first, the United States Supreme Court "broadly" interpreted the terms "work" and
"workweek" under the FLSA. Integrity Staffing Sols., Inc. v. Busk, 574 U.S. 27, 31, 135 S. Ct. 513, 190 L. Ed. 2d
410 (2014). It defined "work" as "physical or mental exertion (whether burdensome or not) controlled or required by
the employer and pursued necessarily and primarily for the benefit of the employer and his business." Tennessee
Coal, Iron, & R. Co. v. Muscoda Local No. 123, 321 U.S. 590, 598, 64 S. Ct. 698, 88 L. Ed. 949 (1944); see Armour
& Co. v. Wantock, 323 U.S. 126, 132-34, 65 S. Ct. 165, 89 L. Ed. 118 (1944) (holding that time firefighters spent "in
playing cards and other amusements, or in idleness" while on call at the fire station was working time); Jewell Ridge
Coal Corp. v. Local No. 6167, United Mine Workers of Am., 325 U.S. 161, 163, 65 S. Ct. 1063, 89 L. Ed. 1534
(1945) (applying Tennessee Coal).
In a 1946 case, workers sought compensation [**13] for time spent walking to their respective work benches in a
pottery factory. Anderson v. Mt. Clemens Pottery Co., 328 U.S. 680, 691, 66 S. Ct. 1187, 90 L. Ed. 1515 (1946).
The Anderson Court defined "workweek" to include "all time during which an employee is necessarily required to be
on the employer's premises, on duty or at a prescribed work place." Id. at 690-91. It then held that time spent
walking to the work benches was compensable "work" under the Tennessee Coal standard, reasoning that the
"employee's convenience and necessity . . . bore no relation whatever to this walking time." Id. at 691. Rather,
employees "walked on the employer's premises only because they were compelled to do so by the necessities of
the employer's business." Id.
"These decisions provoked a flood of litigation." Busk, 574 U.S. at 31; see also Heimbach, 255 A.3d at 195
(discussing Anderson). Congress responded by passing the federal Portal-to-Portal Act (PPA) in 1947. See Busk,
574 U.S. at 31-32; Sec'y U.S. Dep't of Labor v. Nursing Home Care Mgmt., No. 23-2284, 2025 U.S. App. LEXIS
2219, 2025 WL 351599, at *2 (3d Cir. Jan. 31, 2025). The PPA states that employers cannot be liable under the
FLSA for failure to pay overtime compensation for the time spent "walking . . . to and from the actual place of
performance of the principal activities which such employee is employed to perform" and doing "activities which are
preliminary to or postliminary to said principal activity or activities." 29 U.S.C. § 254(a)(1)-(2); see Nursing Home
explicitly rejected by the Pennsylvania Supreme Court. See Heimbach, 255 A.3d at 203 n.12 ("As our Court has recognized, the
computation of overtime pay for a "workweek" depends on a determination of the actual number of "hours worked" by an
employee in that "workweek"; thus, ascertaining whether a particular employee activity constitutes "hours worked" is an
indispensable part of that assessment." (citing Chevalier v. Gen. Nutrition Ctrs., Inc., 656 Pa. 296, 220 A.3d 1038, 1058 (Pa.
2019))).
Page 7 of 15
Davis v. Target Corp.
Care, 2025 U.S. App. LEXIS 2219, 2025 WL 351599, at *2. Applying the PPA, the Supreme Court in [**14] Busk
held that time spent waiting for and undergoing security screening at a Nevada warehouse was not compensable
under the FLSA because security screening was not the workers' principal activity, or "integral and indispensable"
to their duties. 574 U.S. at 35.13
[*196] Twenty-one years after Congress enacted the PPA, the Pennsylvania legislature passed the PMWA.
Heimbach, 255 A.3d at 196. The PMWA does not contain the PPA's "specific classification of certain employee
activities as being exempt from compensation." Id. at 201; see 43 Pa. Stat. § 333.104; 34 Pa. Code § 231.1(b).
In Heimbach, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court addressed the question, certified from the Sixth Circuit, of "whether
time spent on an employer's premises waiting to undergo, and undergoing, mandatory security screening is
compensable as 'hours worked' under the PMWA." 255 A.3d at 192.14 The facts in Heimbach were not in dispute.
Amazon warehouse workers in Pennsylvania claimed they were owed compensation for the time spent waiting for
and undergoing security screening at the end of their shifts. Id. at 193. The state supreme court recognized that the

generous protections provided by a state are not precluded." Id. at 201 (quoting Chevalier, 220 A.3d at 1055).
Because the Busk decision [**15] interpreted the FLSA and not the PMWA, the state supreme court viewed it as
neither binding nor persuasive. Id. at 201. The court reasoned that the Pennsylvania legislature's decision not to
adopt the PPA was "wholly consistent" with the PMWA's stated purpose of addressing unfair ages and
"ameliorat[ing] employer practices which serve to artificially depress those wages." Id. at 202 (quoting 43 Pa. Stat. §
333.101).
The Heimbach court then proceeded to interpret the PMWA "in accordance with its own specific terms." Id. It
reasoned that the "plain language" of § 231.1(b) provides "four separate categories of an employee's time":
• "time during which an employee is required by the employer to be on the premises of the employer,"
• "[time during which an employee is required by the employer] to be on duty or to be at the prescribed work
place,"
• [*197] "time spent in traveling as part of the duties of the employee during normal working hours,"
• "and time during which an employee is employed or permitted to work".
Heimbach, 255 A.3d at 203 (quoting 34 Pa. Code § 231.1). "[A]ll time which an employee spends performing any
one of these four types of activity constitutes hours worked." Id. at 203-04 (emphasis added). The Heimbach court
"accept[ed] the Sixth Circuit's finding [**16] of fact that Amazon 'requires' employees to remain on their premises"
13 In Busk, the Supreme Court held that an activity is compensable under the FLSA, as amended by the PPA, if it is an "intrinsic
element of [principal] activities and one with which the employee cannot dispense if he is to perform his principal activities." 574

41, 126 S. Ct. 514, 163 L. Ed. 2d 288 (2005)).
14 The workers brought suit in Pennsylvania state court under both the FLSA and PMWA. Heimbach, 255 A.3d at 193-94. The
case was removed to the Eastern District of Pennsylvania and then consolidated with a multidistrict litigation matter in the
Western District of Kentucky. Id. at 194. After the Supreme Court decided Busk, the district court dismissed the workers' FLSA
claims. See Fulfillment Ctr. Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) v. Amazon.com, Inc. (In re Amazon.com, Inc.), No. 3:14-cv-204-
DJH, 2018 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 148140, 2018 WL 4148856, at *3 (W.D. Ky. Aug. 30, 2018), vacated and remanded, 856 Fed. Appx.
42 (6th Cir. 2021). The district court interpreted the PMWA claims in line with post-PPA decisions interpreting the FLSA,
reasoning that "[i]f the Pennsylvania legislature had intended to expose employers to liability foreclosed by the [PPA], one may
reasonably assume it would have done so affirmatively." Id. (internal quotations omitted). The workers appealed to the Sixth
Circuit, which certified two controlling questions of law to the Pennsylvania Supreme Court: (1) "Is time spent on an employer's
premises waiting to undergo and undergoing mandatory security screening compensable as 'hours worked' within the meaning
of the [PMWA]?" and (2) "Does the doctrine of de minimus non curat lex . . . apply to bar claims brought under the [PMWA]?" In
re Amazon, Inc., 942 F.3d 297, 304 (6th Cir. 2019).
Page 8 of 15
Davis v. Target Corp.
during security screenings and held that time spent waiting for and undergoing the screenings constituted "hours
worked." Id. at 204.
Target contends that "other comments" in Heimbach concerning the definition of "hours worked," but unrelated to
security screening, are dicta. DI 64 at 8-9; see DI 60-1 at 14; DI 68 at 13-14.15 We disagree. Dicta is "generally
regarded as information in an opinion which is not necessary to the determination of the case." BouSamra v. Excela
Health, 653 Pa. 365, 210 A.3d 967, 976 n.5 (Pa. 2019) (internal quotations omitted); see In Re Nat'l Football
Players Concussion Injury Litig., 775 F.3d 570, 583 n.18 (3d Cir. 2014) (defining dictum as "a statement in a judicial
opinion that could have been deleted without seriously impairing the analytical foundations of the holding" (quoting
In re McDonald, 205 F.3d 606, 612 (3d Cir. 2000))). Here, the Heimbach court's analysis of the definition of "hours
worked" was necessary to its ultimate determination about security screening. By its own words, the Heimbach
court examined the text of the PMWA and its regulations "in order to" answer the certified question. 255 A.3d at 202
(emphasis added). After analyzing the text of § 231.1, it determined that "hours worked" includes four categories of
time. Id. at 203. Only then, the court held that security screening falls within one of those categories. Id. at 203-04.
Target's attempt [**17] to distinguish Heimbach also falls flat. See DI 64 at 7-8; DI 60-1 at 13-15; DI 68 at 12-15.
True, the question certified in Heimbach concerned security screening and not walking time. This difference does
not justify completely disregarding the Pennsylvania Supreme Court's legal rationale. The Heimbach court could
have confined its holding to the security screening fact pattern before it, which it did not.16 The court used
expansive language, such as "Meaning of 'hours worked' under the PMWA," to guide its analysis. Heimbach, 255
A.3d at 196. And like Heimbach, this matter concerns time that warehouse workers spend on a ubiquitous activity
that occurs after (and here, before) their primary job-related tasks. Therefore, we are obligated to follow Heimbach's
directive that the definition of "hours worked" under the PMWA includes "four separate categories of time," including
"time during which an employee is required by the employer to be on the premises of the employer." Id. at 203.
2. Section 231.1(b) is not unconstitutionally vague.
Target next argues that § 231.1(b), as applied to the facts of this [*198] case, is void for vagueness. See DI 64 at
9-15; DI 60-1 at 15-25, 23 n.11. "In a void-for vagueness challenge, we must ensure that a statute or standard is
fair [**18] in that it is not so vague that a party would not know what conduct is prohibited." Borden v. School Dist.
of Tp. of East Brunswick, 523 F.3d 153, 166-67 (3d Cir. 2008) (citing San Filippo v. Bongiovanni, 961 F.2d 1125,
1136 (3d Cir. 1992)). "A statute or regulation is void for vagueness if "(1) it fails to give a person of ordinary
intelligence a reasonable opportunity to know what is prohibited, or (2) it fails to provide explicit standards to the
enforcing officer." Trojan Techs., Inc. v. Pennsylvania, 916 F.2d 903, 914 (3d Cir. 1990); Hall v. Zickefoose, 448
Fed. Appx. 184, 186 (3d Cir. 2011) (per curiam); see Coulter v. Lindsay, 2017 PA Super 92, 159 A.3d 947, 953 (Pa.
Super. Ct. 2017). "
IRAC_summ:
Case Name: Davis v. Target Corp., 767 F. Supp. 3d 185 (E.D. Pa. 2025).
Court + Jurisdiction: United States District Court, Eastern District of Pennsylvania.
Area of Law: Employment Law (Wage and Hour).
Procedural Posture: Cross-Motions for Summary Judgment.
Issue
Whether time spent by warehouse employees walking between the facility entrance and their assigned home departments before and after their shifts constitutes compensable "hours worked" under the Pennsylvania Minimum Wage Act (PMWA).
Rule
Under PMWA regulations (34 Pa. Code § 231.1(b)), "hours worked" includes all time during which an employee is "required by the employer to be on the premises of the employer" [194]. This is a distinct category from time spent "on duty" or "permitted to work" [196]. Unlike the federal Fair Labor Standards Act, which was amended by the Portal-to-Portal Act to exclude preliminary walking time, the PMWA contains no such exclusion [196]. The Pennsylvania Supreme Court in Heimbach v. Amazon.com established that if an employer requires an employee to be on the premises for a specific activity, that time is compensable regardless of whether it is a "principal activity" of the job [196-197].
Application
The court applied the Heimbach framework to the undisputed facts of Target’s Chambersburg distribution center. The facility is 1.3 million square feet, and all employees must enter and exit through a single security location [190]. Target requires employees to report to "home departments" for start-up meetings and instructs them to follow a specific, demarcated walking path for safety reasons [190-191]. Employees are trained on this path and can be disciplined for failing to use the time clocks located at their home departments [191].
Target argued that the employees were not "required" to be on the premises because they chose to work there of their own free will [200]. The court rejected this as an "absurd" interpretation, defining "required" as "demanded as necessary or essential" [200-201]. Because Target’s facility configuration and safety policies made the walk indispensable to reaching the workstation, the court found the employees were "required" to be on the premises during that time [201]. The court also dismissed Target’s "convenience" exception argument, noting that walking to a workstation is a necessity of the employer’s business, not a personal choice like using a breakroom [202]. Finally, the court held that Target could not assert a de minimis defense, as Heimbach categorically barred that defense under the PMWA [192].
Conclusion
The court granted partial summary judgment for the plaintiff, holding that the walking time is compensable under the PMWA because Target requires employees to be on the premises to navigate the facility to their assigned work areas.

Judgment, Supreme Court, Bronx County (Audrey E. Stone, J.), rendered January 12, 2024, convicting defendant,

a term of probation of five years, unanimously affirmed.

Defendant made a valid waiver of the right to appeal (see People v Thomas, 34 NY3d 545 [2019], cert denied 589 
US &, 140 S Ct 2634 [2020]; People v Bryant, 28 NY3d 1094 [2016]), which forecloses his claim that his sentence 
is excessive. In any event, we perceive no basis for reducing the sentence.

Defendant's challenge to the condition of his probation requiring him to "[a]void injurious or vicious habits; refrain 
from frequenting unlawful or disreputable places; and . . . not consort with disreputable people" under Penal Law &;

Hakes, 32 NY3d 624, 628 n 3 [2018]). Nevertheless, where defendant was found in possession of a loaded [*2]  
gun and ammunition, and given the Department of Probation's concerns that defendant was "engaging in 
disreputable behavior with the potential for dangerous consequences that poses a potential risk to public safety," 
the court providently concluded that this condition was "reasonably necessary to insure that the defendant will lead 
a law-abiding life or to assist him to do so" (Penal Law &; 65.10[1]; see People v Letterlough, 86 NY2d 259, 263 
[1995]; People v Lowndes, 239 AD3d 574, 575 [1st Dept 2025]).

Case Name: New York v. Berry [2025] N.Y. App. Div. LEXIS 6047
Court: Supreme Court of New York, Appellate Division, First Department
Area of law: Criminal Sentencing—Probation Conditions; Waiver of Appeal
Procedural posture: Appeal from a judgment convicting the defendant of attempted criminal possession of a weapon.
Issue
(1) Whether the defendant's waiver of the right to appeal precludes his claim that the sentence is excessive; and (2) whether the probation condition requiring the defendant to refrain from consorting with "disreputable people" or frequenting "disreputable places" is legal and reasonably necessary for rehabilitation.
Rule
A valid waiver of the right to appeal forecloses a defendant's claim that a sentence is excessive (People v. Thomas). However, a challenge to the legality of a sentence—including the legality of specific probation conditions—survives a valid waiver and does not require preservation (People v. Alvarez).
Regarding the merits of probation conditions, Penal Law § 65.10(1) authorizes courts to impose conditions reasonably necessary to ensure the defendant leads a law-abiding life or to assist in doing so. Conditions prohibiting association with disreputable persons or places are permissible if factually justified (People v. Letterlough).
Application
First, the court determines that the defendant executed a valid waiver of the right to appeal. Consequently, the court holds that the defendant is procedurally barred from arguing that the term of the sentence itself is excessive.
Second, the court addresses the challenge to the specific probation condition. The court acknowledges that this claim survives the appeal waiver because it implicates the legality of the sentence. However, on the merits, the court finds the condition was providently imposed. The court relies on the specific facts of the case: the defendant was convicted of possessing a loaded gun and ammunition. Additionally, the Department of Probation had expressed specific concerns that the defendant was engaging in "disreputable behavior" posing a risk to public safety. Given these facts, the court reasons that the condition requiring him to avoid disreputable people and places was reasonably necessary to ensure he leads a law-abiding life. Finally, the court notes that any constitutional challenge to the condition (as opposed to the statutory legality challenge) was waived by the appeal waiver and unpreserved, and the court declines to review it in the interest of justice.
Conclusion
The judgment is unanimously affirmed.

Lloyd v Google [2021] All ER (D) 39 (Nov)
[2021] UKSC 50
Supreme Court
Lord Reed P, Lady Arden, Lord Sales, Lord Leggatt, Lord Burrows  SCJJ
10 November 2021
PRACTICE – SERVICE OUT OF JURISDICTION – SERVICE OUT OF JURISDICTION
Abstract
The Supreme Court allowed the appeal of Google from a decision of the Court of Appeal, Civil Division, giving 
permission to the claimant to serve a claim form on Google outside the jurisdiction. The claimant was seeking 
compensation under s 13 of the Data Protection Act 1998 (DPA 1988) for damage allegedly suffered by a class of 
Apple iPhone users as a result of unlawful processing by Google of their personal data, in breach of the 
requirements of the DPA 1988. The Supreme Court restored the order of the High Court (refusing permission to 
serve out of the jurisdiction) and found that in order to recover compensation under the DPA 1998 for any given 
individual, it would be necessary to show both that Google had made some unlawful use of personal data relating to 
that individual and that the individual had suffered some damage as a result. The claimant's attempt to recover 
compensation under the DPA 1988, without proving either matter, in any individual case, was doomed to fail. 
Digest
The judgment is available at: [2021] UKSC 50
  Background     
The claimant, backed by a commercial litigation funder, issued proceedings against the defendant, Google, on 
behalf of a class of more than 4m Apple iPhone users. He alleged that Google had secretly tracked some of their 
internet activity, for commercial purposes, on certain dates. He further alleged that Google had breached the 
statutory duty, under s 4(4) of the Data Protection Act 1998 (the DPA 1998) (see [9]-[14] of the judgment). The 
claimant claimed a uniform amount by way of damages on behalf of each person within the defined class, without 
seeking to allege or prove any distinctive facts affecting any of them, save that they did not consent to the 
abstraction of their data. The claimant was entitled to advance a claim against Google on that basis in his own right 
which had a real prospect of success, the issue was, however, whether he could do so on behalf of all other iPhone 
users who fell within the represented class. As Google was a Delaware corporation, the claimant needed the court's 
permission to serve the claim form on Google outside the jurisdiction. 
The judge dismissed the claimant's application for permission to serve outside the jurisdiction on the basis that: (i) 
none of the represented class had suffered 'damage' under the DPA 1998 s 13; (ii) the members of the class had 
not had the 'same interest' within CPR 19.6(1) so as to justify allowing the claim to proceed as a representative 
action; and (iii) of his own initiative, he exercised his discretion under CPR 19.6(2) against allowing the claim to 
proceed. The claimant appealed. The Court of Appeal reversed that decision under the CPR 19.6(2) discretion. 
Google appealed. 
  Issues and decisions     
*Lloyd v Google [2021] All ER (D) 39 (Nov)
Page 2 of 5
(1) Representative and class actions in the UK. 
Class actions, in which a single person was permitted to bring a claim and obtain redress on behalf of a class of 
people who had been affected in a similar way by alleged wrongdoing, had long been possible in the United States 
and, more recently, in Canada and Australia. The only sector for which such a regime had so far been enacted in 
the UK was that of competition law. Parliament had not legislated to establish a class action regime in the field of 
data protection. A group of people who wished to bring claims which give rise to common or related issues of fact or 
law could apply to the court for a Group Litigation Order to be made under CPR 19.11, providing for the claims to be 
managed together, usually by a single designated judge. 
The other option was CPR 19.6. In its current form CPR 19.6 imposed no limit (either as a minimum or maximum) 
on the number of people who might be represented. Only one condition had to be satisfied before a representative 
claim could be begun or allowed to continue: namely, that the representative had 'the same interest' in the claim as 
the person(s) represented. Where the same interest requirement was satisfied, the court had a discretion whether 
to allow a claim to proceed as a representative action. The court in exercising discretion had to  give effect to the 
overriding objective of dealing with cases justly and at proportionate cost (see [3], [4], [24], [69]-[75] of the 
judgment).

(2) Whether the claimant could bring a claim against Google in a representative capacity seeking compensation 
under DPA 1988 s 13 for damage allegedly suffered by a class of Apple iPhone users as a result of unlawful 
processing by Google of their personal data in breach of the requirements of DPA 1998. The claimant argued that 
the principles identified in Gulati v MGN Ltd [2015] All ER (D) 199 (May), as applicable to the assessment of 
damages for misuse of private information at common law, also applied to the assessment of compensation under 
DPA 1998 s 13(1). The claimant submitted that, as a matter of principle, the same approach to the damage for 
which compensation could be awarded should apply under the data protection legislation as, where the claim had 
been brought in tort for misuse of private information because the two claims, although not coterminous, had a 
common source. Both had sought to protect the same fundamental right to privacy guaranteed by art 8 of the 
European Convention on Human Rights. 
The decision in Gulati was not applicable by analogy to the DPA 1998. To the contrary, there were significant 
differences between the privacy tort and the data protection legislation which made such an analogy positively 
inappropriate. Even if the suggested analogy between the privacy tort and the data protection regime were 
persuasive, DPA 1998 s 13(1) could not properly be interpreted as having the meaning for which the claimant 
contended. The logic of the argument, by analogy, was, in any event, flawed (see [113], [135] of the judgment). 
The detailed scheme for regulating the processing of personal data extended beyond the scope of art 8 and much 
more widely than the English domestic tort of misusing private information. An important difference was that the 
data legislation applied to all 'personal data' with no requirement that the data were of a confidential or private 
nature or that there was a reasonable expectation of privacy protection. By contrast, information was protected 
against misuse by the domestic tort only where there was a reasonable expectation of privacy. The reasonable 
expectation of privacy was an essential element of the decision in Gulati. It could not properly be inferred that the 
same entitlement should arise where a reasonable expectation of privacy was not a necessary element of the claim 
(see [130] of the judgment). 
What  the claimant was seeking to do was to claim for each member of the represented class a form of damages 
the rationale for which depended on there being a violation of privacy, while avoiding the need to show a violation of 
privacy in the case of any individual member of the class. That was a flawed endeavour (see [131] of the judgment). 
It 
was unnecessary to decide whether the Court of Appeal had been entitled to interfere with the judge's 
discretionary ruling or whether it would be desirable for a commercially funded class action to be available on the 
facts alleged in this case. Regardless of what view of it was taken, the claim had no real prospect of success. That 
in turn was because, of the way the claim had been framed in order to try to bring it as a representative action. The 
seeking of damages under DPA 1998 for each individual member of the represented class without attempting to 
*Lloyd v Google [2021] All ER (D) 39 (Nov)
Page 4 of 5
show that any wrongful use had been made by Google of personal data relating to that individual or that the 
individual suffered any material damage or distress as a result of a breach of the requirements of the DPA 1998 by 
Google, was flawed. Without proof of these matters, a claim for damages could not succeed (see [159] of the 
judgment). 
In order to recover compensation under the DPA 1998 for any given individual, it would be necessary to show both 
that Google had made some unlawful use of personal data relating to that individual and that the individual had 
suffered some damage as a result (see [8] of the judgment).
DPA 1998 s 13 could not reasonably be interpreted as conferring on a data subject a right to compensation for any 
(non-trivial) contravention by a data controller of any of the requirements of the DPA 1998, without the need to 
prove that the contravention had caused material damage or distress to the individual concerned (see [138] of the 
judgment). 
Even if it were unnecessary in order to recover compensation under the provision to show that an individual had 
suffered material damage or distress as a result of unlawful processing of his or her personal data, it would still be 
necessary to establish the extent of the unlawful processing in his or her individual case. In deciding what amount 
of damages, if any, should be awarded, relevant factors would include: over what period of time had Google tracked 
the individual's internet browsing history; what quantity of data had been unlawfully processed; had any of the 
information been unlawfully processed of a sensitive or private nature; what use had Google made of the 
information and what commercial benefit, if any, had Google obtained from such use (see [144] of the judgment). 
Gulati and others v MGN Ltd [2015] EWHC 1482 (Ch), 165 NLJ 7655, [2015] All ER (D) 199 (May) distinguished
The appeal would be allowed (see [160] of the judgment).

IRAC_summ:
Case Name: Lloyd v Google [2021] UKSC 50
Court + jurisdiction: United Kingdom Supreme Court
Area of law: Data Protection – Representative Actions – Damages
Procedural posture: Appeal from the Court of Appeal, Civil Division.
Issue
Whether a claimant can bring a representative action under CPR 19.6 on behalf of a class of data subjects to recover uniform compensation under section 13 of the Data Protection Act 1998 for "loss of control" of data, without proving individual damage or distress.
Rule
Under section 13(1) of the Data Protection Act 1998 (DPA 1998), a data subject is entitled to compensation for "damage" suffered by reason of a contravention of the Act. "Damage" under this section requires proof of material damage (financial loss) or distress; it does not include a standalone right to compensation for the mere "loss of control" of personal data irrespective of any consequent harm. To proceed as a representative action under CPR 19.6, the representative and the class members must have the "same interest" in the claim.
Application
The Court rejected the claimant's attempt to use the representative action procedure to claim a uniform sum for 4 million iPhone users based solely on Google's unlawful tracking. The claimant argued that "loss of control" of data was itself a form of compensable damage under the DPA 1998, analogous to the tort of misuse of private information (Gulati v MGN Ltd).
The Court distinguished the DPA 1998 from the misuse of private information tort. The tort protects a reasonable expectation of privacy, whereas the DPA 1998 regulates all personal data regardless of privacy expectations. Consequently, the damages principles from Gulati (awarding damages for loss of right to control private information) could not be imported into the statutory scheme [113], [130]. Section 13 requires proof that the individual suffered actual damage or distress caused by the breach; a non-trivial contravention alone does not trigger compensation [138].
Because section 13 requires individualized assessment of damage—considering the nature of the data, the duration of tracking, and the specific impact on each user—the members of the proposed class did not have the "same interest" [144]. The claimant’s strategy of disavowing individual circumstances to create a uniform claim was legally flawed because it sought compensation without proving the essential element of damage for each class member [159]. Without proof of unlawful use and resulting damage for each individual, the representative claim was doomed to fail.
Conclusion
The Court held that section 13 of the DPA 1998 requires proof of individual damage or distress and does not permit uniform compensation for mere loss of control of data, precluding the representative action; the appeal was allowed.

Adoption of Paco
Appeals Court of Massachusetts

October 28, 2025, Entered

24-P-1464

Reporter
2025 Mass. App. Unpub. LEXIS 796 *; 2025 LX 482097

ADOPTION OF PACO.1

Notice: Summary decisions issued by the Appeals Court pursuant to M.A.C. Rule 23.0, as appearing in 97 Mass. 
App. Ct. 1017 (2020) (formerly known as rule 1:28, as amended by 73 Mass. App. Ct. 1001 [2009]), are primarily 
directed to the parties and, therefore, may not fully address the facts of the case or the panel's decisional rationale. 
Moreover, such decisions are not circulated to the entire court and, therefore, represent only the views of the panel 
that decided the case. A summary decision pursuant to rule 23.0 or rule 1:28 issued after February 25, 2008, may 
be cited for its persuasive value but, because of the limitations noted above, not as binding precedent. See Chace 
v. Curran, 71 Mass. App. Ct. 258, 260 n.4, 881 N.E.2d 792 (2008).

Disposition: Decree affirmed.

Core Terms

father's, unfitness, best interests of the child, mental health, violence, terminate, prescription, appointment, 
symptom

Judges: Meade, Walsh & Hodgens, JJ. [*1] 

Opinion

MEMORANDUM AND ORDER PURSUANT TO RULE 23.0

Following a trial, and entry of the mother's stipulation terminating her parental rights, a Juvenile Court judge found 
the father unfit to parent the child, awarded custody of the child to the Department of Children and Families 
(department), determined that the department's adoption plan was in the child's best interests, and entered a 
decree terminating the father's parental rights. The father appeals, and we affirm.

Background. The child, born prematurely in December 2017 at twenty-six weeks, spent the first three months of his 
life in the hospital's neonatal intensive care unit. Due to his premature birth, the child (age five at conclusion of trial) 

1 A pseudonym.



Page 2 of 5
Adoption of Paco, 2025 Mass. App. Unpub. LEXIS 796

has several significant needs around feeding and nutrition, sleep, asthma, and allergies. He also has behavioral 
and emotional difficulties. These needs require frequent appointments with specialists, prescribed medication, and 
follow-up care. He began preschool, completed an early intervention service, and started an assessment for an 
individualized education plan due to a concern about his ability "to follow regular instructions." The child has been in 
the same foster home [*2]  since January 2020.

The father reported being diagnosed with mental health conditions (including posttraumatic stress disorder, 
depression, anxiety, schizophrenia, and multiple personality disorder). He testified that he has had an imaginary 
friend since the age of fourteen. He receives some treatment for the persistent symptoms of these mental health 
conditions but struggles to recall taking medications and rarely accounted for prescription medications during home 
visits by an ongoing social worker. In addition to having difficulty managing his prescriptions, the father self-
medicates with marijuana and oxycodone. The father also experienced periods of housing instability, has been 
involved in multiple instances of domestic violence, has been the subject of three restraining orders, has violated 
the terms of his probation, and has been incarcerated.

The department first became involved with the child in the days following his birth based on a report filed pursuant 
to G. L. c. 119, § 51A. The department opened a case for services after an investigation of the report resulted in a 
decision to support allegations that the mother used marijuana during her pregnancy, both parents experienced 
significant symptoms [*3]  of untreated mental health conditions, and both parents engaged in domestic violence 
resulting in the loss of housing. The father reported to the department that he did not remember the domestic 
violence incident because he experienced two seizures and "was out of it." The mother obtained a restraining order 
against him that remained in effect for more than two years, until February 14, 2019.

On December 10, 2019, the father was arrested and charged with two counts of assault and battery by means of a 
dangerous weapon, assault and battery on a family or household member, threatening to commit a crime, and 
larceny, with the mother listed as the victim. Following his arrest, another restraining order issued, requiring the 
father to stay away and have no contact with the mother and the child. While in custody awaiting trial, the father 
reported to a department investigator that he "never touched" the mother. He later pleaded guilty and was placed 
on probation.

On January 21, 2020, the mother left the child in the care of his maternal aunt, who subsequently took him to the 
hospital with an eye infection. The father, who was at the same hospital for medical care, took the child and left 
the [*4]  hospital. Soon after, the police located the father and arrested him for violating the restraining order. The 
following day, the department obtained emergency custody of the child. The child has remained in department 
custody since that time.

The next month, the department established a family action plan for the father. The action plan included 
requirements that the father maintain contact with the department, participate in a parenting course, complete an 
intimate partner violence education program, and identify and consistently meet with a therapist and psychiatrist. 
Complying with part of the action plan, the father completed an intimate partner violence education program and 
parenting course. Not complying with other parts of the plan, the father failed to consistently meet with a therapist, 
provide the department with his psychological evaluation, and provide adequate proof of his income. Additionally, 
the father missed over twenty visits with the child, resulting in over a month between some visits.

On February 12, 2024, following a trial held over five nonconsecutive days and during which the father testified, a 
judge adjudicated the child in need of care and protection, found [*5]  the father unfit, and found that termination of 
the father's parental rights was in the child's best interests. The judge approved the department's plan for adoption 
of the child by his current foster parents and allowed for limited posttermination and postadoption visitation with the 
child by the father.

Discussion. To terminate parental rights to a child and to dispense with parental consent to adoption, "a judge must 
find by clear and convincing evidence, based on subsidiary findings proved by at least a fair preponderance of 
evidence, that the parent is unfit to care for the child and that termination is in the child's best interests." Adoption of 
Jacques, 82 Mass. App. Ct. 601, 606, 976 N.E.2d 814 (2012). "In determining whether the best interests of the 



Page 3 of 5
Adoption of Paco, 2025 Mass. App. Unpub. LEXIS 796

child[] will be served by issuing a decree dispensing with the need for consent, a 'court shall consider the ability, 
capacity, fitness and readiness of the child's parents.'" Adoption of Nancy, 443 Mass. 512, 515, 822 N.E.2d 1179 
(2005), quoting G. L. c. 210, § 3 (c). "We give substantial deference to a judge's decision that termination of a 
parent's rights is in the best interest of the child, and reverse only where the findings of fact are clearly erroneous or 
where there is a clear error of law or abuse of discretion." Adoption of Ilona, 459 Mass. 53, 59, 944 N.E.2d 115 
(2011). Based on these standards, we discern no error or abuse [*6]  of discretion.

We disagree with the father's contention that the judge "relie[d] on the father's stale history of assaultive behavior[.]" 
While "stale information cannot be the basis for a finding of current parental unfitness . . .[p]rior history . . . has 
prognostic value." Adoption of Jacques, 82 Mass. App. Ct. at 607, quoting Adoption of George, 27 Mass. App. Ct. 
265, 268, 537 N.E.2d 1251 (1989). The judge considered the father's history of violence against the mother and 
others, while also acknowledging the improvements made by the father. Specifically, the judge noted that since 
completing an intimate partner abuse prevention course in 2020, "[t]here is no evidence that [the father] was 
involved in any domestic violence incident[.]" Even so, the father admitted at trial that he had a pending assault and 
battery charge following an altercation with a tow truck driver. The evidence also showed that the father reacted 
aggressively to department staff on at least one occasion while visiting the child. In light of such repeated incidents, 
the father's violent and aggressive behavior served as prognostic evidence that was "within the purview of the judge 
to consider." Adoption of Jacques, supra at 607-608.

Next, the father argues that the judge erred in finding that he did not understand, nor was he able to meet, the 
child's needs. [*7]  The father points to several of the judge's findings in advancing this argument, including that he 
did not understand the child's medical, emotional, and behavioral conditions requiring specialized care; that he did 
not attend medical appointments; and that he "willfully" missed visits with the child. We discern no error. The father 
testified generally about the child's medical needs, and that the child took medication. Despite this general 
understanding, the father did not know what medications the child needed, nor did he ever ask about the 
medications. As the father acknowledges in his brief, his lack of knowledge likely comes from his absence from the 
child's medical appointments — a circumstance he blames on "hurdles" beyond his control such as lack of 
transportation. The record, however, shows that the father repeatedly turned down offers by the department to 
assist with attending medical appointments. Additionally, there was ample evidence of the father's failure to 
consistently attend scheduled visits with the child. While some visits were canceled by the department, several 
visits were missed because the father failed to confirm or even show up. Where the father did not consistently [*8]  
attend medical appointments or visits with the child, or express any understanding of the child's care regimens, the 
record supports the judge's findings that the father did not understand and could not meet the child's complex 
needs. See Adoption of Mary, 414 Mass. 705, 711, 610 N.E.2d 898 (1993) (parental unfitness must be determined 
on consideration of child's particular needs).

We disagree with the father's contention that there is insufficient evidence that he "misuse[d]" prescription 
medication at the time of trial, and that there was no nexus between the substance use and his ability to parent the 
child. While this case was pending, the father tested positive for a component of marijuana, tetrahydrocannabinol 
(THC), and the department expressed concerns about his substance use. Evidence showed that the father needed 
help maintaining his regimen of prescribed medications and rarely accounted for these medications during 
department visits. The father admitted at trial that he lied to the department about his substance use, leading the 
judge to conclude that the "[f]ather does not recognize that he misuses unprescribed substances and thus has not 
engaged in any services to address it[.]" Based on the father's inability to manage his own [*9]  prescription 
medications to address persistent negative symptoms of his mental health conditions, the positive drug test and use 
of marijuana, the admitted lying about having a prescription for oxycodone, and the father's explanation to the 
ongoing social worker that he failed to answer several calls because he was sleeping during the day, the judge 
could properly conclude that the father's unabating substance misuse constituted "a contributing factor" to his 
current and future unfitness. Adoption of Xarissa, 99 Mass. App. Ct. 610, 618, 171 N.E.3d 737 (2021).

We also disagree with the father's argument that the record does not support the judge's findings regarding his 
housing. The judge carefully traced a timeline of the father's varied housing arrangements: he lived approximately 
one year with the mother and child until his arrest and incarceration in 2020; he was "homeless" and living in a 



Page 4 of 5
Adoption of Paco, 2025 Mass. App. Unpub. LEXIS 796

shelter placement starting in September 2020; he lived with another person from January 2021 through at least 
September 2022 when he fell behind in rent and utilities; and finally, following his marriage, he lived with his wife 
and her three sons. While the record supports that the father's housing stabilized in the time leading up to the trial, it 
also showed an [*10]  unwillingness by the father to inform the department of changes in housing or to schedule 
home visits, both of which were required by his action plans. Even when he had stable housing, the father testified 
that he owed several thousand dollars in overdue rent and utility payments, ultimately causing his electricity service 
to be disconnected. Thus, the record supports the judge's finding that the father's housing instability contributed to 
his parental unfitness. See Adoption of Abigail, 23 Mass. App. Ct. 191, 196, 499 N.E.2d 1234 (1986) ("A past 
pattern of behavior . . . has prognostic value"). See also Adoption of Yvonne, 99 Mass. App. Ct. 574, 581, 170 
N.E.3d 1178 (2021) (judge properly considered housing instability where department was unable to verify parent's 
living situation or conduct home visits).

Contrary to the father's claim, the record also supports the judge's findings regarding untreated symptoms of mental 
health conditions. The father argues that the department's difficulties in contacting his providers was not sufficient to 
find him unfit. While the judge found that the father "shielded his providers from the [d]epartment[,]" this finding was 
only one of many findings bearing on the father's mental health. For example, as previously discussed, the judge 
found that the father was unable to manage his own [*11]  medications. One department worker testified that the 
father was unable to produce his medication during several home visits, and on the few occasions that he could, the 
medication bottles had old labels or were empty. This evidence supported the judge's logical conclusion that the 
"[f]ather's inability to manage his own medication is a predictor that he will also be unable to manage [the child's] 
medications." See Adoption of Frederick, 405 Mass. 1, 9, 537 N.E.2d 1208 (1989) (symptoms of parent's mental 
health conditions may impair "capacity to assume parental responsibility, and ability to deal with a child's . . . 
needs").

The evidence also supported the judge's finding that the father's unfitness was likely to continue indefinitely. By the 
time the trial concluded, the department had been involved with the father for over three years. After all that time, as 
the judge noted, the concerns precipitating the department's involvement remained. Although commending the 
father's improvements, including completing the "nurturing fathers" program and attempting to comply with the 
action plan, the judge ultimately concluded that the father "falls short from making observable changes," and "there 
still exists a substantial risk of harm to the child." [*12]  See Adoption of Paula, 420 Mass. 716, 730, 651 N.E.2d 
1222 (1995) (absent evidence that services have "appreciably improved" capacity to meet needs of child, mere 
participation in services does not equate with fitness); Adoption of Jacques, 82 Mass. App. Ct. at 608 (judge entitled 
to consider evidence of parent's recent improvements within context of earlier and continuing deficits). We do not 
substitute our judgment for that of the judge who heard the evidence.

Lastly, the father contends that the judge abused his discretion in finding that termination served the child's best 
interests, arguing that "dispositive" weight was given to the child's bond with his foster parents. We disagree. The 
judge considered the factors set forth in G. L. c. 119, § 26, and G. L. c. 210, § 3 (c), in determining the best 
interests of the child. While the judge acknowledged the child's bond with his foster parents and the emotional and 
psychological harm that removal would cause, there is nothing in the record to support that such consideration was 
dispositive. The judge also considered the father's mental health, his history of violence, his history of housing 
instability, and his failure to consistently cooperate with the department. Therefore, the judge did not abuse his 
discretion in determining that freeing the child for adoption was in the [*13]  best interests of the child. See Adoption 
of Quentin, 424 Mass. 882, 886 n.3, 678 N.E.2d 1325 (1997) (parent's "dissatisfaction with the judge's weighing of 
the evidence and his credibility determinations" is not sufficient basis to warrant relief on appeal).

Decree affirmed.

By the Court (Meade, Walsh & Hodgens, JJ.2),

Entered: October 28, 2025.

IRAC_summ:
Case Name: Adoption of Paco
Jurisdiction / Court: Appeals Court of Massachusetts
Citation: 2025 Mass. App. Unpub. LEXIS 796
Date: October 28, 2025
I. Issue(s)
Was there clear and convincing evidence to support the judge's finding that the father was currently unfit to parent the child?
Did the judge abuse his discretion in determining that terminating the father's parental rights was in the child's best interests?
II. Rule(s)
Standard for Termination of Parental Rights: To terminate parental rights, a judge must find by clear and convincing evidence that the parent is currently unfit to care for the child and that termination is in the child's best interests. This determination must be based on subsidiary findings proved by a preponderance of the evidence. (G. L. c. 210, § 3 (c); Adoption of Jacques, 82 Mass. App. Ct. 601).Prognostic Value of Past Conduct: While stale information alone cannot support a finding of current unfitness, a parent's prior history and past patterns of behavior have "prognostic value" in determining future fitness. (Adoption of George, 27 Mass. App. Ct. 265).
Child's Specific Needs: Parental unfitness must be evaluated in the context of the child's particular needs. (Adoption of Mary, 414 Mass. 705).
Best Interests of the Child: The court must consider the parent's ability, capacity, fitness, and readiness, as well as the child's bond with foster parents and the potential harm of removal. (G. L. c. 210, § 3 (c)).
III. Application (Analysis)
Parental Unfitness: The court found sufficient evidence to support the finding of unfitness, based on a combination of factors:
History of Violence: The father had a history of domestic violence and a pending assault charge. The court held that this was not "stale" information but rather prognostic evidence of his ongoing aggressive behavior.
Inability to Meet Child's Needs: The child had significant and complex medical needs. The father demonstrated a lack of understanding of these needs, did not know the child's medications, and failed to consistently attend medical appointments despite the department offering assistance. His inconsistent attendance at visits further supported this finding.
Substance Misuse: The father tested positive for THC, admitted to using unprescribed oxycodone, and lied to the department about his substance use. This misuse, combined with his inability to manage his own prescribed medications for his mental health conditions, was a contributing factor to his unfitness.
Housing and Mental Health Instability: The father had a history of housing instability and an inability to manage his own mental health, evidenced by his failure to consistently take prescribed medications. The judge properly concluded that his inability to manage his own medication regimen was a predictor of his inability to manage the child's complex medical care. The court found that despite some improvements, the father's unfitness was likely to continue indefinitely.
Best Interests of the Child: The court found no abuse of discretion. The judge did not give "dispositive" weight to the child's bond with his foster parents but properly considered it as one of several factors. The decision was also based on the father's ongoing unfitness, including his mental health issues, history of violence, and failure to consistently cooperate with the department.
IV. Conclusion
Yes. The evidence was sufficient to support the judge's finding that the father was unfit to parent the child, based on his history of violence, inability to meet the child's complex needs, substance misuse, and mental health instability.
No. The judge did not abuse his discretion in finding that termination of the father's parental rights was in the child's best interests. The decree terminating the father's parental rights was affirmed.

case:
*Tesco Stores Ltd v Union of Shop, Distributive and Allied Workers and others [2024] All ER (D) 24 (Sep)
*Tesco Stores Ltd v Union of Shop, Distributive and Allied Workers and 
others [2024] All ER (D) 24 (Sep)
[2024] UKSC 28
Supreme Court
Lord Reed, President, Lord Lloyd-Jones, Lord Leggatt, Lord Burrows and Lady Simler
12 September 2024
EMPLOYMENT – COLLECTIVE AGREEMENT – WHETHER LOWER COURT ERRING IN FINDING 
RESPONDENT COMPANY ENTITLED TO TERMINATE CERTAIN EMPLOYMENT CONTRACTS FOR SPECIFIC 
PURPOSE OF DEPRIVING EMPLOYEES OF RETAINED PAY, AND OFFERING RE-ENGAGEMENT ON TERMS 
OMITTING IT
Abstract
The Supreme Court allowed the appellant employees' (and their union's) appeal, concerning whether the Court of 
Appeal, Civil Division, had erred in finding that the respondent company (Tesco) had been entitled to terminate its 
employees' employment contracts for the specific purpose of depriving them of 'retained pay' (RP) (a financial 
contractual entitlement which was described as a 'permanent' benefit), and to offer re-engagement on terms without 
RP (the 'fire and re-hire' mechanism). The High Court had granted an injunction to restrain Tesco from terminating 
the employees' employment to remove the RP term. The Court of Appeal had allowed Tesco's appeal. The court 
ruled among other things, that: (i) on the true construction of the express RP term in the relevant employment 
contracts, the word 'permanent' conveyed that the right to RP was not time-limited in any way and would continue to 
be paid to employees for as long as their employment in the same role continued, subject only to the other two 
qualifications set out in the RP term; (ii) however, applying the test of business efficacy (or obviousness), Tesco 
was precluded by an implied term from exercising the contractual right to dismiss the claimants on notice for the 
purpose of removing or diminishing their right to receive permanent RP; (iii) the exception to the general rule that a 
contract of employment was not specifically enforceable was engaged, in circumstances where there had been no 
breakdown of mutual trust and confidence (Tesco was prepared to re-engage the relevant employees), and where 
damages would be inadequate; and (iv) accordingly, the injunction which the High Court had granted in favour of 
the employees would be reinstated.
Digest
The judgment is available at: [2024] UKSC 28
  Background     
The appeal concerned whether the respondent company, Tesco Stores Ltd (Tesco), could terminate the 
employment contracts of its employees, for the specific purpose of depriving them of 'retained pay' (RP), a financial 
contractual entitlement which was agreed to be permanent.
The appeal raised fundamental questions about an employer's right, under contract law, to terminate a contract of 
employment by giving the requisite notice to the employee and about an employee's remedies for breach of an 
employment contract. 
Page 2 of 5
*Tesco Stores Ltd v Union of Shop, Distributive and Allied Workers and others [2024] All ER (D) 24 (Sep)
In 2007, Tesco closed certain of its distribution centres, to expand or restructure others, and to open new sites. It 
sought to incentivise existing employees at the centres being closed to relocate to another site. Tesco and its 
recognised trade union, the Union of Shop, Distributive and Allied Workers (USDAW), made a collective agreement 
under which Tesco agreed to provide retained pay (RP) to employees who agreed to relocate. The right to receive 
RP was then incorporated into the relevant employment contracts as an express term, which stated that RP would 
'remain a permanent feature' of an employee's contractual entitlement, subject to certain qualifications. A separate 
term in the employment contracts gave Tesco a contractual right to dismiss the employee without cause, on 
provision of specified notice. 
In 2021, Tesco sought to end RP. It informed employees that, if they did not consent to the removal of their right to 
receive it, they would be dismissed and offered re-engagement. The re-engagement terms would be identical, save 
for the removal of the RP term. Together with USDAW, several employees in receipt of RP applied to the High 
Court for declarations as to the true meaning of the RP term, and an injunction to restrain Tesco from terminating 
their employment to remove the RP term. The High Court allowed the claim and granted the injunction.
The Court of Appeal, Civil Division, unanimously allowed Tesco's appeal. 
The appellants, the union and the employees, appealed to the Supreme Court 
  Issues and decisions     
Whether the Court of Appeal had erred in finding that Tesco had been entitled to terminate certain employment 
contracts of its employees for the specific purpose of depriving them of RP and offer re-engagement on terms 
without it (the so-called 'fire and re-hire' mechanism).
The court considered: (i) the correct interpretation of an express term, concerning RP, as agreed in a collective 
agreement, which stated that: 'Retained pay will remain a permanent feature of an individual's contractual eligibility 
subject to the following principles' (see [17] of the judgment); (ii) whether Tesco was precluded by an implied term 
from exercising the contractual right to dismiss the claimants on notice for the purpose of removing or diminishing 
their right to receive permanent RP; and (iii) the correct remedy: damages or an injunction.
The appeal would be allowed and the injunction granted by the High Court would be reinstated (see [85] of the 
judgment). 
(i) The word 'permanent' in the RP term conveyed that the right to RP was not time-limited in any way and would 
continue to be paid to employees for as long as their employment in the same role continued (that it had to continue 
in the same role followed from the subsequent qualification that 'on promotion to a new role it will cease') and 
subject only to the other two qualifications set out in the RP term. However, if Tesco's case were correct, that 
promise was defeated (or deprived of its value) as there was nothing to prevent Tesco from removing it unilaterally 
by dismissal on notice at any time of Tesco's choosing and offering re-engagement on contractual terms that did 
not include RP. Accordingly, the real question was whether there was a term implied by fact that qualified Tesco's 
otherwise unrestricted contractual right to terminate the employment contracts on notice in order to deprive 
employees of the right to permanent RP (see [36]-[42] of the judgment).
(ii) Applying the test of business efficacy (or obviousness), Tesco was precluded by an implied term from exercising 
the contractual right to dismiss the claimants on notice for the purpose of removing or diminishing their right to 
receive permanent RP (see [57] of the judgment).
It was necessary, applying the business efficacy test, to imply a term in the contracts to qualify Tesco's right to 
dismiss on notice so that it could not be exercised for the purpose of depriving the claimants of their right to 
permanent RP. That implied term was necessary (or, alternatively, it was so obvious that it went without saying) in 
order not to undermine the promise that RP would be a 'permanent' feature of contractual entitlements for the 
relevant employees (subject only to the qualifications specified by the RP term). The circumstances in which the 
right to RP was agreed made clear that the offer of permanent RP was intended as an inducement to employees to 
accept the terms of the collectively negotiated agreement and make permanent changes to their lives by relocating 
Page 3 of 5
*Tesco Stores Ltd v Union of Shop, Distributive and Allied Workers and others [2024] All ER (D) 24 (Sep)
to the new distribution centres, rather than accepting redundancy. The implied term was that Tesco's contractual 
right to terminate the contract on notice could not be exercised for the purpose of removing or diminishing the right 
of that employee to receive RP. It operated to qualify (rather than contradict) the express contractual right to 
terminate on notice. It did not mean that Tesco could not dismiss for any other unrelated reason (including lack of 
capability, misconduct, or redundancy). The stringent tests applicable to the implication of a term by fact were 
satisfied (see [43]-[48] of the judgment).
The court's view as to there being an implied term was supported by a line of cases concerning employment 
contracts offering valuable long-term sickness or permanent health insurance benefits (the PHI cases), which had 
established that '... employer ought not to terminate the employment as a means to remove the employee's 
entitlement to benefit but the employer can dismiss for good cause whether that be on the ground of gross 
misconduct or, more generally, for some repudiatory breach by the employee ...'. Plainly there were limits to the 
principle established by the PHI cases, and it should be sparingly and cautiously used to avoid turning the 
traditional principles of contract upside down. It should not be used to imply a term that conflicted with the express 
terms of the contract. The clear, consistent requirements for a term to be implied by fact into a contract were not in 
dispute. It was clear that, for such a term to be implied, either the business efficacy or obviousness test must be 
satisfied. A term should not be implied by fact on the basis that it was reasonable to do so (see [34], [35], [51]-[56] 
of the judgment).
(iii) The general rule was that a contract of employment was not specifically enforceable. The court had recognised 
two exceptions: where damages were inadequate; and where there was no breakdown in mutual confidence 
between employer and employee. In the present case, the grant of the injunction would amount to indirect specific 
performance of Tesco's obligation to continue to employ the employees on RP. The question was whether indirect 
specific performance be ordered against Tesco even though one was dealing with a contract of employment. 
Applying settled law to the facts of the present case, there had been no breakdown of mutual confidence. Tesco 
had no complaints about the employees' work performance and maintained confidence in them. The clear proof of 
that was that Tesco was offering the employees a new contract on the same terms except as to RP. Further, 
damages would be an inadequate remedy in the case because of the difficulties of assessment and because non
pecuniary loss would be irrecoverable (see [58]-[84] of the judgment).

IRAC_summ:
Case Name: Tesco Stores Ltd v Union of Shop, Distributive and Allied Workers and others [2024] UKSC 28
Court + jurisdiction: United Kingdom Supreme Court
Area of law: Employment Law – Contract Interpretation – Implied Terms
Procedural posture: Appeal from the Court of Appeal, Civil Division
Issue
Whether an employer is precluded by an implied term from exercising an express contractual right to dismiss employees on notice for the specific purpose of depriving them of a financial benefit explicitly described in the employment contract as “permanent”.
Rule
The court applies the principles of contract interpretation and implied terms, specifically the "business efficacy" and "obviousness" tests (Marks and Spencer plc v BNP Paribas). Where a contract confers a "permanent" benefit alongside a general right to dismiss on notice, a term may be implied to prevent the right of dismissal from being used solely to negate that benefit. Regarding remedies, an injunction against dismissal is available as an exception to the general rule against specific performance of employment contracts where there is no breakdown of mutual trust and confidence and damages would be an inadequate remedy (Powell v Brent London Borough Council).
Application
The Court first addressed the construction of the express term "Retained Pay" (RP), which the contract stated would remain a "permanent feature" of the individual's eligibility. The Court reasoned that "permanent" meant the entitlement was not time-limited and would continue as long as the employee remained in the specific role, subject only to express qualifications like promotion [36]–[42].
Applying the business efficacy test, the Court found that Tesco’s interpretation—that it could dismiss employees on notice purely to re-hire them without RP—would defeat the purpose of the "permanent" promise. The Court emphasised that the RP was an inducement for employees to relocate, involving significant life changes. Therefore, it was necessary to imply a term that qualified Tesco's right to dismiss. Specifically, the right to terminate on notice could not be exercised for the purpose of removing or diminishing the right to RP [43]–[48]. This implied term did not contradict the express termination clause but limited its scope; Tesco retained the right to dismiss for other reasons, such as redundancy or misconduct [48].
Regarding the remedy, the Court held that the exception to the rule against specific performance of employment contracts applied. There was no breakdown in mutual trust and confidence because Tesco was willing to re-engage the same employees in the same roles, merely on different financial terms [78]. Furthermore, damages were inadequate because the loss involved a "permanent" entitlement that was difficult to quantify and included non-pecuniary elements of job security. Consequently, an injunction restraining the dismissal was the appropriate remedy [82]–[84].
Conclusion
The Court held that an implied term prevented the employer from exercising its contractual right to dismiss solely to remove the permanent retained pay entitlement and reinstated the injunction preventing such dismissal; the appeal was allowed.

case_name: X v Kuoni Travel Ltd [2021] UKSC 34
case:
FS Cairo (Nile Plaza) LLC v Brownlie (as dependant and executrix of Sir Ian Brownlie CBE QC) [2021] All ER 
(D) 105 (Oct)
FS Cairo (Nile Plaza) LLC v Brownlie (as dependant and executrix of Sir Ian 
Brownlie CBE QC) [2021] All ER (D) 105 (Oct)
[2021] UKSC 45
Supreme Court
Lord Reed P, Lord Lloyd-Jones, Lord Briggs, Lord Leggatt and Lord Burrows SCJJ
20 October 2021
Claim form – Service – Service out of the jurisdiction
Abstract
The Supreme Court dismissed the appellant Egyptian company's appeal against the lower court's dismissal of it's 
appeal, concerning whether permission should have been given to the respondent widow to serve proceedings out 
of the jurisdiction. The respondent's claim in contract and in tort sought damages from the appellant, which 
operated a hotel in Egypt that had provided an excursion, during which the respondent had been injured and her 
husband had been killed in an accident while on holiday. The court held that the gateway in para 3.1(9)(a) of CPR 
PD 6B (the tort gateway), namely that 'damage was sustained ... within the jurisdiction', related to actionable harm 
suffered in the jurisdiction as a result of the wrongful acts alleged, and that the three heads of claim in the present 
case ((i) a claim for damages for personal injury in the respondent's own right; (ii) a claim for damages in her 
capacity as executrix of the estate of her late husband for wrongful death; and (iii) a claim for damages for 
bereavement and loss of dependency in her capacity as her late husband's widow) should be considered to relate 
to actionable harm suffered in the jurisdiction of England and Wales as a result of the wrongful acts alleged and, 
therefore, to pass through the tort gateway. The court held that England and Wales was the proper jurisdiction in 
which to bring the claim and, further, that the respondent's claims were pleaded under Egyptian law, such that there 
was no scope for applying English law by default. The court ruled that, in the absence of any evidence of Egyptian 
law, there was no basis for challenging the judge's decision that, at the present stage of the proceedings, reliance 
on the presumption of similarity with English law was sufficient to show that the pleaded claims had a real prospect 
of success.
Digest
The judgment is available at: [2021] UKSC 45
  Background     
In January 2010, the respondent (Lady B) and her husband, Sir B, were on holiday in Egypt. They stayed at the 
Four Seasons Hotel Cairo at Nile Plaza. 
On 3 January 2010, they went on a guided driving tour which Lady B had booked through the hotel. The vehicle 
they were travelling in during the tour crashed, killing Sir B and seriously injuring Lady B. 
Lady B issued a claim in England, seeking damages in contract and tort. The case reached the Supreme Court, 
which found that the company sued by Lady B was not the operator of the hotel, and the matter was remitted to the 
High Court. 
Page 2 of 7
*FS Cairo (Nile Plaza) LLC v Brownlie (as dependant and executrix of Sir Ian Brownlie CBE QC) [2021] All ER 
(D) 105 (Oct)
Lady B successfully sought permission to substitute the present defendant (the appellant) company and to serve 
the proceedings on them out of the jurisdiction. 
The appellant appealed on the question of whether permission should have been given to serve the proceedings 
out of the jurisdiction. The Court of Appeal, Civil Division, dismissed the appeal. 
The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court.
  Issues and decisions     
(1) Whether Lady B's claims in tort satisfied the requirements of the relevant jurisdictional 'gateway' in the CPR (the 
tort gateway issue).
Consideration was given to Regulation (EC) No 44/2001 (Brussels Regulation I) and to Regulation (EU) No 
1215/2012 (the Brussels Recast Regulation).
The appeal would be dismissed on the first issue (see [84] of the judgment).
The present proceedings were outside the scope of the Brussels system for determining jurisdiction in civil and 
commercial matters, so the present court was concerned with the domestic rules of England and Wales. Those 
required that, in order to obtain permission to serve proceedings out of the jurisdiction in a case to which the 
Brussels system did not apply, a claimant had to establish: (i) a good arguable case that the claims fell within one of 
the gateways in CPR PD 6B, para 3.1; (ii) a serious issue to be tried on the merits; and (iii) that England was the 
appropriate forum for trial and that the court ought to exercise its discretion to permit service out of the jurisdiction 
(see [25], [29] of the judgment).
In the present case, the court was directly concerned with the domestic rules in England and Wales relating to 
service of civil proceedings on a defendant [the appellant] out of the jurisdiction. Those rules were set out in the 
CPR and the Practice Directions made under them, and they were previously to be found in the Rules of the 
Supreme Court. Those rules required the claim to pass through one of a number of statutory gateways and, in 
addition, that there should be shown to be a serious issue to be tried and that England and Wales was the proper 
place to bring the claim. The inquiry as to the proper place to bring the claim was referred to as forum non 
conveniens. That requirement was reflected in CPR 6.37(3) and the applicable principles were stated in authority 
(see [28], [29] of the judgment).
CPR PD 6B para 3.1(9) provided that: 'The claimant may serve a claim form out of the jurisdiction with the 
permission of the court under rule 6.36 where ... A claim is made in tort where (a) damage was sustained, or will be 
sustained, within the jurisdiction; or (b) damage which has been or will be sustained results from an act committed, 
or likely to be committed, within the jurisdiction' (see [30] of the judgment).
In the present case, the issue was whether each of the tort claims advanced was a claim where damage had been 
sustained within the jurisdiction. It was common ground between the parties that sub-para (b) could not apply as the 
relevant conduct (the 'act committed') had occurred entirely in Egypt, and not in England (see [30] of the judgment).
The word 'damage' in Practice Direction 6B para 3.1(9)(a) referred to actionable harm, direct or indirect, caused by 
the wrongful act alleged. That reading reflected the ordinary and natural meaning of the word and it was in 
accordance with the purpose of the provision and with principle. There was no reason to apply, within English 
domestic rules, the distinction between direct and indirect damage which had developed in the Brussels system. 
Fundamental differences between the two systems would have made such an assimilation totally inappropriate. 
There was no justification, in principle or in practice, for limiting 'damage' in para 3.1(9)(a) to damage which was 
necessary to complete a cause of action in tort, or for according any special significance to a place simply because 
it was where the cause of action had been completed. That approach was unduly restrictive (see [49]-[53], [81] of 
the judgment).
Page 3 of 7
*FS Cairo (Nile Plaza) LLC v Brownlie (as dependant and executrix of Sir Ian Brownlie CBE QC) [2021] All ER 
(D) 105 (Oct)
Provided that the discretionary test was correctly applied, there should be no danger that the wider reading of 
'damage' would establish a jurisdiction simply on the basis of the English identity of the claimant or that it would 
permit foreign defendants to be brought before the English courts in cases where there was no substantial 
connection between the wrongdoing and the jurisdiction. In that regard, the domestic system was markedly different 
from the Brussels regime which did not possess such a safety valve. As a result, there was no need to adopt an 
unnaturally restrictive reading of the domestic gateways (see [77] of the judgment).
The discretionary test of forum non conveniens, well established in English law, was an appropriate and effective 
mechanism which could be trusted to prevent the acceptance of jurisdiction in situations where there was merely a 
casual or adventitious link between the claim and England. Where a claim passed through a qualifying gateway, 
there remained a burden on the claimant to persuade the court that England and Wales was the proper place in 
which to bring the claim. Unless that was established, permission to serve out of the jurisdiction would be refused 
(CPR  6.37(3)). In addition, the forum non conveniens principle was not a mere general discretion, the application of 
which might vary according to the differing subjective views of different judges creating a danger of legal 
uncertainty. On the contrary, the principle applied a structured discretion, the details of which had been refined in 
the decided cases, in a readily predictable manner (see [78], [79] of the judgment).
In the present case, Lady B had made claims under three heads: (i) a claim for damages for personal injury in her 
own right; (ii) a claim for damages in her capacity as executrix of the estate of her late husband for wrongful death; 
and (iii) a claim for damages for bereavement and loss of dependency in her capacity as her late husband's widow. 
All three heads of claim should be considered to relate to actionable harm suffered in the jurisdiction as a result of 
the wrongful acts alleged and, therefore, to pass through gateway 9(a). In that regard, there was no reason to 
distinguish between the different heads of claim. So far as the first head was concerned, the pain, suffering and 
physical injury had been suffered sequentially, first in Egypt and then in England. If a person was seriously injured 
in a road accident, the pain, suffering and loss of amenity which he suffered were all part of the same injury and, in 
cases of permanent disability, it would be with him wherever he was. The damage was, in a very real sense, 
sustained in the jurisdiction. That was equally true of the second and third heads of claim. The injury to Sir B's 
estate and Lady B's bereavement and loss of dependency could properly be regarded as having been sustained in 
the present jurisdiction. Damage in that context was not confined to the element necessary to complete a cause of 
action, but included all the detriment, physical, financial and social which Lady B had suffered as a result of the 
appellant's tortious conduct. Further, England and Wales was the proper jurisdiction in which to bring the claim (see 
[83] of the judgment).
