months before beginning judicial forfeiture proceedings.  Respondents, six individuals who had cars and cash 
seized under that law, brought this federal civil rights action, claiming that the failure of the State to provide a 
speedy postseizure hearing violated the federal Due Process Clause.  The District Court dismissed the case based 
on Circuit precedent, but, on appeal, the Seventh Circuit departed from that precedent and ruled for respondents.  
This Court granted certiorari to review the Seventh Circuit's due process determination, but at oral argument the 
Court learned that all of the actual property disputes between the parties had been resolved. 
Held:
1. The case is moot.  The Constitution permits this Court to decide legal questions only in the context of actual 
"Cases" or "Controversies," Art. III, § 2, and an actual controversy must exist at all stages of  [****2] review, not just 
when the complaint is filed, Preiser v. Newkirk, 422 U.S. 395, 401, 95 S. Ct. 2330, 45 L. Ed. 2d 272.  Here there is 
no longer any actual controversy regarding ownership or possession of the underlying property.  There is no claim 
for damages before this Court; there is no properly certified class or dispute over class certification; and this case 
does not fit within the category of cases that are "capable of repetition" while "evading review."  Only an abstract 
dispute about the law remains.  Pp. 92-94 175 L. Ed. 2d, at 452-453. 
2. The judgment below is vacated.  In moot cases, this Court normally vacates the lower court judgment, which 
clears the path for relitigation of the issues and preserves the rights of the parties, while prejudicing none by a 
preliminary decision.  United States v. Munsingwear, Inc., 340 U.S. 36, 40,  [***450]  71 S. Ct. 104, 95 L. Ed. 36. 
 [**578]  Where mootness is the result of settlement rather than happenstance, however, the losing party forfeits the 
equitable remedy of vacatur.  U.S. Bancorp Mortgage Co. v. Bonner Mall Partnership, 513 U.S. 18, 25, 115 S. Ct. 
386, 130 L. Ed. 2d 233.  This case more closely resembles mootness through happenstance than through 
settlement.  In Bancorp, the party seeking review caused the mootness by voluntarily settling the  [*88]  issue 
contested throughout the litigation.   [****3] Here, the Court believes that the presence of the federal case played no 
significant role in the termination of plaintiffs' state-court forfeiture proceedings.  Plaintiffs' forfeiture cases took 
place with no procedural link to the case before this Court; apparently terminated on substantive grounds in their 
ordinary course; and, to the Court's knowledge, no one raised the procedural question at issue here in those cases.  
This Court therefore concludes that it should follow its ordinary practice and order vacatur.  Pp. 94-97, 175 L. Ed. 
2d, at 453-455.

Illinois law provides for forfeiture of movable personal property (including cars and cash) used "to facilitate" a drug

the State up to 142 days, nearly five months, to begin judicial forfeiture proceedings--during which time the statute 
permits the State to keep the car or cash within its possession. 
On November 22, 2006, six individuals (the respondents or "plaintiffs") brought this federal civil rights action against 
defendants the city of Chicago, the Superintendent of the Chicago Police Department, and the Cook County State's 
Attorney (the petitioner here, whom we shall call the "State's Attorney").  See Rev. Stat. § 1979, 42 U.S.C. § 1983.

U.S. Bancorp Mortg. Co. v. Bonner Mall Pshp., 
513 U.S. 18, 21, 115 S. Ct. 386, 130 L. Ed. 2d 233 (1994).  Applying this statute, we normally do vacate the lower

Applying these principles to the case before us, we conclude that the terminations here fall on the "happenstance"

proceedings.  In the three automobile cases, the State voluntarily dismissed the proceedings and returned the cars

IL) (Brunston's car returned on July 27, 2009); People v. Smith, No. 2006-COFO-000036 (Cook County, IL) (Smith's

dismissed the proceedings after 14 months, again a long enough time for the State to have weighed the evidence 
and  [***455] found a compromise settlement appropriate on the merits.  See Docket in People v. $1,500 in U. S. 
Currency, No. 2006-COFO-000201 (Cook County, IL) (Waldo's cash returned on Mar. 19, 2007).  The disparate 
dates at which  [****16] the plaintiffs' forfeiture proceedings terminated--11, 14, 27, and 40 months after the 
seizures--indicate that the State's Attorney did not coordinate the resolution of the plaintiffs' state-court cases, either 
with each other or with the plaintiffs' federal civil rights case.  Cf. Munsingwear, 340 U.S., at 39-40, 71 S. Ct. 104, 
95 L. Ed. 36 (stating that a lower court judgment would have been vacated [**583]  even though an action of the 
party seeking review had brought about the mootness because that action--a commodity being decontrolled by

judgments that have become moot because the parties settled. 
Bancorp set forth the basic principles for determining  [****18] whether to vacate a case that has become moot.  
The overriding concern is equitable:  "From the beginning we have disposed of moot cases in the manner '"most 
consonant  [*98]  to justice" . . . in view of the nature and character of the conditions which have caused the case to 
become moot.'"  Id., at 24, 115 S. Ct. 386, 130 L. Ed. 2d 233 (quoting

quoting South Spring Hill Gold Mining Co. v. Amador Medean Gold Mining Co., 145 U.S. 300, 302, 12 S. Ct. 921, 
36 L. Ed. 712 (1892) (alteration in original)). 
The "public interest" must be considered as part of this equitable 
inquiry, Bancorp, 513 U.S., at 26, 27, 115 S. Ct. 386, 130 L. Ed. 2d 233, and that interest is generally better served 
by leaving appellate judgments intact.  "'Judicial precedents are presumptively correct and valuable to the legal 
community as a whole.  They are not merely the property of private litigants . . . .'"  Id., at 26, 115 S. Ct. 386, 130 L. 
Ed. 2d 233 (quoting 
Izumi Seimitsu Kogyo Kabushiki Kaisha v. U.S. Philips Corp., 510 U.S. 27, 40, 114 S. Ct. 425, 
126 L. Ed. 2d 396 (1993) (Stevens, J., dissenting)). 
Hence, we will typically vacate a judgment when the party 
seeking review has been "frustrated by the vagaries of circumstance" or "when mootness results from unilateral 
action of  [****19] the party who prevailed below."  Bancorp, 513 U.S., at 25, 115 S. Ct. 386, 130 L. Ed. 2d 233.

IRAC_summ:
Case Name: Alvarez v. Smith [2009] 558 U.S. 87
Court + jurisdiction: Supreme Court of the United States
Area of law: Constitutional Law – Article III Mootness – Civil Procedure – Vacatur
Procedural posture: On writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
Issue
Whether a case challenging the constitutionality of state forfeiture procedures becomes moot when the underlying property disputes are resolved, and if so, whether the appellate court’s judgment should be vacated where the mootness resulted from the "happenstance" of independent state-court proceedings rather than a voluntary settlement of the federal litigation.
Rule
Under Article III, § 2 of the Constitution, federal courts may only decide actual "Cases" or "Controversies." An actual controversy must exist at all stages of review. A case is moot when the dispute is no longer embedded in any actual controversy about the plaintiffs' particular legal rights (Preiser v. Newkirk). When a case becomes moot, the standard practice is to vacate the lower court’s judgment (United States v. Munsingwear, Inc.), unless the mootness was caused by the voluntary action (settlement) of the party seeking review, in which case the equitable remedy of vacatur is forfeited (U.S. Bancorp Mortgage Co. v. Bonner Mall Partnership).
Application
The plaintiffs challenged Illinois' forfeiture procedures after their cars and cash were seized. By the time the case reached the Supreme Court, the state had returned the cars and the cash disputes were resolved [92]. The Court held the case was moot because there was no longer an actual controversy regarding the property. The plaintiffs' claims for declaratory and injunctive relief were abstract disputes about the law, unconnected to any concrete harm, and they had not appealed the denial of class certification [92]–[93]. The "capable of repetition, yet evading review" exception did not apply because there was no showing the plaintiffs would be subjected to the seizure procedures again [93].
Regarding disposition, the Court applied the Munsingwear doctrine to vacate the Seventh Circuit’s judgment. Although the property disputes were resolved by agreement (settlement) in state court, the Court distinguished this from the Bancorp settlement exception. The mootness here resembled "happenstance" more than voluntary forfeiture of the right to review because the state forfeiture proceedings were separate from the federal litigation and terminated on independent substantive grounds [95]–[96]. There was no evidence the state settled the individual cases to manipulate federal jurisdiction or avoid review of the constitutional issue. Therefore, the equitable balance favored clearing the path for future relitigation of the legal issues [96]–[97].
Conclusion
The Court vacated the judgment of the Court of Appeals and remanded with instructions to dismiss the case as moot.

IRAC_summ:
Case Name: In the Int. of J.E. [2025] PA Super 245
Court: Superior Court of Pennsylvania
Area of law: Evidence—Privilege; Juvenile Law
Procedural posture: Appeal from dispositional order of the Court of Common Pleas.
Issue
Whether a juvenile delinquency proceeding constitutes a "civil matter" within the meaning of 42 Pa.C.S.A. § 5929, such that the statutory physician-patient privilege precludes the admission of a juvenile’s inculpatory statements made to a treating physician.
Rule
Under 42 Pa.C.S.A. § 5929, a physician is prohibited from disclosing information acquired in a professional capacity "in any civil matter" without the patient's consent. Statutory interpretation requires courts to ascertain legislative intent; when words are clear, they must be read in accordance with their plain meaning. While juvenile proceedings are not "criminal proceedings" (In re S.A.S.), they are governed by the Juvenile Act, which creates a distinct legal system separate from the civil and criminal courts (In re J.B.).
Application
The court determines that the physician-patient privilege does not apply because a juvenile delinquency hearing is not a "civil matter" under the statute. J.E., a minor, sought to suppress medical records containing his admission to a surgeon that he accidentally shot himself with his own gun. J.E. argued that because juvenile proceedings are not criminal, they must be civil, thereby triggering the § 5929 privilege.
The court rejects this binary classification. It reasons that the legislature created a distinct system for juvenile offenders under the Juvenile Act. The court observes that § 5929 explicitly applies to "civil matters," a term typically referring to common law claims for damages or equity. The court notes that the Juvenile Act itself distinguishes between civil, criminal, and juvenile proceedings. Because the legislature did not include juvenile proceedings within the text of § 5929, and because precedent establishes juvenile court as a distinct venue neither wholly civil nor criminal, the privilege is inapplicable. Consequently, the trial court properly admitted the medical records containing the confession.
Conclusion
The dispositional order is affirmed; the physician-patient privilege does not apply in juvenile delinquency proceedings.

Syllabus
Viking River Cruises, Inc. v. Moriana
Page 8 of 20
 [**1910]   [***185]   [*639]  The question for decision is whether the Federal Arbitration Act, 9 U. S. C. §1 et seq., 
preempts a rule of California law that invalidates contractual waivers of the right to assert representative claims 
under California’s Labor Code Private Attorneys General Act of 2004, Cal. Lab. Code §2698 et seq. PAGA enlists 
employees as private attorneys general to enforce California labor law. By its terms, PAGA authorizes any 
“aggrieved employee” to initiate an action against a former employer “on behalf of himself or herself and other 
current or former employees” to obtain civil penalties that previously could have been recovered only by the State in 
an enforcement action brought by California’s Labor and Workforce Development Agency (LWDA). California 
precedent holds that a PAGA suit is a “‘representative action’” in which the employee plaintiff sues as an “‘agent or 
proxy’” of the State. Iskanian v. CLS Transp. Los Angeles, LLC, 59 Cal. 4th 348, 380, 173 Cal. Rptr. 3d 289, 327 
P.3d 129. California precedent also interprets the statute to contain what is effectively a rule of claim joinder—
allowing a party to unite multiple claims against an opposing party in a single action. An employee with PAGA 
standing may “seek any civil penalties the state can,  [**1911]  including penalties for violations involving 
employees other than [****2]  the PAGA litigant herself.” ZB, N. A. v. Superior Court, 8 Cal. 5th 175, 185, 252 Cal. 
Rptr. 3d 228, 448 P.3d 239.
Respondent Angie Moriana filed a PAGA action against her former employer Viking River Cruises, alleging a 
California Labor Code violation. She also asserted a wide array of other violations allegedly sustained by other 
Viking employees. Moriana’s employment contract with Viking contained a mandatory arbitration agreement. 
Important here, that agreement contained both a “Class Action Waiver”—providing that the parties could not bring 
any dispute as a class, collective, or representative action under PAGA—and a severability clause—specifying that 
if the waiver was found invalid, such a dispute would presumptively be litigated in court. Under the severability 
clause, any “portion” of the waiver that remained valid would be “enforced in arbitration.” Viking moved to compel 
arbitration of Moriana’s individual PAGA claim and to dismiss her other PAGA claims. Applying California’s Iskanian 
precedent, the California courts denied that motion, holding that categorical waivers of PAGA standing are contrary 
to California  [*640]  policy and that PAGA claims cannot be split into arbitrable “individual” claims and nonarbitrable 
“representative” claims. This Court granted certiorari [****3]  to decide whether the FAA preempts the California 
rule.
Held: The FAA preempts the rule of Iskanian insofar as it precludes division of PAGA actions into individual and 
non-individual claims through an agreement to arbitrate. Pp. 7-21.
(a) Based on the principle that “[a]rbitration is strictly ‘a matter of consent,’” Granite Rock Co. v. Teamsters, 561 U. 
S. 287, 299, 130 S. Ct. 2847, 177 L. Ed. 2d 567, this Court has held that “a party may not be compelled under the 
FAA to submit to class arbitration unless there is a contractual basis for concluding that the  [***186]  party agreed 
to do so,” Stolt-Nielsen S. A. v. AnimalFeeds Int’l Corp., 559 U. S. 662, 684, 130 S. Ct. 1758, 176 L. Ed. 2d 605. 
Because class-action arbitration mandates procedural changes that are inconsistent with the individualized and 
informal mode of bilateral arbitration contemplated by the FAA, see AT&T Mobility LLC v. Concepcion, 563 U. S. 
333, 347, 131 S. Ct. 1740, 179 L. Ed. 2d 742, class procedures cannot be imposed by state law without presenting 
unwilling parties with an unacceptable choice between being compelled to arbitrate using such procedures and 
forgoing arbitration all together.
Viking contends that the Court’s FAA precedents require enforcement of contractual provisions waiving the right to 
bring PAGA actions because PAGA creates a form of class or collective proceeding. If this is correct, Iskanian’s 
prohibition on PAGA waivers presents parties with an impermissible choice: Either arbitrate [****4]  disputes using a 
form of class procedures, or do not arbitrate at all. Moriana maintains that any conflict between Iskanian and the 
FAA is illusory because PAGA creates nothing more than a substantive cause of action.
This Court disagrees with both characterizations of the statute. Moriana’s premise that PAGA creates a unitary 
private cause of action is irreconcilable with the structure of the statute and the ordinary legal meaning of the word 
“claim.” A PAGA action asserting multiple violations under California’s Labor Code affecting a range of different 
employees does not constitute “a single claim” in even the broadest possible sense. Viking’s position, on the other 
hand, elides important structural differences between PAGA actions and class actions. A class-action plaintiff can 
raise a  [**1912]  multitude of claims because he or she represents a multitude of absent individuals; a PAGA 
Viking River Cruises, Inc. v. Moriana
Page 9 of 20
plaintiff, by contrast, represents a single principal, the LWDA, that has a multitude of claims. As a result, PAGA suits 
exhibit virtually none of the procedural characteristics of class actions.
This Court’s FAA precedents treat bilateral arbitration as the prototype of the individualized and informal form of 
arbitration [****5]  protected  [*641]  from undue state interference by the FAA. See, e.g., Epic Systems Corp. v. 
Lewis, 584 U. S. ___, ___, 138 S. Ct. 1612, 200 L. Ed. 2d 889. Viking posits that a proceeding is “bilateral” only if it 
involves two and only two parties and “is conducted by and on behalf of the individual named parties only.” Wal
Mart Stores, Inc. v. Dukes, 564 U. S. 338, 348, 131 S. Ct. 2541, 180 L. Ed. 2d 374. Thus, Iskanian’s prohibition on 
PAGA waivers is inconsistent with the FAA because PAGA creates an intrinsically representational form of action 
and Iskanian requires parties either to arbitrate in that format or forgo arbitration altogether.
This Court disagrees. Nothing in the FAA establishes a categorical rule mandating enforcement of waivers of 
standing to assert claims on behalf of absent principals. Non-class representative actions in which a single agent 
litigates on behalf of a single principal necessarily deviate from the strict ideal of bilateral dispute resolution posited 
by Viking, but this Court has never held that the FAA imposes a duty on States to render all forms of representative 
standing waivable by contract or that such suits deviate from the norm of bilateral arbitration. Unlike procedures 
distinctive to multiparty litigation, single-principal,  [***187]  single-agent representative actions are “bilateral” in two 
registers: They involve the rights of only the absent [****6]  real party in interest and the defendant, and litigation 
need only be conducted by the agent-plaintiff and the defendant. Nothing in this Court’s precedent suggests that in 
enacting the FAA, Congress intended to require States to reshape their agency law governing who can assert 
claims on behalf of whom to ensure that parties will never have to arbitrate disputes in a proceeding that deviates 
from bilateral arbitration in the strictest sense. Pp. 7-17.
(b) PAGA’s built-in mechanism of claim joinder is in conflict with the FAA. Iskanian’s prohibition on contractual 
division of PAGA actions into constituent claims unduly circumscribes the freedom of parties to determine “the 
issues subject to arbitration” and “the rules by which they will arbitrate,” Lamps Plus, Inc. v. Varela, 587 U. S. ____, 
____, 139 S. Ct. 1407, 203 L. Ed. 2d 636, and does so in a way that violates the fundamental principle that 
“arbitration is a matter of consent,” Stolt-Nielsen, 559 U. S., at 684, 130 S. Ct. 1758, 176 L. Ed. 2d 605. For that 
reason, state law cannot condition the enforceability of an agreement to arbitrate on the availability of a procedural 
mechanism that would permit a party to expand the scope of the anticipated arbitration by introducing claims that 
the parties did not jointly agree to arbitrate. A state rule imposing an expansive rule of joinder in [****7]  the arbitral 
context would defeat the ability of parties to control which claims are subject to arbitration by permitting parties to 
superadd new claims to the proceeding, regardless of whether the agreement committed those claims to arbitration. 
When made compulsory by way of Iskanian, PAGA’s joinder rule functions in exactly this way. The effect is to 
coerce parties into withholding PAGA claims from arbitration. Iskanian’s indivisibility  [*642]  rule effectively coerces 
parties to opt for a judicial forum rather than “forgo[ing] the procedural rigor and appellate review of the courts to 
realize the benefits of private dispute resolution.”  [**1913]  Stolt-Nielsen, 559 U. S., at 685, 130 S. Ct. 1758, 176 L. 
Ed. 2d 605. Pp. 17-19.
(c) Under this Courts holding, Iskanian’s prohibition on wholesale waivers of PAGA claims is not preempted by the 
FAA. But Iskanian’s rule that PAGA actions cannot be divided into individual and non-individual claims is 
preempted, so Viking was entitled to compel arbitration of Moriana’s individual claim. PAGA provides no 
mechanism to enable a court to adjudicate non-individual PAGA claims once an individual claim has been 
committed to a separate proceeding. And under PAGA’s standing requirement, a plaintiff has standing to maintain 
non-individual PAGA claims in an action [****8]  only by virtue of also maintaining an individual claim in that action. 
As a result, Moriana would lack statutory standing to maintain her non-individual claims in court, and the correct 
course was to dismiss her remaining claims. Pp. 20-21.
Reversed and remanded.

IRAC_summ:
Case Name: Viking River Cruises, Inc. v. Moriana [2022] 596 U.S. 639
Court + jurisdiction: Supreme Court of the United States
Area of law: Constitutional Law – Federal Preemption – Arbitration (FAA)
Procedural posture: On writ of certiorari to the Court of Appeal of California, Second Appellate District
Issue
Whether the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA) preempts a rule of California law (Iskanian) that invalidates contractual waivers of the right to assert representative claims under the Private Attorneys General Act (PAGA), specifically insofar as that rule prohibits dividing a PAGA action into individual and non-individual claims.
Rule
The FAA preempts state laws that discriminate against arbitration or that effectively coerce parties into forgoing arbitration by imposing procedures inconsistent with the traditional individualized, bilateral nature of arbitration (AT&T Mobility LLC v. Concepcion; Epic Systems Corp. v. Lewis). Arbitration is strictly a matter of consent, and parties cannot be compelled to arbitrate issues or disputes they have not agreed to submit (Stolt-Nielsen S. A. v. AnimalFeeds Int’l Corp.).
Application
The Court analyzed the structural conflict between PAGA's procedural mechanism and the FAA. PAGA actions allow an "aggrieved employee" to join claims for violations they suffered personally with claims for violations suffered by other employees [646]. The Court held that the FAA does not preempt the Iskanian rule prohibiting wholesale waivers of representative standing, reasoning that single-agent representative actions are not inherently inconsistent with the norms of bilateral arbitration [657].
However, the Court found that PAGA's "built-in mechanism of claim joinder"—enforced by Iskanian's secondary rule prohibiting the division of PAGA actions—violates the FAA [659]. This "indivisibility rule" effectively coerces parties into arbitrating a wide range of claims (non-individual claims) that they did not agree to arbitrate, or forgoing arbitration entirely [661]. By conditioning the enforceability of an arbitration agreement on the availability of this expansive joinder, California law unduly circumscribes the parties' freedom to design their own dispute resolution procedures [660]. Consequently, the FAA preempts the Iskanian rule to the extent it precludes dividing the action into individual and non-individual claims. Viking was entitled to compel arbitration of the plaintiff's individual claim [662]. Regarding the remaining non-individual claims, the Court noted that under PAGA's specific standing rules, a plaintiff loses statutory standing to maintain non-individual claims in court once their individual claim is pared away to a separate proceeding [663].
Conclusion
The FAA preempts the Iskanian rule insofar as it precludes dividing PAGA actions into individual and non-individual claims; the judgment is reversed and remanded.

 [***713]  With respect to original action brought in Supreme Court against state by another state--seeking equitable 
apportionment of interstate river--standard for intervention held (1) satisfied by water-supply project and energy 
company; but (2) not satisfied by city in one state. 
Summary
 [*256]  Procedural posture:  Plaintiff State of South Carolina brought an original action in the U.S. Supreme Court 
against defendant State of North Carolina seeking equitable apportionment of river water flowing between the 
States.  South Carolina presented exceptions to the recommendation of a Special Master that motions to intervene 
by a water district, a power company, and a North Carolina municipality be granted. 
Overview:  The water district was a governmental joint venture which supplied water from the river to one county in 
each State, the power company operated dams on the river to generate electricity under a federal license, and the 
municipality drew water from the river under a permit from North Carolina.  The Court held that the water district and 
the power company demonstrated sufficiently compelling interests that were unlike the interests of other citizens of 
the States to warrant intervention, but the municipality failed to make such a showing.  The water district was an 
unusual bi-state entity which was jointly owned and regulated by the counties, and protecting the viability of its 
operations was premised on a fine balance between two participating counties which would likely be upset without 
representation of its interests in the litigation.  Further, it was likely that any equitable apportionment of the river 
would need to take into account the amount of  [***714] water that the power company needed to sustain its 
operations and obtain a license renewal.  However, the municipality was part of a class of North Carolina users and 
North Carolina could adequately protect the municipality's interests. 
Outcome:  South Carolina's exceptions to the recommendation of the Special Master were overruled in part and 
sustained in part, the motions to intervene of the water district and the power company were granted, and the 
motion to intervene of the municipality was denied.  Unanimous Decision with regard to municipality; 5-4 Decision 
with regard to water district and power company; 1 Concurrence in part and Dissent in part.

Case Name: South Carolina v. North Carolina [2010] 558 U.S. 256
Court + jurisdiction: Supreme Court of the United States
Area of law: Civil Procedure – Intervention – Original Jurisdiction
Procedural posture: On exceptions to the First Interim Report of the Special Master
Issue
Whether non-state entities—specifically a bi-state water project, a public utility, and a municipality—may intervene as parties in an original jurisdiction equitable apportionment suit between states, where the proposed intervenors claim interests distinct from the general population represented by the state parens patriae.
Rule
In original jurisdiction actions between states, the standard for intervention by non-state entities is high due to respect for state sovereignty. Under New Jersey v. New York, an intervenor whose state is a party must demonstrate a “compelling interest in his own right,” apart from his interest in a class with all other citizens and creatures of the state, which interest is “not properly represented by the state” [266].
Application
The Court applied the New Jersey v. New York standard to three entities seeking to intervene in a dispute over the Catawba River.
First, the Court allowed intervention by the Catawba River Water Supply Project (CRWSP). The Court found CRWSP possessed a compelling interest because it is a bi-state entity, jointly owned by counties in North Carolina and South Carolina, relying on authority from both states to operate [269]. Neither state could adequately represent CRWSP’s interests because the states have opposing interests in maximizing their own equitable share of the water, which threatens the delicate bi-state balance upon which CRWSP operates [270]–[271].
Second, the Court allowed intervention by Duke Energy. Duke Energy demonstrated a unique and compelling interest as the operator of 11 dams controlling the river’s flow and the holder of a federal license [272]. Furthermore, Duke Energy orchestrated a Comprehensive Relicensing Agreement (CRA) signed by 70 entities. Because North Carolina did not sign the CRA and intended to challenge it, the state could not properly represent Duke Energy’s specific interest in preserving that agreement [273].
Third, the Court denied intervention by the City of Charlotte. Charlotte is a municipality of North Carolina, and its water usage constitutes part of the state's equitable share. Although the complaint specifically identified Charlotte’s water transfers, the Court held that Charlotte occupies the same class as other water users represented by the state as parens patriae [274]. Charlotte’s interest was not unique in kind from other citizens, and North Carolina expressly stated it would defend Charlotte’s authorized transfer, ensuring adequate representation [275].
Conclusion
The Court overruled the exceptions regarding CRWSP and Duke Energy (permitting intervention) but sustained the exception regarding Charlotte (denying intervention).

On September 30, 2024, Abalkhad moved to vacate the trial court's order to arbitrate pursuant to section 1281.98. 
He argued that under section 1281.98, defendants materially breached the arbitration agreement and waived their 
right to arbitrate by failing to pay the arbitration fees within 30 [*8]  days of the due date (July 15, 2024). He also 
sought sanctions in the sum of

6

$10,217.26. In opposition, defendants contended that the deadline to pay the arbitration fees ran from the revised 
invoice date (Sept. 6, 2024), not the earlier, incorrect invoice (July 15, 2024). Also, the parties agreed to delegate 
such "gateway questions of arbitrability to the arbitrator, not the [trial] court." Moreover, section 1281.98 was 
preempted by the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA; 9 U.S.C. 1 et seq.). In reply, Abalkhad argued that there was "no 
evidence that the July 15, 2024 invoice was cancelled, 'deemed null,' or 'clawed back by JAMS.'" Abalkhad 
disagreed that the issue of payment was delegated to the arbitrator. He also disagreed that section 1281.98 was 
preempted by the FAA.

On October 30, 2024, the trial court granted the motion and awarded monetary sanctions. The court found 
defendants had failed to timely pay the required arbitration fees and therefore materially breached the arbitration 
agreement as provided in section 1281.98. The court explained that the July 15, 2024 invoice did not become void 
"the minute someone disputes" it. The court rejected the JAMS Case Deposit Summary presented by defendants, 
wherein it showed the amount requested on the July 15, 2024 invoice as zero. [*9]  The court stated that 
defendants admitted the summary was generated on October 15, 2024, "long after the present motion was filed." 
And according to Abalkhad, defendants "specifically requested JAMS administration reflect that the invoice amount 
was $0." The court found there was no evidence that the amount was zero before Abalkhad filed the motion to 
vacate. The court noted that the reissued invoice, dated September 6, 2024, specifically stated that "the due date 
was not affected by the reissue." The court concluded that defendants "cite no law that an invoice is made void by 
simply disputing it." The court also rejected defendants' arguments that the parties agreed to

7

delegate arbitrability to an arbitrator and that the FAA preempted section 1281.98.

Defendants timely appealed.

After briefing in this appeal was complete, the California Supreme Court decided Hohenshelt, which we discuss 
below. We requested, and the parties filed, supplemental letter briefs addressing the impact of Hohenshelt on this 
appeal. 4

DISCUSSION

I. Governing Statue and Standard of Review

In 2019, the Legislature enacted section 1281.98 to assist consumers and employees who find themselves in 
"procedural limbo" because they are required to submit a dispute [*10]  to arbitration, but the entity enforcing the 
arbitration agreement has not paid the arbitration fees required to proceed. (Gallo v. Wood Ranch USA, Inc. (2022) 
81 Cal.App.5th 621, 634, disapproved on another ground in Hohenshelt, supra, 18 Cal.5th at p. 349.)

Section 1281.98 provides that where "an employment or consumer arbitration . . . requires . . . the drafting party" to 
"pay certain fees and costs," those fees or costs must be "paid within 30 days after the due date." (Id. subd. (a)(1).) 
If the fees are not timely paid, "the drafting party is in material breach of the arbitration agreement, is in default of 
the arbitration, and waives its right to compel the employee or consumer to proceed with the arbitration as a result 
of the material breach." (Ibid.) The consumer or employee may then "unliterally elect" to "[w]ithdraw the claim from

4 Defendants contended on appeal that section 1281.98 was preempted 



Page 5 of 9
Abalkhad v. Lithia Motors, 2025 Cal. App. Unpub. LEXIS 6875

by the FAA. However, in their supplemental briefing, defendants "concede that the FAA does not preempt section 
1281.98." (See Hohenshelt, supra, 18 Cal.5th at p. 323.) Therefore, we do not address this issue on appeal.

8

arbitration and proceed in a court of appropriate jurisdiction" (id., subd. (b)(1)) or "[c]ontinue the arbitration 
proceeding, if the arbitration provider agrees to continue administering the proceeding, notwithstanding the drafting 
party's failure [*11]  to pay fees or costs" (id., subd. (b)(2)). If the employee or consumer chooses to withdraw the 
claim from arbitration, he or she may bring a motion to recover all attorney's fees and all costs associated with the 
abandoned arbitration proceedings. (Id., subd. (c)(1).) The imposition of sanctions on the drafting party is 
mandatory upon the finding of material breach. (Id., subd. (c)(2), 1281.99, subd. (a).)

"Ordinarily, a trial court's determination that a party has waived the right to arbitrate is subject to substantial 
evidence review. [Citation.] However, where the parties do not dispute the factual support for the trial court's ruling, 
but instead dispute the proper interpretation of section 1281.98, the appellate court's review is de novo. [Citations.]" 
(Doe v.Superior Court (2023) 95 Cal.App.5th 346, 397-398, disapproved on another ground in Hohenshelt, supra, 
18 Cal.5th at p. 349.)

II. Applicability of Section 1281.98

On appeal, defendants argue for the first time that section 1281.98 is inapplicable because the parties did not 
submit to arbitration pursuant to a pre-dispute agreement. Rather, defendants contend the parties submitted to 
arbitration pursuant to a post-dispute stipulation and therefore fell outside the purview of section 1281.98. In 
support, defendants exclusively rely on

Trujillo v. J-M Manufacturing Co., Inc. (2024) 107 Cal.App.5th 56 (Trujillo),which was decided several months after 
the trial court's decision [*12]  in this case. In that case, the court held that "the Legislature intended to limit section 
1281.98's applicability to arbitration arising from a pre-dispute agreement."

9

(Id. at p. 70, disapproved on another ground in Hohenshelt, supra, 18 Cal.5th at p. 349.)

As a preliminary matter, Abalkhad contends the argument is forfeited because it was not raised in the trial court. 
While we agree with Abalkhad that the trial court was not presented with this argument, we elect to reach the merits 
as it involves a question of law. (See Ward v. Taggart (1959) 51 Cal.2d 736, 742 [new theory pertaining to question 
of law on facts appearing in the record may be raised for the first time on appeal].) Moreover, "Courts of Appeal 
routinely consider newly published case law that was not available until after entry of judgment in the trial court. 
(See, e.g., Hattersley v.American Nucleonics Corp. (1992) 3 Cal.App.4th 397, 402 [rejecting claim that appellant 
should be foreclosed from relying on theory of law espoused in newly decided Court of Appeal opinion]; . . .)" 
(Waller v. Truck Ins. Exchange,Inc. (1995) 11 Cal.4th 1, 23-24; Guardianship of Stephen G. (1995) 40 Cal.App.4th 
1418, 1422 ["Courts have often entertained new arguments on appeal when they rest on new authority that the 
appellant could not fairly be expected to anticipate"].)

Regardless, we find Trujillo distinguishable from, and inapplicable to, the facts of this case. In Trujillo, the plaintiff 
filed a complaint against her former employer and [*13]  four former coworkers. (107 Cal.App.5th at p. 60.) The 
employer reminded the plaintiff that she executed an arbitration agreement that required her to resolve any 
employment disputes by private arbitration. A dispute arose regarding the applicability and validity of some of the 
terms of the pre-dispute arbitration agreement. (Id. at pp. 60-61.) The plaintiff eventually circulated a draft of her 
proposed stipulation to arbitrate her claims. (Id. at p. 61.) After weeks of negotiating, the parties agreed to the

10

terms of the stipulation, which was later entered as an order by the trial court. (Id. at pp. 61-62.)



Page 6 of 9
Abalkhad v. Lithia Motors, 2025 Cal. App. Unpub. LEXIS 6875

Over a year into the arbitration, the employer paid an arbitration fee beyond the 30-day window after receiving the 
arbitrator's invoice. (Trujillo,supra, 107 Cal.App.5th at p. 62.) The plaintiff then moved to withdraw from arbitration 
due to the employer's late payment, which was granted by the trial court. (Id. at p. 63.) The Court of Appeal 
reversed the trial court's order, holding that "section 1281.98, subdivision (a) does not apply because the parties did 
not submit to arbitration pursuant to any pre-dispute agreement and because [the employer] does not qualify as a 
'drafting party' as defined by section 1280, subdivision (e)." (Id. at p. 60.) The court reasoned that while the parties 
were previously bound by a mandatory pre-dispute arbitration agreement, that [*14]  was not the operative 
arbitration agreement and did not govern the arbitration proceedings between the parties. (Trujillo,supra, 107 
Cal.App.5th at pp. 69-70.) Rather, after weeks of negotiations with her former employer, the plaintiff drafted and 
circulated a post-dispute stipulation for arbitration that was substantively distinguishable from the prior arbitration 
agreement. (Id. at pp. 70-71.)

Unlike the parties in Trujillo, Abalkhad and defendants expressly stipulated to arbitration pursuant to their prior, 
binding arbitration agreement. Moreover, the original arbitration agreement was never revised or edited by any 
party. The drafting parties of the stipulation were defendants and Abalkhad simply reviewed and signed the 
stipulation. While the arbitration agreement was not attached to the stipulation, it was expressly incorporated in the 
stipulation and there was no language deviating from the prior agreement. We find defendants' argument to the 
contrary disingenuous. As expressly acknowledged by defendants in another

11

section of their opening brief, "to the extent that the . . . [s]tipulation itself is silent as to any terms, the only 
reasonable conclusion is counsel knew . . .

they were agreeing to the same terms as those in the [p]re-[d]ispute [*15]  [a]ribtration [a]greement." (Italics added.) 
Therefore, we conclude section 1281.98, subdivision (a)(1) applies to this case because the operative arbitration 
agreement that governed the arbitration proceedings between the parties was a pre-dispute agreement, not a 
revised post-dispute one.

III. Forum

Next, defendants contend that the issue of whether there has been a material breach of the arbitration agreement 
for failure to timely pay the required fees was delegated to the arbitrator, not the trial court. Defendants' contention 
lacks merit.

"Nothing in the plain language of section 1281.98 purports to condition the consumer's unilateral election upon an 
initial arbitral determination of breach. Nor does anything in section 1281.98's concrete definition of breach, default, 
and waiver require such a determination: at issue is payment, or not, by a specified date, comparable to the failure 
of a litigant to pay jury fees or to timely file an answer, which are typically matters of ministerial record keeping 
rather than adjudicative factfinding." (Williams v. West CoastHospitals, Inc. (2022) 86 Cal.App.5th 1054, 1066 
(Williams), disapproved on another ground in Hohenshelt, supra, 18 Cal.5th at p. 349.) "Requiring the employees or 
consumers to remain in arbitration to secure a default-from an arbitrator who did not receive timely payment and 
may still remain unpaid- invites [*16]  the very abuse that the statute is intended to eradicate. We decline to impose 
this burden on the intended beneficiaries of the statute, even if they may independently elect to submit the issue of 
default to the arbitrator." (Id.

12

at p. 1068; see Cvejic v. Skyview Capital, LLC (2023) 92 Cal.App.5th 1073, 1079 ["The point [of 1281.98] was to 
take this issue away from arbitrators, who may be financially interested in continuing the arbitration and in pleasing 
regular clients."].)

The fact that the arbitration agreement provided for the arbitrator to determine disputes pertaining to the 
"interpretation and/or application" of the terms of the agreement does not support a contrary conclusion. "[S]ection 
1281.98 sets forth the consequences of a failure of the drafting party to timely pay arbitration fees, vesting the 



Page 7 of 9
Abalkhad v. Lithia Motors, 2025 Cal. App. Unpub. LEXIS 6875

employee or consumer with the right 'unilaterally' to 'proceed in a court of appropriate jurisdiction.' Nothing is left for 
the arbitrator to decide. The fact the default is described in the statute as a 'material breach' does not mean there is 
a factual issue for the arbitrator." (Sanders v. Superior Court (2025) 110 Cal.App.5th 1304, 1317 (Sanders), 
disapproved on another ground in Hohenshelt, supra, 18 Cal.5th at p. 349.) The Legislature's intent for the trial 
court to decide the issue of material breach controls. (Cvejic, supra, 92 Cal.App.5th at p. 1079; see Williams,supra, 
86 Cal.App.5th at p. 1069 [ 1281.98's provision for employees and consumers [*17]  to unilaterally withdraw from 
arbitration and proceed in a court of appropriate jurisdiction "compels the conclusion that the Legislature intended 
courts to exercise jurisdiction over such proceedings, as a matter of positive law"].) Contrary to defendants' 
assertion, "nothing in JAMS rule 11 limits or overrides a trial court's authority to apply section 1281.98." (Sanders, 
supra, at p. 1318.)

IV. Material Breach

Defendants alternatively argue that assuming section 1281.98 applies, they did not materially breach the arbitration 
agreement. We disagree.

13

On July 15, 2024, JAMS sent an invoice to defendants for the November hearing. The invoice stated the payment 
of $126,600 was "due upon receipt," which meant the deadline was 30 days later, on August 15, 2024. No payment 
was made by defendants for the amount before or by August 15, 2024. Moreover, when JAMS reissued the invoice 
on September 6, 2024, it explicitly stated that the reissued invoice "is not intended to and does not extend the due 
date for payment of the July [15], 2024 invoice." JAMS also stated, "This date is not intended to and does not 
extend the due date for payment of the outstanding invoice(s)" because "[t]he outstanding invoice(s) was due upon 
receipt." Therefore, payment was still [*18]  due on or before August 15, 2024, despite the reissuance of the invoice 
on September 6, 2024.

Defendants contend that at the August 5, 2024 hearing, the arbitrator agreed the July 15, 2024 invoice was 
excessive and nullified it. We find no evidence to support this assertion in the record. There was no transcript of the 
hearing or any corroborating evidence the arbitrator nullified the July 15, 2024 invoice. Rather, a September 6, 2024 
email exchange with the JAMS administrator and defendants' counsel establishes the parties were "still waiting on a 
ruling" and that the arbitrator reduced the number of hearing dates during the August 5, 2024 hearing. Defendants 
also assert that the JAMS Case Deposit Summary shows the July 15, 2024 invoice lists a zero balance due. 
Therefore, there was no pending invoice for defendants to pay on August 15, 2024. Reliance on the Case Deposit 
Summary is misleading. As aptly noted by the trial court, "defendant[s] admit[] that summary was generated 
October 15, 2024, long after the [motion to vacate] was filed." We agree with the trial court that there is no evidence 
the amount was zero prior to the filing of the motion. Therefore, we conclude the trial court [*19]  correctly

14

found that defendants failed to timely pay the arbitration fees. However, in light of the California Supreme Court's 
recent decision in Hohenshelt, our analysis of material breach does not stop there.

After briefing was complete on appeal, the Supreme Court issued Hohenshelt. The question in Hohenshelt was 
whether the FAA preempts section 1281.98's provision that drafting parties waive their right to arbitrate if they fail to 
timely pay arbitration fees. (Hohenshelt, supra, 18 Cal.5th at pp. 322-323.) The FAA sets forth "'"an equal-treatment 
principle"'" that allows courts to "'"invalidate an arbitration agreement based on 'generally applicable contract 
defenses,'"'" but preempts state rules that "'"'apply only to arbitration or that derive their meaning from the fact that 
an agreement to arbitrate is at issue.'"' [Citation.]" (Hohenshelt, supra, at p. 327.)

Our Supreme Court agreed with the employer's argument "that if section 1281.98 were construed to mean that any 
failure to make timely payment, regardless of the circumstances, invariably results in forfeiture of arbitral rights, the 
statute would be anomalous in the context of general contract law principles." (Hohenshelt, supra, 18 Cal.5th at p. 
343.) However, the court held that "section 1281.98, properly construed, is not preempted by the FAA." 
(Hohenshelt, supra, at p. 323.) The court reasoned that "the statute does [*20]  not abrogate the longstanding 



Page 8 of 9
Abalkhad v. Lithia Motors, 2025 Cal. App. Unpub. LEXIS 6875

principle, established by statute and common law, that one party's nonperformance of an obligation automatically 
extinguishes the other party's contractual duties only when nonperformance is willful, grossly negligent, or 
fraudulent." (Ibid.) As examples of this "longstanding principle," the court cited Civil Code section 3275, which 
"excuses a failure to perform an 'obligation'" if the breaching party "'mak[es] full compensation to the other party, 
except in case of a grossly negligent, willful, or fraudulent breach of duty.'" (Hohenshelt, supra,

15

18 Cal.5th at p. 332, quoting Civ. Code, 3275.) The court also cited section 473, subdivision (b) as a "path by which 
a drafting party that does not timely pay fees can be relieved from forfeiting its right to arbitration." 
(Hohenshelt,supra, at pp. 334-335.)

The Supreme Court disapproved of construing section 1281.98 as imposing an "inflexible rule that deems any 
failure to make timely payment a material breach, regardless of circumstances, with the automatic consequence 
that the drafting party loses its arbitral rights." (Hohenshelt,supra, 18 Cal.5th at p. 331, citing Doe v. Superior Court, 
supra, 95 Cal.App.5th at p. 357; Espinoza v. Superior Court (2022) 83 Cal.App.5th 761, 776; Williams, supra, 86 
Cal.App.5th at p. 1074.) The court concluded the Legislature did not intend "to strip companies and employers of 
their contractual right to arbitration where nonpayment of fees results from a good faith mistake, inadvertence, or 
other excusable [*21]  neglect." (Hohenshelt, supra, 18 Cal.5th at p. 323.) Rather, the intent was "to deter 
companies and employers from engaging in strategic nonpayment of arbitration fees." (Ibid.) The Supreme Court 
directed the Court of Appeal "to remand the matter to the trial court for consideration of whether [the employer] may 
be excused for its failure to timely pay arbitration fees, such that the stay of litigation should not be lifted and the 
parties should be returned to arbitration, and whether the delay resulted in compensable harm to [the employee]." 
(Hohenshelt, supra, 18 Cal.5th at p. 349.)

Because the trial court did not have the benefit of Hohenshelt, we remand the matter to the trial court to consider, 
for the first time, whether defendants' failure to timely pay the arbitration fees was defensible. 5

5 At oral argument, Abalkhad's counsel requested that this court decide 

this issue on appeal and not remand the matter back to the trial court. In 16

DISPOSITION

We affirm the trial court's ruling that it had jurisdiction to decide whether section 1281.98 applies. However, in light 
of Hohenshelt, we reverse the trial court's order granting the motion to vacate as to the issue of material breach. 
The matter is remanded for the trial court's consideration of whether defendants may be excused for their 
failure [*22]  to timely pay arbitration fees, and whether the delay in payment resulted in compensable harm to 
Abalkhad. Based on our conclusion, the trial court's order awarding monetary sanctions is also reversed. The 
parties are to bear their own costs on appeal.

NOT TO BE PUBLISHED IN THE OFFICIAL REPORTS

ZUKIN, P. J.

WE CONCUR:

MORI, J.

TAMZARIAN, J.

support, counsel cited to a recently published decision, Wilson v. TapWorldwide, LLC (Sept. 22, 2025, B334533) __ 
Cal.App.5th ___ [2025 WL 2802617] (Wilson). In that case, the court held "remand is unnecessary . . .



Page 9 of 9
Abalkhad v. Lithia Motors, 2025 Cal. App. Unpub. LEXIS 6875

because unlike in Hohenshelt, the trial court's findings establish, as a matter of law, that defendant's untimely 
payment was not willful, grossly negligent, or fraudulent." Unlike Wilson, the trial court here did not make factual 
findings regarding the reasons for the untimely payment. Therefore, we decline counsel's request.

17

End of Document
IRAC_summ:
Case Name: Abalkhad v. Lithia Motors, Inc.
Jurisdiction / Court: Court of Appeal of California, Second Appellate District, Division Four
Citation: 2025 Cal. App. Unpub. LEXIS 6875
Date: October 28, 2025
I. Issue(s)
1.	Does Code of Civil Procedure section 1281.98, which governs material breach for non-payment of arbitration fees, apply to an arbitration initiated via a post-dispute stipulation that expressly incorporates a pre-dispute arbitration agreement?
2.	Is the determination of whether a party materially breached an arbitration agreement by failing to timely pay fees a question for the arbitrator or the trial court?
3.	Did the defendants materially breach the arbitration agreement by failing to pay an invoice for arbitration fees within 30 days of its due date, despite a dispute over the amount and the subsequent reissuance of a corrected invoice?
4.	In light of the California Supreme Court's decision in Hohenshelt, what is the proper remedy when a trial court finds a material breach under section 1281.98 without considering whether the non-payment was willful, grossly negligent, or fraudulent?
II. Rule(s)
1.	Applicability of § 1281.98: California Code of Civil Procedure section 1281.98 applies to employment and consumer arbitrations where the drafting party is required to pay fees. If payment is not made within 30 days of the due date, the drafting party is in material breach and waives its right to compel arbitration. (Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1281.98(a)(1)).
2.	Forum for Determining Breach: The plain language of § 1281.98 vests the employee or consumer with the unilateral right to withdraw from arbitration and proceed in court upon a material breach. This legislative intent grants the trial court jurisdiction to determine whether a breach occurred, removing the issue from the arbitrator. (Williams v. West Coast Hospitals, Inc. (2022) 86 Cal.App.5th 1054).
3.	Standard for Material Breach: In Hohenshelt v. Superior Court (2025) 18 Cal.5th 310, the California Supreme Court held that a failure to timely pay arbitration fees under § 1281.98 does not automatically result in a forfeiture of the right to arbitrate. A party may be excused from the breach unless its nonperformance was "willful, grossly negligent, or fraudulent." The statute was intended to deter strategic nonpayment, not to punish good faith mistakes or excusable neglect.
III. Application (Analysis)
1.	Applicability of § 1281.98: The court distinguished this case from Trujillo v. J-M Manufacturing Co., Inc. (2024) 107 Cal.App.5th 56, where the parties negotiated a new, substantively different post-dispute arbitration agreement. Here, the parties' stipulation expressly incorporated and was governed by the terms of the original pre-dispute arbitration agreement. The court found that because the original pre-dispute agreement was the operative one, § 1281.98 applied.
2.	Forum for Determining Breach: The court rejected the defendants' argument that the arbitrator should decide the issue of material breach. Citing precedent, the court affirmed that the Legislature intended for trial courts to have jurisdiction over such determinations. Section 1281.98's provision allowing a party to "unilaterally elect" to proceed in court compels the conclusion that the issue is for the court, not the arbitrator, whose financial interests might be conflicted.
3.	Existence of Material Breach: The court found that a material breach occurred. JAMS issued an invoice on July 15, 2024, making payment due by August 15, 2024. The defendants failed to pay by this deadline. The subsequent reissuance of a corrected invoice on September 6 did not extend the original due date, as JAMS explicitly stated in writing. The court found no evidence in the record to support the defendants' claim that the arbitrator had nullified the July 15 invoice.
4.	Impact of Hohenshelt: Although the court agreed that a breach occurred, its analysis was incomplete under the new standard established by Hohenshelt. The trial court had granted the motion to vacate based solely on the untimely payment, without considering the defendants' reason for the delay. Because Hohenshelt requires an inquiry into whether the non-payment was "willful, grossly negligent, or fraudulent," the matter had to be remanded. The trial court must now consider, for the first time, whether the defendants' failure to pay was excusable.
IV. Conclusion
1.	Yes. Section 1281.98 applies because the parties' arbitration was governed by the terms of the original pre-dispute agreement, which was expressly incorporated into their post-dispute stipulation.
2.	The trial court. The Legislature intended for trial courts, not arbitrators, to determine whether a material breach for non-payment of fees under § 1281.98 has occurred.
3.	Yes. The defendants materially breached the agreement by failing to pay the arbitration fees within 30 days of the original invoice's due date.
4.	Reversal and Remand. The trial court's order vacating the arbitration is reversed. The case is remanded for the trial court to apply the Hohenshelt standard and determine whether the defendants' failure to timely pay was willful, grossly negligent, or fraudulent, and therefore not excusable. The associated award of monetary sanctions is also reversed pending this determination.

case_name: Lonon v. State [2025] Tex. App. LEXIS 8267
case:
Page 1 of 4
Lonon v. State, 2025 Tex. App. LEXIS 8267

Lonon v. State
Court of Appeals of Texas, Fourteenth District, Houston

October 28, 2025, Memorandum Opinion Filed

NO. 14-23-00956-CR

Reporter
2025 Tex. App. LEXIS 8267 *; 2025 LX 424522

ALEXANDER O'BRIAN LONON, Appellant V. THE STATE OF TEXAS, Appellee

Notice: Decision text below is the first available text from the court; it has not been editorially reviewed by 
LexisNexis. Publisher's editorial review, including Headnotes, Case Summary, Shepard's analysis or any 
amendments will be added in accordance with LexisNexis editorial guidelines.

Core Terms

trial court, community supervision, ineffective, counsel's, intoxicate, interview, probation, driving

Opinion

 [*1] On Appeal from the 458th District Court

Fort Bend County, Texas

Trial Court Cause No. 18-DCR-084582

MEMORANDUM OPINION

In this appeal from a judgment adjudicating guilt, appellant argues in two issues that the judgment should be 
reversed because the trial court abused its discretion by granting the motion to adjudicate, or alternatively, because 
trial counsel was ineffective. For the reasons given below, we overrule both issues and affirm the trial court's 
judgment.

BACKGROUND

Appellant was indicted for possession of methamphetamine. He pleaded guilty to that charge in exchange for the 
prosecution's recommendation that his adjudication be deferred. The trial court accepted that recommendation and 
placed appellant on community supervision for a period of two years.

Less than five months later, the prosecution moved to adjudicate appellant's guilt, based on allegations that 
appellant had violated eleven conditions of his community supervision. The prosecution subsequently amended its 
motion and alleged a total of thirty violations. Many of those allegations concerned failures to report and failures to 
pay certain fees, but the leading allegations concerned an incident of driving while intoxicated. [*2] 



Page 2 of 4
Lonon v. State, 2025 Tex. App. LEXIS 8267

Appellant pleaded not true to all thirty of the allegations. But following an evidentiary hearing, the trial court found 
every allegation to be true. The trial court then adjudicated appellant's guilt and assessed his punishment at thirty 
months' imprisonment.

REVOCATION OF COMMUNITY SUPERVISION

In a hearing on a motion to adjudicate, the prosecution has the burden of proving that the defendant violated a 
condition of his community supervision "by a preponderance of the evidence." See Hacker v. State, 389 S.W.3d 
860, 864-65 (Tex. Crim. App. 2013). This evidentiary burden is not as rigorous as the burden required to obtain a 
criminal conviction, which requires proof "beyond a reasonable doubt." Id. at 865. To satisfy the lesser 
preponderance standard, the prosecution need only prove that the "greater weight of the credible evidence . . . 
would create a reasonable belief that the defendant has violated a condition of his probation." Id.

2

We review a trial court's finding in an adjudication proceeding for an abuse of discretion. Id. The test for abuse of 
discretion is not whether, in the opinion of the reviewing court, the facts present an appropriate case for the trial 
court's action; rather, it is a question of whether the trial court acted without reference [*3]  to any guiding rules or 
principles. See Howell v. State, 175 S.W.3d 786, 792 (Tex. Crim. App. 2005).

One condition of appellant's community supervision was that he was required to "avoid any use of dangerous 
drugs, controlled substances, substances with THC (including CBD oils), and alcoholic beverages." The 
prosecution alleged in its motion to adjudicate that appellant violated this condition when he was "arrested for 
driving while intoxicated" and "admitted to a '12 ounce Corona.'"

To prove this allegation, the prosecution relied on the testimony of an officer, who said that he conducted a traffic 
stop after he witnessed appellant pull out from a bar at two o'clock in the morning and drive erratically. According to 
the officer, appellant weaved between lanes, exited without signaling, and drove on the shoulder.

After appellant brought his vehicle to a rest, the officer observed that appellant's eyes were glassy, his stare was 
blank, and his speech was slurry. Appellant was wearing a wristband from the bar, and he had the slight odor of 
alcohol. He also admitted to the officer that, earlier in the day, he had taken a muscle relaxer, and that he had also 
consumed a Corona.

The officer conducted the three standard field sobriety tests, which were [*4]  recorded on video and published for 
the trial court's consideration. Appellant exhibited six clues of intoxication in the horizontal gaze nystagmus test, five 
clues on the walk-and-turn test, and three clues on the one-legged stand test.

3

Testifying in his own defense, appellant said that he had not been drunk on the night in question. In fact, he testified 
multiple times that he does not drink. Nevertheless, he admitted that he had consumed "a little bit of beer" earlier in 
the day before he was pulled over.

Based on the foregoing, we conclude that there was sufficient evidence from which the trial court could have formed 
a reasonable belief that appellant had violated the terms of his community supervision by consuming alcohol and 
driving while intoxicated. And because proof of just a single violation is sufficient to support the revocation of 
community supervision, we likewise conclude that the trial court did not abuse its discretion by granting the 
prosecution's motion to adjudicate. SeeMoore v. State, 605 S.W.2d 924, 926 (Tex. Crim. App. 1980).

Appellant suggests that the record is somehow deficient because the trial court did not make any specific findings. 
We disagree. At the end of the evidentiary hearing on the motion to adjudicate, the [*5]  trial court told appellant, 
"You violated your probation." The trial court then explained that the violation concerned appellant's apparent 
intoxication: "There is nothing good that happens with one of my probationers . . . being at a bar at 2:00 o'clock in 
the morning. And I watched that video and you did not have the normal use of your mental and physical faculties." 



Page 3 of 4
Lonon v. State, 2025 Tex. App. LEXIS 8267

Appellant acknowledges these statements, but he contends that the trial court's finding was not "specific enough." 
To whatever extent that appellant believes that the trial court should have explicitly cross-referenced this finding 
with the number of the allegation from the motion to adjudicate, the written judgment leaves nothing to question-it 
recites that every single allegation from the motion to adjudicate was found to be true.

Appellant also suggests that his due process rights were somehow violated. Over the course of three pages in his 
brief, appellant quotes-without proper

4

attribution-to a lengthy passage from Brumit v. State, 206 S.W.3d 639, 645 (Tex. Crim. App. 2006), which 
addressed the alleged bias and partiality of a certain trial court. And at the end of that passage, appellant asserts in 
his own words, "It violates Appellant's due process when all parties including [*6]  the Court know when the plea is 
accepted that immediate violation will result." Appellant does not elaborate on that assertion in any way, nor does 
he attempt to apply Brumit to the facts of his case. We overrule this argument as inadequately briefed. See Tex. R. 
App. P. 38.1(i); Gibson v. State, Nos. 16-23-00425-CR, 13-23-00426-CR, 13-23-00427-CR, 13-23-00428-CR, & 13-
23-00429-CR, 2024 WL 2066825, at *3 (Tex. App.-Corpus Christi May 9, 2024, pet. ref'd) (mem. op., not 
designated for publication) (concluding that an identically worded argument, which also failed to incorporate any 
facts of the case into the analysis, was "entirely devoid of merit").

INEFFECTIVE ASSISTANCE OF COUNSEL

In his next issue, appellant raises what appears to be two complaints of ineffective assistance of counsel: first, that 
counsel failed to inquire into mitigating evidence or interview potential witnesses; and second, that counsel was not 
a zealous advocate.

We review such complaints under the standard set forth in Strickland v.Washington, 466 U.S. 668 (1984). Under 
that standard, appellant must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that his counsel's performance was 
deficient, and that the deficient performance was so prejudicial that it deprived him of a fair trial. Id. at 687. Failure 
to make the required showing of either deficient performance or sufficient prejudice defeats the claim of 
ineffectiveness. Id. at 700.

Beginning with the first complaint that counsel had [*7]  failed to inquire into mitigating evidence or interview 
potential witnesses, even if we assumed for the sake of argument that counsel's performance had been deficient, 
appellant has not

5

identified any mitigating evidence that could have been produced, nor he has identified any witnesses whom 
counsel should have interviewed or that the interview would have revealed any information favorable to his defense. 
Absent such facts, appellant has not demonstrated prejudice. See Stokes v. State, 298 S.W.3d 428, 432 (Tex. 
App.-Houston [14th Dist.] 2009, pet. ref'd) ("A claim for ineffective assistance based on trial counsel's general 
failure to investigate the facts of the case fails absent a showing of what the investigation would have revealed that 
reasonably could have changed the result of the case. Likewise, a claim for ineffective assistance based on trial 
counsel's failure to interview a witness cannot succeed absent a showing of what the interview would have revealed 
that reasonably could have changed the result of the case.").

As for the second complaint, appellant contends that counsel was not a zealous advocate because "he did not 
challenge any of the State's allegations" and he "essentially conceded to the allegations." Appellant does not 
support these assertions with [*8]  any analysis, and the record plainly refutes them. Counsel challenged the officer 
about whether appellant's driving had actually been erratic and whether certain clues of intoxication were visible in 
the video evidence. Counsel also challenged the prosecution's other witness, a probation officer, about appellant's 
alleged failure to report and pay fees. Counsel elicited testimony, for instance, that appellant's community 
supervision coincided with the COVID-19 lockdown, and that the probation officer did not return appellant's calls. 



Page 4 of 4
Lonon v. State, 2025 Tex. App. LEXIS 8267

Counsel also elicited testimony that, despite missing an occasional payment, appellant made a lump sum payment 
that satisfied his entire financial obligation.

Appellant relatedly contends that counsel was not a zealous advocate because counsel offered him as a witness 
"seemingly without preparation."

6

Our review of counsel's performance is highly deferential, and begins with the strong presumption that counsel's 
decisions were reasonably professional and motivated by sound trial strategy. See Jackson v. State, 877 S.W.2d 
768, 771 (Tex. Crim. App. 1994). Appellant had the burden of overcoming that presumption with affirmative proof 
regarding counsel's actions and omissions. See Thompson v. State, 9 S.W.3d 808, 813 (Tex. Crim. App. 1999) 
("Any allegation of ineffectiveness [*9]  must be firmly founded in the record, and the record must affirmatively 
demonstrate the alleged ineffectiveness.").

The record here affirmatively shows that counsel called appellant as a witness, but the record is silent as to the 
measures taken by counsel to prepare appellant for testifying. Appellant did not move for a new trial, and counsel 
did not otherwise file an affidavit explaining those measures. Moreover, appellant does not even explain in his brief 
why he believes that the measures, if any, were inadequate. Without any factual support or basis, his complaint is 
conclusory.

We conclude that appellant has failed to overcome the presumption that counsel's performance was motivated by 
sound trial strategy. We likewise conclude that all of appellant's claims of ineffectiveness must fail.

CONCLUSION

The trial court's judgment is affirmed.

/s/ Tracy Christopher

Chief Justice

Panel consists of Chief Justice Christopher and Justices Wise and Jewell. Do Not Publish - Tex. R. App. P. 47.2(b).

7
