Appellants filed a motion for judgment notwithstanding the verdict, asking the trial court to disregard the jury's 
damages finding and instead award the entire $71,071.49 in damages they insisted were undisputed. The trial court 
signed a judgment in accord with the jury's verdict.

Analysis

A. Partial Reporter's Record

Appellants filed a partial reporter's record. Appellants did not file a written request with the court reporter to prepare 
a partial reporter's record, but they did communicate directly with the reporter regarding the portions of the record 
they requested. Each volume of the reporter's record is conspicuously identified as "Excerpt of Jury Trial," but none 
of the exhibits admitted during trial or in the offer of proof are included in our record.

Under our Rules of Appellate Procedure, when an appellant requests a partial reporter's record, the appellant must 
designate the issues to be presented on appeal

8

and will then be limited to those points or issues. See Tex. R. App. P. 34.6(c)(1);

Bennett v. Cochran, 96 S.W.3d 227, 229 (Tex. 2002) (explaining that statement of issues on appeal need not be 
included in the request for the reporter's record so long as it is made in time for other parties to designate [*13]  any 
additional portions of the record and to prepare their appellate briefs). If the appellant complies with rule 34.6(c)'s 
requirements, this court presumes that the partial reporter's record constitutes the entire record for purposes of the 
stated points or issues. Tex. R. App. P. 34.6(c)(4). Absent compliance with this rule, however, we will not apply the 
presumption and instead will presume that the omitted portions of the reporter's record are relevant and support the 
trial court's judgment. See Bennett, 96 S.W.3d at 229; McCartney v. McCartney, -S.W.3d-, 2025 WL 2213213, at *3 
(Tex. App.-Houston [14th Dist.] Aug. 5, 2025, no pet. h.); DeWolf v. Kohler, 452 S.W.3d 373, 393-94 (Tex. App.-
Houston [14th Dist.] 2014, pet. denied); Brown v.McGuyer Homebuilders, Inc., 58 S.W.3d 172, 176 (Tex. App.-
Houston [14th Dist.] 2001, pet. denied).

Here, appellants did not include a statement of issues on appeal in their request for the reporter's record. However, 
in their notice of appeal, they stated that they

"desire to appeal the award of damages . . . ." We construe this statement as one identifying the points or issues to 
be presented on appeal. See Tex. R. App. P. 34.6(c)(1). Accordingly, we presume the partial reporter's record 
constitutes the entire record for purposes of this stated issue. See Tex. R. App. P. 34.6(c)(4). But we do not apply 
this presumption to any of appellants' issues unrelated to damages and will instead presume that the omitted 
portions of the record-i.e., the exhibits- are relevant and support the trial court's judgment. See Bennett, 96 S.W.3d 
at 229;

McCartney, 2025 WL 2213213, at *3; DeWolf, 452 S.W.3d at 393-94; Brown, 58 S.W.3d at 176.

9



Page 6 of 7
Bayou Bait Camp, LLC v. Wasserloos, 2025 Tex. App. LEXIS 8295

B. Exclusion of Evidence

In their first issue, appellants [*14]  contend the trial court erred by excluding their proffered evidence of 
Wasserloos's licensure status and history. We review the trial court's exclusion of evidence for an abuse of 
discretion. Caffe Ribs, Inc. v. State, 487 S.W.3d 137, 142 (Tex. 2016); JLG Trucking, LLC v. Garza, 466 S.W.3d 
157, 161 (Tex. 2015). Error in excluding evidence is reversible only if it probably caused the rendition of an 
improper judgment. Tex. R. App. P. 44.1(a)(1); see Caffe Ribs,Inc., 487 S.W.3d at 144-45; JGL Trucking, 466 
S.W.3d at 161. Although there is no specific test for determining whether evidentiary error resulted in an improper 
judgment, "an appellate court must review the entire record, 'considering the state of the evidence, the strength and 
weakness of the case, and the verdict.'" JGLTrucking, 466 S.W.3d at 165 (quoting Reliance Steel & Aluminum Co. 
v. Sevcik, 267 S.W.3d 867, 771 (Tex. 2008)); accord Brown, 58 S.W.3d at 176.

Appellants refer to and attach to their brief several exhibits that they contend were included in their offer of proof. 
Though the record is clear that the court excluded appellants' evidence, the exhibits attached to appellants' brief are 
not in our official record. This court cannot consider documents that are not included in the record on appeal. See 
Yeske v. Piazza Del Arte, Inc., 513 S.W.3d 652, 672 n.5 (Tex. App.-Houston [14th Dist.] 2016, no pet.) ("[T]his court 
cannot consider documents attached to an appellate brief that are not contained in the appellate record."); 
WorldPeace v. Comm'n for Lawyer Discipline, 183 S.W.3d 451, 465 (Tex. App.-Houston [14th Dist.] 2005, pet. 
denied). Thus, we cannot consider any exhibits attached to appellants' brief.

Consequently, the absence of a complete reporter's record [*15]  prevents us from determining whether appellants 
were harmed by any error in the exclusion, and we presume the omitted exhibits support the judgment. See Tex. R. 
App. P. 44.1(a)(1);

10

cf. also DeWolf, 452 S.W.3d at 398 (presuming that omitted portions of record support judgment; "[T]he absence of 
a complete record would prevent us from determining that Tammy was probably harmed by the erroneous 
admission of evidence."); see also Brown, 58 S.W.3d at 175-76; Soard v. Univ. of Tex. Health Sci.Ctr., No. 14-01-
01110-CV, 2002 WL 31835094, at *2 (Tex. App.-Houston [14th Dist.] Dec. 19, 2002, no pet.) (mem. op., not 
designated for publication) (holding that failure to comply with Rule 34.6 meant that court could not conclude 
whether the claimed erroneous exclusion of evidence was reversible). We must presume that the evidence omitted 
from our record would have shown that the trial court's error, if any, was harmless. See DeWolf, 452 S.W.3d at 398; 
Brown, 58 S.W.3d at 175-76.

We overrule appellants' first issue.

C. Damages

In issue two, appellants contend the trial court erred by denying their JNOV motion in which they sought judgment 
for "undisputed damages proved up in liquidated form." Appellants suggest that the trial court erred by failing to set 
aside the jury's $7,657.50 damage finding and instead should have signed a judgment awarding them the entire 
amount of attorney's fees that they incurred in the Christie Lawsuit. Because appellants included in their 
notice [*16]  of appeal that they wished to challenge the damages awarded in the judgment, we presume that the 
partial reporter's record constitutes the entire record for purposes of reviewing this issue.

See Tex. R. App. P. 34.6(c)(4).

A trial court may disregard a jury's verdict and render judgment notwithstanding the verdict pursuant to Texas Rule 
of Civil Procedure 301 if a directed verdict would have been proper, which means that the evidence conclusively 
establishes a party's right to judgment as a matter of law. See Tex. R. Civ. P. 301; Sherman v. Elkowitz, 130 
S.W.3d 316, 319 (Tex. App.-Houston [14th

11



Page 7 of 7
Bayou Bait Camp, LLC v. Wasserloos, 2025 Tex. App. LEXIS 8295

Dist.] 2004, no pet.). We review the denial of a JNOV motion for legal sufficiency, and evidence is conclusive "only 
if reasonable people could not differ in their conclusions, a matter that depends on the facts of each case." See City 
of Keller v.Wilson, 168 S.W.3d 802, 816, 823 (Tex. 2005).

"A jury has broad discretion to award damages within the range of evidence presented at trial." MEMC Pasadena, 
Inc. v. Riddle Power, LLC, 472 S.W.3d 379, 408 (Tex. App.-Houston [14th Dist.] 2015, no pet.). The evidence need 
not show exactly how the jury arrived at the specific amount awarded, nor is a jury tied to awarding damages 
exactly as requested by the injured party. See id. Instead, a jury is entitled to decide whether or how much of a 
witness's testimony to accept. E.g.,

McGalliard v. Kuhlmann, 722 S.W.2d 694, 697 (Tex. 1986) ("[T]he trier of fact is afforded considerable discretion in 
evaluating opinion testimony on the issue of damages.").

Appellants contend [*17]  that they provided undisputed evidence of their

"liquidated" damages. Appellants' alleged damages, however, were not "liquidated" because the parties did not 
stipulate to them in advance. See Flores v. MillenniumInts., Ltd., 185 S.W.3d 427, 431 (Tex. 2005) (explaining that 
"liquidated damages" ordinarily refers to an acceptable measure of damages that parties stipulate in advance will 
be assessed).

Neither were appellants' alleged damages undisputed. Appellants insist that the only "range" of evidence of 
damages introduced at trial was "the exact figure of $71,071.49." But Wasserloos's counsel cross-examined 
appellants' counsel extensively regarding whether and to what extent the fees claimed were necessary or 
reasonable. The court directed the jury to consider as damages only those reasonable and necessary attorney's 
fees incurred in defending the Christie Lawsuit. Thus, the jury was tasked with determining the reasonableness and 
necessity of all

12

the attorney's fees claimed, and it had discretion to find that appellants reasonably and necessarily incurred only 
$7,651.50 because of the wrongful acts found against Wasserloos. Cf. 4922 Holdings, LLC v. Rivera, 625 S.W.3d 
316, 330-31 (Tex. App.-Houston [14th Dist.] 2021, pet. denied) ("Horizon's argument presupposes that the jury was 
required to accept Jones's testimony and remedial cost figure in full [*18]  and could not have found that remedial 
costs were less than Jones estimated. But this disregards the jury's prerogatives."). Contrary to appellants' position, 
$7,651.50 is within the range of evidence presented at trial, and the jury had discretion to award this amount. See, 
e.g., id.

Because legally sufficient evidence supports the jury's damage award, the trial court did not err in denying 
appellants' motion for judgment notwithstanding the verdict. We overrule appellants' second issue.

Conclusion

Having overruled both of appellants' issues, we affirm the trial court's judgment.

/s/ Kevin Jewell

Justice

Panel consists of Chief Justice Christopher and Justices Wise and Jewell.

13

IRAC_summ:
Case Name: Bayou Bait Camp, LLC v. Wasserloos
Jurisdiction / Court: Court of Appeals of Texas, Fourteenth District, Houston
Citation: 2025 Tex. App. LEXIS 8295
Date: October 28, 2025
I. Issue(s)
Can an appellate court find reversible error in the trial court's exclusion of evidence when the excluded exhibits are not included in the appellate record?
Did the trial court err in denying the plaintiffs' motion for judgment notwithstanding the verdict (JNOV) to award the full amount of requested damages, when the jury awarded a much smaller amount?
II. Rule(s)
Partial Appellate Record: When an appellant files a partial reporter's record without complying with the procedural rules for doing so (i.e., by not including a statement of issues covering all points on appeal), the appellate court must presume that the omitted portions of the record are relevant and support the trial court's judgment. An appellate court cannot consider documents attached to a brief that are not part of the official record.
Review of JNOV (Damages): A JNOV is proper only if the evidence conclusively establishes a party's right to judgment as a matter of law. A jury has broad discretion to award damages within the range of evidence presented at trial. It is the trier of fact's role to evaluate witness credibility and decide how much of the testimony to accept, especially regarding the reasonableness and necessity of claimed damages like attorney's fees.
III. Application (Analysis)
Exclusion of Evidence: The appellants argued the trial court erred by excluding evidence of their accountant's (Wasserloos's) troubled CPA licensure history. However, the appellants filed a partial reporter's record and failed to include the actual exhibits from their offer of proof. Because the notice of appeal only mentioned an intent to appeal the damages award, the presumption of a complete record did not apply to the evidentiary issue. Therefore, the court had to presume the missing exhibits supported the trial court's ruling. Without the exhibits, the court could not determine if the exclusion of evidence was harmful, and thus it could not find reversible error.
Damages Award: The appellants sought over $70,000 in damages, representing the attorney's fees they incurred in a prior lawsuit allegedly caused by Wasserloos's misconduct. The jury awarded only $7,657.50. The appellants argued their damages were "undisputed" and "liquidated," and the court should have awarded the full amount. The court rejected this. The damages were not liquidated, as they were not stipulated to in advance. More importantly, they were not undisputed. Wasserloos's counsel had extensively cross-examined the appellants' attorney about the reasonableness and necessity of the fees, challenging numerous billing entries. The jury had the discretion to believe that only a small portion of the fees were actually and necessarily caused by Wasserloos's wrongful conduct. The jury's award was within the range of evidence presented (from $0 to the full amount claimed), and therefore the trial court did not err in upholding it.
IV. Conclusion
No. Due to the incomplete record, the court must presume the omitted evidence supports the trial court's judgment and cannot determine if any error was harmful.
No. The amount of damages was disputed, and the jury's award was within the broad discretion afforded to it as the trier of fact.
The Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court's judgment.

Kennedy (Appellant) v Cordia (Services) LLP (Respondent) (Scotland)
before
Lady Hale, Deputy President
