(3) Whether the phrase 'other charges incurred in respect of the carriage of the goods' in CMR 23.4 was to be 
interpreted broadly or narrowly. The 'broad interpretation' was that it encompassed charges incurred because of the 
way that the goods had actually been carried and lost, so that the cargo claimant could recover excise duty levied 
on goods stolen in transit. The 'narrow interpretation' was that it was limited to those charges which would have 
been incurred if the carriage had been performed without incident and so did not include excise duty levied as a 
result of the loss of the goods in transit through theft.
There were powerful arguments in favour of the narrow interpretation. In particular, there was considerable force in 
the arguments based on the object and purpose of CMR Ch IV and the structure of the compensation scheme for 
JTI Polska Sp. Z o.o. and others v Jakubowski and others [2023] All ER (D) 45 (Jun)
Page 4 of 5
loss of goods under the CMR. However, it was impossible to find that the broad interpretation was not tenable (see 
[98] of the judgment).
That was supported by the fact that it reflected the conclusion of the judges at all levels in Buchanan (other than the 
minority in the House of Lords) and that reached by the Supreme Courts of Denmark, the Czech Republic, 
Lithuania and (arguably) Belgium as well as the Italian Court of Appeal (see [99] of the judgment).
It was also supported by the majority in Buchanan. As to ordinary meaning, there could be little doubt that the 
relevant wording was widely drawn (see [100], [101] of the judgment).
Further, the wording of art 23.4 was different to that in art 6.1(i). Charges 'incurred from the making of the contract 
to the time of delivery' were more readily understood as charges incurred for the purpose of carriage. That 
formulation was not, however, used in art 23.4 (see [102] of the judgment).
Some of the criticisms of the broad interpretation were unjustified or overstated (see [103] of the judgment).
Buchanan (James) & Co Ltd v Babco Forwarding and Shipping (UK) Ltd [1978] AC 141, [1977] 3 All ER 1048, 
[1978] 1 Lloyd's Rep 119 considered
(4) Whether it was appropriate in the present case for the court to exercise its power under the practice statement. 
The appellants contended that the narrow interpretation was to be preferred and that the 
court should exercise its power to depart from the Buchanan decision pursuant to the practice statement. They 
submitted that uncertainty in the law had arisen following the decision in Sandeman Coprimar SA v Transitos y 
Transportes Integrales SL[2002] 3 All ER 108 (Sandeman) in which the Court of Appeal had stated that Buchanan 
ought not to be applied any more widely than respect for the doctrine of precedent required. However, any resulting 
uncertainty arose from that statement in Sandeman, which was inappropriate and should not be followed, and not 
from Buchanan. The appellants further argued that there had been a material change in circumstances given: the 
Sandeman decision; academic disapproval of Buchanan; German and Swedish Supreme Court decisions upholding 
the narrow interpretation; and the emergence of a settled view in relation to the same issue when it arose under the 
CIM.
None of those arguments was persuasive. Sandeman's disapproval of Buchanan was inappropriate. Academic 
disapproval was not unanimous and in any event was somewhat muted and was not in itself a material change. The 
German and Swedish Supreme Court decisions had to be balanced against contrary decisions reached in other 
jurisdictions. The emergence of a settled view under the CIM had been achieved through amendment to that treaty. 
That might be a reason for the parties to the CMR convening to consider making a similar amendment, but it did not 
inform the proper interpretation of art 23.4. It had not been shown that the Buchanan decision worked 
unsatisfactorily in the market place, nor had it been suggested that Buchanan produced manifestly unjust results. It 
was not appropriate case for the court to exercise its power under the practice statement and so depart from 
Buchanan in the present case (see [116]-[118] of the judgment).
Although it was desirable that there be a uniform view as to the proper interpretation of are 23.4, reversing 
Buchanan would not achieve that, as the broad interpretation either was or might be followed in many other 
countries. In order to achieve uniformity, it would be necessary to amend art 23.4 to the CMR. That, however, was a 
matter for the parties to the CMR (see [120] of the judgment).
Consequently, the appeal would be dismissed (see [121] of the judgment).
Buchanan (James) & Co Ltd v Babco Forwarding and Shipping (UK) Ltd [1978] AC 141, [1977] 3 All ER 1048, 
[1978] 1 Lloyd's Rep 119 considered
Sandeman Coprimar SA v Transitos y Transportes Integrales SL [2003] All ER (D) 136 (Feb), [2003] 3 All ER 108, 
[2003] 1 All ER (Comm) 504, [2003] EWCA Civ 113, [2003] QB 1270 considered

IRAC_summ:
Case Name: JTI Polska Sp. Z o.o. v Jakubowski [2023] UKSC 19
Court + jurisdiction: United Kingdom Supreme Court
Area of law: International Transport – CMR Convention – Treaty Interpretation
Procedural posture: Appeal from the High Court (permission to appeal directly to Supreme Court).
Issue
Whether excise duty levied on goods stolen during international transit constitutes "other charges incurred in respect of the carriage of the goods" recoverable under Article 23.4 of the CMR Convention, and whether the Court should depart from its prior decision in Buchanan v Babco.
Rule
Under Article 23.4 of the CMR Convention, a carrier is liable to refund carriage charges, customs duties, and "other charges incurred in respect of the carriage of the goods." The Supreme Court (formerly House of Lords) previously held in James Buchanan & Co Ltd v Babco Forwarding and Shipping (UK) Ltd that this includes excise duty levied on goods lost in transit. The Court may depart from its own precedent under the 1966 Practice Statement only where it appears right to do so, such as where the previous decision causes manifest injustice, uncertainty, or impedes the development of the law.
Application
The Court reaffirmed the "broad interpretation" of Article 23.4 adopted in Buchanan, which interprets "charges incurred in respect of the carriage" to include charges incurred because of the way the carriage was performed (i.e., resulting from the theft), rather than just charges incurred for the carriage itself. While the appellants presented powerful arguments for a "narrow interpretation" (supported by the text's context and some foreign judgments), the Court found the broad interpretation remained "tenable" [98]–[102].
The Court declined to exercise its power under the Practice Statement to overrule Buchanan. The appellants failed to show that Buchanan had caused uncertainty or worked unsatisfactorily in the marketplace. While some foreign courts (e.g., Germany, Sweden) had adopted the narrow view, others (e.g., Denmark, Czech Republic) followed the broad view, meaning overruling Buchanan would not achieve international uniformity [116]–[120]. The Court noted that interpretation of international conventions often involves impression, and mere disagreement with a prior decision is insufficient to overturn it, especially where the prior view is tenable and has stood for decades [40]–[42].
Conclusion
The Court held that excise duty on stolen goods is recoverable under Article 23.4 of the CMR as interpreted in Buchanan, and declined to depart from that precedent; the appeal was dismissed.

case:
Clear Spring Prop. & Cas. Co. v. Wello & Mom, LLC
United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida
February 26, 2025, Decided; February 26, 2025, Entered on Docket
CASE NO. 21-cv-24234-ALTMAN/Reinhart
Reporter
768 F. Supp. 3d 1360 *; 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 34408 **; 2025 LX 34871; 2025 AMC 91
CLEAR SPRING PROPERTY AND CASUALTY COMPANY, Plaintiff, v. WELLO AND MOM, LLC, Defendant.
Core Terms
magistrate judge, vessel, spring, fire extinguisher, warranty, tagging, material fact, engine, summary judgment, void,
renewal, genuine, maritime, choice-of-law, marine insurance, usher, expire, questionnaire, certificate, fire
suppression, report and recommendation, summary judgment motion, underwriter, replace, fidei, insurance risks,
uberrimae, novo, fire-extinguishing, misrepresent
Counsel: [**1] For Clear Spring Property and Casualty Company, Plaintiff: Jacqueline Louise Goldman, Steven
Eric Goldman, The Goldman Maritime Law Group, Fort Lauderdale, FL.
For Wello and Mom, LLC, Defendant, Counter Claimant, Counter Defendant: Raul Morales, Raul Morales, Esq.,
Coral Gables, FL.
Judges: ROY K. ALTMAN, UNITED STATES DISTRICT JUDGE.
Opinion by: ROY K. ALTMAN
Opinion
[*1363] ORDER ADOPTING REPORT AND RECOMMENDATION
On September 27, 2021, Wello and Mom, LLC's vessel suffered a "partial sinking." Second Amended Complaint
("SAC") [ECF No. 74] ¶ 9. Although our Plaintiff, Clear Spring Property and Casualty Company, issued Wello a
marine insurance policy (the "Policy"), Clear Spring declined to cover the loss after it concluded that Wello "failed to
disclose facts which would have been material to the judgment of the underwriter who made the decision to issue
the Policy." Id. ¶ 15. Clear Spring sought declaratory relief in this Court, and both parties subsequently moved for
summary judgment—with Clear Spring arguing that the Policy was void ab initio and Wello insisting that Clear
Spring breached the Policy by refusing to cover the loss. See Clear Spring's Motion for Summary Judgment
("Clear Spring MSJ") [ECF No. 81] at 1 ("The [**2] Plaintiff seeks summary judgment . . . the policy is void due to
misrepresentation and/or nondisclosure of material fact[s] made at the time of the time of the application process.");
Wello and Mom, LLC's Motion for Summary Judgment ("Wello MSJ") [ECF No. 85] at 1 ("Wello . . . [contends]
that [Clear Spring] breached a valid and enforceable contract between the parties—the marine insurance policy.").
Page 2 of 17
Clear Spring Prop. & Cas. Co. v. Wello & Mom, LLC, 768 F. Supp. 3d 1360
We referred these cross-motions for summary judgment to U.S. Magistrate Judge Bruce E. Reinhart for a Report
and Recommendation. See Order of Referral [ECF No. 98]. After reviewing the parties' briefing, Magistrate Judge
Reinhart recommended that we "grant Clear Spring's Motion for Summary Judgment and deny Wello's Motion
for Summary Judgment." Report and Recommendation ("R&R") [ECF No. 101] at 15. Magistrate Judge Reinhart
agreed with Clear Spring (1) that the Policy is void ab initio because "Wello failed to disclose prior losses" and (2)
that "Clear Spring relied on the facts disclosed in [Wello's] applications in issuing a policy to cover the [Vessel]." Id.
at 9-10. Magistrate Judge Reinhart also found, in the alternative, that Wello had voided the Policy before the Vessel
sunk when [**3] it breached the Policy's "Fire Extinguisher Warranty." See id. at 14 ("A 2019 inspection tag means
the [Vessel's] fire suppression system and handheld fire extinguisher certification and tagging would have expired in
May [sic] 2020—a year before the reported loss. So, at the time of the loss, the policy was void and Clear Spring's
Motion for Summary Judgment should be granted."). Magistrate Judge Reinhart then cautioned the parties as
follows:
A party shall serve and file written objections, if any, to this Report and Recommendation with the Honorable
Roy K. Altman, United States District Court Judge for the Southern District of Florida, [*1364] within
FOURTEEN (14) DAYS of being served with a copy of this Report and Recommendation. Failure to timely file
objections shall constitute a waiver of a party's "right to challenge on appeal the district court's order based on
unobjected-to factual and legal conclusions." 11TH CIR. R. 3-1 (2016).
Id. at 16.
Wello timely objected to Magistrate Judge Reinhart's R&R. See Objections to Report and Recommendation
("Objections") [ECF No. 102]. Clear Spring has now responded to those Objections. See Plaintiff's Response to the
Defendant's Objections ("Objections Response") [**4] [ECF No. 105]. After careful review, we OVERRULE Wello's
Objections and ADOPT Magistrate Judge Reinhart's R&R in full.
BACKGROUND
I. The Undisputed Facts1
On July 23, 2016, Wello purchased a "2003 37' Sunseeker vessel, bearing [Hull Identification Number]
XSK02857F304" (the "Vessel"). Plaintiff's Statement of Material Facts ("PSOF") [ECF No. 80] ¶ 1; see also
Defendant's Response to PSOF ("PSOF Response") [ECF No. 87] ¶ 1 ("Undisputed"). Wello is an LLC with only
two members: Amelina Cisneros and Roy Cisneros. See PSOF ¶ 2; see also PSOF Response ¶ 2 ("Undisputed.").
Shortly after the Vessel was purchased, Wello "submitted an application for a policy of marine insurance to Concept
Special Risks Ltd. . . . which was then acting as underwriting and claims handling agent for another marine insurer,
Great Lakes Insurance SE[.]" PSOF ¶ 4; see also PSOF Response ¶ 4 ("Undisputed."). Acting on behalf of Great
1 "The facts are described in the light most favorable to the non-moving party." Plott v. NCL Am., LLC, 786 F. App'x 199, 201
(11th Cir. 2019); see also Lee v. Ferraro, 284 F.3d 1188, 1190 (11th Cir. 2002) ("[F]or summary judgment purposes, our analysis
must begin with a description of the facts in the light most favorable to the [non-movant]."). We accept these facts for summaryjudgment
purposes only and recognize that "[t]hey may not be the actual facts that could be established through live testimony at
trial." Snac Lite, LLC v. Nuts 'N More, LLC, 2016 WL 6778268, at *1 n.1 (N.D. Ala. Nov. 16, 2016) (Proctor, J.); see also Cox
Adm'r US Steel & Carnegie Pension Fund, 17 F.3d 1386, 1400 (11th Cir. 1994) ("[W]hat we state as 'facts' in this opinion for
purposes of reviewing the rulings on the summary judgment motion may not be the actual facts. They are, however, the facts
for present purposes[.]" (cleaned up)). "Cross-motions for summary judgment will not, in themselves, warrant the court in
granting summary judgment unless one of the parties is entitled to judgment as a matter of law on facts that are not genuinely
disputed." United States v. Oakley, 744 F.2d 1553, 1555 (11th Cir. 1984) (cleaned up). In adjudicating cross-motions, then, we
consider each motion separately and, of course, resolve all reasonable inferences against the movant. See Am. Bankers Ins.
Grp. v. United States, 408 F.3d 1328, 1331 (11th Cir. 2005).
Page 3 of 17
Clear Spring Prop. & Cas. Co. v. Wello & Mom, LLC, 768 F. Supp. 3d 1360
Lakes, Concept issued "a policy of marine insurance to Wello, Policy No. CSRYP/157469, for the policy period of
July 26, 2016 through July 26, 2017." Defendant's Statement of Material Facts ("DSOF") [ECF No. 86] ¶ 7.2
[*1365] The Vessel suffered [**5] "two losses—one in 2016 and one in 2018." R&R at 3. The first loss occurred
on September 1, 2016, when the Vessel "suffered damage related to a fuel tank leak[.]" DSOF ¶ 8. Great Lakes
denied "coverage for the loss suffered in 2016" and subsequently "elected not to renew insurance coverage for the
[Vessel]" in July 2017. Id. ¶¶ 11, 13. Thus, on July 28, 2017, Wello "entered into a marine insurance policy with
Certain Underwriters at Lloyd's . . . for the 2017 through 2018 policy period[.]" Id. ¶ 15. On May 6, 2018, the Vessel
"suffered an engine loss." Id. ¶ 16.3 As a consequence of this loss, Wello "completely replaced the [Vessel's]
Yamaha 250 2-stroke engines with Suzuki triple 300hp gas engines[.]" Id. ¶ 18.
Around the same time, Wello prepared "a marine insurance application to obtain coverage for the [Vessel] for the
2018-19 policy period." Id. ¶ 20. This application described the Vessel as a "Sunseeker with Suzuki triple 300hp gas
engines" and affirmed that the Vessel had not been involved "in a Loss in the last 10 years[.]" Id. ¶¶ 22-23; see also
PSOF ¶ 19 ("In response to a question on the 2018 Application requiring disclosure of 'Loss History.' Wello
answered, 'None.'"). [**6] "Thereafter, Concept issued on behalf of Great Lakes a marine insurance policy to Wello
to cover the [Vessel], Policy No. CSRYP/169671, for the policy period of July 31st, 2018, through July 31st, 2019."
DSOF ¶ 24. Wello renewed the Policy in 2019, 2020, and 2021—each time claiming that the Vessel had not
suffered a loss in the preceding ten years. See R&R at 3-4 ("In 2019, 2020, and 2021 a renewal application for [the
Vessel] was filed. The 2019, 2020, and 2021 renewal applications listed 'Roy Cisneros' under operator and 'none'
under 'all losses in the past 10 years.'"); see also DSOF ¶¶ 25-35 (same). In 2021, "Concept issued on behalf of
Clear Spring a marine insurance policy, Policy No. CSRYP/204845, for the policy period of July 31st, 2021, through
July 31st, 2022[.]" DSOF ¶ 36.
On September 27, 2021, "during the period of coverage afforded under the Policy, the [Vessel] suffered a partial
sinking." PSOF ¶ 39; see also PSOF Response ¶ 39 ("Undisputed."). "The sinking occurred at around 2:00-4:00 AM
while the [Vessel] was docked at Amelina and Roy Cisneros' vacation home in Marathon, Florida. The [V]essel was
completely submerged in water and [was] deemed a total loss." DSOF ¶ 44. [**7] Clear Spring assigned Revel
Boulon "to undertake a full investigation into the causes and circumstances of the loss." PSOF ¶ 40; see also PSOF
Response ¶ 40 ("Undisputed."). After investigating Wello's claim, Clear Spring denied coverage. See Joint
Statement of Material Facts ("Joint SOF") [ECF No. 84] ¶ 3 ("Clear Spring informed Wello in writing that it denied
the claim and did not pay for the alleged damages.").
II. The Procedural History and the R&R
Clear Spring's operative SAC seeks "declaratory relief pursuant to [28 U.S.C. § 2201] . . . to adjudicate and
determine the rights of the parties to a contract of marine insurance which is in dispute." [*1366] SAC ¶ 1. The
2 Clear Spring never responded to the DSOF. See generally Docket. Our Local Rules require litigants to respond to the opposing
party's statement of material facts to the extent that factual issues are disputed. See S.D. Fla. L.R. 56.1(b)(2)(B)-(C) ("An
opponent's Statement of Material Facts shall use, as the very first word in each paragraph-by-paragraph response, the word
'disputed' or 'undisputed.' If an opponent's Statement of Material Facts disputes a fact in the movant's Statement of Material
Facts, then the evidentiary citations supporting the opponent's position must be limited to evidence specific to that particular
dispute."). We'll therefore deem every fact Wello asserted in its SOF "admitted" unless that fact is contradicted by the PSOF or
other evidence in the record. See Ibezim v. GEO Grp., Inc., 2018 WL 8222121, at *7 (S.D. Fla. July 6, 2018) (Marra, J.) ("Failure
of a respondent to file a statement of disputed facts, in the format as required [by the Local Rules] causes all material facts set
forth in the movant's statement to be deemed admitted unless controverted by the opposing party's statement." (cleaned up));
see also S.D. Fla. L.R. 56.1(c) (same).
3 Clear Spring alleges that this "engine loss" occurred when the Vessel "ran aground and suffered approximately twenty
thousand dollars ($20,000.00) in damages." PSOF ¶ 15; see also PSOF Response ¶ 15 ("Disputed as phrased. Wello suffered a
loss in 2018 and its damages exceeded $20,000.00."). How exactly the Vessel suffered an engine loss in 2018 is irrelevant to
the issues in this case.
Page 4 of 17
Clear Spring Prop. & Cas. Co. v. Wello & Mom, LLC, 768 F. Supp. 3d 1360
SAC asks us—across six causes of action—to find: (1) that the Vessel's partial sinking "does not constitute an
accidental physical loss for which coverage would be afforded under the express terms and provisions of the
Policy," id. ¶ 20; (2) that the sinking "was due to wear and tear, gradual deterioration, lack of maintenance, etc., for
which coverage is excluded under the express terms and provisions of Plaintiff's policy of marine insurance," id. ¶
27; (3) that the damage to the Vessel's engines "was not caused by an accidental external [**8] event such as a
collision, impact with a fixed or floating object, grounding, stranding, ingestion of a foreign object, lightning strike or
fire," id. ¶ 34; (4) that "[t]he Vessel was unseaworthy at the time of the partial sinking on September 27, 2021," id. ¶
42; (5) that Wello breached its duty of uberrimae fidei by "fail[ing] to disclose material facts at the time that it
submitted the Renewal Questionnaire and prior to the issuance of the Policy," id. ¶ 49; and (6) that Wello breached
the Policy's "Fire Extinguisher Warranty" because "the inspection and certification tags on the Vessel's fire
extinguishers and fire suppression system had been expired since March 2020," id. ¶ 60.
Both parties moved for summary judgment on different portions of the SAC. Clear Spring moved for summary
judgment on Counts 5 and 6 (viz., the breach of uberrimae fidei and the breach of the Fire Extinguisher Warranty).
See Clear Spring MSJ at 1. Wello, by contrast, moved for summary judgment on Counts 1 through 5. See Wello
MSJ at 1-2. After reviewing the cross-motions for summary judgment, Magistrate Judge Reinhart sided with
Clear Spring and recommended that we grant Clear Spring's MSJ in full and deny [**9] Wello's. See R&R at 15.
Magistrate Judge Reinhart first found that Wello "failed to disclose prior losses and therefore the [P]olicy is void ab
initio." Id. at 9. In reaching this conclusion, Magistrate Judge Reinhart rejected Wello's argument "that the vessel in
2019 was not the same vessel that experienced the 2016 and 2018 losses because the engines were since
replaced." Id. at 10. "New engines or not," Magistrate Judge Reinhart explained, "there is no dispute that the Hull
Identification number remained the same, so the response to the loss question was inaccurate." Ibid. Magistrate
Judge Reinhart also found that "there is no genuine dispute that Clear Spring relied on the facts disclosed in
[Wello's] applications in issuing a policy to cover the [Vessel]" and that "any reasonable juror would find that the
answer 'none' is material to the insurer's decision assessing the risk." Ibid. Since "no reasonable jury could
conclude that Wello's omission did not materially affect the calculation of insurance risk," Magistrate Judge Reinhart
recommends that we grant summary judgment in favor of Clear Spring and declare the Policy void ab initio. Id. at
11.
Magistrate Judge Reinhart also found [**10] that Wello had voided the Policy by breaching its Fire Extinguisher
Warranty. Magistrate Judge Reinhart divided this analysis in two parts. First, the Magistrate Judge determined that
the Policy's "New York choice of law provision is presumptively enforceable" and, therefore, that the Policy "is
subject to the substantive laws of the State of New York"—not Florida. Ibid. Although Wello argued that the Policy's
"choice of law provision is unreasonable and unjust," Magistrate Judge Reinhart found the choice-of-law provision
"presumptively enforceable" and concluded that Wello had failed to surmount its "burden to overcome that
presumption." Id. at 11, 13. Second, Magistrate Judge Reinhart applied the relevant New York law, which holds that
a "breach of an express warranty in a marine insurance policy voids the policy, even where the breach played no
[*1367] role in the loss." Id. at 13. Based on evidence that "Wello does not dispute," Magistrate Judge Reinhart
concluded that the Fire Extinguisher Warranty was breached because the Vessel's "fire suppression system and
handheld fire extinguisher certification and tagging would have expired in May [sic] 2020—a year before the
reported loss." Id. [**11] at 13-14.4 Accordingly, "at the time of the loss, the policy was void and Clear Spring's
Motion for Summary Judgment should be granted." Id. at 14.5

THE LAW
District courts must review de novo any part of a magistrate judge's disposition that has been properly objected to.
See Fed. R. Civ. P. 72(b)(3). Although Rule 72 itself is silent on the standard of review, the Supreme Court has
acknowledged that Congress's intent was to require a de novo review only where objections have been properly
filed—and not when neither party objects. See Thomas v. Arn, 474 U.S. 140, 150, 106 S. Ct. 466, 88 L. Ed. 2d 435
(1985) ("It does not appear that Congress intended to require district court review of a magistrate [judge]'s factual or
legal conclusions, under a de novo or any other standard, when neither party objects to those findings."). "If no
objection or only [a] partial objection is made to the magistrate judge's report, the district judge reviews those
unobjected portions for clear error." Macort v. Prem, Inc., 208 F. App'x 781, 784 (11th Cir. 2006) (quoting Johnson
v. Zema Sys. Corp., 170 F.3d 734, 739 (7th Cir. 1999) (cleaned up)).
When a party timely objects to a magistrate judge's report and recommendation, the district judge must make a de
novo determination "of those portions of the report or specified proposed findings or recommendations to which
objection is made." 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1); see also [**12] Leonard v. Polk Cnty. Sheriff's Dep't, 2019 WL
11641375, at *1 (M.D. Fla. Apr. 16, 2019) (Jung, J.). "Parties filing objections to a magistrate's report and
recommendation must specifically identify those findings objected to. Frivolous, conclusive, or general objections
need not be considered by the district court." United States v. Tardon, 493 F. Supp. 3d 1188, 1209 (S.D. Fla. 2020)
(Lenard, J.) (quoting Marsden v. Moore, 847 F.2d 1536, 1548 (11th Cir. 1988)). The "[f]ailure to object to the
magistrate [judge]'s factual findings after notice precludes a later attack on these findings." [*1368] Lewis v. Smith,
855 F.2d 736, 738 (11th Cir. 1988) (citation omitted).
Summary judgment is appropriate when "there is no genuine dispute as to any material fact and the movant is
entitled to judgment as a matter of law." Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(a). "By its very terms, this standard provides that the
mere existence of some alleged factual dispute between the parties will not defeat an otherwise properly supported
motion for summary judgment; the requirement is that there be no genuine issue of material fact." Anderson v.
Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242, 247-48, 106 S. Ct. 2505, 91 L. Ed. 2d 202 (1986). An issue of fact is "material" if
it might affect the outcome of the case under the governing law. Id. at 248. A dispute about a material fact is
"genuine" if the evidence could lead a reasonable jury to find for the non-moving party. See ibid.
At summary judgment, the moving party bears the initial burden of "showing the absence of a genuine issue as to
any material fact." Allen v. Tyson Foods, Inc., 121 F.3d 642, 646 (11th Cir. 1997); see also [**13] Celotex Corp. v.
Catrett, 477 U.S. 317, 323, 106 S. Ct. 2548, 91 L. Ed. 2d 265 (1986) ("[A] party seeking summary judgment always
bears the initial responsibility of informing the district court of the basis for its motion [ ] and identifying those
portions of [the record] which it believes demonstrate the absence of a genuine issue of material fact."). Once the
moving party satisfies its initial burden, the burden then shifts to the non-moving party to "come forward with
'specific facts showing there is a genuine issue for trial.'" Bailey v. Allgas, Inc., 284 F.3d 1237, 1243 (11th Cir. 2002)
(quoting Matsushita Elec. Indus. Co. v. Zenith Radio Corp., 475 U.S. 574, 587, 106 S. Ct. 1348, 89 L. Ed. 2d 538
(1986) (emphasis omitted)).
The Court, in ruling on a motion for summary judgment, "need consider only the cited materials, but it may
consider other materials in the record." Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(c)(3); see also Green v. Northport, 599 F. App'x 894, 895
(11th Cir. 2015) ("The district court could consider the record as a whole to determine the undisputed facts on
summary judgment."); HRCC, Ltd. v. Hard Rock Cafe Int'l (USA), Inc., 703 F. App'x 814, 817 (11th Cir. 2017)
(noting that a "court may decide a motion for summary judgment without undertaking an independent search of
the record" (quoting Fed. R. Civ. P. 56 advisory committee's note to 2010 amendment)). In any event, on summary
judgment, the Court must "review the facts and all reasonable inferences in the light most favorable to the non-
Judgment should be denied. . . . A reasonable jury viewing the undisputed facts in the light most favorable to Clear Spring could
find that Wello's insurance application omission violated its burden to disclose all facts material to a calculation of the insurance
risk and therefore the policy was void ab initio. In the alternative, even if the policy was not void ab initio, there is no genuine
dispute of material fact that Wello breached the fire suppression warranty, therefore rendering the policy void. And for these
reasons, I do not reach Wello's argument that Clear Spring breached its policy coverage contract.").

moving party." Pennington v. City of Huntsville, 261 F.3d 1262, 1265 (11th Cir. 2001). Where, as here, there are
competing cross-motions for summary judgment, "the facts are viewed in the light [**14] most favorable to the
non-moving party on each motion[.]" Chavez v. Mercantil Commercebank, N.A., 701 F.3d 896, 899 (11th Cir. 2012).
"Cross-motions for summary judgment will not, in themselves, warrant the court in granting summary judgment
unless one of the parties is entitled to judgment as a matter of law on facts that are not genuinely disputed." United
States v. Oakley, 744 F.2d 1553, 1555 (11th Cir. 1984) (cleaned up).
In sum, if there are any genuine issues of material fact, the Court must deny summary judgment and proceed to
trial. Whelan v. Royal Caribbean Cruises Ltd., 2013 WL 5583970, at *2 (S.D. Fla. Aug. 14, 2013) (Ungaro, J.). On
the other hand, the Court must grant summary judgment if a party "has failed to make a sufficient showing on an
essential element of her case." Celotex, 477 U.S. at 323; see also Lima v. Fla. Dep't of Children & Families, 627 F.
App'x 782, 785-86 (11th Cir. 2015) ("If no reasonable jury could return a verdict in favor of the nonmoving party,
there is no genuine issue of [*1369] material fact and summary judgment will be granted." (quoting Beal v.
Paramount Pictures Corp., 20 F.3d 454, 459 (11th Cir. 1994))).
ANALYSIS
Wello advances six objections to Magistrate Judge Reinhart's R&R: two on the doctrine of uberrimae fidei (Count
5), see Objections at 5-10; two relating to the alleged breach of the Fire Extinguisher Warranty (Count 6), see id. at
10-15; and the final two about the evidence Magistrate Judge Reinhart may (or may not) have considered in
reaching his decision, see id. at 16-17.6 We'll address Wello's objections to Magistrate Judge Reinhart's [**15]
process first. After that, we'll go through the substantive legal objections Wello has offered as to each count.
I. Objections to Judge Reinhart's Methodology
Wello has identified two flaws that (it says) infect Magistrate Judge Reinhart's entire R&R. First, Wello claims that
"the Report . . . does not comment on whether Wello's objections to Clear Spring's summary evidence were welltaken,
or disregarded." R&R at 16. Wello argues that "it is unclear to what extent the Magistrate Judge's findings
and conclusions are the result of or are supported by these objected-to documents" and insists that, because of this
uncertainty, we must review the entire Report de novo to ensure that Magistrate Judge Reinhart's findings weren't
tainted by objectionable evidence. Ibid. Second, Wello again asserts that we must "review the cross-MSJs de novo"
because Magistrate Judge Reinhart failed to "consider[ ] the fact that Clear Spring admitted each and every fact in
[the DSOF] . . . by not filing an opposing Statement of Material Facts[.]" Id. at 17.
We reject Wello's transparent attempt to avoid Magistrate Judge Reinhart's unfavorable recommendation by
forcing [**16] us to conduct a full de novo review of the summary-judgment record. Wello's complaints are based
on the flawed premise that the entire R&R is tainted because it's "unclear to what extent" Magistrate Judge Reinhart
relied on "objected-to documents[.]" Id. at 16. Magistrate Judge Reinhart's R&R is replete with detailed citations to
the parties' briefing, and he painstakingly described the evidence he relied on in making his findings. See generally
R&R. If the Magistrate Judge did, in fact, incorrectly rely on objected-to evidence, Wello could easily have identified
6 Wello's Objections also contain a bullet-point list titled "Portions of the Report to Which Objection is Made." Objections at 3-4.
Wello expands on most of these general and conclusory objections in later portions of its Objections, so we find that many of
these one-line complaints have been preserved for our review. Compare, e.g., id. at 3 ("The conclusion that the undisclosed
losses would be material to Clear Spring's determination of the risk in insuring the Vessel."), with id. at 8 ("Here, not only did the
Report did [sic] not make any findings that the alleged misrepresentation was material in light of the facts presented, it does not
conduct any factual analysis at all."). But as to those one-sentence objections that aren't discussed in more detail, we find this
list of one-liners (submitted without citations to the record or to caselaw) insufficient to trigger de novo review. See Marsden v.
Moore, 847 F.2d 1536, 1548 (11th Cir. 1988) ("Parties filing objections to a magistrate's report and recommendation must
specifically identify those findings objected to. Frivolous, conclusive, or general objections need not be considered by the district
court.").
Page 7 of 17
Clear Spring Prop. & Cas. Co. v. Wello & Mom, LLC, 768 F. Supp. 3d 1360
those errors by referring to the R&R's citations and checking Magistrate Judge Reinhart's work. But Wello hasn't
done that. In fact, it hasn't identified even a single specific instance in which Magistrate Judge Reinhart relied on
objected-to evidence. Instead, Wello merely speculates that he might have done that. See Objections [*1370] at
16 ("In the Report, it is unclear to what extent the Magistrate Judge's findings and conclusions are the result of or
are supported by these objected-to documents—in particular, to what extent the Magistrate relied on the
Underwriting Manual to conclude that Wello's alleged misrepresentations affected [**17] the insurance risk.").
That's not good enough. See Marsden, 847 F.2d at 1548 ("Parties filing objections to a magistrate's report and
recommendation must specifically identify those findings objected to. Frivolous, conclusive, or general objections
need not be considered by the district court."); United States v. Schultz, 565 F.3d 1353, 1360 (11th Cir. 2009)
("After a magistrate judge has issued a report and recommendation under § 636(b)(1)(B), a party that wishes to
preserve its objection must clearly advise the district court and pinpoint the specific findings that the party disagrees
with.").7
Wello's related objection about Clear Spring's failure to respond to the DSOF is similarly unavailing. Wello contends
that the "failure to dispute Wello's factual statement is extremely important and should have been taken into
consideration by the Magistrate Judge" and that "the report is silent on this front." Objections at 17. Again, however,
Wello doesn't identify any portion of the R&R in which Magistrate Judge Reinhart failed to give proper deference to
"Wello's proffered facts as admitted by Clear Spring[.]" Ibid. Wello also misapprehends the scope of the relevant
Local [**18] Rule. Although Wello says that "Clear Spring admitted each any every fact" in the DSOF when it failed
to respond, ibid., we still can't take the facts alleged in the DSOF as a given unless "the material fact at issue is
supported by properly cited record evidence," S.D. Fla. L.R. 56.1(c); see also ante, at note 2 ("Accordingly, we'll
deem every fact Wello asserted in their SOF 'admitted' unless that fact is contradicted by the PSOF or the other
evidence in the record.").
We therefore OVERRULE Wello's two objections to Magistrate Judge Reinhart's methodology insofar as Wello
demands a second (and complete) de novo review of the cross-motions for summary judgment. However, if we
determine that Magistrate Judge Reinhart made a specific factual finding that either relied on a document [*1371]
Wello had objected to or failed to afford proper deference to an admitted fact from the DSOF, we'll review that
finding de novo. See Garvey v. Vaughn, 993 F.2d 776, 779 n.9 (11th Cir. 1993) ("Because Johnson did not file
specific objections to factual findings by the magistrate judge, there was no requirement that the district court de
novo review those findings.").
II. The Uberrimae Fidei (Count 5) Objections
Wello's next objections [**19] concern Magistrate Judge Reinhart's recommendation that we grant summary
judgment in favor of Clear Spring on Count 5 because (in Judge Reinhart's words) Wello's material omissions
"void[ed] the [P]olicy ab initio under uberrimae fidei." R&R at 11. According to Wello, Magistrate Judge Reinhart's
7 Wello mistakenly believes that, "regardless of whether specific objections are filed, the magistrate's legal conclusions must be
reviewed de novo." Objections at 3 (citing Tran v. Waste Mgmt., Inc., 290 F. Supp. 2d 1286, 1291 (M.D. Fla. 2003) (Conway,
J.)). Wello's misunderstanding of the law derives from the Tran Court's own misreading of the Eleventh Circuit's opinion in
Cooper-Houston v. Southern Railroad Co., which held that a district court must "review [a magistrate judge's] legal conclusions
de novo"—but only if the case "was tried by a magistrate judge sitting as a special master[.]" 37 F.3d 603, 604 (11th Cir. 1994)
(emphasis added). That's not the situation we have here. And the Eleventh Circuit has been clear that a party's general
objections to an R&R aren't sufficient to invoke our de novo review of a magistrate judge's legal conclusions. See Marsden, 847
F.2d at 1548 ("Parties filing objections to a magistrate's report and recommendation must specifically identify those findings
objected to."); Schultz, 565 F.3d at 1360 ("[A] party that wishes to preserve its objection must clearly advise the district court and
pinpoint the specific findings that the party disagrees with."). And this makes sense. To hold otherwise would be to permit an
unhappy litigant (like Wello) to double judicial labor by forcing both the magistrate judge and the district judge to conduct a full de
novo review of the record simply by asserting an omnibus objection about the magistrate judge's methodology. That's plainly not
the law. See Schultz, 565 F.3d at 1361 ("It is reasonable to place upon the parties the duty to pinpoint those portions of the
magistrate's report that the district court must specially consider. This rule facilitates the opportunity for district judges to spend
more time on matters actually contested and produces a result compatible with the purposes of the Magistrates Act.").

Case Name: Clear Spring Prop. & Cas. Co. v. Wello & Mom, LLC, 768 F. Supp. 3d 1360 (S.D. Fla. 2025).
Court + Jurisdiction: United States District Court, Southern District of Florida.
Area of Law: Marine Insurance.
Procedural Posture: Cross-Motions for Summary Judgment.
Issue
Whether a marine insurance policy is void ab initio due to the insured’s failure to disclose prior vessel losses under the doctrine of uberrimae fidei or due to a breach of an express fire extinguisher warranty.
Rule
The maritime doctrine of uberrimae fidei (utmost good faith) requires an insured to disclose all facts material to the insurance risk; failure to do so, even if by mistake or negligence, renders the policy void ab initio [1371]. A fact is "material" if it would influence a prudent insurer’s decision to accept the risk [1371]. Additionally, under New York law (applicable via the policy’s choice-of-law clause), an express promissory warranty in a marine insurance policy must be literally complied with; any breach voids the policy regardless of whether the breach caused the loss [1376, 1381].
Application
The court first analyzed the uberrimae fidei claim. It was undisputed that Wello’s renewal applications from 2019–2021 listed "none" for losses in the past ten years, despite the vessel suffering a fuel tank leak in 2016 and an engine loss in 2018 [1372]. The court rejected Wello’s argument that the 2018 loss was irrelevant because the engines had been replaced, noting that the Hull Identification Number remained the same and the vessel was the same legal entity [1373]. Materiality was established through the unrebutted declaration of the insurer’s underwriter, who testified that loss history is a primary indicator of future risk and would have influenced the decision to issue the policy [1375].
The court then addressed the Fire Extinguisher Warranty, which required that equipment be "maintained in good working order," including "certification/tagging... as necessary" [1380]. Evidence showed the vessel’s fire suppression system was last tagged in March 2019, meaning the tags had expired by March 2020—well before the 2021 loss [1381]. Wello argued that the owners personally weighed the tanks and believed them to be functional [1380]. The court held this was irrelevant under New York’s "literal compliance" standard; the fact that the official tags were expired meant the warranty was breached as a matter of law [1382]. The court also upheld the New York choice-of-law provision, finding a "reasonable basis" for it because the insurer was licensed in New York and maintained bank accounts there [1378-1379].
Conclusion
The court granted summary judgment for the insurer, declaring the policy void ab initio due to both the material misrepresentations regarding loss history and the breach of the express fire equipment warranty.

Interrogation, Miranda Rights
Maryland v. Shatzer, 559 U.S. 98
Page 2 of 23
In Miranda v. Arizona, the U.S. Supreme Court adopted a set of prophylactic measures to protect a suspect's Fifth 
Amendment right from the inherently compelling pressures of custodial interrogation. Incommunicado interrogation 
in an unfamiliar, police-dominated atmosphere involves psychological pressures which work to undermine the 
individual's will to resist and to compel him to speak where he would not otherwise do so freely. Consequently, 
unless adequate protective devices are employed to dispel the compulsion inherent in custodial surroundings, no 
statement obtained from the defendant can truly be the product of his free choice. To counteract the coercive 
pressure, Miranda announced that police officers must warn a suspect prior to questioning that he has a right to 
remain silent, and a right to the presence of an attorney. After the warnings are given, if the suspect indicates that 
he wishes to remain silent, the interrogation must cease. Similarly, if the suspect states that he wants an attorney, 
the interrogation must cease until an attorney is present. Critically, however, a suspect can waive these rights. To 
establish a valid waiver, the State must show that the waiver was knowing, intelligent, and voluntary under the high 
standard of proof for the waiver of constitutional rights.
Criminal Law & Procedure > ... > Interrogation > Miranda Rights > Voluntary Waiver
HN3[
]  
Miranda Rights, Voluntary Waiver
In Edwards v. Arizona, the U.S. Supreme Court determined that the traditional standard for waiver was not sufficient 
to protect a suspect's right to have counsel present at a subsequent interrogation if he had previously requested 
counsel; additional safeguards were necessary. The Court therefore superimposed a second layer of prophylaxis. 
When an accused has invoked his right to have counsel present during custodial interrogation, a valid waiver of that 
right cannot be established by showing only that he responded to further police-initiated custodial interrogation even 
if he has been advised of his rights. He is not subject to further interrogation by the authorities until counsel has 
been made available to him, unless the accused himself initiates further communication, exchanges, or 
conversations with the police. Under this rule, a voluntary Miranda waiver is sufficient at the time of an initial 
attempted interrogation to protect a suspect's right to have counsel present, but it is not sufficient at the time of 
subsequent attempts if the suspect initially requested the presence of counsel. The Edwards presumption of 
involuntariness ensures that police will not take advantage of the mounting coercive pressures of prolonged police 
custody by repeatedly attempting to question a suspect who previously requested counsel until the suspect is 
badgered into submission.

Decision
 [***1045]  Suppression of inculpatory statements of state prisoner--whose initial interrogation was terminated after 
he invoked counsel right--made after waiving right during later interrogation held not required, because of break of 
over 2 weeks in Miranda custody between interrogations. 
Summary
Procedural posture:  Respondent inmate moved to suppress statements he had made pursuant to Edwards v. 
Arizona.  The trial court held a suppression hearing and denied the motion holding a presumption of involuntariness 
did not apply due to a break in custody; it found the inmate guilty of sexual child abuse.  Over the dissent of two 
judges, the Court of Appeals of Maryland reversed and remanded.  Petitioner Maryland filed a petition for certiorari 
which was granted. 
Overview:  In 2003, a police detective tried to question the inmate, who was incarcerated at a Maryland prison 
pursuant to a prior conviction, about allegations that he had sexually abused his son.  The inmate invoked his 
Miranda right to have counsel present during interrogation, so the interview was terminated.  The inmate was 
released back into the general prison population, and the investigation was closed.  Another detective reopened the 
investigation in 2006 and attempted to interrogate the inmate, who was still incarcerated.  The inmate waived his 
Miranda rights and made inculpatory statements.  The Court held that extending the Edwards presumption was not 
justified.  It held that a 14 day break-in-custody provided plenty of time for a suspect to get reacclimated to his 
normal life, to consult with friends and counsel, and to shake off any residual coercive effects of his prior custody.  
The inherently compelling pressures of custodial interrogation ended when the inmate returned to his normal prison 
life, so his release back into the general  [***1046] prison population after the 2003 interview constituted a break in 
custody.  The two-and-a-half year break was long enough to render Edwards inapplicable. 
Outcome:  The judgment of the Court of Appeals of Maryland was reversed, and the case was remanded for 
further proceedings not inconsistent with the opinion.  9-0 decision; two concurrences.

was convicted of sexual child abuse.  The Court of Appeals of Maryland reversed, holding that the mere passage of 
time does not end the Edwards protections, and that, assuming, arguendo, a break-in-custody exception to

We consider whether a break in custody ends the presumption of involuntariness established in Edwards v. 
Arizona, 451 U.S. 477, 101 S. Ct. 1880, 68 L. Ed. 2d 378 (1981). 
I 
In August 2003, a social worker assigned to the Child Advocacy Center in the Criminal Investigation Division of the 
Hagerstown Police Department referred to the department allegations that respondent Michael Shatzer, Sr., had 
sexually abused his 3-year-old son.  At that time, Shatzer was  [*101]  incarcerated at the Maryland Correctional 
Institution-Hagerstown, serving a sentence for an unrelated child-sexual-abuse offense.  Detective  [****5] Shane 
Blankenship was assigned to the investigation and interviewed Shatzer at the correctional institution on August 7, 
2003.  Before asking any questions, Blankenship reviewed  [***1051] Shatzer's Miranda rights with him, and 
obtained a written waiver of those rights.  When Blankenship explained that he was there to question Shatzer about 
sexually abusing his son, Shatzer expressed confusion--he had thought Blankenship was an attorney there to 
discuss the prior crime for which he was incarcerated.  Blankenship clarified the purpose of his visit, and Shatzer 
declined to speak without an attorney.  Accordingly, Blankenship ended the interview, and Shatzer was released 
back into the general prison population.  Shortly thereafter, Blankenship closed the investigation. 
Two years and six months later, the same social worker referred more specific allegations to the department about 
the same incident involving Shatzer.  Detective Paul Hoover, from the same division, was assigned to the 
investigation.  He and the social worker interviewed the victim, [**1218]  then eight years old, who described the 
incident in more detail.  With this new information in hand, on March 2, 2006, they went to the Roxbury Correctional 
 [****6] Institute, to which Shatzer had since been transferred, and interviewed Shatzer in a maintenance room 
outfitted with a desk and three chairs.  Hoover explained that he wanted to ask Shatzer about the alleged incident 
involving Shatzer's son.  Shatzer was surprised because he thought that the investigation had been closed, but 
Hoover explained they had opened a new file.  Hoover then read Shatzer his Miranda rights and obtained a written 
waiver on a standard department form. 
Hoover interrogated Shatzer about the incident for approximately 30 minutes.  Shatzer denied ordering his son to 
perform fellatio on him, but admitted to masturbating in  [*102]  front of his son from a distance of less than three 
feet.  Before the interview ended, Shatzer agreed to Hoover's request that he submit to a polygraph examination.  
At no point during the interrogation did Shatzer request to speak with an attorney or refer to his prior refusal to 
answer questions without one. 
Five days later, on March 7, 2006, Hoover and another detective met with Shatzer at the correctional facility to 
administer the polygraph examination.  After reading Shatzer his Miranda rights and obtaining a written waiver, the 
other detective administered  [****7] the test and concluded that Shatzer had failed.  When the detectives then 
questioned Shatzer, he became upset, started to cry, and incriminated himself by saying, "'I didn't force him.  I didn't 
force him.'"  405 Md. 585, 590, 954 A.2d 1118, 1121 (2008).  After making this inculpatory statement, Shatzer 
requested an attorney, and Hoover promptly ended the interrogation. 
The State's Attorney for Washington County charged Shatzer with second-degree sexual offense, sexual child 
abuse, second-degree assault, and contributing to conditions rendering a child in need of assistance.  Shatzer 
moved to suppress his March 2006 statements pursuant to Edwards.  The trial court held a suppression hearing

IRAC_summ:
Case Name: Maryland v. Shatzer [2010] 559 U.S. 98
Court + jurisdiction: Supreme Court of the United States
Area of law: Criminal Procedure – Miranda Rights – Right to Counsel
Procedural posture: On writ of certiorari to the Court of Appeals of Maryland
Issue
Whether the presumption of involuntariness established in Edwards v. Arizona—which prohibits police from re-initiating interrogation after a suspect invokes the right to counsel—persists after a substantial break in custody, specifically where a suspect returns to the general prison population for two years between interrogations.
Rule
Under Edwards v. Arizona, once a suspect invokes the right to have counsel present during custodial interrogation, any subsequent waiver of that right during a police-initiated interrogation is presumed involuntary. However, this is a judicially prescribed prophylactic rule, not a constitutional mandate, and applies only where its benefits outweigh its costs [106]. The Edwards presumption ends when there is a break in Miranda custody. To provide certainty to law enforcement, the Court establishes that the appropriate duration for this break is 14 days [110]. Lawful imprisonment imposed upon conviction constitutes a break in Miranda custody if the inmate returns to the general prison population [113].
Application
The Court reasoned that the Edwards presumption is designed to counteract the "inherently compelling pressures" of prolonged isolation in a police-dominated atmosphere [106]. When a suspect is released from custody and returns to normal life, these coercive pressures dissipate because the suspect is no longer isolated and can consult with counsel, family, or friends [107–108]. Consequently, extending the Edwards prohibition indefinitely would provide meager benefits while imposing the high cost of suppressing voluntary confessions [108].
To avoid case-by-case litigation regarding how long a break is sufficient, the Court adopted a bright-line 14-day rule. This period provides ample time for a suspect to reacclimate to normal life and shake off the residual coercive effects of prior custody [110].
Applying this rule to the prison context, the Court held that Shatzer’s return to the general prison population between the 2003 and 2006 interrogations constituted a break in custody. Unlike the "paradigm Edwards case" involving uninterrupted investigative custody, lawful imprisonment allows an inmate to return to a familiar routine and environment where their detention is unconnected to their willingness to cooperate with interrogators [113–114]. Because the break in custody lasted two and a half years—well beyond the 14-day limit—the Edwards presumption did not bar the second interrogation, and Shatzer’s subsequent waiver of rights was valid [117].
Conclusion
A break in custody of 14 days or more terminates the Edwards presumption of involuntariness, and return to the general prison population constitutes such a break; the judgment is reversed.

insurance coverage.

provisions as presumptively valid and enforceable. 521 F. Supp. 3d 580, 585-586 (ED Pa. 2021). The court

maritime law, but nonetheless must yield to a strong public policy [****7]  of  [*69]  the State in which suit is 
brought—here, Pennsylvania’s public policy regarding insurance. Id., at 230, 233.

Case Name: Great Lakes Ins. SE v. Raiders Retreat Realty Co., LLC [2024] 601 U.S. 65
Court + jurisdiction: Supreme Court of the United States
Area of law: Admiralty & Maritime Law – Contract Law – Choice-of-Law Provisions
Procedural posture: On writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
Issue
Whether, under federal maritime law, a choice-of-law provision in a maritime contract is rendered unenforceable if enforcing the chosen law would contravene the strong public policy of the state where the suit is brought.
Rule
Under federal maritime law, choice-of-law provisions in maritime contracts are presumptively enforceable. This presumption of enforceability yields only to narrow exceptions: (1) where the chosen law contravenes a controlling federal statute; (2) where the chosen law conflicts with an established federal maritime policy; or (3) where the parties can furnish no reasonable basis for the chosen jurisdiction. There is no recognized exception allowing the public policy of a specific state to override a valid federal maritime choice-of-law provision.
Application
The parties entered into a marine insurance contract that selected New York law to govern disputes. After the insured's boat ran aground in Florida, the insurer denied coverage. The insured (a Pennsylvania company) sued in Pennsylvania, arguing that Pennsylvania public policy should override the New York choice-of-law clause. The Third Circuit held that the clause must yield to the strong public policy of the forum state [68]. The Supreme Court reversed, emphasizing that Article III contemplates a uniform system of maritime law [69].
The Court analogized choice-of-law provisions to forum-selection clauses, noting that both are prima facie valid under The Bremen and Carnival Cruise because they reduce legal uncertainty and lower costs in maritime commerce [71]–[72]. The Court rejected the respondent's reliance on Wilburn Boat, clarifying that Wilburn Boat only authorizes the application of state law as a gap-filler when no established federal maritime rule exists. Here, the presumption of enforceability is the established federal rule, so there is no gap to fill [74]. The Court reasoned that allowing the public policy of 50 different states to invalidate choice-of-law clauses would destroy the uniformity and predictability essential to maritime commerce [77]. Furthermore, the Court declined to adopt the approach of the Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws § 187(2)(b), noting it was designed for interstate conflicts, not the federal-state dynamic inherent in maritime law [79].
Conclusion
The Court held that choice-of-law provisions in maritime contracts are presumptively enforceable and cannot be defeated by the public policy of the forum state; the judgment was reversed.

Our Supreme Court presumes judges of this Commonwealth are honorable, fair and competent, and, when 
confronted with a recusal demand, have the ability to determine whether they can rule impartially and without

As a general rule, a motion for recusal is initially directed to and decided by the jurist whose impartiality is being 
challenged. In considering a recusal request, the jurist must first make a conscientious determination of his or her 
ability to assess the case in an impartial manner, free of personal bias or interest in the outcome. The jurist must 
then consider whether his or her continued involvement in [*14]  the case creates an appearance of impropriety 
and/or would tend to undermine public confidence in the judiciary. This is a personal and unreviewable decision that 
only the jurist can make. Where a jurist rules that he or she can hear and dispose of a case fairly and without 
prejudice, that decision will not be overruled on appeal but for an abuse of discretion.

IRAC_summ:
Case Name: Commonwealth v. Barnett, 2025 Pa. Super. Unpub. LEXIS 2784.
Court: Superior Court of Pennsylvania.
Area of Law: Criminal Procedure—Waiver; Jurisdiction; Recusal.
Procedural Posture: Appeal from a judgment of sentence following a jury trial conviction.
Issue
The appellant, proceeding pro se, appeals his judgment of sentence for possession with intent to deliver heroin and related drug offenses following a jury trial where he represented himself. The appeal presents multiple procedural and substantive questions, including whether the appellant was denied the right to inspect tangible evidence against him and whether the Commonwealth committed a Brady violation by failing to disclose promises made to a cooperating witness. Furthermore, the court must address whether the trial judge abused his discretion by refusing to recuse himself based on allegations of bias and a "cover-up," and whether the trial court was divested of subject-matter jurisdiction under Pa.R.A.P. 1701 when the appellant filed a notice of appeal from a non-appealable interlocutory pre-trial order that was subsequently quashed.
Rule
Pro se litigants must comply with procedural rules; appellate courts will not develop arguments for an appellant (Vurimindi; Westlake). Claims not supported by citation to authority or the record are waived (Johnson). A Brady violation requires showing suppression of favorable evidence and ensuing prejudice (King). A trial court retains jurisdiction to proceed in a matter despite the filing of an appeal from a non-appealable interlocutory order (Pa.R.A.P. 1701(b)(6)).
Application
The court found that the appellant waived his first four issues—regarding inspection of evidence, Brady violations, suppression discovery, and recusal—due to his failure to develop coherent arguments or cite relevant authority and the record [*9]–[*15]. The court noted that the appellant made only "bald accusations" of a police cover-up and evidence planting without substantiation. Regarding the Brady claim, the court alternatively noted that the appellant failed to demonstrate prejudice or request a remedy when the witness's cooperation agreement was disclosed at trial [*11].
On the jurisdictional issue, the court held that the trial court was not divested of jurisdiction when the appellant attempted to appeal a pre-trial discovery order. Because that order was interlocutory and the appeal was quashed, Pa.R.A.P. 1701(b)(6) expressly permitted the trial court to proceed with the case [*18].
Conclusion
The judgment of sentence is affirmed.

Opinion

Before TOTH, Judge [*1] .

MEMORANDUM DECISION

Note: Pursuant to U.S. Vet. App. R. 30(a), this action may not be cited as precedent.

TOTH, Judge: Under Jones v. Shinseki, the Board may not deny a higher rating based on relief provided by 
medication when those effects are not contemplated by the rating criteria. 26 Vet.App. 56, 61 (2012). But where a 
DC does contemplate the effects of medication, "then Jones is inapplicable." McCarroll v. McDonald, 28 Vet.App. 
267, 271 (2016). Army veteran Joseph Allen Joshua contends that the Board failed to consider the ameliorative 
effects of his hepatitis B medications when it denied a higher rating for that condition. 1 He argues that a 20% rating 
is appropriate because, under his interpretation of the diagnostic code (DC), he only needs to show that he takes 
daily medication that controls his symptoms. But the 20% rating under the DC for hepatitis B very clearly 
contemplates the use of medication, along with requiring the presence of daily symptoms that the Board found the 
veteran did not experience. So, the Board did not need to consider the ameliorative effects of medications and, 
therefore, the Court finds no error and affirms.

The veteran served from 1967 to 1970. Decades later, he filed a service-connection claim for hepatitis B. VA 
ordered an exam [*2]  in March 2017, at which the veteran reported that his treating

doctor in 2016 told him that he had hepatitis B but that "[i]f they hadn't told me, I would have never known. I don't 
know how I got it." R. at 1572. Mr. Joshua denied any symptoms from his condition. He was told to take Viread daily 
for hepatitis B and to not "stop taking it." Id. The examiner confirmed that the veteran took continuous medication 
for control of his liver condition, but found that he did not exhibit cirrhosis, incapacitating episodes, or chronic 
symptoms. She determined that the veteran's hepatitis B was asymptomatic and caused no functional limitations. 
R. at 1576.

In 2021, the Agency granted his claim and assigned an initial 10% rating based on "[c]ontinuous medication." R. at 
1446-47. In April 2023, Mr. Joshua filed an increased rating claim, asserting that his hepatitis B condition worsened. 
He attended a June 2023 exam, where, again, the [*3]  examiner noted that the veteran was on a daily medication 
(Tenofovir) to treat his hepatitis B condition. The examiner also found that Mr. Joshua did not exhibit any symptoms 
related to his liver condition nor had any incapacitating episodes. Finally, the examiner found that the veteran did 
not have any signs or symptoms attributable to chronic liver diseases. VA denied a higher rating, so the veteran 
appealed to the Board.

In its 2024 decision, the Board determined that the veteran's hepatitis B condition did not cause daily fatigue, 
malaise, and anorexia that needed dietary restriction or continuous medication, as required by the higher 20% 
rating criteria. The Board determined that the medical evidence was "devoid of complaints" for symptoms or 
incapacitating episodes associated with his hepatitis B condition. R. at 27. The decision relied on the 2017 and 
2023 exams, which found that the veteran took daily medication but exhibited no hepatitis B symptoms or showed 
that he had incapacitating episodes. Indeed, the Board noted that the veteran's lack of symptoms more nearly 
corresponded with a noncompensable rating rather than his current 10% rating, but the Board did not disturb 
that [*4]  rating. Id. Mr. Joshua appealed to the Court.

On appeal, the veteran contends generally that the Board erred in denying a 20% rating because of its failure to 
properly consider his use of daily medication. Specifically, he first seems to contend that the Board erred by failing 
to discount the effects of his medication under Jones and

McCarroll. Compare Jones, 26 Vet.App. at 56 (discussing symptom relief from medications when the rating criteria 
do not encompass medication use) with McCarroll, 28 Vet.App. at 267 (discussing evaluations when the rating 
criteria do encompass medication use). This Court has long held that the Board may not deny a higher rating based 
on relief provided by medication when

2

Case: 24-4282 Page: 3 of 4 Filed: 10/28/2025

those effects are not contemplated by the rating criteria. See Jones, 26 Vet.App. at 63. More specifically, "if [a DC] 
does not specifically contemplate the effects of medication, the Board is required . . . to discount the ameliorative 
effects of medication." McCarroll, 28 Vet.App. at 271; see also Ingram v. Collins 38 Vet.App. 130, 135 (2025). 
Conversely, where a DC does contemplate the effects of medication, "then Jones is inapplicable." McCarroll, 28 
Vet.App. at 271.

Here, the veteran's hepatitis B is rated under DC 7345 for "Chronic liver disease without cirrhosis (including 
hepatitis B[)]." 38 C.F.R. § 4.114 (2023). 2 A 10% rating is met when [*5]  the predominant disability picture reflects 
"[i]ntermittent fatigue, malaise, and anorexia, or; incapacitating episodes (with symptoms such as fatigue, malaise, 
nausea, vomiting, anorexia, arthralgia, and right upper quadrant pain) having a total duration of at least one week, 
but less than two weeks, during the past 12-month period." Id. To meet 20%, the predominant disability picture 
should reflect



Page 3 of 4
Joshua v. Collins, 2025 U.S. App. Vet. Claims LEXIS 1461

Daily fatigue, malaise, and anorexia (without weight loss or hepatomegaly), requiring dietary restriction or 
continuous medication, or; incapacitating episodes (with symptoms such as fatigue, malaise, nausea, vomiting, 
anorexia, arthralgia, and right upper quadrant pain) having a total duration of at least two weeks, but less than four 
weeks, during the past 12-month period.

Id.

It's clear from the text of the DC that it contemplates the use of medication (at the very least, within the 20% rating 
criteria), rendering Jones inapplicable. See McCarroll, 28 Vet.App. at 271. Thus, the Board had no duty to discount 
the ameliorative effects of the veteran's medication usage to determine his "baseline" level of disability without the 
medication under Jones. Cf.Ingram, 38 Vet.App. at 137.

Next, Mr. Joshua asks the Court to interpret the 20% rating criteria [*6]  in DC 7345 as saying that such a rating is 
warranted when "the veteran has these symptoms and that these symptoms require continuous medication." 
Appellant's Br. at 8. In other words, he says that a 20% rating is warranted if a veteran "use[s] medication to prevent 
fatigue, malaise, and anorexia." Id. Thus, he contends that the 20% rating criteria does not require both daily 
symptoms and medication usage. Rather, he concludes that a "20[%] rating should be applicable so long as the 
Appellant is taking this medication to prevent symptoms." Id. at 9.

2 The rating criteria for DC 7345 have since been amended and retitled as "Chronic liver disease without cirrhosis," 
effective May 19, 2024, which is shortly after the appealed decision was issued. See 89 Fed. Reg. 19,735 (2024). 
The parties do not dispute that the pre-amended version applies here.

3

Case: 24-4282 Page: 4 of 4 Filed: 10/28/2025

"The starting point in interpreting a statute [or regulation] is its language." Good SamaritanHosp. v. Shalala, 508 
U.S. 402, 409 (1993). "Where a statute [or regulation's] language is plain, and its meaning clear, no room exists for 
construction." Gardner v. Derwinski, 1 Vet.App. 584, 587-88 (1991), aff'd sub nom. Brown v. Gardner, 513 U.S. 115 
(1994). Without ambiguity, "[t]he regulation then just means what it means-and the court must give it effect." Kisor v. 
Wilkie, 588 U.S. 558, 575 (2019). And here, the [*7]  DC plainly states that a 20% rating is warranted when a 
veteran suffers from "daily fatigue, malaise, and anorexia" that "require[es] dietary restriction or continuous 
medication." 38 C.F.R. § 4.114, DC 7345. It is clear from the regulation that all three symptoms must be present 
daily, and the severity of those symptoms is indicated by the requirement of dietary restriction or continuous 
medication. Indeed, each rating level builds off the other-a veteran goes from showing "intermittent fatigue, malaise, 
and anorexia" (10%) to "daily fatigue, malaise, and anorexia" (20%). Id. (emphasis added). The Court is not 
persuaded by the veteran's argument that daily medication usage alone, without the presence of daily symptoms 
(fatigue, malaise, and anorexia), is all that the 20% rating criteria require.

As a final note, even if Mr. Joshua's interpretation was correct and the 20% rating contemplates symptoms that are 
controlled by daily medication, the record supports the Board's finding that he suffers from no symptoms at all. The 
2017 and 2023 exams repeatedly state that Mr. Joshua's hepatitis B condition is asymptomatic and the veteran 
even stated that he "would have never known" that he had hepatitis B [*8]  before his 2016 diagnosis. R. at 1572. 
So, even if the Court accepts the veteran's interpretation, he would still face the additional hurdle of explaining how 
his symptoms are controlled by medication in the absence of any indication from the record that he suffered such 
symptoms.

Given the foregoing, the May 9, 2024, Board decision is AFFIRMED.

IRAC_summ:
Case Name: Joshua v. Collins [2025] U.S. App. Vet. Claims LEXIS 1461
Court: United States Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims
Area of law: Veterans Law—Disability Ratings (Hepatitis B)
Procedural posture: Appeal from a decision of the Board of Veterans' Appeals denying an increased rating.
Issue
Whether the Board erred in denying a 20% rating for hepatitis B by failing to consider the ameliorative effects of medication under Jones v. Shinseki. The specific question is whether Diagnostic Code (DC) 7345 contemplates the use of medication, thereby rendering the Jones rule inapplicable.
Rule
Under Jones v. Shinseki, the Board generally cannot deny a higher rating based on symptom relief provided by medication if the rating criteria do not contemplate medication use. However, if the DC does specifically contemplate the effects of medication, Jones is inapplicable (McCarroll v. McDonald). DC 7345 (Chronic liver disease) assigns a 20% rating for "Daily fatigue, malaise, and anorexia... requiring dietary restriction or continuous medication."
Application
The court affirms the Board's denial of the 20% rating. The veteran argued that because he takes daily medication to control his hepatitis B, he is entitled to the 20% rating, and the Board should have evaluated him as if he were unmedicated.
The court rejects this argument because the text of DC 7345 explicitly includes "continuous medication" as a criterion for the 20% rating. Because the regulation contemplates medication, the Jones rule requiring the Board to discount ameliorative effects does not apply. Furthermore, the court rejects the veteran's interpretation that medication use alone warrants the rating. The plain language of the regulation requires both "daily fatigue, malaise, and anorexia" and the requirement of medication/dietary restriction. Since the record consistently showed the veteran was asymptomatic (no fatigue, malaise, or anorexia), he did not meet the criteria for the 20% rating, regardless of his medication use.
Conclusion
The Board's decision is affirmed.

Decision
 [***1009]  Advice that suspect had "the right to talk to a lawyer before answering any of [the law enforcement 
officers'] questions" and could invoke right "at any time . . . during th[e] interview," held to satisfy Miranda 
requirement to warn of right to presence of attorney. 
Summary
Procedural posture:  Defendant was convicted in state court of unlawful possession of a weapon but asserted that 
the defendant was not properly advised of his right to counsel prior to admitting ownership of the weapon.  Upon the 
grant of a writ of certiorari, respondent State of Florida appealed the judgment of the Supreme Court of Florida 
which held that the advice given the defendant concerning his right to counsel was misleading. 
Overview:  The defendant contended that federal jurisdiction was lacking because the state court relied on the 
Florida Constitution in addition to the U.S. Constitution, and thus there was an independent and adequate state-law 
basis for the state court's decision.  The defendant also argued that the advice that the defendant could consult 
counsel prior to questioning, and that the defendant could invoke his rights at any time, failed to advise the 
defendant that he could have counsel present during questioning.  The U.S. Supreme Court first held that, although 
the state court invoked both state and federal law in its decision, federal jurisdiction was not precluded since the 
state court treated state and federal law as interchangeable and did not assert that state law gave the defendant 
distinct or broader rights.  Further, although the advice given to the defendant was not the clearest possible 
formulation of the right to counsel, the two advisements that the defendant could consult counsel prior to 
questioning and invoke his right to counsel at any time, in combination, reasonably conveyed the defendant's right 
to have counsel present, not only at the outset of interrogation, but at all times. 
 [***1010]  Outcome:  The judgment holding that the advisement of the defendant's right to counsel was 
inadequate was reversed, and the case was remanded for further proceedings.  7-2 Decision; 1 Dissent.
