case:
Popoviciu v Curtea De Apel Bucharest (Romania) - [2023] All ER (D) 35 (Nov)
Page 1 of 5
Popoviciu v Curtea De Apel Bucharest (Romania) [2023] All ER (D) 35 (Nov)
[2023] UKSC 39
Supreme Court
Lord Hodge, Deputy President, Lord Lloyd-Jones, Lord Kitchin, Lord Hamblen and Lord Stephens
8 November 2023
EXTRADITION – HUMAN RIGHTS – STANDARD OF PROOF
Abstract
The Supreme Court dismissed the appellant's appeal against the decision of the Administrative Court which allowed 
the respondent's extradition appeal pursuant to s 27(1)(a) of the Extradition Act 2003, discharged the respondent 
pursuant to s 27(5)(a) of that Act and quashed the order for the respondent's extradition to Romania to serve a 
sentence of seven years' imprisonment for two offences: accessory to aggravated abuse of power, and bribery, 
pursuant to s 27(5)(b) (see [2021] EWHC 1584 (Admin)). That decision was made on the basis that there were 
substantial grounds for believing there was a real risk that the respondent's trial was so flagrantly unfair that his 
right to liberty under art 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention) would be violated if he 
were returned to Romania, having considered fresh evidence relating to the propriety of the judge who had heard 
the respondent's trial in Romania. Subsequently, the European Arrest Warrant had been withdrawn. In those 
circumstances, the Supreme Court made an order pursuant to s 43(4) dismissing the appeal. The Supreme Court, 
nevertheless, decided the certified question holding that the earlier court had applied the wrong standard of proof 
when it decided the case. In a conviction extradition case, the respondent had to show that the allegations of bias 
and corruption that he made against the trial judge were true on the balance of probabilities, rather than showing 
merely that there were substantial grounds for believing that there was a real risk that they were true. Where a 
requested person alleged that they had been convicted in a trial that was so flagrantly unfair that it deprived them of 
the essence of their right to a fair trial under art 6 of the Convention, and that accordingly extradition would violate 
their right to liberty under art 5, they had to prove on the balance of probabilities that the trial was flagrantly unfair.
Digest
The judgment is available at: [2023] UKSC 39
  Background     
The respondent appealed against his extradition to Romania to serve a sentence of seven years' imprisonment for 
two offences: accessory to aggravated abuse of power, and bribery relating to a conspiracy to transfer a plot of land 
from state ownership to a private company in which he had an interest. Before the district judge, the respondent 
had challenged his extradition on numerous grounds. The essence of his case had been, and was, that his 
prosecution was politically motivated and wholly unfair, and that he faced risk of death, or detention in inhumane 
prison conditions, if returned to Romania. On appeal, the respondent renewed the challenges he had advanced 
before the judge and added further grounds in respect of which he sought to rely on fresh evidence relating to the 
propriety of the judge who had heard the respondent's trial in Romania. The Administrative Court allowed the 
respondent's appeal pursuant to s 27(1)(a) of the Extradition Act 2003 (EA 2003), discharged the respondent 
pursuant to EA 2003 s 27(5)(a) and quashed the order for the respondent's extradition to Romania pursuant to EA 
2003 s 27(5)(b) (see [2021] EWHC 1584 (Admin)) having held that there were substantial grounds for believing 
*Popoviciu v Curtea De Apel Bucharest (Romania) - [2023] All ER (D) 35 (Nov)
Page 2 of 5
there was a real risk that the respondent's trial was so flagrantly unfair that his right to liberty under art 5 of the 
European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention) would be violated if he were returned to Romania. The 
Administrative Court certified that its decision involved a point of law of general public importance about the 
standard of proof in cases where a person alleged that extradition would violate their human rights because the trial 
where they were convicted was flagrantly unfair (the certified question). It refused permission for the Court of 
Appeal in Romania to appeal to the Supreme Court, but the Supreme Court later granted permission to appeal. 
Following the completion of the hearing of the appeal, the Supreme Court was informed by the designated authority 
that the European Arrest Warrant (EAW) dated 3 August 2017 had been withdrawn. In those circumstances, the 
Supreme Court made an order dated 24 July 2023 pursuant to EA 2003 s 43(4) dismissing the appeal. The 
Supreme Court, nevertheless, decided to deliver its judgment on this appeal, in order to answer the certified 
question and to address other important issues which arose.
  Issues and decisions     
Whether, in a conviction extradition case, substantial grounds should be shown for believing that there was a real 
risk that the person's trial was so flagrantly unfair as to deprive him of the essence of his art 6 rights, and therefore 
a real risk that his imprisonment in the requesting state would violate his art 5 rights.
The respondent submitted that there was a good reason to extend the relaxed approach in the case of evidence 
obtained by torture to cases where corruption and bias were alleged on the basis that: (i) the gravity of the resulting 
injustice if the allegations were true was so great that it sufficed for there to be credible evidence that that might be 
the case; (ii) as in the case of torture, bias and partiality were difficult to prove; (iii) where a judge, in breach of duty, 
had failed to disclose the true position, it was not reasonable to impose a greater burden on the fugitive than to 
establish credible evidence that the judge might well have been corrupt or biased. Alternatively, he submitted that 
the Administrative Court in its assessment of the evidence did not take account of the failure of the Romanian 
authorities to put forward any evidence or information to dispel the concerns that arose from the evidence in relation 
to the respondent's trial.
The extension for which the respondent contended would be totally inappropriate. The exceptional relaxation of the 
standard of proof in the case of evidence which might have been obtained by torture reflected the unique 
wickedness of torture and the abhorrence in which its corrupting influence was rightly held. The Administrative 
Court had misdirected itself and applied the wrong standard of proof when it decided the case. In a conviction 
extradition case, the respondent had to show that the allegations of bias and corruption that he made against the 
trial judge were true on the balance of probabilities, rather than showing merely that there were substantial grounds 
for believing that there was a real risk that they were true. Where a requested person alleged that they had been 
convicted in a trial that was so flagrantly unfair that it deprived them of the essence of their right to a fair trial under 
art 6 of the Convention, and that accordingly extradition would violate their right to liberty under art 5, they had to 
prove on the balance of probabilities that the trial was flagrantly unfair (see [78] of the judgment).  
The assessment of the response from the Prosecutor's Office of the High Court of Cassation and Justice in 
Romania had clearly been a factor taken into account by the judge in the Administrative Court in coming to his 
overall conclusion. He had drawn inferences from the inadequacy of the response. However, they were weak 
inferences, and he clearly did not consider them sufficient to carry the allegations made by the respondent over the 
line of establishing on the balance of probabilities a flagrant violation of fundamental rights. That conclusion was 
reached on his evaluation of all the evidence in the case. He was entitled to come to that conclusion and there was 
no basis on which the present court could properly interfere with it (see [82], [84] of the judgment).
The further evidence was of limited significance when considered against the earlier evidence and could not have 
the decisive effect required by the strict test in Szombathely City Court v Fenyvesi [2009] 4 All ER 324. As a result, 
the present case was not a case in which a degree of latitude in applying the criteria must be introduced in order to 
comply with the Human Rights Act 1998 (HRA 1998). Had the appellant not withdrawn the EAW, further evidence 
would have been refused to be admitted and the application that the proceedings be remitted to the Administrative 
Court for consideration of the further evidence would have been dismissed (see [87], [92], [93] of the judgment).
*Popoviciu v Curtea De Apel Bucharest (Romania) - [2023] All ER (D) 35 (Nov)
Page 3 of 5
Further, the Romanian authorities stated that even if the impropriety of the trial judge were proven, it would not 
constitute a reason to review a final decision under Romanian legislation. The experts for the parties had disagreed 
about whether there was an effective remedy, as required by art 5(4) of the Convention under Romanian law for the 
respondent to challenge the lawfulness of his detention in Romania if he were extradited, and the fairness of the 
criminal proceedings. If the EAW had not been withdrawn, the Supreme Court would therefore have remitted the 
issue to be decided by the Administrative Court, where the parties' experts could be cross-examined (see [30], [85], 
[104], [107], [108] of the judgment).
The appeal would be dismissed pursuant to EA 2003 s 43(4) on the basis of the appellant's withdrawal of the EAW 
(see [109] of the judgment).

IRAC_summ:
Case Name: Popoviciu v Curtea De Apel Bucharest (Romania) [2023] UKSC 39
Court + jurisdiction: United Kingdom Supreme Court
Area of law: Extradition – Human Rights – Standard of Proof
Procedural posture: Appeal from the Administrative Court (High Court).
Issue
Whether a requested person alleging that extradition would violate their Article 5 rights (liberty) because of a flagrantly unfair trial in the requesting state must prove the unfairness on the balance of probabilities, or merely show "substantial grounds for believing" there is a real risk of such unfairness.
Rule
In a conviction extradition case (where the person has already been convicted), if the requested person relies on evidence that the trial was flagrantly unfair (a violation of Article 6) to argue that extradition would violate Article 5, they must prove that the trial was flagrantly unfair on the balance of probabilities. The lower "substantial grounds for believing" test applies to future risks (e.g., risk of future torture or unfair trial), but not to past facts occurring in the requesting state, unless the evidence was obtained by torture (where a special rule applies).
Application
The Court clarified the standard of proof for past events in extradition. The respondent argued that his Romanian trial was unfair due to judicial bias/corruption. The Administrative Court had applied the "substantial grounds for believing" test, effectively lowering the bar for the respondent. The Supreme Court held this was an error of law. The "substantial grounds" test is predictive, used for assessing future risks upon return. For past events (like the fairness of a completed trial), the standard is the balance of probabilities [78].
The Court rejected the argument that the exceptional approach used for evidence obtained by torture (where "real risk" suffices) should extend to allegations of judicial bias. Torture holds a unique status of abhorrence in law; this exception does not apply to other forms of unfairness [78]. Therefore, the respondent was required to prove, on the balance of probabilities, that the judge in his trial was actually biased or corrupt. The Administrative Court’s findings, which relied on weak inferences from the Romanian prosecutor's inadequate response, were insufficient to meet this standard [82]–[84].
Although the appeal was formally dismissed because the European Arrest Warrant was withdrawn, the Court decided the legal point to correct the lower court's error.
Conclusion
The Court held that a requested person must prove on the balance of probabilities that a past trial was flagrantly unfair; the appeal was dismissed on procedural grounds (withdrawal of warrant) but the legal principle was decided in favour of the appellant.

Symeonides v. Trump Ruffin Commer., LLC
Sebastian Symeonides got stuck in a malfunctioning elevator at the Trump International Hotel in Las Vegas for 20
minutes on Valentine's Day 2022, which also happened to be his wedding day. So he sues Trump Ruffin
Commercial LLC and its affiliated entities,1 along with Otis Elevator Corporation for negligence and products
liability.2 His claims are based primarily on the opinions of his retained elevator-maintenance expert, John Koshak.
Otis now moves for summary judgment on all claims3 and seeks to exclude Koshak's opinions.4 Symeonides
concedes that his products-liability claim should be dismissed but argues that Koshak's opinions are not excludable
and fully support his negligence claims. Trump Ruffin seeks to join in Otis's summary-judgment motion with
additional substantive arguments,5 an effort that Symeonides opposes.6
While Koshak will not be permitted to offer the legal conclusions that Otis's actions constituted a breach of contract
or fraud, his opinions are otherwise not excludable, so I largely deny Otis's motion to exclude Koshak's testimony.
Because Symeonides has shown that Koshak's non-excluded testimony and other evidence in the record create
genuine [**3] issues of material fact to support Symeonides's negligence theories, I deny Otis's motion for
summary judgment on them. And because Trump Ruffin's joinder in Otis's summary-judgment motion is not a
true joinder but instead a late substantive motion of its own, I grant Symeonides's motion to strike it. So this case
proceeds to trial on Symeonides's negligence theories, but first I refer the parties to the magistrate judge for a
mandatory settlement conference.
Background
A. Symeonides and his friends got trapped in the hotel elevator for 20 minutes.
Sebastian Symeonides got married in the penthouse on the 64th floor of the [*1012] Trump International Hotel in
Las Vegas on Valentine's Day 2022.7 He was also a guest at the hotel and, after a wedding rehearsal in the
penthouse that morning, he and his friends got in public elevator # 3 (PE3) and pushed the buttons to go back to
their rooms to get ready for the wedding.8 But the elevator malfunctioned, keeping the six passengers trapped
inside it for about 20 minutes.9

IRAC_summ:
Case Name: Symeonides v. Trump Ruffin Commer., LLC, 789 F. Supp. 3d 1005 (D. Nev. 2025).
Court + Jurisdiction: United States District Court for the District of Nevada.
Area of Law: Tort—Negligence (Elevator Malfunction and Expert Admissibility).
Procedural Posture: Motion for summary judgment and motion to exclude expert testimony.
Issue
Whether the plaintiff’s elevator-maintenance expert’s opinions are admissible under Federal Rule of Evidence 702 and whether genuine issues of material fact exist regarding negligent maintenance and the application of res ipsa loquitur following an elevator malfunction.
Rule
Under Federal Rule of Evidence 702, the court acts as a gatekeeper to ensure expert testimony is relevant and reliable [1013]. For non-scientific testimony, reliability depends on the expert’s specialized knowledge and experience rather than a strictly scientific methodology [1014]. To prevail on a negligence claim, a plaintiff must demonstrate a duty of care, breach, legal causation, and damages [1018]. Under Nevada law, a res ipsa loquitur inference of negligence is permitted if: (1) the event ordinarily does not occur without negligence; (2) it was caused by an instrumentality within the defendant’s exclusive control; and (3) it was not due to the plaintiff’s voluntary contribution [1021].
Application
The court first addressed the admissibility of the plaintiff’s expert, John Koshak. Otis argued Koshak’s opinions were unreliable because he did not use the scientific method [1014]. The court rejected this, reasoning that Koshak’s opinions were based on forty years of experiential practice in the elevator industry, making them "non-scientific" testimony governed by the Kumho Tire standard rather than the Daubert scientific factors [1014-1015]. The court further found that Koshak’s causation theory—that a compensation sheave switch tripped due to stretched ropes—was rooted in a review of business records and witness accounts, not "cherry-picked" evidence [1015-1016]. While Koshak was barred from offering legal conclusions regarding "fraud" or "breach of contract," his technical opinions on maintenance frequency and pit conditions were deemed helpful to the jury [1018].
Regarding the negligence claim, Otis argued there was no evidence the compensation sheave caused the stop because the elevator allegedly restarted, which would be impossible without a manual reset [1019]. The court found a genuine dispute because passenger accounts were not uniform; some described "bouncing" rather than a restart, and the interpretation of these subjective perceptions required the "expert’s lens" provided by Koshak [1019-1020]. On the issue of breach, the court noted that while the elevator passed state inspections, Koshak’s testimony that the maintenance time was "grossly inadequate" to cover the sheave created a triable issue regarding the standard of care [1020-1021].
Finally, the court held that res ipsa loquitur could apply. Koshak’s testimony established that sudden elevator stops are "very, very low" probability events in the absence of negligent maintenance [1022]. Although the elevator was located in a hotel, the "exclusive control" element was a question of fact because hotel staff testified that Otis was "exclusively" responsible for maintenance [1022].
Conclusion
The court denied summary judgment on the negligence theories and largely denied the motion to exclude the expert, while dismissing the products liability claim by concession.

Appellant presents the following questions for our review:

1. Whether Appellant should have been served with the petition to remove [*6]  him from the property where he

4. Whether Appellant, as an heir, was entitled to notice of the petition to remove the executrix of the estate[?]

2 The record reflects that the orphans' court's order was dated October 8,

See In re Trust of John S. Middleton, 313 A.3d 1090, 1095 (Pa. Super. 2024) (citations omitted). "This Court has

right; (3) an interlocutory order by permission; or (4) a collateral order." Id. (citation and brackets omitted).

Pennsylvania Rule of Appellate Procedure 342 governs the appealability of interlocutory orphans' court's orders and 
provides, in relevant part: "An appeal may be taken as of right from … [a]n order determining the status of 
fiduciaries, beneficiaries, or creditors in an estate, trust, or guardianship[.]"

3 Appellant lists four questions in his statement of questions presented, but his brief contains only one co-mingled

Pa.R.A.P. 2119(a). Failure to do so may result in waiver. Ramalingam v.Keller Williams Realty Group, Inc., 121 
A.3d 1034, 1042 (Pa. Super. 

2015). While we do not condone Appellant's failure to comply with the Rules of Appellate Procedure, the deficiency 
does not impede our appellate review; therefore, we decline to find waiver. See id.

4 No appellee brief has been filed. See Letter, 6/23/25, at 1 (single page) (Attorney Derrico's indicating that Ms. 
Miller is not taking a position on this appeal and would not be filing an appellate brief).

Pa.R.A.P. 342(a)(5); see also 20 Pa.C.S. 102 (providing that the term

"fiduciary" includes "personal representatives … subject to the jurisdiction of the orphans' court division"); id. 
(defining a "personal representative" as "an executor or administrator of any description"). The note to Rule 342 
explains that subsection (a)(5) "stat[es] definitively that an order removing or refusing to remove a fiduciary is an

Note. Hence, we deem the October 30, 2024 order granting the petition to remove Ms. Cheroke as executrix to be

As to the orphans' court's declaration that Appellant lacks standing to appeal, we observe that no party or 
participant has independently raised this issue. [*9]  The orphans' court raised the issue of Appellant's standing sua

(citations omitted); Interest of R.P., A.3d , 2025 PA Super 189, *4 (filed Aug. 29, 2025) (determining that the trial

Thus, we consider the issue of Appellant's standing to be waived and will

(Pa. Super. 2024) ("Pennsylvania courts view the issue of standing as non-

jurisdictional and waivable.") (citations omitted).

Our standard of review of an orphans' court's decree is deferential.

When reviewing a decree entered by the orphans' court, this Court must determine whether the record is free from 
legal error and the court's factual findings are supported by the [*10]  evidence. Because the orphans' court sits as 
the fact-finder, it determines the credibility of the witnesses and, on review, we will not reverse its credibility 
determinations absent an abuse of that discretion. However, we are not constrained to give the same deference to 
any resulting legal conclusions. Where the rules of law on which the court relied are palpably wrong or clearly 
inapplicable, we will reverse the court's decree.

In re Estate of Hooper, 80 A.3d 815, 818 (Pa. Super. 2013) (cleaned up).

Additionally, we recognize that "[t]he removal of an executrix is a

matter vested in the sound discretion of the [orphans'] court, and thus we will

disturb such a determination only upon a finding of an abuse of that

discretion." In re Estate of Mumma, 41 A.3d 41, 49 (Pa. Super. 2012)

(citation omitted); see also In re Estate of Tomcik, 286 A.3d 748, 764 (Pa.

Super. 2022) ("An abuse of discretion occurs when the court misapplies

existing law, makes a manifestly unreasonable judgment, or rules with

partiality, prejudice or ill will."). The grounds for removal of a personal

representative are delineated in Section 3182 of the Probate, Estates and

Fiduciaries ("PEF") Code, 20 Pa.C.S. 101-8816. See 20 Pa.C.S. 3182.

That statute permits the orphans' court to remove a personal representative

when he or she "is wasting or mismanaging the estate, is or is likely [*11]  to become

insolvent, or has failed to perform any duty imposed by law[,]" as well as "when, for any other reason, the interests 
of the estate are likely to be jeopardized by his [or her] continuance in office." 20 Pa.C.S. 3182(1), (5).5

It is well-established that a personal representative owes a fiduciary duty to collect the assets of the estate and 
distribute them according to the law and the testator's intent. See In re Estate of Lorent, No. 2630 EDA 2024, 
unpublished memorandum at 4 (Pa. Super. filed Sept. 11, 2025);6 seealso 20 Pa.C.S. 3311 ("A personal 
representative shall … take possession of, maintain and administer all the real and personal estate of the 
decedent….");7 In re Kurkowski's Estate, 409 A.2d 357, 360-61 (Pa. 1979)

("A decedent's personal representative is under a duty to take custody of the estate and administer it in such a way 
as to preserve and protect the property for distribution to the proper persons within a reasonable time."); In re

Wallis' Estate, 218 A.2d 732, 736 (Pa. 1966) (stating that the "primary duty"

5 There are other bases for removal that are not pertinent here.

6 See Pa.R.A.P. 126(b) (unpublished non-precedential decisions of the Superior Court filed after May 1, 2019, may 
be cited for their persuasive value).

7 Section 3311 provides an exception for real estate occupied at [*12]  the time of death by an heir or devisee with 
the consent of the decedent. See 20 Pa.C.S. 3311(a). However, in such a situation, "the court may direct the 
personal representative to take possession of, administer and maintain [the] real estate

… if this is necessary to protect the rights of claimants or other parties." Id.

Moreover, the statute expressly states that "[n]othing in this section shall affect the personal representative's power 
to sell real estate occupied by an heir or devisee." Id.

of an executor of a will is "to marshal[] the assets and to liquidate and

terminate as soon as possible").

Regarding removal of a personal representative, Section 3183 of the

PEF Code provides, in pertinent part:

The court on its own motion may, and on the petition of any party in interest alleging adequate grounds for removal 
shall, order the personal representative to appear and show cause why he [or she] should not be removed, or, 
when necessary to protect the rights of creditors or parties in interest, may summarily remove him [or her]. Upon 
removal, the court may direct the grant of new letters testamentary or of administration by the register to the person 
entitled and may, by summary attachment of the person or other appropriate [*13]  orders, provide for the security 
and delivery of the assets of the estate, together with all books, accounts and papers relating thereto.

20 Pa.C.S. 3183.

Here, Ms. Miller filed a petition pursuant to Section 3183, seeking the

removal of Ms. Cheroke as the executrix of the decedent's estate.8 Therein,

the petitioners averred that the decedent's will called for the residuary of her

estate to be divided equally among her eight children and listed the names

and addresses of each of the heirs, including Appellant. Petition, 9/11/24, at

¶¶ 4-5. Additionally, they averred that Appellant is currently residing in the

McDonald Property, "the single largest asset of the estate[,]" id. at ¶ 6, and

that Ms. Cheroke had failed to fulfill her fiduciary duties by, inter alia, "refusing

to put the real estate on the market for sale[,]" id. at ¶ 10. They alleged that

Ms. Cheroke admitted to "'holding the land hostage' in an effort to deny the

8Since Ms. Lewis, Ms. O'Rourke, and Ms. Winter joined in Ms. Miller's petition, we refer to the four siblings 
collectively as "the petitioners."

other heirs from receiving their rightful shares of the estate to benefit herself

and … [Appellant]." Id. The petitioners requested that the orphans' court

remove Ms. [*14]  Cheroke as executrix and take "other action … to ensure a fair

and prompt administration for the benefit of all the heirs." Id. at 3



Page 7 of 8
In re Est. of Zupancic, 2025 Pa. Super. Unpub. LEXIS 2780

(unpaginated).

Appellant claims that he was never served with a copy of the removal

petition or notice of the subsequent hearing, and therefore was deprived of

the opportunity to participate in the proceedings. See Appellant's Brief at 4-

6. He notes that there is no certificate of service attached to the petition, nor

does the record contain any proof that he was served with the petition or

notice of the hearing. Id. at 7. Appellant elaborates that he

should have been served with a copy of the petition and a notice of the hearing. He could have then objected to the 
petition. He could have attended the hearing and participated. The record is devoid of notice or service to Appellant. 
These are fundamental due process rights for the heir of an estate. The petitioner[s] listed him as an heir but gave 
him no notice of [their] plan to subvert the will and install [Ms. Miller] as the executor.

Id. (unnecessary capitalization omitted). Thus, he asserts that the orphans'

court's October 30, 2024 order was entered in error. Id. at 4.

Pennsylvania Orphans' Court Rule 3.5(b) governs notice of petitions and

provides, [*15]  in relevant part, "the petitioner shall, either in advance of filing or

contemporaneously therewith, provide a copy of the petition to the interested

parties identified in the petition." Pa.O.C.R. 3.5(b)(1); see also Pa.O.C.R.

1.3 (defining "Interested Party" as "one or more individuals or entities having

or claiming an interest in the estate, trust, person or other entity that is the

subject of the legal proceeding"). As a named heir and occupant of estate property which the petitioners seek to 
sell, Appellant clearly has an interest in the administration of the decedent's estate. Moreover, he was specifically 
identified in the petition. Thus, we agree with Appellant that he was entitled to notice of the petition to remove the 
existing executrix of the estate. See

Pa.O.C.R. 3.5(b)(1); see also Appeal of Lancaster, 4 A. 333, 335 (Pa.

1886) ("All parties interested in a proceeding in the orphans' court are entitled to notice of every petition or motion 
not grantable of course, as provided by the statutes. … Where an order, decree, or judgment has been wrongfully 
entered, without notice to a party who was entitled to notice, such party may demand its vacation, at least to the 
extent that it affects his interest.").

Based on our review, the record lacks [*16]  proof that Appellant was served with a copy of the petition to remove 
Ms. Cheroke as executrix of the estate or notice of the related October 8, 2024 hearing. Consequently, we are 
constrained to vacate the October 30, 2024 order and remand for further proceedings.9

Order vacated. Case remanded. Jurisdiction relinquished.

9 Due to our disposition, we need not address Appellant's remaining issues.

IRAC_summ:
Case Name: In re Est. of Zupancic, 2025 Pa. Super. Unpub. LEXIS 2780
Court: Superior Court of Pennsylvania
Area of law: Probate – Removal of Executor; Due Process – Notice
Procedural posture: Appeal from an orphans' court order removing an executrix and ordering the appellant to vacate estate property.
Issue
Whether the orphans' court erred in granting a petition to remove the executrix and ordering the appellant (an heir and occupant of estate property) to vacate the premises, where the appellant was not served with notice of the petition or the hearing.
Rule
Under Pennsylvania Orphans' Court Rule 3.5(b), a petitioner must provide a copy of the petition to all "interested parties" identified in the petition. An "interested party" includes any individual having a claim or interest in the estate or property subject to the proceeding. Fundamental due process requires that parties with an interest in the proceeding be given notice and an opportunity to be heard before an order affecting their rights is entered.
Application
The petitioners (four siblings) sought to remove the executrix for failing to sell the estate's main asset, a residential property occupied by their brother, the appellant. The petition specifically identified the appellant as an heir and the current occupant of the property [*13]. The orphans' court granted the petition and ordered the appellant to vacate the home within 30 days.
The appellant argued he was never served with the petition or notice of the hearing. The record confirmed the lack of service. The court held that as a named heir and the current occupant of the property the petitioners sought to sell, the appellant was clearly an "interested party" entitled to notice under Rule 3.5(b) [*15]. The failure to provide notice deprived him of the opportunity to object or participate, violating his due process rights.
Conclusion
The court vacated the order and remanded for further proceedings to ensure proper notice.

case_name: Armstead v Royal & Sun Alliance Insurance Company Ltd [2024] UKSC 6
case:
George v Cannell and another - [2024] All ER (D) 39 (Jun)
Page 1 of 5
George v Cannell and another [2024] All ER (D) 39 (Jun)
[2024] UKSC 19
Supreme Court
Lord Hodge, Deputy President, Lord Hamblen, Lord Leggatt, Lord Burrows and Lord Richards
12 June 2024
MALICIOUS FALSEHOOD – DAMAGES – WHETHER FINANCIAL LOSS BEING A NECESSARY 
REQUIREMENT TO ESTABLISH LIABILTY FOR MALICIOUS FALSEHOOD
Abstract
The Supreme Court (by a majority) ruled on appeal concerning whether s 3(1) of the Defamation Act 1952 (DA 
1952) removed the need, in specified circumstances, for a claimant to prove their financial loss in order to establish 
a defendant's liability for malicious falsehood and, if so, whether a claimant who successfully relied on s 3(1) could 
recover damages for injury to feelings related to the publication of the malicious falsehood, even if no financial loss 
had been caused to them. The respondent had worked as a recruitment consultant for the second appellant 
agency, which the first appellant owned and operated. After the respondent had resigned and had started working 
for a different agency, the first appellant had spoken to one of the respondent's clients and she had emailed the 
respondent's new employer, alleging that she had been in breach of certain restrictions in her contact with her 
former employer. The respondent  sued the appellants, alleging libel, slander and malicious falsehood. The High 
Court dismissed the malicious falsehood claim, having found that the relevant statements had not caused the 
respondent any financial loss. The Court of Appeal, Civil Division, had reversed that decision, holding that the claim 
fell within s 3(1); that  liability could be established where false statements were likely to cause financial loss, even 
though no such loss had, in fact, occurred; and that, because liability had been made out, the respondent could 
recover damages for injury to her feelings. In allowing the appellants' appeal (in part), the court ruled, among other 
things that the effect of s 3(1), where it applied, was to create a presumption of law that the publication of the words 
complained of had caused financial loss. That presumption was irrebuttable as far as liability was concerned, but 
did not necessarily lead to an award of substantial damages. If the court concluded, as the judge had in the present 
case, that no financial loss had actually been caused, the respondent would be entitled only to nominal damages. 
The court held that the Court of Appeal had correctly held that the test was whether, viewed at the time of 
publication, the words complained of were likely to cause financial loss to the claimant; and that the respondent had 
been entitled to succeed on the question of liability, but that that did not affect the judge's finding that the 
publications complained of had caused her no financial loss. Further, the court held that damages could not be 
recovered for the hurt, indignation or other injured feelings simply from discovering that the defendant has published 
false and malicious words about them; and that there was nothing in the circumstances of the case which could 
reasonably be said to justify an award of aggravated damages. Accordingly, the Court of Appeal's order for an 
assessment of damages for injury to feelings was set aside, and the court directed that the judgment entered for the 
claimant should be a judgment for nominal damages only, in a sum of £5. 
Digest
The judgment is available at: [2024] UKSC 19
  Background     
*George v Cannell and another - [2024] All ER (D) 39 (Jun)
Page 2 of 5
The appeal concerned the civil wrong of malicious falsehood, which was committed when someone maliciously 
published words that caused another person financial loss.
Section 3 of the Defamation Act 1952 (DA 1952), so far as material, provided that: '(1) In an action for slander of 
title, slander of goods or other malicious falsehood, it shall not be necessary to allege or prove special damage - (a) 
if the words upon which the action is founded are calculated to cause pecuniary damage to the plaintiff and are 
published in writing or other permanent form; or (b) if the said words are calculated to cause pecuniary damage to 
the plaintiff in respect of any office, profession, calling, trade or business held or carried on by him at the time of the 
publication' (see [18] of the judgment).
The respondent worked as a recruitment consultant for the second appellant agency (LCA Jobs Ltd), which the first 
appellant owned and operated.
The respondent resigned from LCA Jobs Ltd and she was employed by another recruitment agency. She soon 
began targeting LCA Jobs Ltd's clients.
The first appellant spoke to one of the respondent's clients and sent an email to her new employer, alleging that the 
respondent was acting in breach of restrictions in her contact with LCA Jobs Ltd, which prevented her from 
contacting LCA Jobs Ltd's clients. In fact, as the first appellant knew, there was no term of that contract which 
prohibited the respondent from soliciting business from LCA Jobs Ltd's clients.
The respondent sued the appellants for libel, slander and malicious falsehood. The present appeal concerned the 
claim for malicious falsehood.
The High Court dismissed the claim for malicious falsehood, having found that, while the relevant statements were 
false and malicious, they had not caused the respondent any financial loss.
The Court of Appeal, Civil Division, reversed that decision, holding that: (i) it was sufficient to establish liability that 
the false statements were likely to cause financial loss, even though no such loss had in fact occurred; (ii) the claim 
fell within s 3(1); and (iii) because liability was made out, the respondent could recover damages for injury to her 
feelings.
The appellants appealed to the Supreme Court.
  Issues and decisions     
Whether DA 1952 s 3(1) removed the need, in specified circumstances, for a claimant to prove their financial loss to 
establish a defendant's liability for malicious falsehood. If so, whether a claimant who successfully relied on s 3(1) 
could recover damages for injury to feelings related to the publication of the malicious falsehood, even if no financial 
loss had been caused to them.
(Per Lord Leggatt, Lord Hamblen and Lord Burrows dissenting) The appeal would be allowed. The order made by 
the Court of Appeal for an assessment of damages for injury to feelings would be set aside and it would be directed 
that the judgment entered for the respondent should be a judgment for nominal damages only, in a sum of £5 (see 
[120] of the judgment). 
The effect of s 3(1), where it applied, was to create a presumption of law that the publication of the words 
complained of had caused financial loss. That presumption was irrebuttable as far as liability was concerned, but 
did not necessarily lead to an award of substantial damages. If the court concluded, as the judge had in the present 
case, that no financial loss had actually been caused, the claimant would be entitled only to nominal damages (see 
[51], [89] of the judgment).
That conclusion was inescapable when s 3(1) was read together with s 2. All a claimant need show to establish a 
cause of action was that words of the relevant kind were spoken by the defendant to a third person. If that was 
shown, the damage necessary to found the action was presumed by law and, therefore, need not be proved. It was 
*George v Cannell and another - [2024] All ER (D) 39 (Jun)
Page 3 of 5
then a matter for the jury (or nowadays the judge) to assess the amount of damages (see [52], [53] of the 
judgment).
When the formulation 'it shall not be necessary to allege or prove special damage' was used in s 3(1), that did not 
mean merely that damage need not be alleged and proved with certainty and precision. Rather, those words were 
to be understood as having the same meaning as they do in s 2. The term 'special damage' referred to actual 
pecuniary loss. As with slander actionable per se, where the words published fall within the scope of the statutory 
provision the damage necessary to found an action was presumed by law and so need not be alleged or proved 
(see [54] of the judgment).
The aim of s 3(1) was to make it easier to bring actions for malicious falsehood by removing the need to allege and 
prove (on the balance of probability) that special (i.e. pecuniary) damage had actually been caused. It would 
completely defeat that purpose if, to avoid the need to allege and prove that a malicious falsehood - more probably 
than not - had caused pecuniary damage, it were necessary to prove that it probably had caused pecuniary 
damage. Such an interpretation would make s 3(1) vacuous (see [63] of the judgment).
The appropriate test in determining whether the words complained of 'are calculated to cause pecuniary damage' to 
a claimant was to ask whether, on the facts known or which should reasonably have been known to the defendant 
at the time of publication, it was objectively likely that the words published would cause financial loss. Subject to 
that constraint, potentially relevant matters included prior publications, other statements made in the same 
publication, and steps which the publishee would be likely to take in response to the publication (see [80]-[82], [199] 
of the judgment).
Judged, therefore, by reference to the facts known (or which ought to have been known) to the first appellant, her 
false statements made to the third parties had been calculated to cause financial loss to the respondent. The Court 
of Appeal had, therefore, been right to have concluded that both publications had fallen within s 3(1) (see [83], [84] 
of the judgment).
In the present case, the Court of Appeal had been right to have rejected the historical approach and to have held 
that the test was whether, viewed at the time of publication, the words complained of were likely to cause financial 
loss to the respondent (see [68] of the judgment). 
It followed that the respondent had been entitled to succeed on the question of liability. However, that did not affect 
the judge's finding that the publications complained of had caused her no financial loss. Where an action 
succeeded, but no loss had been sustained, only nominal damages could be awarded (see [89] of the judgment).
The respondent contended that, if only she could pass through the gateway of s 3(1), she was entitled to 
compensation for injury to her feelings caused by the two publications complained of, even though it had been 
found as a fact that they had no economic effect. However, the interests protected by the common law tort of 
malicious falsehood were purely economic interests. Pecuniary damage was an essential element of the cause of 
action. The tort consisted in the infliction of financial loss by maliciously publishing false words. Where the 
commission of the tort caused mental distress, if the law was to provide full compensation for the wrong done and 
its consequences, the damages awarded should include compensation for such mental distress. If the injury to a 
claimant's feelings was not causally connected with the financial damage on which the action was founded, then it 
was not an injury caused by the tort and it was not compensable. In almost every case of malicious falsehood 
claimants would experience hurt, indignation or other injured feelings simply from discovering that the defendant 
has published false and malicious words about them. On principle, however, damages could not be recovered for 
that injury because it was not an injury caused by the tort. That analysis required was no different in principle in a 
case where s 3(1) applied. There was nothing in the content of DA 1952 or in the background to the enactment of s 
3(1) which provided any reason to infer that it was intended to transform an economic tort into a psychological one. 
In cases where s 3(1) applied, it remained necessary, if an award of damages for injury to feelings was to be 
justified, to show that financial damage had been suffered which had caused such injury to feelings (see [90], [102]
[112] of the judgment).
*George v Cannell and another - [2024] All ER (D) 39 (Jun)
Page 4 of 5
In the present case, it had been found as a fact that no financial loss was actually caused by the relevant 
publications. Although s 3(1) applied, the presumption that the words published caused financial damage to the 
respondent was purely notional and attracted only token damages. Accordingly, there was no financial loss that 
could have given rise to injury to feelings for which compensation might be awarded. Although the respondent 
claimed in her particulars of claim to have suffered 'huge emotional distress as a result of the publications 
complained of', and gave evidence at the trial to that effect, such distress could not have been - and on the judge's 
findings was not - a consequence of financial loss inflicted by those publications. There had been no such financial 
loss. The respondent's emotional distress was therefore not a matter for which the appellants could be held 
responsible. It was not suffered as a consequence (foreseeable or otherwise) of the tort of malicious falsehood (see 
[113] of the judgment).
Aggravated damages had been recognised as a separate category of damages which could be awarded where the 
conduct or motives of the defendant aggravate the injury done to the claimant. However, there was nothing in the 
circumstances of the present case which could reasonably be said to justify an award of aggravated damages (see 
[114]-[119] of the judgment).

IRAC_summ:
Case Name: Armstead v Royal & Sun Alliance Insurance Company Ltd [2024] UKSC 6
Court + jurisdiction: United Kingdom Supreme Court
Area of law: Tort – Negligence – Damages – Burden of Proof
Procedural posture: Appeal from the Court of Appeal, Civil Division
Issue
Whether a claimant, whose credit-hire vehicle is damaged by a negligent driver, can recover a contractually agreed sum owed to the hire company for "loss of use," and whether the burden of proving that such a sum is too remote or unreasonable lies with the defendant.
Rule
In the tort of negligence, a claimant is entitled to recover monies they are contractually liable to pay a third party resulting from the damage, provided the contractual liability is a reasonable pre-estimate of the third party's loss (Network Rail Infrastructure Ltd v Conarken Group Ltd). Once the claimant proves the tort and factual causation, the legal burden lies on the defendant to plead and prove that the loss is irrecoverable due to remoteness, failure to mitigate, or that the contractual sum is not a reasonable pre-estimate of loss.
Application
The Court addressed the "loss of use" clause (Clause 16), which required the claimant to pay the hire company the daily hire rate for up to 30 days while the damaged vehicle was being repaired. The Court of Appeal had rejected the claim, reasoning that the sum was not a reasonable estimate of the hire company's loss of profit.
The Supreme Court held this approach was procedurally and legally flawed because it reversed the burden of proof. Once the appellant established that the respondent's negligence caused the physical damage and the subsequent contractual liability, the onus shifted to the respondent (RSA) to prove that this liability was too remote [59]–[63]. This allocation of the burden is justified by fairness and efficiency; it is the wrongdoer who seeks to limit full compensation [63].
In this case, RSA had neither pleaded nor adduced evidence that Clause 16 was an unreasonable estimate of the hire company's loss (e.g., by showing the company had a surplus of cars). Without such evidence, the Court of Appeal was not entitled to assume the clause was unreasonable [65], [71]. On its face, a clause calculating loss of use based on the daily hire rate (essentially extending the hire period) is a simple and reasonable method of estimation [70]. Because the defendant failed to discharge its burden of proof, the damages were recoverable.
Conclusion
The Court held that the burden of proving the contractual liability was too remote or unreasonable rested on the defendant, who failed to discharge it; the appeal was allowed and judgment entered for the Clause 16 sum.

Opinion

 [*1] DECISION

APPEAL from the Franklin County Court of Common Pleas, Division of Domestic Relations and Juvenile Branch

DINGUS, J.

{¶ 1} Appellant, M.O., putative father of A.O., appeals from a judgment of the Franklin County Court of Common 
Pleas, Division of Domestic Relations and Juvenile Branch, awarding legal custody of A.O. to a family friend. For 
the following reasons, we affirm.

I. Facts and Procedural History

{¶ 2} A.O. is the youngest of five siblings born to V.R. ("mother") while she was married to J.R. ("legal father"). The 
legal father lives in Florida, and the children lived with their mother and M.O. in the years leading up to involvement 
with Franklin County Children Services and the National Youth Advocate Program (collectively, "the agency"). M.O. 
is the putative father of A.O. and is not the putative father of the other children. The rights and interests of A.O.'s 
mother, legal father, and siblings are not at issue in this appeal.

{¶ 3} The agency became involved with the children in response to reports of homelessness and substance abuse 
by both the mother and M.O., physical abuse by M.O.



Page 2 of 6
In re A.O., 2025 Ohio App. LEXIS 3658

 No. 24AP-712 2 

against the mother, and physical abuse by the mother against one of A.O.'s [*2]  siblings. The agency obtained a 
temporary order of custody for A.O. in February 2020. The agency's complaint alleged that A.O. was a dependent 
child. A.O. was placed in the care of K.R., a maternal family friend.

{¶ 4} The case plan for the family identified both the legal father and M.O. as parents. M.O.'s objectives under the 
case plan included completing a domestic violence assessment and following all recommendations, completing an 
alcohol and drug assessment and following all recommendations, participating in drug screening, and participating 
in housing services and following all recommendations. The trial court appointed a guardian ad litem ("GAL") and 
attorneys for A.O., the mother, and M.O.

{¶ 5} On September 21, 2021, the trial court entered a temporary order of court custody to the agency and 
adjudicated A.O. as a dependent minor. The GAL's reports leading up to the trial court's decision indicated that 
M.O. was attending most visitations with A.O. and he had been linked with a suboxone clinic and counseling 
services. However, M.O. was not compliant with most other case plan goals; M.O. had not appeared for any drug 
screens in 2021, and his drug screens in 2020 showed positive [*3]  results for gabapentin, benzodiazepines, 
barbiturates, opiates, and THC. He did not complete a domestic violence assessment, and he reportedly argued 
that domestic violence services were not necessary because his criminal domestic violence charges had been 
dismissed. He had not obtained housing and continued to stay at friends' houses.

{¶ 6} In February 2022, the agency filed a motion to terminate temporary custody and recommended that the trial 
court place A.O. in the legal custody of her caregiver, K.R., pursuant to R.C. 2151.415(B). The agency asserted that 
this placement was in A.O.'s best interest because, among other reasons, M.O. had failed to comply with the case 
plan objectives related to domestic violence services, drug screens, the release of information to the case worker, 
and housing. After several continuances, the trial court scheduled hearings on the motion for October 2022.

{¶ 7} From February to August 2022, reports to the trial court indicated that M.O. was not working toward 
completing case plan objectives. He continued to miss drug screens and reportedly claimed that he had been 
railroaded into drug treatment, despite never having taken opiates in his life. M.O. finally completed [*4]  a domestic 
violence

 No. 24AP-712 3 

assessment but had not followed through on the subsequent requirement to attend classes. He repeatedly failed to 
work with housing services and was living in hotels and a co-worker's basement. A significant unpaid utility bill in 
the mother's name was potentially hampering their ability to obtain housing. By the end of September 2022, M.O. 
had begun to attend domestic violence classes and submitted to drug screenings, though the results showed 
inconsistent use of suboxone and occasional use of THC.

{¶ 8} The matter proceeded to a hearing before a magistrate. The first day of hearings took place on October 7, 
2022, and included testimony by the caseworker and the GAL. The caseworker testified that M.O. was compliant 
with some of his case plan, including consistent visitation with A.O., mental health counseling, and consistent 
employment. However, the caseworker recommended against allowing A.O. to return to M.O.'s custody because 
M.O. had not adequately followed through with services, did not have stable housing, and did not comply with 
enough drug screens for the caseworker to be able to verify an adequate period of sobriety. He recommended 
granting [*5]  legal custody to K.R. The GAL testified that A.O. is bonded with M.O. A.O. indicated that she wanted 
to live with her mother and M.O., and if that was not possible, she wanted to live with K.R. The GAL recommended 
that A.O. stay in K.R.'s custody as M.O. was only just beginning to work on various case plan objectives and was 
not in a position to take custody of A.O.

{¶ 9} A second day of hearings took place three weeks later, on October 28, 2022, and included testimony by M.O. 
and the mother. M.O. testified that he and the mother had secured an apartment a week and a half prior to the date 
of the second hearing and were in the process of obtaining furniture. He testified that the delay in finding housing 
from February 2020 to October 2022 was due to COVID and its effect on the economy. He testified that he has 



Page 3 of 6
In re A.O., 2025 Ohio App. LEXIS 3658

consistently complied with his suboxone prescription, though he thought he should not have been prescribed 
suboxone in the first place. He took opiates from 2004 to 2011 for injuries sustained from falling off a cliff but 
maintained he had not taken any opiates since 2011. He admitted to smoking marijuana and taking Xanax, though 
he claimed the Xanax was prescribed by a doctor. [*6]  He testified that his work schedule prevented him from 
appearing for drug screens until August 2022. He testified that he completed a domestic violence assessment once 
it was added to the case plan and that his delay in following through with classes was due to a miscommunication.

 No. 24AP-712 4 

{¶ 10} At the end of the second hearing day, the magistrate announced from the bench that she was awarding 
custody of A.O. to K.R. M.O. requested findings of fact and conclusions of law in November 2022. The magistrate 
filed her decision on January 6, 2023, which did not include findings of fact and conclusions of law. M.O. filed 
objections to the magistrate's decision, and the trial court remanded the matter to the magistrate in April 2023 to 
provide findings of fact and conclusions of law. The magistrate retired after the remand, and after various delays, 
the parties appeared before the trial court in April 2024 and consented to the court reviewing the transcripts and 
ruling on the objections without conducting further evidentiary hearings. In November 2024, the court entered 
judgment overruling M.O.'s objections.

{¶ 11} The trial court noted the case plan objectives regarding A.O. included [*7]  requirements that M.O. (1) 
participate in services related to domestic violence, (2) participate in services related to substance abuse, (3) 
comply with drug screening, (4) participate in services related to housing, (5) inform the caseworker of address 
changes, (6) sign releases of information regarding the foregoing services for the caseworker, (7) maintain stable 
housing, (8) provide for A.O.'s basic needs and safety, (9) meet with the caseworker every month, and (10) 
maintain visitations with A.O. The court found that M.O. had complied with the requirements that he keep his 
address updated, meet with his caseworker, sign releases, establish the ability to provide for A.O. by maintaining 
employment, and visit consistently with A.O. However, the court found that M.O. had failed to comply with the 
remaining requirements. Specifically, M.O. did not move forward on a domestic violence assessment from February 
2020 to March 2022, and he did not begin domestic violence classes until July or August 2022. The record of 
repeated orders for M.O. to address domestic violence contradicted M.O.'s claim that domestic-violence-related 
services were only recently added to his case plan objectives. [*8]  M.O. refused to complete drug screens 
throughout most of his case plan. When M.O. began to comply with drug screens starting in August 2022, he tested 
positive for THC and did not consistently test positive for suboxone, indicating that he was not complying with his 
drug treatment program. He repeatedly refused to participate in services related to housing. M.O. did not have a 
home from the beginning of the case in February 2020 until a week and a half before the final hearing date in 
October 2022; he had been moving between hotels and friends'

 No. 24AP-712 5 

houses for over two and a half years while this case was pending. Although M.O. had obtained housing at the last 
minute that had the potential to be stable, he did not establish actual stability.

{¶ 12} After determining that A.O.'s mother and her legal father had likewise failed to substantially comply with their 
respective case plan goals, the trial court proceeded to consider A.O.'s best interests regarding placement. The 
court noted A.O.'s first choice regarding placement was to be with her mother and M.O., her second choice was to 
remain with K.R., and her third and fourth choices were to be placed with other relatives. It [*9]  noted the GAL's 
recommendation that K.R. be awarded legal custody of A.O. It also noted that K.R. had consistently coordinated 
visits between A.O. and her siblings, her mother, M.O., and M.O.'s mother. A.O. had lived with K.R. since March 
2020, had bonded with K.R. and K.R.'s family, and was flourishing in her placement. In contrast, M.O. and the 
mother had not completed their case plan objectives. The court concluded that the magistrate did not err in finding 
that it was in A.O.'s best interest to grant legal custody to K.R.

{¶ 13} M.O. filed a timely appeal, and the matter is now properly before this court.

II. Assignment of Error



Page 4 of 6
In re A.O., 2025 Ohio App. LEXIS 3658

{¶ 14} M.O. assigns the following sole assignment of error for our review:

The weight of the evidence does not support the juvenile court's decision to grant legal custody to a nonparent 
where the child wanted to reunify and the parents were ready for reunification.

III. Discussion

{¶ 15} When, as here, a court adjudicates a child a dependent child and awards temporary custody of the child to 
an agency under R.C. 2151.353(A)(2), the temporary custody order eventually expires unless the agency files a 
motion requesting an extension or a disposition order under R.C. 2151.415. R.C. 2151.353(G). Among the 
dispositional [*10]  orders that the agency may request is "[a]n order that the child be placed in the legal custody of 
a relative or other interested individual." R.C. 2151.415(A)(3). See also R.C. 2151.353(A)(3) (authorizing a trial 
court to award legal custody to an interested individual who has met certain requirements).

{¶ 16} An award of legal custody is significantly different than an award of permanent custody, as legal custody 
merely confers the right and responsibility for the care and supervision of the child, while "residual parental rights, 
privileges, and responsibilities"

 No. 24AP-712 6 

remain intact. R.C. 2151.011(B)(21); 2151.353(A)(3)(c). A parent retaining residual rights has "far different 
procedural safeguards in [a] legal-custody proceeding than those that would be afforded a parent in a permanent-
custody proceeding through which parental rights could be completely terminated." In re R.G.M., 2024-Ohio-2737, ¶ 
17. Unlike the clear and convincing burden of proof that applies to permanent custody proceedings, the burden in 
legal custody actions is merely a preponderance of the evidence. In re G.H., 2016-Ohio-1188, ¶ 19 (10th Dist.); 
Juv.R. 29(E)(4). It is well settled that "a preponderance of evidence means the greater weight of evidence . . . The 
greater weight may be infinitesimal, and it is only necessary that it be sufficient to destroy the equilibrium." [*11] 

Travelers' Ins. Co. v. Gath, 118 Ohio St. 257, 261 (1928). See also State ex rel. Doner v. Zody, 2011-Ohio-6117, ¶ 
54 (a preponderance of evidence indicates that the existence of a fact "is more likely than its nonexistence").

{¶ 17} The preponderance of the evidence standard of proof is generally subject to the manifest weight standard of 
review. Eastley v. Volkman, 2012-Ohio-2179, ¶ 19. An appellate court can reverse a judgment on manifest weight 
grounds only in exceptional circumstances where the evidence weighs heavily against the judgment. State 
v.Thompkins, 1997-Ohio-52, ¶ 25. And an appellate court cannot reverse a judgment on manifest weight grounds if 
it is "supported by some competent, credible evidence going to all the essential elements of the case." C.E. Morris 
Co. v. Foley Constr. Co., 54 Ohio St.2d 279 (1978), syllabus. However, in the context of juvenile legal custody 
determinations, the trial court's award of legal custody has traditionally been subject to an abuse-of-discretion 
standard of review. In re Gales, 2003-Ohio-6309, ¶ 12 (10th Dist.); In re Z.M., 2021-Ohio-3744, ¶ 33 (10th Dist.) .1 
An appellate court can reverse a judgment for abuse of discretion only where the decision is unreasonable, 
arbitrary, or unconscionable. State v. Beasley, 2018-Ohio-16, ¶ 12.

{¶ 18} The two standards of review-abuse of discretion and manifest weight- differ in their application and focus. 
See In re F.M., 2021-Ohio-3039, ¶ 16 (8th Dist.); Jonesv. Jones, 2007-Ohio-4255, ¶ 32 (4th Dist.). There could 
possibly be some scenario in which

1 The Supreme Court of Ohio has rejected the abuse-of-discretion standard of review in the context of permanent 
custody [*12]  decisions, which involve the clear-and-convincing burden of proof. In re Z.C., 2023-Ohio-4703, ¶ 18. 
However, the court in Z.C. declined to extend its holding to custody decisions that involve lesser burdens of proof. 
See id. at ¶ 12.

 No. 24AP-712 7 

the two standards clash, but this case doesn't present an opportunity to explore that possibility; under either 
standard of review, the result is the same in this appeal.



Page 5 of 6
In re A.O., 2025 Ohio App. LEXIS 3658

{¶ 19} The trial court's decision to grant legal custody to a relative or other interested individual under R.C. 
2151.415(A)(3) must be "in accordance with the best interest of the child as supported by the evidence." R.C. 
2151.415(B). Following a dependency adjudication and a disposition awarding temporary custody to an agency, a 
trial court's decision to grant legal custody of the child to anyone-parent or nonparent-is based solely on the best 
interest of the child. In re Z.M. at ¶ 30; R.C. 2151.415(B); R.C. 2151.42(A) ("At any hearing in which a court is 
asked to modify or terminate an order of disposition . . . the court, in determining whether to return the child to the 
child's parents, shall consider whether it is in the best interest of the child.").

{¶ 20} The statutory scheme governing legal custody does not provide specific factors for a trial court to consider 
when determining the child's [*13]  best interests, but it is generally appropriate for a trial court to consider the best 
interest factors contained in the statute governing the allocation of parental rights and responsibilities in divorce 
actions, R.C. 3109.04(F)(1). See In re Z.M. at ¶ 31, citing In re I.M., 2013-Ohio-5549, ¶ 11-12 (10th Dist.), In re 
C.W., 2020-Ohio-6849, ¶ 6 (2d Dist.), In re A.L.H., 2010-Ohio-5425, ¶ 9 (12th Dist.), and In re G.M., 2011-Ohio-
4090, ¶ 14-16 (8th Dist.). When determining the best interest of a child, R.C. 3109.04(F)(1) instructs the trial court 
to "consider all relevant factors, including, but not limited to" an enumerated list. The factors within R.C. 
3109.04(F)(1) that are relevant to a legal custody decision include

(1) the wishes of the child's parents regarding the child's care;

(2) the wishes and concerns of the child, as expressed to the juvenile court; (3) the child's interaction and 
interrelationship with the child's parents, siblings, and any other person who may significantly affect the child's best 
interest; (4) the child's adjustment to the child's home, school, and community; and

(5) the mental and physical health of all persons involved.

In re Z.M. at ¶ 32, citing C.W. at ¶ 6.

{¶ 21} Some appellate courts have held that a trial court determining legal custody may also consider the best 
interest factors contained in the statute governing permanent custody determinations, R.C. 2151.414(D)(1). See In 
re D.L., 2023-Ohio-1125, ¶ 15 (1st Dist.); In re W.W., 2024-Ohio-878, ¶ 30 (4th Dist.). To determine the best 
interest of a

 No. 24AP-712 8 

child, R.C. 2151.414(D)(1) directs [*14]  the court to consider "all relevant factors," including those enumerated in 
R.C. 2151.414(D)(1)(a) through (e) and R.C. 2151.414(E)(7) through (11). The factors in R.C. 2151.414 relevant to 
a legal custody decision under R.C. 2151.353(A)(3) include (1) the child's interactions and interrelationship with 
family members, caregivers, and anyone else who significantly affects the child; (2) the wishes of the child; (3) the 
custodial history of the child, including whether the child has been in temporary agency custody for over 12 of 22 
months; (4) whether the parent has been convicted of certain criminal offenses; (5) whether the parent repeatedly 
withheld medical treatment or food from the child; (6) whether the parent put the child at a substantial risk of harm 
due to substance abuse; (7) whether the parent abandoned the child; and (8) whether the parent's rights were 
terminated regarding a sibling of the child.

{¶ 22} The relevant statutory scheme governing legal custody is silent regarding best-interest factors. See R.C. 
2151.353; 2151.415(B); 2151.42(A). When facing such statutory silence, "we must presume that the legislature did 
not intend to require the consideration of certain factors as a predicate for granting legal custody." In re G.M. at ¶ 
16. Accordingly, although the factors in R.C. 3019.04(F)(1) and 2151.414(D)(1) may be instructive on the issue 
of [*15]  a child's best interests, the trial court is not required to consider those factors when determining legal 
custody.

{¶ 23} M.O. argues that the trial court's decision regarding A.O.'s best interests was against the manifest weight of 
the evidence because most of the foregoing best-interest factors weighed in favor of granting legal custody to M.O. 
rather than K.R. Specifically, M.O. notes that he and A.O. both wanted reunification and maintained a strong familial 



Page 6 of 6
In re A.O., 2025 Ohio App. LEXIS 3658

bond. He did not legally abandon A.O., and he does not have any criminal convictions related to abuse or neglect. 
He was consistently employed throughout the period of agency involvement, and there were no negative reports 
regarding M.O.'s interactions with family members, caretakers, or agency employees. Additionally, M.O. maintains 
he has "never gotten in trouble with the law." (Appellant's Brief at 19.) He claims there was no evidence to support 
concerns over alcohol and drug use, and he had no screens showing drug use apart from THC. He acknowledges 
that he did not have stable housing from the inception of temporary agency custody in February 2020 until the final 
hearing at the end of October

 No. 24AP-712 9 

2022, but he [*16]  contends that the COVID pandemic was to blame and notes that he obtained appropriate 
housing before the final hearing date.

{¶ 24} Although many of M.O.'s cited factors are undisputed, some do not appear to be supported by the record. 
For example, the factual allegations in the agency's complaint- which were uncontested and formed the basis for 
the trial court's dependency adjudication-indicate that M.O. has a history of one or more criminal convictions, 
including breaking and entering. The caseworker and GAL indicated that M.O. did not comply with drug screens for 
almost the entirety of the agency's involvement. When he appeared for screens during a short period in 2020, he 
tested positive for gabapentin, benzodiazepines, barbiturates, opiates, and THC. When he appeared for screens in 
August 2022, his results indicated that he was not complying with his suboxone regimen. The agency repeatedly 
attempted to link M.O. with services to find appropriate housing, but those services failed due to M.O.'s 
noncompliance.

{¶ 25} Additionally, M.O. fails to mention other factors that the trial court considered when determining A.O.'s best 
interests. Specifically, the court considered that the GAL [*17]  recommended that A.O. be placed in K.R.'s legal 
custody. It noted that A.O. has lived with K.R. since March 2020 and has flourished under her care. K.R. has 
consistently facilitated visitation between A.O. and her parents, siblings, and other relatives. In contrast, M.O. did 
not complete domestic violence classes, comply with a drug treatment plan and drug screens, or establish stable 
housing.

{¶ 26} Based on our own thorough review of the evidence, we conclude that the record supports the trial court's 
findings regarding A.O.'s best interests. Although M.O. has identified a few factors that weigh in his favor, he did not 
establish that this is one of those exceptional cases where the evidence weighed heavily against the trial court's 
determination of A.O.'s best interests, nor did he establish that the determination of A.O.'s best interests was 
unreasonable, arbitrary, or unconscionable. The trial court's decision finding that A.O.'s best interests were served 
by awarding legal custody to K.R. was not against the manifest weight of the evidence and did not involve an abuse 
of discretion.

Accordingly, we reject M.O.'s sole assignment of error.

IV. Conclusion

 No. 24AP-712 10 

{¶ 27} Having [*18]  overruled M.O.'s sole assignment of error, we affirm the judgment of the Franklin County Court 
of Common Pleas, Division of Domestic Relations and Juvenile Branch.

Judgment affirmed.

MENTEL and BOGGS, JJ., concur.

IRAC_summ:
Case Name: In re A.O., 2025 Ohio App. LEXIS 3658
Court: Court of Appeals of Ohio, Tenth Appellate District, Franklin County
Area of law: Family Law – Legal Custody; Child Dependency
Procedural posture: Appeal from a judgment awarding legal custody of a dependent child to a non-parent.
Issue
Whether the trial court's decision to award legal custody of a dependent child to a family friend, rather than the putative father, was against the manifest weight of the evidence regarding the child's best interest.
Rule
Following a dependency adjudication, a trial court may award legal custody to a relative or interested individual if it is in the best interest of the child (R.C. 2151.415(B)). Unlike permanent custody termination, legal custody leaves residual parental rights intact and is reviewed under a preponderance of the evidence standard.
While the legal custody statute does not list specific best-interest factors, courts look to factors in R.C. 3109.04(F)(1) (custody disputes) and R.C. 2151.414(D) (permanent custody) for guidance. These include the child's interaction with parents/custodians, the child's adjustment to home/school, the mental/physical health of all involved, and the parent's compliance with case plan objectives. An appellate court will not reverse a custody determination unless it is against the manifest weight of the evidence or constitutes an abuse of discretion.
Application
The putative father (M.O.) appealed the award of custody to a family friend (K.R.). M.O. argued the decision was against the manifest weight of the evidence because he had bonded with the child, wanted reunification, and had obtained housing shortly before the hearing.
The court reviewed the evidence and found the trial court's decision supported by the record. M.O. failed to comply with critical case plan objectives for over two years. Specifically, he failed to complete domestic violence classes, consistently refused drug screens (testing positive for multiple substances when he did screen), and lacked stable housing for the majority of the case [*11]. In contrast, the child had lived with K.R. since March 2020, was flourishing, and K.R. facilitated visits with the family. The Guardian ad Litem recommended custody to K.R. Although M.O. made last-minute efforts, the court found he had not demonstrated stability. Therefore, the best-interest determination was not unreasonable or against the manifest weight of the evidence [*26].
Conclusion
The court affirmed the judgment awarding legal custody to the family friend.
