granted.

9. That the herein Order is final and appealable.

Appellants' Appendix Volume II at 31-32.

Discussion

[6] Plaintiffs contend that the trial court erred in entering summary judgment in favor of Head. Our standard of 
review is [*5]  well settled. Summary judgment is appropriate only where there is no genuine issue of material fact 
and the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. Ind. Trial Rule 56(C);

Mangold ex rel. Mangold v. Ind. Dep't of Natural Res., 756 N.E.2d 970, 973 (Ind. 2001). Our review is de novo, 
drawing all reasonable inferences from the evidence in favor of the nonmovant. Ind. Dep't of Ins. v. Doe, 247 
N.E.3d 1204, 1210 (Ind. 2024) (citing Hughley v. State, 15 N.E.3d 1000, 1003 (Ind. 2014)). "A fact is 'material' if its 
resolution would affect the outcome of the case, and an issue is 'genuine' if a trier of fact is required to resolve the 
parties' differing accounts of the truth . . . ." Williams v. Tharp, 914 N.E.2d 756, 761 (Ind. 2009). In reviewing a trial 
court's ruling on a motion for summary judgment, we may affirm on any grounds supported by the Indiana Trial Rule 
56 designated materials. Catt v. Bd. of Commr's of Knox Cnty., 779 N.E.2d 1, 3 (Ind. 2002).

[7] The party appealing the trial court's summary judgment determination bears the burden of persuading the 
appellate court the ruling was erroneous. Ryan v.TCI Architects/Eng'rs/Contractors, Inc., 72 N.E.3d 908, 913 (Ind. 
2017). In the summary judgment context, we are not bound by the trial court's specific

findings of fact and conclusions of law. Rice v. Strunk, 670 N.E.2d 1280, 1283 (Ind. 1996). They merely aid our 
review by providing us with a statement of reasons for the trial court's actions. Id.

[8] As noted by Head, the Argument section of Plaintiffs brief is "slightly more than half a page, and [Plaintiffs] do 
not identify any facts (or genuine disputes of material fact) affecting the trial [*6]  court's entry of summary 
judgment." Appellee's Brief at 13. Indeed, "[Plaintiffs] fail to even mention [Head's] bankruptcy and discharge, which 
forms the basis for the trial court's decision, much less cite any case law that could show summary judgment was 
improper." Id. Other than a bald request for us to simply "transfer the present case" to the court that presided over 
the settlement involving other plaintiffs, the sole assertion in Plaintiffs' brief is that "the liability of [Head] is based 
upon insurance that he (Head) purchased specifically to cover [Dickerson]-the driver of [Head's] vehicle." 
Appellant's Brief at 7. The Argument section contains no citation to the record or to any legal authority.

[9] Appellate Rule 46(A)(8)(a) provides "[t]he argument must contain the contentions of the appellant on the issues 
presented, supported by cogent reasoning" and "[e]ach contention must be supported by citations to the authorities, 
statutes, and the Appendix or parts of the Record on Appeal relied on . . . ." Appellate Rule 46(A)(8)(b) provides the 
argument "must include for each issue a concise statement of the applicable standard of review" and "a brief 
statement of the procedural and substantive facts necessary for consideration of [*7]  the issues presented on 
appeal, including a statement of how the issues relevant

to the appeal were raised and resolved by any . . . trial court." It is well established that failure to present a cogent 
argument constitutes waiver of an issue on appellate review. Finnegan v. State, 240 N.E.3d 1265, 1269 n.1 (Ind. 
2024) (citing Davis v. State, 835 N.E.2d 1102, 1113 (Ind. Ct. App. 2005)), reh'gdenied. We have little difficulty 
determining that Plaintiffs have waived their challenge to the trial court's summary judgment ruling for failure to 
make cogent argument.

[10] Notwithstanding waiver, the record makes clear that Plaintiffs submitted the issue of Head's 2023 bankruptcy 
filing, and its effect on their negligence claim, to the trial court for consideration when they filed their second 
response to Head's motion for summary judgment. On appeal, Plaintiffs neither address nor dispute that Head 
named them as creditors in the Chapter 7 bankruptcy proceedings, that they failed to pursue any stay or relief in the 
bankruptcy case, and that Head's March 2024 bankruptcy discharge relieves him of all personal liability, if any, to 
Plaintiffs. See generally McCullough v. CitiMortgage, Inc., 70 N.E.3d 820, 827 (Ind. 2017) (citing Ruth v. First Fed. 



Page 4 of 4
Hicks v. Head, 2025 Ind. App. Unpub. LEXIS 1347

Sav. & Loan Ass'n of LaPorteCty., 492 N.E.2d 1105, 1109 (Ind. Ct. App. 1986) (noting, "[a] discharge in bankruptcy 
has the effect of releasing the bankrupt from any personal liability upon his debts")). In failing to address [*8]  
Head's bankruptcy discharge, Plaintiffs

have not met their burden to persuade us that the trial court's summary

judgment ruling on that basis was erroneous. 4

[11] To the extent that Plaintiffs appear to have abandoned the negligence claim asserted in their complaint and 
attempt to base their claim against Head on a contract theory, namely Head's purchase of insurance for Dickerson, 
we observe that they have cited no authority to support any such theory of liability. Moreover, as pointed out by 
Head in his reply in support of summary judgment, it is undisputed that Plaintiffs were not parties to the insurance 
agreement between Head and American Family. Additionally, as observed by Head on appeal, Plaintiffs have 
alleged no facts in support of a breach of contract claim. Appellee's Brief at 16 (citing Franciscan Alliance, Inc. v. 
Padgett, 180 N.E.3d 518, 522 (Ind. 2021) (observing that breach of contract claim requires existence of a contract 
and breach of that contract)). Under the circumstances presented, we cannot say that the trial court erred in 
granting Head's motion for summary judgment.

[12] For the foregoing reasons, we affirm the court's entry of summary judgment.

4 The trial court, in reaching its conclusion, apparently relied upon documents relating [*9]  to the bankruptcy 
proceedings that were not designated but have been included in the Appellee's Appendix, and we take judicial 
notice of the same pursuant to Ind. Evidence Rule 201. See Horton v. State, 51 N.E.3d 1154, 1160 (Ind. 2016) 
(observing that Evidence Rule 201 "permits courts to take judicial notice of certain material, including facts 'not 
subject to reasonable dispute' and facts 'readily determined from sources whose accuracy cannot reasonably be 
questioned[,]'" but noting that it is "the preferable practice to enter into the record the particular documents of which 
the court is taking notice").

[13] Affirmed.

Bailey, J., and Weissmann, J., concur.

ATTORNEY FOR APPELLANT

John H. Davis

John H. Davis & Associates Merrillville, Indiana

ATTORNEYS FOR APPELLEE

Matthew L. Hinkle Alex Emerson

Coots, Henke & Wheeler, P.C. Carmel, Indiana

End of Document
IRAC_summ:
Case Name: Hicks v. Head, 2025 Ind. App. Unpub. LEXIS 1347
Court: Court of Appeals of Indiana
Area of law: Bankruptcy – Discharge; Civil Procedure – Summary Judgment
Procedural posture: Appeal from a grant of summary judgment in favor of the defendant.
Issue
Whether the trial court correctly granted summary judgment to a defendant in a negligence action on the grounds that his liability had been discharged in a Chapter 7 bankruptcy proceeding.
Rule
A discharge in bankruptcy under 11 U.S.C. § 727 releases the debtor from personal liability for debts that arose before the date of the order for relief. Once a debt is discharged, a state court is barred from entering a judgment determining the debtor's personal liability for that debt. Summary judgment is appropriate where the undisputed evidence shows the claim has been discharged and the plaintiff failed to seek relief from the bankruptcy stay or object to the discharge.
Application
The plaintiffs sued the defendant (Head) for negligence arising from a car accident. During the pendency of the suit, Head filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy, listing the plaintiffs as creditors. The plaintiffs did not seek relief from the automatic stay or object in the bankruptcy court. Head subsequently received a discharge [*5].
Head moved for summary judgment. The trial court granted the motion based on the bankruptcy discharge. On appeal, the plaintiffs failed to present a cogent argument addressing the bankruptcy issue, resulting in waiver [*9]. Notwithstanding waiver, the court noted that the undisputed record showed the debt was discharged, relieving Head of personal liability. The plaintiffs' attempt to reframe the claim as a "contract" claim based on insurance was unsupported by law or fact. Therefore, the trial court properly granted summary judgment.
Conclusion
The court affirmed the summary judgment in favor of the defendant.

Page 1 of 9
Barry v. Loandepot.Com, LLC, P.C.F. Props. in TX, LLC, 2025 Tex. App. LEXIS 8281

Barry v. Loandepot.Com, LLC, P.C.F. Props. in TX, LLC
Court of Appeals of Texas, Fourteenth District, Houston

October 28, 2025, Memorandum Opinion Filed

NO. 14-24-00352-CV

Reporter
2025 Tex. App. LEXIS 8281 *; 2025 LX 491159

SCOTT BARRY, Appellant V. LOANDEPOT.COM, LLC, P.C.F. PROPERTIES IN TX, LLC, AND ANTONY 
HALARIS, Appellees

Notice: Decision text below is the first available text from the court; it has not been editorially reviewed by 
LexisNexis. Publisher's editorial review, including Headnotes, Case Summary, Shepard's analysis or any 
amendments will be added in accordance with LexisNexis editorial guidelines.

Core Terms

loandepot, summary judgment motion, summary judgment, pet, trial court, no-evidence, default, fiduciary, mesne 
profits, trial court's grant, notice, trespass, conspiracy claim, foreclosure sale, declaratory judgment action, 
declaratory judgment, breach of contract, gross negligence, mortgage payment, misrepresent, forbearance, 
conspiracy, no evidence, foreclosure, deposition, lender, modify, holder, rental, rend

Opinion

 [*1] On Appeal from the 190th District Court

Harris County, Texas

Trial Court Cause No. 2022-50283

MEMORANDUM OPINION

Appellant Scott Barry challenges the trial court's grant of summary judgment in favor of appellees loanDepot.com, 
LLC (loanDepot); P.C.F. Properties in TX, LLC (PCF); and Antony Halaris (collectively, appellees). In his first two 
issues, Barry argues that genuine issues of material fact precluded summary judgment in favor of loanDepot and 
PCF. In his third and fourth issues, Barry argues that the trial court erred in awarding more than $40,000 in 
damages to PCF and in denying his

motion for continuance. Because we conclude that Barry failed to produce more than a scintilla of evidence to 
support his claims against appellees and that the trial court did not err in awarding damages, we affirm.

BACKGROUND



Page 2 of 9
Barry v. Loandepot.Com, LLC, P.C.F. Props. in TX, LLC, 2025 Tex. App. LEXIS 8281

In November 2017, Barry obtained a Veterans Administration (VA) loan in the amount of $133,336. The loan was 
serviced by loanDepot and secured by a deed of trust on Barry's home located at 11251 Wild Goose Drive in 
Tomball, Texas (the Property). During the COVID-19 pandemic, the VA offered a forbearance program to 
borrowers, which allowed them to temporarily suspend their loan payments. [*2]  Barry's loan entered forbearance 
beginning with his May 2020 payment. LoanDepot initially suspended Barry's loan payments through June 2020, 
and subsequent agreements extended forbearance through October 2021.

In November 2021, loanDepot sent Barry a notice explaining that his forbearance plan had expired and outlining his 
options: pay the entire amount due for the forbearance period, increase his monthly payment amount, or modify the 
loan agreement. Barry claims that he reached out to loanDepot on multiple occasions to inquire about making 
payments, but the representatives repeatedly told him he did not need to make any payments until his loan 
modification was finalized. LoanDepot claims that Barry failed to submit the required paperwork to complete a 
modification.

Barry did not make any further payments, and loanDepot sent Barry a notice of default and opportunity to cure in 
January 2022. After Barry failed to cure the default, loanDepot sent him a notice of acceleration and notice of 
trustee's sale. Ultimately, PCF purchased the Property at the trustee's sale in August 2022.

2

Barry then filed suit against loanDepot, PCF, and Halaris (PCF's corporate representative), asserting claims [*3]  for 
breach of contract, breach of fiduciary duty, fraud, conspiracy, negligent misrepresentation, negligence, gross 
negligence, and declaratory relief. Barry's allegations focused on loanDepot; he only asserted the conspiracy claim 
against PCF and Halaris. PCF filed a counterclaim against Barry for trespass and asked the trial court to award 
mesne profits representing the value of Barry's possession of the Property to compensate it for Barry's refusal to 
surrender possession of the Property.

Thereafter, loanDepot, PCF, and Halaris each filed motions for summary judgment. 1 The trial court granted each 
motion via separate order, and this appeal followed.

MOTION FORCONTINUANCE

We consider Barry's fourth issue first because it affects our determination of whether the trial court properly granted 
summary judgment in favor of appellees. In a few conclusory sentences, Barry asserts that the trial court erred in 
denying his motion for continuance of the summary judgment hearing. The record reflects that Barry filed two 
motions styled as motions for continuance. His briefing does not specify which of these he believes the trial court 
should have granted. 2 To further obfuscate the issue, Barry's [*4]  record citations direct us to his combined 
response to

1 On appeal, Barry refers to PCF and Halaris collectively as "PCF." Though Halaris filed his own traditional 
summary judgment motion challenging Barry's declaratory judgment action and conspiracy claim, Barry does not 
address Halaris's independent motion on appeal. PCF did not move for summary judgment on the conspiracy claim. 
Thus, we affirm the trial court's grant of Halaris's motion as it relates to the conspiracy claim because Barry does 
not challenge that portion of the judgment on appeal. See Brown v. Hensley, 515 S.W.3d 442, 446 (Tex. App.- 
Houston [14th Dist.] 2017, no pet.) (stating that appellate court must uphold summary judgment as to particular 
claims if appellant fails to challenge their disposition on appeal).

2 Though no order appears in our record, the record suggests that the trial court granted Barry's first motion for 
continuance.

3

loanDepot and PCF's summary judgment motions (not to his motion for continuance), which included a request to 
continue the summary judgment determination as to the conspiracy claim alone because PCF had not produced a 
representative for deposition.



Page 3 of 9
Barry v. Loandepot.Com, LLC, P.C.F. Props. in TX, LLC, 2025 Tex. App. LEXIS 8281

On appeal, Barry does not cite any legal authority to support his contention, and he does not explain why the 
deposition [*5]  was essential to his opposition to any of appellees' summary judgment motions. See Tex. R. Civ. P. 
166a(g) (stating that court may grant continuance to permit nonmovant to conduct depositions or additional 
discovery if nonmovant provides affidavit explaining why he cannot present facts essential to justify opposition). An 
appellant's brief must contain a clear and concise argument including appropriate citations to legal authority. Tex. 
R. App. P. 38.1(i). This requirement is not satisfied by conclusory statements unsupported by legal citations, and 
the failure to cite legal authority results in waiver of the complaint. See San Saba Energy, L.P. v. Crawford, 171 
S.W.3d 323, 338 (Tex. App.-Houston [14th Dist.] 2005, no pet.) (holding that "parties asserting error on appeal still 
must put forth some specific argument and analysis showing that the record and the law supports their 
contentions"). Even construing Barry's brief liberally, we conclude that he did not brief his fourth issue adequately. 
See Tex. R. App. P. 38.1(i); San Saba Energy, 171 S.W.3d at 338.

We overrule his fourth issue.

SUMMARYJUDGMENT

In his first and second issues, Barry contends that the trial court erred in granting loanDepot and PCF's summary 
judgment motions. Specifically, Barry argues that he presented more than a scintilla of evidence to support his 
claims for breach of contract, breach of fiduciary duty, fraud, [*6]  conspiracy, negligent

4

misrepresentation, negligence, gross negligence, and declaratory judgment. We disagree.

A. Standard of Review

We review a summary judgment de novo. Rosetta Res. Operating, LP v.Martin, 645 S.W.3d 212, 218 (Tex. 2022). 
When a party moves for summary judgment on both traditional and no-evidence grounds, we first review the no-
evidence summary judgment. Ford Motor Co. v. Ridgway, 135 S.W.3d 598, 600 (Tex. 2004). If the trial court 
properly granted the no-evidence motion, we do not reach the arguments made for traditional summary judgment. 
Id. The non-movant must produce summary judgment evidence raising a genuine issue of material fact to defeat a 
no-evidence motion. Id. "A genuine issue of material fact exists if more than a scintilla of evidence establishing the 
existence of the challenged element is produced." Id.

If, as here, the trial court does not specify the grounds relied upon for its ruling, we will affirm on any meritorious 
ground. See Martin, 645 S.W.3d at 226 ("When a trial court's order granting summary judgment does not specify 
the grounds on which its order is based, the appealing party must negate each ground upon which the judgment 
could have been based."). We review the record in the light most favorable to the nonmovant, indulging every 
reasonable inference and resolving any doubts against the [*7]  movant. Sudan v. Sudan, 199 S.W.3d 291, 292 
(Tex. 2006) (per curiam).

B. LoanDepot's Motion

LoanDepot moved for summary judgment on all of Barry's claims against it on both traditional and no-evidence 
grounds. In its no-evidence motion, loanDepot

5

contended that Barry failed to present evidence of at least one element of each of his claims.

1. Breach of Contract

The elements of a breach of contract claim are: (1) a valid contract; (2) performance or tendered performance by 
the plaintiff; (3) breach of the contract by the defendant; and (4) damages to the plaintiff resulting from that breach. 
West v.Triple B Servs., LLP, 264 S.W.3d 440, 446 (Tex. App.-Houston [14th Dist.] 2008, no pet.). The no-evidence 



Page 4 of 9
Barry v. Loandepot.Com, LLC, P.C.F. Props. in TX, LLC, 2025 Tex. App. LEXIS 8281

portion of loanDepot's motion challenged Barry's evidence as to all but the first element of his breach of contract 
claim.

As to the second and third elements, Barry argues that loanDepot breached the contract by barring him from 
making mortgage payments. Barry claims that he tried to recommence his loan payments, but loanDepot's 
representatives informed him he could wait to make further payments until a loan modification was finalized. Barry 
points to notes from loanDepot's internal system documenting "payment inquiries" he made beginning in November 
2021, along with emails he sent to loanDepot, deposition testimony from its representatives, [*8]  and his own 
affidavit.

Barry's arguments ignore his own breach of the contract in failing to make his mortgage payments as required by 
his loan agreement. See Ramex Constr. Co. v.Tamcon Servs., Inc., 29 S.W.3d 135, 137 (Tex. App.-Houston [14th 
Dist.] 2000, no pet.) ("Generally, a party who is in default of a contract cannot maintain a suit for its breach."); 
Mustang Pipeline Co. v. Driver Pipeline Co., 134 S.W.3d 195, 196 (Tex. 2004) ("It is a fundamental principle of 
contract law that when one party to a contract commits a material breach of that contract, the other party is 
discharged or excused from further performance.").

6

This court addressed a similar situation in Moe v. Option One MortgageGroup, No. 14-07-00550-CV, 2009 WL 
136892 (Tex. App.-Houston [14th Dist.] Jan. 20, 2009, no pet.) (mem. op.). There, the plaintiffs defaulted on their 
home loan and entered into a forbearance agreement. Id. at *1. The plaintiffs then failed to make a required 
payment, or any thereafter. Id. When they inquired with their servicer about further payments, the servicer gave 
incorrect information about receipt of a past payment and advised that the loan was in default. Id. The plaintiffs 
made no further payments and later sued the servicer for breach of contract, among other claims. Id. at *1-2. This 
court affirmed the trial court's grant of the loan servicer's no-evidence summary judgment as to the breach of 
contract claim, rejecting the plaintiffs' arguments as to elements two and three:

The evidence is uncontroverted [*9]  . . . that the [plaintiffs] failed to make the mortgage payment that was due on 
February 1, 2005 . . . [and] failed to make any payment thereafter. . . . Thus, the [plaintiffs] did not perform or tender 
performance, but instead breached the contract.

Id. at *3. Here, like the plaintiffs in Moe, Barry failed to make mortgage payments due under the contract. The 
record reflects that Barry has not made any payments since at least May 2020. 3

The Dallas court of appeals reached an analogous conclusion in Shellnut v.Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., No. 02-15-
00204-CV, 2017 WL 1538166 (Tex. App.- Dallas Apr. 27, 2017, pet. denied) (mem. op.). As in Moe and the present 
case, the homeowner in Shellnut defaulted on his loan. Id. at *2. Shellnut repeatedly contacted the lender to discuss 
modification and repayment assistance. Id. When the lender ultimately advised Shellnut he was not eligible for a 
modification attempted to

3 LoanDepot representative Steven Roark testified that he believed Barry's last payment was May 1, 2020. 
However, past due notices sent to Barry reflect that he did not make the May 2020 payment.

7

foreclose, Shellnut sued for breach of contract, among other claims. Id. at *3. The appellate court affirmed the trial 
court's grant of summary judgment as to the breach of contract claim, concluding that none of Shellnut's 
evidence [*10]  showed a prior material breach by the lender that would excuse his default. Id. at *10. The evidence 
reflected that at the time of the conduct complained of by Shellnut, he was already behind on his loan payments. Id. 
at *8-9.

Here, Barry has failed to present any evidence of a prior material breach by loanDepot that would excuse his 
performance. Instead, the evidence reflects that Barry did not make any payments after April or May 2020 and 
defaulted on his loan. Contrary to Barry's assertions, there is no evidence that loanDepot refused to accept 



Page 5 of 9
Barry v. Loandepot.Com, LLC, P.C.F. Props. in TX, LLC, 2025 Tex. App. LEXIS 8281

payments from him. Rather, LoanDepot produced various letters, statements, and notices sent to Barry that 
included payment instructions.

Because Barry did not perform or tender performance, but instead breached the contract, we conclude that the trial 
court did not err in granting loanDepot's motion for summary judgment as to Barry's breach of contract claim.

2. Breach of Fiduciary Duty

To prevail on a claim for breach of fiduciary duty, a plaintiff must establish:

(1) a fiduciary relationship between the plaintiff and defendant; (2) a breach by the defendant of his fiduciary duty to 
the plaintiff; and (3) an injury to the plaintiff or benefit to the defendant due [*11]  to the defendant's breach. Zhu v. 
Lam, 426 S.W.3d 333, 339 (Tex. App.-Houston [14th Dist.] 2014, no pet.). LoanDepot's no-evidence summary 
judgment motion challenged each of the elements of Barry's breach of fiduciary duty claim. In his response, Barry 
noted the elements of a breach of fiduciary duty claim but did not directly address the first element: the existence of 
a fiduciary relationship. Instead, Barry summarily stated that "Defendants owed a fiduciary duty to plaintiff" and then 
addressed the remaining elements.

8

"[N]ot every relationship involving a high degree of trust and confidence rises to the stature of a fiduciary 
relationship." Schlumberger Tech. Corp. v. Swanson, 959 S.W.2d 171, 176-77 (Tex. 1997). As loanDepot points 
out, Texas courts (including this one) have generally declined to recognize a fiduciary relationship between a lender 
and borrower. See, e.g., Bank One, Tex., N.A. v. Stewart, 967 S.W.2d 419, 442 (Tex. App.-Houston [14th Dist.] 
1998, pet. denied); Farah v.Mafrige & Kormanik, P.C., 927 S.W.2d 663, 675 (Tex. App.-Houston [1st Dist.] 1996, no 
pet.). As we noted in Stewart, when courts have recognized such a relationship, that determination rested on 
extraneous facts and conduct, including excessive lender control or influence in the borrower's business activities. 
Stewart, 967 S.W.2d at 442 (citing Farah, 927 S.W.2d at 675). Here, Barry has not presented any such evidence to 
support imposition of a fiduciary relationship on these facts. See Meyer v. Cathey, 167 S.W.3d 327, 331 (Tex. 2005) 
(noting that to impose informal fiduciary duty in business transaction, special relationship of trust must exist 
prior [*12]  to and apart from agreement made basis of suit). We therefore affirm the trial court's grant of 
loanDepot's no-evidence summary judgment motion as to his breach of fiduciary duty claim.

3. Fraud and Negligent Misrepresentation

Barry also contends that he presented sufficient evidence of each element of his fraud and negligent 
misrepresentation claims. These claims share the following common elements: (1) a material, false statement; (2) 
reliance on that statement; and

(3) damages as a result. See Moe, 2009 WL 136892, at *4 (noting common elements of fraud and false 
representation claims); Atlantic Lloyds Ins. Co. v. Butler, 137 S.W.3d 199, 215 (Tex. App.-Houston [1st Dist.] 2004, 
pet denied) (same). To support either claim, the plaintiff must demonstrate that his reliance was justifiable.

9

See JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. v. Orca Assets, G.P., L.L.C., 546 S.W.3d 648, 653- 54 (Tex. 2018).

While justifiable reliance is ordinarily a question of fact, it may be negated as a matter of law when circumstances 
demonstrate that the reliance cannot be justified. Wyrick v. Bus. Bank of Tex., N.A., 577 S.W.3d 336, 348 (Tex. 
App.-Houston [14th Dist.] 2019, no pet.). For example, a party to a contract cannot justifiably rely on an oral 
representation that is directly contradicted by the express terms of the written agreement. DRC Parts & 
Accessories, L.L.C. v. VM Motori, S.P.A., 112 S.W.3d 854, 858 (Tex. App.-Houston [14th Dist.] 2003, pet denied).

Specifically, Barry alleged that loanDepot's representatives "repeatedly made material representations by telling 
[him] that they were working on modifying his loan and that he did not need to make [*13]  any mortgage 



Page 6 of 9
Barry v. Loandepot.Com, LLC, P.C.F. Props. in TX, LLC, 2025 Tex. App. LEXIS 8281

payments." He also claimed that loanDepot told him "to ignore the foreclosure notices." We conclude that Barry 
could not justifiably rely on these alleged misrepresentations, given the express terms of the loan agreement. The 
note executed by Barry provided as follows:

(B) Default

If I do not pay the full amount of each monthly payment on the date it is due, I will be in default.

(C) Notice of Default

If I am in default, the Note Holder may send me a written notice telling me that if I do not pay the overdue amount 
by a certain date, the Note Holder may require me to pay immediately the full amount of Principal which has not 
been paid and all the interest that I owe on that amount. That date must be at least 30 days after the date on which 
the notice is mailed to me or delivered by other means.

10

(D) No Waiver By Note Holder

Even if, at a time when I am in default, the Note Holder does not require me to pay immediately in full as described 
above, the Note Holder will still have the right to do so if I am in default at a later time.

Further, the Deed of Trust signed by Barry stated that "[a]ny forbearance by Lender in exercising any right or 
remedy . . . shall not be a waiver [*14]  of or preclude the exercise of any right or remedy." Thus, the purported oral 
representations made by loanDepot's representatives to the effect that Barry did not need to make his loan 
payments and did not need to worry about foreclosure notices directly contradicted the contract's terms. Barry could 
not justifiably rely on any such representations. SeeOrca Assets, 546 S.W.3d at 660 n.2; DRC Parts & Accessories, 
112 S.W.3d at 858- 59. We affirm the trial court's grant of loanDepot's no-evidence summary judgment motion as to 
Barry's fraud and negligent misrepresentation claims.

4. Conspiracy

The elements of a common law conspiracy claim are: (1) a combination of two or more persons; (2) the persons 
seek to accomplish an object or course of action; (3) the persons reach a meeting of the minds on the object or 
course of action;

(4) one or more unlawful, overt acts are taken in furtherance of the object or course of action; and (5) damages 
occur as a proximate result. First United PentecostalChurch of Beaumont v. Parker, 514 S.W.3d 214, 222 (Tex. 
2017). LoanDepot's no-evidence motion challenged all but the first element of Barry's conspiracy claim. Barry's 
response cited no evidence but generally alleged that loanDepot, PCF, and Halaris worked together to foreclose on 
the Property and to allow PCF to purchase the Property for less than market value.

As outlined [*15]  above, an essential element of a civil conspiracy claim is a meeting of the minds as to the object 
or course of action. See id.; see also Samson v.

11

Manley, No. 14-07-01085-CV, 2009 WL 3790410, at *5 (Tex. App.-Houston [14th Dist.] Oct. 6, 2009, pet. denied) 
(mem. op.). Here, there is no evidence of a meeting of the minds between appellees. Barry does not identify any 
specific facts establishing any of the elements of conspiracy. Further, he did not attach any evidence of conspiracy 
to his summary judgment response as required by rule 166a(i). See Tex. R. Civ. P. 166a(i); Samson, 2009 WL 
3790410, at *5. Specifically, Barry failed to present evidence of the third element-a meeting of the minds. There is 
no evidence of any connection between loanDepot and PCF. Thus, the trial court did not err in granting loanDepot's 
no-evidence motion for summary judgment as to Barry's conspiracy claim.

5. Negligence and Gross Negligence



Page 7 of 9
Barry v. Loandepot.Com, LLC, P.C.F. Props. in TX, LLC, 2025 Tex. App. LEXIS 8281

LoanDepot's no-evidence summary judgment motion also challenged each element of Barry's negligence and gross 
negligence claims. See Durham v. Accardi, 587 S.W.3d 179, 183 (Tex. App.-Houston [14th Dist.] 2019, no pet.) 
(outlining elements of negligence and stating that plaintiff must prove all elements of negligence as prerequisite to 
gross negligence claim). In response, Barry needed to present more than a scintilla of evidence as to each 
challenged element to defeat loanDepot's no-evidence motion. See Alarcon v. Alcolac Inc., 488 S.W.3d 813, 819 
(Tex. App.-Houston [14th Dist.] 2016, pet. denied). However, Barry's [*16]  response failed to identify any evidence 
to support his negligence or gross negligence claims. We must therefore affirm the trial court's grant of loanDepot's 
no-evidence motion as to the negligence and gross negligence claims. See Tex. R. Civ. P. 166a(i); Alarcon, 488 
S.W.3d at 819.

12

We affirm the trial court's grant of summary judgment as to each of Barry's claims against loanDepot, 4 and we 
overrule his first issue.

C. PCF's Motion

PCF separately moved for summary judgment on both traditional and no-evidence grounds. In its motion, PCF 
argued that Barry's declaratory judgment claim failed as a matter of law because a trespass-to-try-title is the correct 
method of determining title to land, not a declaratory judgment action. PCF also contended that Barry had no 
evidence that the foreclosure sale was invalid. Lastly, PCF argued that it was entitled to mesne profits, a judgment 
on its trespass claim, and reasonable and necessary fees and costs under the Uniform Declaratory Judgments Act. 
5

In response, Barry argued that a declaratory judgment action was an appropriate method for determining the 
parties' rights related to the Property, he had sufficient evidence demonstrating that the foreclosure was improper, 
PCF was not entitled to [*17]  mesne profits because the justice court had determined that PCF was not entitled to 
mesne profits in the eviction case, PCF was not entitled to judgment on its trespass claim because the foreclosure 
sale was invalid and PCF was not the record owner of the Property, and PCF was not entitled to attorney's fees.

4 On appeal, Barry does not contest the trial court's grant of loanDepot's summary judgment motion on his 
declaratory judgment claim. Thus, we also affirm the trial court's judgment in that regard. See Brown, 515 S.W.3d at 
446. We address Barry's declaratory judgment claim as it relates to the remaining appellees below.

5 PCF's motion for summary judgment did not expressly challenge Barry's conspiracy claim against it. However, 
PCF's motion stated that it "adopts the argument and authorities in [loanDepot's] motion [for summary judgment], 
along with the evidence in support thereof." As this court has noted, "Texas courts recognize the adoption of a co-
party's motion for summary judgment as a legitimate procedural practice." Sanchez v. Deutsche Bank Nat'l Tr. Co., 
2015 WL 3609100, at *5 (Tex. App.-Houston [14th Dist.] June 9, 2015, no pet.) (mem. op. on reh'g) (citing Lockett 
v. HB Zachry Co., 285 S.W.3d 63, 72 (Tex. App.-Houston [1st Dist.] 2009, no pet.)); see also Tex. R. Civ. P. 58 
(adoption by reference). 

13

The trial court's order granted PCF's summary judgment motion as to its claims for trespass to try title, declaratory 
judgment, and [*18]  quite title against Barry.6 The order awarded title to the Property to PCF, declared PCF the 
owner of the Property, and concluded that the foreclosure sale was valid. Additionally, the order awarded 
possession of the Property to PCF against all other occupants, awarded $40,431.78 in mesne profits as reasonable 
rent through February 12, 2024, and $72.33 per day thereafter. However, the order denied PCF's request for 
attorney's fees and costs, noting that PCF withdrew those claims in open court.

1. Declaratory Judgment

Barry's second issue challenges the trial court's grant of PCF's summary judgment motion as to his declaratory 
judgment action. Barry's declaratory judgment action asked the trial court to determine the proper owner of the 



Page 8 of 9
Barry v. Loandepot.Com, LLC, P.C.F. Props. in TX, LLC, 2025 Tex. App. LEXIS 8281

Property; whether the transfer of the Property to PCF was valid; and whether PCF or Halaris had any right or 
interest in the Property, including a right to occupy the Property. Each aspect of Barry's declaratory judgment action 
turns on the validity of the foreclosure sale. If, as Barry contends, the sale was invalid, then Barry remains the 
owner of the Property, and PCF has no rights to or interest in the Property.

PCF's summary judgment motion argued [*19]  that Barry presented no evidence that the foreclosure sale was 
improper. In his response, Barry did not contend that any aspect of the foreclosure sale was procedurally improper. 
Instead, Barry argued that the foreclosure was invalid because "Defendants literally prevented [him] from making 
any mortgage payments" and "lied to [him] and told him that they were

6 On appeal, Barry does not challenge the trial court's grant of PCF's motion for summary judgment on its trespass 
claim.

14

working to modify his loan and to not make any mortgage payments." However, the evidence Barry points to does 
not support these assertions.

First, Barry cites to a portion of the deposition testimony of loanDepot representative Steven Roark, wherein he 
testified that in November 2021, Barry was no longer eligible to make a payment. However, other portions of 
Roark's testimony explained that although VA guidelines did not permit Barry to make partial payments once his 
loan entered "late-stage default," he could still either reinstate the loan by paying the entire past due amount or 
modify the debt. And as we explained earlier, Barry's arguments on this point do not address his own prior breach 
of the loan agreement. [*20]  See Moe, 2009 WL 136892, at *3; Shellnut, 2017 WL 1538166, at *10. Because Barry 
defaulted on his loan by failing to make the required payments, the loan agreement permitted loanDepot to 
accelerate the loan and proceed with foreclosure. This testimony is not evidence that the foreclosure sale was 
improper.

Barry's response to PCF's summary judgment motion also directed the trial court to his own affidavit, deposition 
testimony from loanDepot representative Danny Oates, and loanDepot's internal notes as evidence of loanDepot's 
misrepresentations that he did not need to make further payments until it finalized his loan modification. We have 
already determined that Barry could not justifiably rely on any such representations because they were contrary to 
the terms of the loan agreement. See Orca Assets, 546 S.W.3d at 660 n.2; DRC Parts & Accessories, 112 S.W.3d 
at 858-59. These alleged representations are not evidence of the illegality of the foreclosure sale.

Because Barry failed to present evidence of wrongful foreclosure, we affirm the trial court's grant of PCF's summary 
judgment motion as to Barry's declaratory judgment action. We overrule his second issue.

15

2. Mesne Profits

Barry's third issue contests the trial court's award of mesne profits to PCF. Specifically, Barry argues that the trial 
court erred in awarding mesne [*21]  profits because the Harris County Justice of the Peace Court concluded that 
PCF was not entitled to any mesne profits in the forcible entry and detainer action. Barry does not cite any legal 
authority in support of his argument on appeal.

In response, PCF argues that the justice court's denial of mesne profits did not preclude the trial court from 
awarding them in the present case. We agree. As PCF points out, "[t]he only issue in a forcible detainer action is 
the right to actual possession of the premises," as it is meant to be a quick and inexpensive means to procure 
immediate possession of property. Marshall v. Hous. Auth. of City of SanAntonio, 198 S.W.3d 782, 787 (Tex. 2006). 
Further, the Texas Property Code specifically states that forcible entry and detainer suits do not preclude an action 
for trespass, damages, waste, rent, or mesne profits. Tex. Prop. Code § 24.008.



Page 9 of 9

Here, PCF attached a declaration from Halaris to its summary judgment motion, which stated the following 
concerning mesne profits:

PCF is entitled to mesne profits, representing reasonable rent PCF would have received but for [Barry's] 
interference with PCF's ownership rights in the property. I believe a rental rate of $2,200 per month is a reasonable 
rent rate for the Property based on comparable rentals in the area [*22]  (See Exhibit 6 attached hereto). PCF is 
entitled to recover monthly rent from August 2, 2022, through the present, in the amount of $26,255.34 (Daily Rate 
of $72.33 for 363 days to 07/31/2023).

Loss of rentals in an appropriate measure of damages for the temporary loss of use of land as a result of a 
trespass. Williams v. Garnett, 608 S.W.2d 794, 797 (Tex. App.-Waco 1980, no pet.) (citing Bradley v. McIntyre, 373 
S.W.2d 389, 390 (Tex. App.-Houston 1963, writ ref'd n.r.e.)); see also Coinmach Corp. v. Aspenwood

16

Apt. Corp., 417 S.W.3d 909, 921 (Tex. 2013) (noting that when trespass causes temporary injury, amount 
necessary to put plaintiff in the position it would have been in but for trespass usually includes cost to repair any 
damage to property, loss of use of property, and loss of any expected profits from use of property). PCF presented 
competent summary judgment evidence of a reasonable rental rate for the Property, considering comparable 
rentals in the area. Barry did not present any controverting evidence in his response to PCF's motion. Instead, 
Barry stated that "[i]f an amount per day is awarded at all, [he] believes that this amount should be less." This is 
insufficient to defeat PCF's motion for summary judgment. SeeWakefield v. Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., No. 14-12-
00686-CV, 2013 WL 6047031, at *4 (Tex. App.-Houston [14th Dist.] Nov. 14, 2013, no pet.) (mem. op.) (noting 
response to summary judgment motion is not summary judgment proof).

We affirm the trial court's award of mesne profits to PCF, and we overrule [*23]  Barry's third issue.

CONCLUSION

We affirm the trial court's judgment.

IRAC_summ:
Case Name: Barry v. Loandepot.Com, LLC
Jurisdiction / Court: Court of Appeals of Texas, Fourteenth District, Houston
Citation: 2025 Tex. App. LEXIS 8281
Date: October 28, 2025
I. Issue(s)
Did the trial court err in granting a no-evidence summary judgment for the lender (loanDepot) on the borrower's (Barry's) claims for breach of contract, fraud, and other torts, where Barry had defaulted on his loan before the lender's alleged misconduct?
Could Barry justifiably rely on the lender's alleged oral representations that he did not need to make mortgage payments when those statements directly contradicted the express terms of the written loan agreement?
Did the trial court err in granting summary judgment for the property purchaser (PCF) on Barry's declaratory judgment action challenging the foreclosure sale's validity?
Did the trial court err in awarding mesne profits (reasonable rental value) to PCF for the period Barry occupied the property after the foreclosure sale?
II. Rule(s)
Breach of Contract: A party who is in material breach of a contract cannot maintain a suit for its breach. The other party is excused from further performance.
Justifiable Reliance (Fraud/Negligent Misrepresentation): A party cannot justifiably rely on an oral representation that is directly contradicted by the express, unambiguous terms of a written agreement. Such reliance is negated as a matter of law.
Wrongful Foreclosure: To challenge a foreclosure sale, a party must present evidence of a defect in the foreclosure sale proceedings or a wrongful act by the lender that caused the sale.
Mesne Profits: A party who wrongfully possesses land after a valid foreclosure is liable for mesne profits, which are damages for the loss of use of the land, typically measured by its reasonable rental value. A ruling in a separate forcible detainer (eviction) action does not preclude an award of mesne profits in a trespass-to-try-title case.
III. Application (Analysis)
Claims Against loanDepot: The court affirmed summary judgment for loanDepot. Barry's breach of contract claim failed because he was the first to materially breach the loan agreement by failing to make payments since May 2020. His fraud and misrepresentation claims failed because he could not have justifiably relied on alleged oral statements from loanDepot representatives telling him not to worry about payments or foreclosure notices. The written loan agreement clearly defined default and gave the lender the right to foreclose, directly contradicting any such oral assurances. His other claims (conspiracy, negligence, etc.) failed for lack of evidence.
Justifiable Reliance: Barry's reliance on the alleged oral statements was unjustifiable as a matter of law because the loan agreement and deed of trust expressly stated that failure to pay constituted default and that any forbearance by the lender did not waive its right to foreclose.
Claims Against PCF: The court affirmed summary judgment for PCF. Barry's declaratory judgment action, which sought to invalidate the foreclosure, failed because he presented no evidence of a procedural defect in the sale. His argument that the sale was invalid because loanDepot wrongfully prevented him from making payments was unsupported by the evidence and defeated by his own prior default.
Mesne Profits: The court affirmed the award of mesne profits to PCF. Barry's argument that a justice court's prior ruling in an eviction case barred the award was incorrect, as the Property Code explicitly allows a separate action for mesne profits. PCF provided competent evidence of the property's reasonable rental value, which Barry failed to controvert with any evidence of his own.
IV. Conclusion
No. Barry's prior material breach of the contract by failing to make payments precluded his claims against the lender.
No. Barry's reliance was unjustifiable as a matter of law because the oral statements were contradicted by the written contract.
No. Barry failed to produce any evidence that the foreclosure sale was procedurally improper or otherwise invalid.
No. The award was proper as damages for Barry's trespass after PCF became the rightful owner of the property.
The Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court's judgment in its entirety.

Petitioners represent a class of current and former Cornell University employees who participated in two defined
contribution retirement plans from 2010 to 2016. In 2017, they sued Cornell and other plan fiduciaries for allegedly 
causing the plans to engage in prohibited transactions for recordkeeping services with the Teachers Insurance and 
Annuity Association of America-College Retirement Equities Fund and Fidelity Investments Inc., in violation of

reasonable recordkeeping fees. The District Court dismissed the prohibited-transaction claim, and the Second 
Circuit affirmed. The Second Circuit held that §1108(b)(2)(A) is incorporated into §1106(a)’s prohibitions, requiring

to dismiss. 86 F. 4th 961, 975.

provision itself, without addressing potential §1108 exemptions. Pp. 700-709.
(a) Section 1106(a)(1)(C) contains three elements: It prohibits fiduciaries from (1) “caus[ing a] plan to engage in a 
transaction” (2) that the fiduciary “knows or should know . . . constitutes a direct or indirect . . . furnishing of goods, 
services, or facilities” (3) “between the plan and a party in interest.” Its bar is categorical and does not remove from 
its scope transactions that were necessary or involved reasonable compensation. The exemptions in §1108 do not 
impose additional pleading requirements  [*694]  for §1106(a)(1) claims. When a statute has “exemptions laid out 
apart from the prohibitions,” and the exemptions “expressly refe[r] to the prohibited conduct as such,” the 
exemptions ordinarily [****3]  constitute “affirmative defense[s]” that are “entirely the responsibility of the party 
raising” them. Meacham v. Knolls Atomic Power Laboratory, 554 U. S. 84, 91, 95, 128 S. Ct. 2395, 171 L. Ed. 2d 
283. Like the exemptions at issue in Meacham, the §1108 exemptions are structured as affirmative defenses that 
must be pleaded and proved by defendants who seek to benefit from them. Pp. 700-702.
(b) Respondents’ contrary arguments are unpersuasive. First, the “[e]xcept as provided in section 1108” language 
in §1106(a) does not incorporate §1108 exemptions as elements of §1106(a) violations. That reading  [***597]  
ignores that Congress wrote the §1108 exemptions “in the orthodox format of an affirmative defense” separate from 
the prohibitions. Meacham, 554 U. S., at 102, 128 S. Ct. 2395, 171 L. Ed. 2d 283. The headings of the sections, 
“Prohibited transactions” for §1106 and “Exemptions from prohibited transactions” for §1108, confirm this 
understanding. Respondents also fail to explain why some but not all §1108 exemptions should be treated as 
elements of §1106(a) claims. Yet requiring plaintiffs to plead and disprove all potentially relevant §1108 exemptions 
would be impractical, given that there are 21 statutory exemptions and hundreds of regulatory exemptions. Pp. 703
706.
(c) Respondents’ reliance on United States v. Cook, 84 U.S. 168, 17 Wall. 168, 21 L. Ed. 538, is misplaced. Cook 
established “a rule of criminal pleading” based  [**1024]  on constitutional considerations not present in the civil 
context. [****4]  United States v. Reese, 92 U. S. 214, 232, 23 L. Ed. 563. Even in criminal cases, it remains settled 
that “‘an indictment or other pleading . . . need not negative the matter of an exception made by a proviso or other 
distinct clause.’” Dixon v. United States, 548 U. S. 1, 13, 126 S. Ct. 2437, 165 L. Ed. 2d 299. Pp. 706-707.
(d) Finally, respondents’ practical concerns about meritless litigation cannot overcome the statutory text and 
structure. District courts have various tools at their disposal to screen out meritless claims, including requiring 
plaintiffs to file a reply addressing exemptions under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 7(a), dismissing claims that fail 
to identify a concrete injury under Article III, limiting discovery, imposing Rule 11 sanctions, and ordering cost 
shifting under §1132(g)(1). Pp. 707-709.
86 F. 4th 961, reversed and remanded.

A

ERISA subjects plan fiduciaries to certain fiduciary duties derived from the common law of trusts. See 
§1104(a);

IRAC_summ:
Case Name: Cunningham v. Cornell Univ. [2025] 604 U.S. 693
Court + jurisdiction: Supreme Court of the United States
Area of law: ERISA – Fiduciary Duties – Prohibited Transactions
Procedural posture: On writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
Issue
Whether a plaintiff stating a claim under 29 U.S.C. § 1106(a)(1)(C) for a prohibited transaction must plead and prove that the transaction was not covered by the exemption in 29 U.S.C. § 1108(b)(2)(A) for necessary services and reasonable compensation.
Rule
Under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA), § 1106(a)(1) categorically prohibits fiduciaries from causing a plan to engage in specific transactions with parties in interest. Section 1108 provides exemptions to these prohibitions, including for arrangements involving "necessary" services and "reasonable compensation." When a statute lays out exemptions separate from prohibitions, the burden of proving the exemption rests on the party claiming its benefit. Consequently, § 1108 exemptions are affirmative defenses.
Application
The Court analyzed the statutory text and structure to determine the pleading burden. Section 1106(a)(1)(C) contains three elements: a fiduciary causing a transaction, involving the furnishing of goods/services, with a party in interest [700]. The Court held that a plaintiff need only allege these three elements to state a claim. The Court rejected the Second Circuit’s view that the exemption in § 1108(b)(2)(A) is effectively an element of the offense that the plaintiff must negate in the complaint.
Relying on Meacham v. Knolls Atomic Power Laboratory, the Court reasoned that when Congress structures a statute with exemptions "laid out apart from the prohibitions," those exemptions are affirmative defenses [701]. The text of § 1108 explicitly refers to "Exemptions," and § 1106’s "except as provided" clause does not shift the burden to the plaintiff [703]–[704]. The Court noted that treating exemptions as elements would be impractical and unfair, as there are 21 statutory exemptions and hundreds of regulatory exemptions; requiring a plaintiff to plead against all potential exemptions would be illogical, particularly where facts regarding reasonableness are often in the fiduciary's possession [705].
The Court dismissed the respondents' reliance on United States v. Cook, clarifying that Cook established a rule of criminal pleading based on constitutional notice requirements not present in civil litigation [707]. Finally, the Court addressed policy concerns regarding meritless litigation, noting that district courts possess sufficient tools—such as Rule 7 replies, discovery limits, and cost-shifting—to manage barebones claims without altering the statutory burden of proof [708].
Conclusion
The Court held that § 1108 exemptions are affirmative defenses that must be pleaded and proved by the defendant, not the plaintiff; the judgment was reversed and remanded.

before
Lord Reed, President
