IRAC_summ:
Case Name: A and another v Criminal Injuries Compensation Authority [2021] UKSC 27
Court + jurisdiction: United Kingdom Supreme Court
Area of law: Human Rights – Discrimination – Criminal Injuries Compensation
Procedural posture: Appeal from the Court of Appeal, Civil Division
Issue
Whether a rule in the Criminal Injuries Compensation Scheme, which automatically disqualifies applicants with unspent custodial convictions from receiving compensation, unjustifiably discriminates against victims of human trafficking in breach of Article 14 (read with Article 4) of the ECHR.
Rule
Article 14 of the ECHR prohibits discrimination in the enjoyment of Convention rights on grounds such as "other status." To succeed, a claimant must show: (1) the issue falls within the ambit of a substantive Convention right (here, Article 4 protection against slavery/trafficking); (2) difference in treatment based on a status; and (3) the difference is not objectively justified. In social welfare policy, a measure is justified unless it is "manifestly without reasonable foundation."
Application
The Court accepted that the Criminal Injuries Compensation Scheme (CICS) falls within the ambit of Article 4 because the state voluntarily provides compensation to trafficking victims, creating a link to the state's protective duties [39]. It also held that having an unspent conviction resulting in a custodial sentence constitutes an "other status" under Article 14, as it is a personal characteristic with independent legal significance [66]–[67].
However, the Court rejected the discrimination claim. First, regarding Thlimmenos discrimination (failure to treat differently those in relevantly different situations), the Court found the appellants were not in a significantly different position from other offenders. Their convictions (burglary/theft) occurred years before they were trafficked and were unrelated to their trafficking. Therefore, they could not rely on the non-punishment principle applicable to crimes committed because of trafficking [69]–[78].
Second, regarding the justification for the exclusionary rule, the Court applied the "manifestly without reasonable foundation" test appropriate for social welfare policy involving the allocation of public funds. The rule's objective—limiting compensation to those deemed "deserving"—was legitimate. The bright-line exclusionary rule was a proportionate means of achieving this aim, avoiding complex individual assessments. The distinction between those with and without unspent convictions was not based on a "suspect" ground, and Parliament had reviewed the scheme. Thus, the exclusion was justified [83]–[92].
Conclusion
The Court held that the exclusionary rule did not constitute unjustifiable discrimination because the difference in treatment was objectively justified and not manifestly without reasonable foundation; the appeal was dismissed.

case_name: Enka Insaat Ve Sanayi AS v OOO Insurance Company Chubb [2020] UKSC 38
case:
Enka Insaat Ve Sanayi AS v OOO Insurance Company Chubb - [2020] All ER (D) 36 (Oct)
Enka Insaat Ve Sanayi AS v OOO Insurance Company Chubb [2020] All ER 
(D) 36 (Oct)
[2020] UKSC 38
Supreme Court
Lord Kerr, Sales, Hamblen, Leggatt and Burrows  SCJJ
9 October 2020
Conflict of laws – Contract – Arbitration
Abstract
Applying the principles applicable to determining the proper law of an arbitration agreement when found in an 
agreement governed by a different system of law, the Supreme Court concluded that the contract from which a 
dispute had arisen in the present case contained no choice of the law that was intended to govern the contract or 
the arbitration agreement within it. Accordingly, the validity and scope of the arbitration agreement at issue (and the 
rest of the dispute resolution clause containing that agreement) was governed by the law of the chosen seat of 
arbitration, as the law with which the dispute resolution clause had been most closely connected. Consequently, the 
decision of the Court of Appeal, Civil Division, that the law applicable to the arbitration agreement at issue was 
English law, would be affirmed, albeit for different reasons. It followed that the appellant company's appeal was 
dismissed.
Digest
The judgment is available at: [2020] UKSC 38
  Background     
The claimant (Enka) was a Turkish company carrying on an international construction and engineering business. It 
had been engaged as a subcontractor to provide works relating to the boiler and auxiliary equipment installation at 
a power plant in Russia under a contract which contained an arbitration agreement. Clause 50.1a of the contract 
provided that the dispute would be referred to international arbitration and finally settled under the Rules of 
Arbitration of the International Chamber of Commerce, that the arbitration would be conducted in the English 
language, and that the place of arbitration would be London. It was common ground that the parties had not chosen 
a system of law specifically to govern the arbitration agreement.
The first defendant (Chubb Russia) was a Russian company and part of the well-known Chubb insurance group. 
Chubb Russia commenced proceedings against Enka and ten other parties in Russia seeking damages in relation 
to a fire at the power plant. Enka issued an arbitration claim form in the Commercial Court in London seeking, 
among other things, an anti-suit injunction restraining Chubb Russia from continuing the Russian proceedings in 
breach of cl 50. The judge dismissed Enka's claims against all the defendants on the main basis that he considered 
the appropriate forum to decide whether Chubb Russia's claim against Enka fell within the arbitration agreement to 
be the Russian courts and not the English Commercial Court.
Enka appealed to the Court of Appeal, Civil Division. In allowing Enka's appeal, the Court of Appeal held that unless 
there had been an express choice of the law that was to govern the arbitration agreement, the general rule should 
Page 2 of 4
*Enka Insaat Ve Sanayi AS v OOO Insurance Company Chubb - [2020] All ER (D) 36 (Oct)
be that the arbitration agreement was governed by the law of the seat, as a matter of implied choice, subject only to 
any particular features of the case demonstrating powerful reasons to the contrary. Consequently, the Court of 
Appeal issued an anti-suit injunction restraining Chubb Russia from continuing the Russian proceedings.
Chubb Russia appealed.
  Issues and decisions     
Which system of national law governed the validity and scope of the arbitration agreement when the law applicable 
to the contract containing it differed from the law of the seat of the arbitration.
Chubb Russia argued that the Court of Appeal's conclusion was heterodox and wrong and that the correct 
approach was that, in the absence of strong indications to the contrary, a choice of law for the contract was a 
choice of that law to govern the arbitration agreement. Chubb Russia contended that in the present case, the 
parties had chosen Russian law to govern the construction contract between them and that the implication that they 
had intended the arbitration agreement included in that contract to be governed by Russian law was not displaced 
by their choice of London as the seat of arbitration. Enka disputed that. Enka accepted that the main body of the 
construction contract was governed by Russian law but maintained that that was so only because of the 
connections between the construction contract and the law of Russia and not as a matter of choice.
The principles applicable to determining the proper law of an arbitration agreement when found in an agreement 
governed by a different system of law were as follows. First, where a contract contained an agreement to resolve 
disputes arising from it by arbitration, the law applicable to the arbitration agreement might not be the same as the 
law applicable to the other parts of the contract and was to be determined by applying English common law rules for 
resolving conflicts of laws rather than the provisions of the Rome I Regulation. Second, according to those rules, 
the law applicable to the arbitration agreement would be: (a) the law chosen by the parties to govern it; or (b) in the 
absence of such a choice, the system of law with which the arbitration agreement was most closely connected. 
third, whether the parties had agreed on a choice of law to govern the arbitration agreement was ascertained by 
construing the arbitration agreement and the contract containing it, as a whole, applying the rules of contractual 
interpretation of English law as the law of the forum. Fourth, where the law applicable to the arbitration agreement 
was not specified, a choice of governing law for the contract would generally apply to an arbitration agreement 
which forms part of the contract. Fifth, the choice of a different country as the seat of the arbitration is not, without 
more, sufficient to negate an inference that a choice of law to govern the contract was intended to apply to the 
arbitration agreement (see [171] of the judgment).
Sixth, additional factors which might, however, negate such an inference and could in some cases imply that the 
arbitration agreement had been intended to be governed by the law of the seat were: (a) any provision of the law of 
the seat which indicated that, where an arbitration was subject to that law, the arbitration would also be treated as 
governed by that country's law; or (b) the existence of a serious risk that, if governed by the same law as the main 
contract, the arbitration agreement would be ineffective. Either factor might be reinforced by circumstances 
indicating that the seat was deliberately chosen as a neutral forum for the arbitration. Seventh, where there was no 
express choice of law to govern the contract, a clause providing for arbitration in a particular place would not by 
itself justify an inference that the contract (or the arbitration agreement) was intended to be governed by the law of 
that place. Eighth, in the absence of any choice of law to govern the arbitration agreement, the arbitration 
agreement was governed by the law with which it was most closely connected. Where the parties had chosen a 
seat of arbitration, that would generally be the law of the seat, even if that differed from the law applicable to the 
parties' substantive contractual obligations. Ninth, the fact that the contract required the parties to attempt to resolve 
a dispute through good faith negotiation, mediation or any other procedure before referring it to arbitration would not 
generally provide a reason to displace the law of the seat of arbitration as the law applicable to the arbitration 
agreement by default in the absence of a choice of law to govern it (see [170] of the judgment).
One of the difficulties with the general rule proposed by the Court of Appeal was that it was not accepted that it was 
only in a minority of cases that an express choice of law to govern the contract should properly be construed as 
being a choice of law to govern an arbitration agreement included in the contract. As discussed, a clause such as 
Page 3 of 4
*Enka Insaat Ve Sanayi AS v OOO Insurance Company Chubb - [2020] All ER (D) 36 (Oct)
'This Agreement is to be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of [a named country]' was 
naturally and sensibly understood to mean that the law of that country should govern and determine the meaning 
and effect of all the clauses in the contract which the parties signed including the arbitration clause. It was unclear 
to us why more should be needed, or what more on the Court of Appeal's approach was required, to make it clear 
that a phrase such as 'This Agreement' meant the whole agreement and not just part of it (see [60] of the 
judgment).
The Court of Appeal had justified its approach on the ground that a choice of law to govern the contract 'has little if 
anything to say about the [arbitration agreement] law choice because it was directed to a different and separate 
agreement'. That was said to follow from the doctrine that an arbitration agreement was separable from the rest of 
the contract. That put the principle of separability of the arbitration agreement too high. For reasons already given, 
the requirement that an arbitration clause was to be treated as a distinct agreement for the purpose of determining 
its validity, existence and effectiveness made it more amenable than other parts of a contract to the application of a 
different law. The rationale underlying the separability principle was also relevant in cases where applying the 
governing law of the contract to the arbitration clause would render the arbitration agreement invalid or ineffective. 
However, it did not follow from the separability principle that an arbitration agreement was generally to be regarded 
as 'a different and separate agreement' from the rest of the contract or that a choice of governing law for the 
contract should not generally be interpreted as applying to an arbitration clause (see [61] of the judgment).
Applying the relevant principles (see [171] of the judgment), the contract from which a dispute had arisen in the 
present case contained no choice of the law that was intended to govern the contract or the arbitration agreement 
within it. In those circumstances, the validity and scope of the arbitration agreement (and the rest of the dispute 
resolution clause containing that agreement) was governed by the law of the chosen seat of arbitration, as the law 
with which the dispute resolution clause had most closely been connected. Accordingly, albeit for different reasons, 
the Court of Appeal's conclusion that the law applicable to the arbitration agreement was English law, would be 
affirmed (see [171] of the judgment).

IRAC_summ:
Case Name: Enka Insaat Ve Sanayi AS v OOO Insurance Company Chubb [2020] UKSC 38
Court + jurisdiction: United Kingdom Supreme Court
Area of law: Arbitration – Conflict of Laws – Contract
Procedural posture: Appeal from the Court of Appeal, Civil Division
Issue
Which system of law governs the validity and scope of an arbitration agreement where the main contract contains no express choice of law for the arbitration agreement itself, but provides for arbitration in London while the substantive contract is (arguably) governed by Russian law.
Rule
The law applicable to an arbitration agreement is determined by common law conflict rules: (1) the law expressly or impliedly chosen by the parties; or (2) in the absence of choice, the law with which the arbitration agreement is most closely connected. A choice of law for the main contract will generally be construed as applying to the arbitration agreement. However, if there is no choice of law for the main contract, the validity and scope of the arbitration agreement are governed by the law of the chosen seat of arbitration, as the law most closely connected to the dispute resolution clause.
Application
The Court clarified the hierarchy of rules. It rejected the Court of Appeal's presumption that the law of the seat generally governs the arbitration agreement even where there is a choice of law for the main contract. Instead, the Supreme Court held that a choice of law for the main contract usually extends to the arbitration clause [170].
However, applying this to the facts, the Court found that the construction contract contained no express or implied choice of law for the contract itself. While the contract had connections to Russia, there was no choice of Russian law agreed by the parties [171]. In the absence of any choice of law (for either the main contract or the arbitration clause), the Court applied the "closest connection" test. The arbitration agreement was part of a dispute resolution clause providing for arbitration in London. The Court held that an arbitration agreement is most closely connected with the law of the seat of arbitration (English law), rather than the law governing the substantive obligations (Russian law) [171].
Therefore, English law governed the arbitration agreement. Consequently, the English court was the appropriate forum to determine whether the claim fell within the arbitration clause and to grant an anti-suit injunction against the Russian proceedings.
Conclusion
The Court held that, in the absence of a choice of law for the contract, the arbitration agreement was governed by the law of the seat (English law), justifying the anti-suit injunction; the appeal was dismissed.

Superior Court of Pennsylvania

IRON AND STEEL REALTY INVESTMENTS, LLC v. TYLER HOBERMAN AND JENNIFER HOBERMAN, 
HUSBAND AND WIFE, AND HOBERMAN HOMES, LLC Appellants 

Notice: Decision text below is the first available text from the court; it has not been editorially reviewed by 
LexisNexis. Publisher's editorial review, including Headnotes, Case Summary, Shepard's analysis or any 
amendments will be added in accordance with LexisNexis editorial guidelines.

tax sale, unjust enrichment, trial court, preliminary objection, rental, rend, steel, format, gate, demurrer, confer a

Opinion

 [*1] Appeal from the Order Entered May 17, 2024

In the Court of Common Pleas of Westmoreland County Civil Division at

No(s): 1559 of 2023

BEFORE: KUNSELMAN, J., NICHOLS, J., and LANE, J.

MEMORANDUM BY NICHOLS, J.: FILED: October 28, 2025

Appellants Tyler Hoberman, Jennifer Hoberman, and Hoberman Homes,

LLC, appeal from an order overruling their preliminary objections to Appellee,

Iron and Steel Realty Investments, LLC's action alleging unjust enrichment.

Appellants claim that the trial court erred in concluding that Appellee had

stated a cause of action in unjust enrichment sufficient to overcome

preliminary objections. We affirm.

By way of background, this matter arises from an upset tax sale of



Page 2 of 7
Iron v. Hoberman, 2025 Pa. Super. Unpub. LEXIS 2790

property located at 1100 Willowbrook Road in Rostraver, Westmoreland

County (the Property). See Trial Ct. Op., 10/18/25, at 1; see also Iron and

Steel Realty Investments v. Westmoreland County Tax Claim Bureau

893 CD 2021, 2022 WL 2336050, at *1 (Pa. Cmwlth. filed Jun. 29, 2022)

(unpublished mem.) (Iron and Steel Tax Sale).1 In 2015, Appellee

purchased the Property as an "investment property to repair and flip for

profit." Iron and Steel Tax Sale, 2022 WL 2336050 at *2 (citation omitted).

On September 9, 2019, the Property was put up for "a tax sale by the

Westmoreland County Tax Claim Bureau for delinquent [*2]  taxes" and was

purchased by Appellant, Hoberman Homes, LLC (Hoberman Homes). See

Appellee's Am. Compl., 12/1/23, at ¶¶ 6-7; see also Iron and Steel Tax

Sale, 2022 WL 2336050 at *1-2. A deed confirming this tax sale to Hoberman

Homes was issued on December 10, 2019. See Appellee's Am. Compl.,

12/1/23, at Ex. "B" (Tax Sale Deed, 12/10/19).

On January 10, 2020, Appellee filed a petition to set aside the tax sale

and alleged that, by this action, Appellants were "placed on notice that

[Appellee] was questioning the legal propriety of the sale and consequently

[Appellants'] legal right of control, possession, and maintenance of [the

Property]." Id. at ¶¶ 11-12. Appellee alleged that Appellants were also placed

"on notice as to [Appellee's] claims" because Appellee "requested a Motion for

Stay, a Request for a Supersedeas and other relief[;]" and had "requested

that any rental amount being received by [Appellants] be placed into an

1 With regard to decisions of our sister Court, the Commonwealth Court, while we are not bound by these 
decisions, "such decisions provide persuasive authority and we may turn to our colleagues on the Commonwealth 
court for guidance when appropriate." Lynn v. Aria Health System, 227 A.3d 22, 32 (Pa. Super. 2020) (citation 
omitted and [*3]  some formatting altered). Further, we may cite to unreported memoranda of the Commonwealth 
Court filed after January 15, 2008 for persuasive value. See Pa.R.A.P. 126(b).

escrow account during the pendency of the appeal to the Commonwealth Court," which was "yet further notice of 
[Appellee's] claim to any rental proceeds generated from the rental of the premises." Id. at ¶¶ 20-21.

On July 6, 2021, the trial court granted Appellee's petition to set aside the tax sale. On August 3, 2021, the trial 
court entered an amended order directing Appellee to pay $9,311.32 to Hoberman Homes as reimbursement for the 
tax sale purchase price. Id. at ¶¶ 17-18; see also Iron and SteelTax Sale, 2022 WL 2336050 at * 3.



Page 3 of 7
Iron v. Hoberman, 2025 Pa. Super. Unpub. LEXIS 2790

Appellants timely appealed the tax sale set aside order to Commonwealth Court. See Appellee's Am. Compl., 
12/10/23, at ¶ 19. A panel of the Commonwealth Court concluded that Appellee's petition "was properly granted 
where the [Westmoreland County Tax Claim] Bureau conceded that it did not comply with the notice requirements 
of the Tax Sale

Law" and affirmed the trial court's set aside order on June 29, 2022. Ironand Steel Tax Sale, 2022 WL 2336050 at 
*10. Appellee regained possession of the Property on or about July 5, 2022. See Appellee's Am. Compl., 
12/10/23, [*4]  at ¶ 23.

After regaining possession of the Property, Appellee commenced the instant action by filing a complaint against 
Appellants on August 9, 2023. Appellee subsequently filed an amended complaint in which it alleged that 
Appellants "did not invest any proceeds into the Property, supply any labor to the Property, or otherwise add any 
value to the Property." Id. at ¶ 30 (some formatting altered).

Additionally, Appellee asserted that Appellants rented the Property to a

third-party tenant for a monthly amount of $1,700.00 from January 1, 2020

through June 30, 2022. Id. at ¶ 13. Because the tax sale was set aside,

Appellees asserted that Appellants "ab initio, had no right, title or interest to

the . . . Property," and "no legal or equitable claim for the receipt or retention

of the rental payments paid from January 1, 2020, through June 30, 2022."

Id. at ¶¶ 28, 34 (some formatting altered). Appellee further asserted that

"[a]s the owner of the . . . Property, [Appellee] is the proper party for

receiving rent for the use of the . . . Property," and that the rental income

"collected . . . and retained by [Appellants] from January 1, 2020, until June

30, 2022, is the rightful property of [Appellee]." [*5]  Id. at ¶¶ 29, 33 (some

formatting altered). Therefore, Appellee argued that Appellants' retention of

$51,000 in rental payments "would be unjust, inequitable, and an outright

deprivation of [Appellee's] property and contractual rights." Id. at ¶ 35.

Finally, Appellant asserted that

[t]he benefit received by [Appellants] did not arise through passivity. Rather, [Appellants] undertook direct concerted 
efforts to rent [the Property] and to collect monthly rent for the use and residence of [the Property] while knowing 
the propriety of the same was being questioned in the [trial court]. Additionally, [Appellants] opposed any and all 
efforts to place the rental money in an escrow account until the litigation was resolved and legal ownership of [the 
Property] could be determined.

Id. at ¶¶ 40, 41 (some formatting altered).2

Appellants subsequently filed preliminary objections to the amended

complaint in the nature of a demurrer. Therein, Appellants argued that

[t]o establish a claim of unjust enrichment, a plaintiff must show some benefit conferred on defendants by the 
plaintiff, appreciation of such benefits by defendants, and acceptance and retention of such benefits under 



Page 4 of 7
Iron v. Hoberman, 2025 Pa. Super. Unpub. LEXIS 2790

circumstances where it [*6]  would be inequitable for defendants to retain the particular benefit without payment of 
value.

Appellants' Prelim. Objs. to Am. Compl., 12/21/23, at 2 (citation omitted).

Appellants further contended that "[Appellee] did not confer any benefit on

[Appellants.]" Id.

After briefing and oral argument, the trial court entered an order

overruling Appellants' preliminary objections and holding that Appellee's

"allegations, when taken in the light most favorable to [Appellee], are

sufficient to set forth a claim at this stage of the pleadings." See Trial Ct.

Order, 5/17/24, at 1; Trial Ct. Op., 10/18/24, at 2-3.

On June 5, 2024, Appellants filed a motion requesting that the trial court

amend its May 17, 2024 order to include language from 42 Pa.C.S. 702(b)

to permit it to file an immediate appeal. After the trial court denied Appellants'

motion, Appellants filed a timely petition for permission to appeal with this

2 The Commonwealth Court, in Iron and Steel Tax Sale, noted that

Hoberman Homes had "represented to the [trial court] that it had paid $8,313.68 for the Property at the tax sale and 
. . . spent a total of $24,845.60 to date on the Property." Iron and Steel Tax Sale, 2022 WL 2336050 at *2 (citation 
omitted).

Court pursuant to Pa.R.A.P. 1311. This [*7]  Court granted Appellants' petition for review on September 12, 2024. 
Both Appellants and the trial court complied with Pa.R.A.P. 1925.

On appeal, Appellants present the following questions:

1. Whether [Appellee's amended complaint] sets forth a cause of action for unjust enrichment under the facts pled 
in that [Appellee] did not confer any "benefit" upon [Appellants].

2. Whether the [trial] court erred in its conclusion that the allegations of [Appellee's amended complaint] are 
sufficient to set forth a claim for unjust enrichment.

Appellants' Brief at 6.

Appellants' issues are related, therefore we address them together.

Appellants argue that Appellee failed to allege "facts suggesting that it conferred a benefit on [Appellants]" and, 
therefore, the trial court should have sustained its demurrer that Appellee failed to state a claim for unjust 
enrichment. Id. at 19 (some formatting altered). Specifically, Appellants argue that Appellee did not plead that it 
gave anything to Appellants, performed any work or services for Appellants, or paid any debt or saved Appellants 
any expense or loss. Id. at 18. Appellants also claim that Appellee did not allege that it was renting out the Property 
at the time of [*8]  the tax sale and, accordingly, Appellee had not pled that it "suffered any 'loss' for which 
restitution may be directed." Id.



Page 5 of 7
Iron v. Hoberman, 2025 Pa. Super. Unpub. LEXIS 2790

Appellants observe that "there appears to be no statutory enactment providing that the purchaser at tax sale is 
liable for rents to the original owner

should the tax sale subsequently be declared void." Id. at 21. In support,

Appellants direct our attention to Dubin v. County of Northumberland, 847

A.2d 769 (Pa. Cmwlth. 2004), in which the Commonwealth Court found that

"the plaintiffs 'failed to state a claim for unjust enrichment because they have

failed to prove that they conferred benefits' on the defendants," where "the

defendants were not liable to the plaintiff landowner for the profits and

benefits received during the lease terms." Id. (quoting Dubin, 847 A.2d at

773). Appellants conclude that the trial court erred in overruling their

preliminary objections because the facts alleged by Appellee, that is, "the use

of [Appellee's] property to collect a monthly rent" to establish "the benefit

conferred on [Appellants,]" is "inconsistent with both appellate authority and

analogous statutory enactments." Id. at 22-23 (citation omitted).

In reviewing a trial court's ruling on preliminary [*9]  objections,

we deem all material facts averred in the complaint, and all reasonable inferences that can be drawn therefrom[] to 
be true. The purpose of our inquiry is to determine the legal sufficiency of the complaint and whether the pleading 
would permit recovery if ultimately proven. When sustaining the trial court's ruling will result in the denial of claim or 
a dismissal of suit, preliminary objections will be sustained only where the case is free and clear of doubt. With 
regard to preliminary objections in the nature of demurrer, we consider whether, on the facts averred, the law says 
with certainty that no recovery is possible. Where a doubt exists as to whether a demurrer should be sustained, this 
doubt should be resolved in favor of overruling it.

Commonwealth by Shapiro v. Golden Gate National Senior Care LLC,

194 A.3d 1010, 1022 (Pa. 2018) (citations omitted and some formatting

altered) (Golden Gate). "We will reverse the trial court's decision regarding

preliminary objections only where there has been an error of law or abuse of

discretion." Ashton v. Aventus Pasteur, Inc., 851 A.2d 908, 911 (Pa.

Super. 2004) (citation omitted).

This Court has explained:

A claim for unjust enrichment arises from a quasi-contract. A quasi-contract [*10]  imposes a duty, not as a result of 
any agreement, whether express or implied, but in spite of the absence of an agreement, when one party receives 
unjust enrichment at the expense of another.

The elements of unjust enrichment are benefits conferred on defendant by plaintiff, appreciation of such benefits by 
defendant, and acceptance and retention of such benefits under such circumstances that it would be inequitable for 
defendant to retain the benefit without payment of value. Whether the doctrine applies depends on the unique 



Page 6 of 7
Iron v. Hoberman, 2025 Pa. Super. Unpub. LEXIS 2790

factual circumstances of each case. In determining if the doctrine applies, we focus not on the intention of the 
parties, but rather on whether the defendant has been unjustly enriched.

Moreover, the most significant element of the doctrine is whether the enrichment of the defendant is unjust. The 
doctrine does not apply simply because the defendant may have benefited as a result of the actions of the plaintiff.

Stoeckinger v. Presidential Financial Corp. of Delaware Valley, 948

A.2d 828, 833 (Pa. Super. 2008) (citations omitted, some formatting altered,

and emphasis in original).

Here, the trial court stated that it

accepted [Appellee's] allegations as true in accordance [*11]  with the standard for preliminary objections" and, in 
so doing, found "that each of the[] elements [of unjust enrichment] were sufficiently ple[d]. [Appellee] allege[d] that 
the benefit conferred on

[Appellants] by [Appellee] was the use of [Appellee's] property to collect a monthly rent. [Appellants] appreciated the 
benefit of using [Appellee's] property by renting the property and collecting

the monthly rental payments. Further, [Appellants] accepted and retained the monthly rental amounts under 
circumstances that would be inequitable as a result of [Appellee's] petition to set aside the tax sale, the actions 
taken by [Appellee] in that matter, the ruling by the [trial court] overturning the tax sale, and the appeal of that ruling 
with no stay during the pendency of that appeal. Based on these allegations, [Appellee's] claims for unjust 
enrichment were sufficiently ple[d].

Trial Ct. Op., 10/18/24, at 4.

Based on our review of the record, we find no abuse of discretion or

error of law in the trial court's order overruling Appellants' preliminary

objections. See Ashton, 851 A.2d at 911. As noted previously, when ruling

on preliminary objections, the trial court must evaluate the sufficiency of the

pleadings, [*12]  treating all material facts alleged as true. See Golden Gate, 194

A.3d at 1022. Here, Appellee raised a claim for unjust enrichment and pled

that Appellees conferred a benefit upon Appellants when Appellants collected

monthly rent for the Property. See Appellee's Am. Compl., 12/10/23, at ¶¶

13-40. Even if, as Appellants contend, no statute or case law establishes that

Appellants were liable to Appellee for the alleged rental income collected for

the use of the Property, the trial court was not required to conclude that it

would be impossible for Appellee to establish that it conferred a benefit upon

Appellants under a claim of unjust enrichment when ruling on a demurrer.

See Golden Gate, 194 A.3d at 1022 (directing that "[w]here a doubt exists

as to whether a demurrer should be sustained, this doubt should be resolved



Page 7 of 7
Iron v. Hoberman, 2025 Pa. Super. Unpub. LEXIS 2790

in favor of overruling it"). Therefore, we agree with the trial court that

Appellee adequately pled its claim for unjust enrichment. See Stoeckinger, 948 A.2d at 833; see also Golden 
Gate, 194 A.3d at 1022.

Further, to the extent Appellants rely on Dubin, that case involved an unjust enrichment claim in the context of 
summary judgment, not preliminary objections. See Dubin, 847 A.2d at 771 n.7 (explaining that "[s]ummary 
judgment [*13]  is only appropriate when, after examining the record in the light most favorable to the non-moving 
party, there is no genuine issue of material fact, and the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law"). 
As noted previously, in ruling on preliminary objections, the trial court was required to assume that all of the 
allegations in Appellee's amended complaint were true. See Golden Gate, 194 A.3d at 1022. Therefore, Dubin 
does not foreclose the possibility that Appellee could establish that it conferred a benefit upon Appellants in support 
of its claim of unjust enrichment. See Dubin, 847 A.2d at 771.

We are mindful that a finding of unjust enrichment depends on "the unique factual circumstances of each case" and 
depends "not on the intention of the parties, but rather on whether the defendant[s, here, Appellants] ha[ve] been 
unjustly enriched." Stoeckinger, 948 A.2d at 833 (citations omitted). At this stage of proceedings, however, the 
facts, and the equitable considerations and conclusions to be drawn from those facts, have not yet been developed. 
Accordingly, Appellants are not entitled to relief on their claims. See Golden Gate, 194 A.3d at 1022; Ashton, 851 
A.2d at 911. For these reasons, we affirm the trial court's order. [*14] 

Order affirmed. Jurisdiction relinquished.

IRAC_summ:
Case Name: Iron v. Hoberman [2025] Pa. Super. Unpub. LEXIS 2790
Court: Superior Court of Pennsylvania
Area of law: Restitution—Unjust Enrichment
Procedural posture: Interlocutory appeal from an order overruling preliminary objections.
Issue
Whether a plaintiff sufficiently pleads the "benefit conferred" element of an unjust enrichment claim against a tax-sale purchaser by alleging that the purchaser collected rent on the plaintiff's property during the period before the tax sale was judicially set aside.
Rule
To state a claim for unjust enrichment, a plaintiff must plead: (1) benefits conferred on the defendant by the plaintiff; (2) appreciation of such benefits by the defendant; and (3) acceptance and retention of such benefits under circumstances where it would be inequitable to do so without payment of value (Stoeckinger). When reviewing preliminary objections in the nature of a demurrer, the court must accept all material facts as true and sustain the objection only if the law says with certainty that no recovery is possible (Golden Gate).
Application
The court affirms the overruling of the preliminary objections. Appellee (the original owner) alleged that Appellants (the purchasers) were unjustly enriched by collecting $51,000 in rent from a third-party tenant during the time Appellants held title under a tax sale that was later voided. Appellants argued that Appellee failed to state a claim because Appellee did not directly "confer" a benefit (such as goods or services) upon them; rather, Appellants collected the rent themselves.
The court rejects this argument at the pleading stage. It reasons that Appellee sufficiently pleaded that the benefit conferred was the use of the property itself to generate income. Because the tax sale was set aside, Appellants had no valid right to the property ab initio. Therefore, retaining the rental income derived from Appellee's property would be inequitable. The court distinguishes the Dubin case relied upon by Appellants, noting it was decided at the summary judgment stage, whereas the current standard requires resolving all doubts in favor of the plaintiff.
Conclusion
The order overruling the preliminary objections is affirmed.

CONSUMER CREDIT – UNFAIR RELATIONSHIP – LIMITATION PERIOD
Abstract
The Supreme Court allowed the appeal of the original claimants from a decision of the Court of Appeal (Civil 
Division) allowing the defendant bank's joined appeals against decisions to allow two claims for compensation 
under the Consumer Credit Act 1974 arising from payment protection insurance (PPI) that had been taken out by 
the claimants at the same time as agreements for credit cards from the defendant bank. The Court held that a claim 
for a remedial order under s 140B of the Consumer Credit Act 1974 could  be made at any time while the credit 
relationship said to be unfair to the debtor was continuing. The relevant relationship was the relationship arising out 
of the credit card agreement between the bank and the claimant, which continued after the PPI policy came to an 
end. The period of limitation began to run only when the relationship ended and expired after six years. Each of the  
claims was brought within that period. So the claims were not time-barred.
Digest
The judgment is available at: [2023] UKSC 34
  Background     
The two claimants, K and D, each had a credit card issued by the defendant bank who also sold them Payment 
Protection Insurance (PPI). The PPI did not go to the insurer, but was retained by the defendant as commission. In 
2007, amendments to the Consumer Credit Act 1974 (CCA 1974) brought about by the Consumer Credit Act 2006 
(CCA 2006) came into effect, which introduced the ability to bring a claim for an unfair credit relationship. The new 
law applied to existing credit agreements if they remained in force after the end of the transitional period provided 
by CCA 2006 paras 14 and 16 of sch 3. S and B had cancelled their PPI agreements before the end of the 
transitional period, although their credit card agreements remained in place for some time after until they were also 
terminated. The defendant offered K and D redress (in 2018 and 2017, respectively) under a scheme for PPI mis
selling established by the Financial Conduct Authority. In 2019, S and B each brought a claim in the county court, 
seeking an order under CCA 1974 s 140B that the defendant repay all the money paid by them for PPI. 
S's claim succeeded before the district judge; and in B's case the district judge made a ruling that the claim had 
been brought in time. Those decisions were both upheld on appeal by the county court. On its appeal to the Court 
of Appeal, the defendant advanced two grounds of appeal. The first was that by reason of the transitional provisions 
which regulated the entry into force in 2007 of the relevant provisions of the CCA 1974, the claimants had no claim. 
The second was that the claims were in any event time-barred by s 9 of the Limitation Act 1980 (LA 1980). The 
Court of Appeal ruled in favour of the defendant holding that in each case the relevant time limit for bringing a claim 
had expired before the claim was brought. S and B appealed to the Supreme Court. The two issues argued before 
the Court of Appeal were raised again. 
Smith and another v Royal Bank of Scotland Plc [2023] All ER (D) 15 (Oct)
Page 2 of 3
  Issues and decisions     
Whether S and B were entitled to bring their claims, or whether they were barred by reason of  the transitional 
provisions or LA 1980. 
The new scheme under CCA 1974 had been intended to provide consumers with greater protection based on the 
concept of an 'unfair relationship' (see [12] of the judgment).
In dealing with a claim by a debtor under the provisions, the court was required to follow a two-stage process. The 
first stage was to determine whether the relationship between the creditor and the debtor arising out of the credit 
agreement was unfair to the debtor because of one or more of the matters specified in CCA 1974 s 140A(1). If the 
court found that the relationship was unfair for that reason, the court had then to proceed to the second stage and 
decide what, if any, order to make, selecting from the list of options in CCA 1974 s 140B(1). There were other 
general points  to be considered (see [16], [17]-[22] of the judgment). 
The possible causes of unfairness in CCA 1974 s 140A(1)(a)-(c) demonstrated that, for the purpose of deciding 
whether the relationship was (or was when it ended) unfair to the debtor, the court had to consider the whole history 
of the relationship - going back not only to the making of the credit agreement but to any relevant act or omission of 
the creditor before the making of that agreement or any related agreement. That was so without any limit on how 
long ago the credit agreement or any related agreement had been made. The matters to which the court was 
obliged to have regard were not limited in time (see [23] of the judgment). 
As well as requiring the court to make a very broad and holistic assessment to decide whether the relationship 
between the creditor and the debtor was unfair to the debtor, the legislation also had given  the court, where a 
determination of unfairness was made, the broadest possible remedial discretion in deciding what order, if any, to 
make under CCA 1974 s 140B. Section 140B gave the court an extensive menu of options from which to select but 
said nothing at all about how that selection should be made. On the face of the legislation the court's discretion was 
entirely unfettered. It was clear that the court was not, in the circumstances, required to engage in the kind of strict 
analysis of causation, loss and so forth that would be required, for example, in deciding what remedy to award in a 
claim founded on the law of contract or tort. Some constraint was, however, imposed by consideration of the 
general purpose of an order under CCA 1974 s 140B (see [25] of the judgment). 
The defendant had not disputed that in each case its failure to disclose the commission that it had received made 
the relationship arising out of the credit agreement (taken with the related PPI agreement) unfair to the claimant and 
that, if the claim had been brought in time, the remedial order made in the case of S was one which the court was 
entitled to make (see [30] of the judgment). 
Its main argument was that the claims were barred by la 1980 s 9 because they were claims to recover money 
brought 'after the expiration of six years from the date on which the cause of action accrued' (see [31]of the 
judgment). 
The defendant argued that the 'cause of action' had  accrued when each of PPI payment had been made. As the 
last such payment had been made in, respectively, April 2006 (by S)  and March 2008 (by B), the six year time limit 
had expired in each case long before their claims had been brought in 2019 (see [32] of the judgment). 
The argument would be rejected, for as long as the credit relationship lasted, no cause of action accrued for which 
the debtor then had a period of time in which to sue for a remedy under CCA 1974 s 140B. Any entitlement to a 
remedial order arose from a set of facts which was complete only at the time when the order was made. Once the 
credit relationship ended, the position changed. A determination that the relationship was unfair to the debtor on the 
date when it ended could be made on that date or any later date. All the facts relevant to the determination were 
fixed when the relationships ended and nothing that occurred subsequently could affect the assessment of fairness. 
It could therefore be said that a cause of action had accrued so that the period of limitation started to run. 
Therefore, the cause of action had not accrued, and 
Smith and another v Royal Bank of Scotland Plc [2023] All ER (D) 15 (Oct)
Page 3 of 3
the six year period for bringing a claim had not commenced until the credit relationship ended 
(in 2015 and 2019, respectively). It followed that both claims were brought in time (see [42]-[45] of the judgment).
As an alternative argument, the defendant relied on the Court of Appeal's reasoning however, that confused the 
question of when the relationship had come to an end with the different 
question of when (if at all before it came to an end) the relationship ceased to be unfair. The Court of Appeal should 
have affirmed the conclusions of the courts below that the relevant credit relationships remained unfair to the 
debtors when they ended and that the claims seeking a remedy for that unfairness had been brought in time (see 
[69] of the judgment).

IRAC_summ:
Case Name: Smith and another v Royal Bank of Scotland Plc [2023] UKSC 34
Court + jurisdiction: Supreme Court of the United Kingdom
Area of law: Consumer Credit – Unfair Relationships – Limitation Periods
Procedural posture: Appeal from the Court of Appeal (Civil Division)
Issue
Whether the six-year limitation period for a claim under s 140B of the Consumer Credit Act 1974 (CCA 1974), alleging an unfair relationship arising from the non-disclosure of PPI commissions, begins to run from the date of the last PPI payment or from the date the underlying credit relationship (e.g., the credit card agreement) ended.
Rule
Under s 9 of the Limitation Act 1980, an action to recover any sum recoverable by virtue of any enactment must be brought within six years from the date on which the cause of action accrued. A claim under s 140B of the CCA 1974 is based on an "unfair relationship" between the creditor and the debtor. The relationship is a continuing one, and the court must assess fairness by looking at the entire history of the relationship up to the point it ends. Therefore, the cause of action for an order under s 140B does not accrue—and the limitation period does not start running—until the credit relationship itself has ended.
Application
The claimants had credit card agreements with the bank and took out PPI policies. They made their last PPI payments in 2006 and 2008, respectively, but their credit card agreements continued until 2015 and 2019. They brought claims in 2019 seeking repayment of PPI commissions, arguing the relationship was unfair due to non-disclosure. The bank argued the claims were time-barred because the cause of action accrued when the last PPI payments were made (more than six years prior).
The Supreme Court rejected the bank's argument. The Court reasoned that the "relationship" under s 140A is a single, continuous legal relationship arising from the credit agreement and any related agreements (like PPI) [42]. The unfairness is an attribute of this ongoing relationship, not a specific historic event. As long as the relationship persists, the unfairness can be remedied, and the court can make an order based on the relationship as it stands at the time of trial or when it ended [43].
Consequently, a debtor does not have a completed cause of action that triggers the limitation clock merely because a specific unfair act (like a payment) occurred. Instead, the right to seek a remedial order continues throughout the relationship. The limitation period only begins to run once the relationship ends, because that is the point at which the facts of the relationship are fixed and the opportunity to seek relief for an ongoing unfair state of affairs ceases [44]–[45]. Since the claimants brought their actions within six years of their credit card agreements ending, their claims were in time.
Conclusion
The Court allowed the appeal, holding that the limitation period for a s 140B claim runs from the end of the credit relationship, not the date of the last payment related to the unfairness.

case_name: In re Verret [2025] Tex. App. LEXIS 8287
case:
Page 1 of 4
In re Verret, 2025 Tex. App. LEXIS 8287

In re Verret
Court of Appeals of Texas, First District, Houston

October 28, 2025, Opinion Issued

NO. 01-25-00390-CV

Reporter
2025 Tex. App. LEXIS 8287 *; 2025 LX 470923

IN RE CHERYL VERRET, Relator

Core Terms

mandamus, new trial, non-jury, default

Counsel:  [*1] For Verret, Cheryl, Relator: Charlotte Dawn Rainwater, Antwonique Turner, Sofia Vlahakos.

For Verret, Chad, Real party in interest: Dennis Marston Slate, Karlene Dunn Poll.

Judges: Panel consists of Justices Rivas-Molloy, Gunn, and Caughey. Justice Gunn, concurring.

Opinion

Original Proceeding on Petition for Writ of Mandamus

MEMORANDUM OPINION

Relator, Cheryl Verret, has filed a petition for writ of mandamus challenging the trial court's order granting new trial 
and setting aside the judgment of the preceding trial court judge following a bench trial.1 We deny the petition.

PER CURIAM

Concur by: David Gunn

Concur

CONCURRING OPINION

1 The underlying case is In the Matter of the Marriage of Chad J. Verret and Cheryl Newman Verret, cause number 2022-67908, 
pending in the 507th District Court of Harris County, Texas, the Honorable Lilian H. Alexander presiding.



Page 2 of 4
In re Verret, 2025 Tex. App. LEXIS 8287

The judge presided over a bench trial and signed a final judgment, but she later left office before plenary power 
expired. Her successor, who had not sat through any of the trial, used that plenary power and ordered a new trial. 
Relator assails that order by petition for writ of mandamus.

Mandamus would be cognizable if the first trial had been to a jury, but things become murkier when the trial takes 
place non-jury. Does the removal of the jury matter to the availability of mandamus relief?

The courts of appeals tend to think so. [*2] 1 They allow mandamus if the new trial order threw out a jury verdict, but 
not otherwise. After all, the last 20 years of supreme court decisions in this area stress the value of the right to a 
jury trial, based on the historic role of juries in American law.2 It is hard to make the same case for non-jury trials. 
For this reason, denying relief appears to be proper. See Ospina v. Garcia Florez, No. 01-19-00465-CV, 2021 WL 
2149334, at *4 (Tex. App.—Houston [1st Dist.] May 27, 2021, pet. denied) (mem. op.) ("This case does not involve 
the same concerns that In re Columbia Medical Center presented. This is not a situation in which the trial court 
granted a motion for new trial and set aside a jury verdict without stating its reasons beyond 'in the interests of 
justice and fairness.' Rather, the divorce case was tried to the bench, not a jury.").

This conclusion admittedly gives me some pause. Relator notes the anomaly that occurs when a new judge 
overturns the old judge's work without having heard the evidence. Fair enough, but that anomaly largely comes as a 
fact of life. Every time a new judge takes office, there is the possibility of undoing the rulings of a predecessor. 
Texas has accepted this anomaly as inherent in the system. Further, our system allows judges to sit for each other 
on various [*3]  occasions. For instance, a judge with a medical issue might have a colleague sit in for a part of the 
trial. These things happen. See id. at *5.

Quite apart from the wrinkle of the successor judge, relator questions why non-jury cases should be exempt from 
mandamus review of new trial orders. One could easily make arguments for expanding mandamus beyond where 
the Toyota line of cases took it. Litigants in bench trials care just as much about the process, benefit just as much 
from a good explanation, and deserve just as much respect as litigants who put themselves upon the country.

However, if we were to open the door to extraordinary relief in non-jury cases, it would undermine the doctrinal 
framework of the Toyota line of cases. Toyota and its progeny placed jury trials on something of a pedestal. If we 
were to give identical treatment to non-jury trials, it would amount to putting all things onto pedestals, which really 
means putting none of them onto a pedestal.

When more years of experience in the post-Toyota world have accumulated, the supreme court will have the benefit 
of those years in evaluating how well the current approach has been working. But that is for another court and 
another day. For the time being, [*4]  my best reading of the high court's extant cases persuades me that those 
cases fit better with a mandamus denial here than with a grant.

All that said, Texas could improve the system with one simple step: allow for review of new trial orders by ordinary 
appeal after the second trial. This would not require expanding mandamus any further. It would simply require the 
parties to get back in the courtroom, get to final judgment without losing another year to mandamus struggles, and 
bring the matter up on appeal.

1 See, e.g., In re Velasquez, No. 04-25-00091-CV, 2025 WL 1063434, at *4 (Tex. App.—San Antonio Apr. 9, 2025, orig. 
proceeding) (mem. op.); In re Foster, No. 05-15-00179-CV, 2015 WL 682335, at *1 (Tex. App.—Dallas Feb. 18, 2015, orig. 
proceeding) (mem. op.); In re Old Am. Cnty. Mut. Fire Ins. Co., No. 13-13-00644-CV, 2014 WL 1633098, at *10-11 (Tex. App.—
Corpus Christi—Edinburg Apr. 23, 2014, orig. proceeding) (mem. op.).

2 See In re Rudolph Auto., LLC, 674 S.W.3d 289, 299-302 (Tex. 2023) (orig. proceeding); In re Bent, 487 S.W.3d 170, 175-78 
(Tex. 2016) (orig. proceeding); In re Toyota Motor Sales, U.S.A., Inc., 407 S.W.3d 746, 755-59, 762 (Tex. 2013) (orig. 
proceeding); In re United Scaffolding, Inc., 377 S.W.3d 685, 686-87 (Tex. 2012) (orig. proceeding); In re Columbia Med. Ctr. of 
Las Colinas, Subsidiary, L.P., 290 S.W.3d 204, 209 (Tex. 2009) (orig. proceeding).



Page 3 of 4
In re Verret, 2025 Tex. App. LEXIS 8287

First, the federal courts have a good track record with allowing such review: "An order granting a new trial is not 
appealable, but it is certainly reviewable. On appeal from the final judgment following the second trial, the appellant 
may claim error in the grant of the new trial. If the appellate court agrees, it will reinstate the verdict reached at the 
first trial." 11 CHARLES ALAN WRIGHT, ARTHUR R. MILLER, MARY KAY KANE & ALLAN STEIN, FEDERAL PRACTICE AND 
PROCEDURE § 2818 (3d ed. 2025).3

Second, adopting the federal approach would strike a sensible balance. It would protect the right to a fair trial while 
also protecting the courts and the parties from the inefficiencies [*5]  of mandamus practice. Mandamus comes with 
costs. For every petition that we grant, there may be ten or twenty more that we deny. The success rate of 
mandamus petitions has historically been in the low single digits. See Patricia J. Askew, "Click Bait" for the Courts, 
and Other Mandamus Practice Tips 44, State Bar of Texas, Advanced Trial Strategies Course (2025). Perhaps the 
rate is higher for new trial grants, but whatever it is, some mandamus petitions will fail, with all the attendant 
expense in time and money.

That expense will be substantial. Start with money. To pursue mandamus review of an order granting a new trial, 
the seasoned practitioner typically files the entire trial record—every exhibit, every scrap of testimony, everything—
rather than face the risk of the petition being dead on arrival for want of an adequate record. The cost of getting a 
full record will outrun the cost of a discovery mandamus about overbroad interrogatories or the like.

Next comes lawyer time, which means more money. Mandamus also takes up court time and resources. In contrast 
to the era when my career began, today's appellate courts have more and more staff attorneys who do more and 
more mandamus, [*6]  with some doing little else.

Finally, review by ordinary appeal after the new trial would be consistent with the twenty-first century world. 
Although some older cases arguably foreclose the position taken here, those precedents strike me as obsolete. 
Shortly before the dawn of the Toyota era, Texas usually said no to review of an order granting a new trial. The two 
exceptions to that rule were so narrow as to be unworthy of attention here. See Johnson v. Fourth Ct. of Appeals, 
700 S.W.2d 916, 918 (Tex. 1985) (orig. proceeding). The saying was that a trial judge could grant a new trial for 
good grounds, bad grounds, or coffee grounds.

The main precedent against ordinary appellate review was a default judgment case called Cummins v. Paisan 
Construction Co., 682 S.W.2d 235 (Tex. 1984) (per curiam). There a trial court set aside a default judgment and 
proceeded to trial on the merits. Id. at 235. On appeal after the (only) trial, this Court examined the new trial order 
and found that the evidence supported setting aside the default judgment. Id. at 235-36; see Cummins v. Paisan 
Constr. Co., 682 S.W.2d 323, 325-26 (Tex. App.—Houston [1st Dist.] 1984, writ ref'd n.r.e.).

The supreme court denied review. Its short per curiam opinion stated that "the trial court's order setting aside the 
default judgment and granting the motion for new trial is not reviewable on appeal." Cummins, 682 S.W.2d at 235-
36. The opinion stated that this Court reached the right result for the wrong reason. [*7]  Id. at 236. Obviously, 
Cummins involved a default, not a trial to the bench, as occurred here, so it may well be distinguishable.

The world of Cummins traced back to at least 1961 and maybe even earlier.4 Today, however, it seems to me that 
the world of Cummins has ceased to exist. That world fell away with the most recent supreme court decisions, from 

3 See, e.g., Latino v. Kaizer, 58 F.3d 310, 314 (7th Cir. 1995) ("An order granting a new trial is not a final order within the 
meaning of 28 U.S.C. § 1291 and is therefore generally not immediately appealable. Nevertheless, after a new trial and entry of 
final judgment an appellate court entertaining an appeal from the final judgment may review the decision to grant a new trial and, 
where appropriate, reinstate the original verdict."); Wallake Power Sys., LLC v. Engine Distribs., Inc., No. 22-3399, 2023 WL 
3966740, at *5 n.7 (6th Cir. June 13, 2023) (similar); Duncan v. Duncan, 377 F.2d 49, 52 (6th Cir. 1967) ("[I]t is clear that such 
orders [granting a new trial] are reviewable on appeal from the final judgment in the second trial.").

4 The decision in Cummins relied on Burroughs v. Leslie, 620 S.W.2d 643, 644 (Tex. Civ. App.—Dallas 1981, writ ref'd n.r.e.), 
which in turn traced back to Ebaugh v. State, 342 S.W.2d 221, 222-23 (Tex. Civ. App.—Austin 1961, writ ref'd n.r.e.), but the 



Page 4 of 4
In re Verret, 2025 Tex. App. LEXIS 8287

the Toyota trilogy to Bent and Rudolph. So to the extent that the federal approach proposed here—allowing 
ordinary appeal after a second trial—faces a wall of older Texas cases, the proper response should be the phrase 
once spoken about a different barrier of roughly the same vintage: "Tear down this wall."

David Gunn

Justice

IRAC_summ:
Case Name: In re Verret [2025] Tex. App. LEXIS 8287
Court: Court of Appeals of Texas, First District
Area of law: Civil Procedure—Mandamus; New Trial
Procedural posture: Original Proceeding on Petition for Writ of Mandamus
Issue
Whether a relator is entitled to mandamus relief to vacate a successor judge’s order granting a new trial following a non-jury bench trial. The specific legal question is whether the heightened standard prohibiting trial courts from granting new trials without specific reasons—which applies to jury verdicts—extends to bench trials.
Rule
Mandamus relief is generally available when a trial court grants a motion for new trial and sets aside a jury verdict without stating its reasons, as such orders must be specific to protect the right to a jury trial (In re Columbia Med. Ctr.; In re Toyota). However, Texas courts of appeals generally hold that this requirement does not extend to non-jury trials (Ospina v. Garcia Florez). A successor judge typically possesses plenary power to undo the rulings of a predecessor, including granting a new trial.
Application
The court denies the petition for writ of mandamus filed by Relator Cheryl Verret. The underlying case involved a divorce tried to the bench. The presiding judge signed a final judgment but left office before plenary power expired. The successor judge, who had not heard the evidence, granted a new trial.
In a concurring opinion providing the substantive analysis for the denial, the court explains that the "Toyota line of cases" is predicated on the historic role and value of the jury in the American legal system. The court reasons that because the underlying trial was a non-jury bench trial, the concerns regarding the sanctity of a jury verdict are absent. Consequently, the successor judge retained the discretion to grant a new trial without the heightened requirement to provide specific reasons that would otherwise be reviewable by mandamus. The court notes that while it may seem anomalous for a judge who did not hear the evidence to overturn a judgment, this is an accepted risk in the system when judges change office. Extending mandamus review to new trial orders in bench trials would undermine the doctrinal distinction established by the Supreme Court of Texas.
Conclusion
The petition for writ of mandamus is denied.
