Kisting-Leung v. Cigna Corp.
This matter is before the court on defendants' motion to dismiss filed on August 23, 2024. (Doc. No. 46.)
Defendants' motion was taken under submission on the papers pursuant to Local Rule 230(g). (Doc. No. 51.) For
the reasons explained below, defendants' motion to dismiss will be granted in part and denied in part.
BACKGROUND
Plaintiffs Suzanne Kisting-Leung, Samantha Dababneh, Randall Rentsch, Christina Thornhill, Amanda Bredlow,
and Abdulhussein Abbas (collectively, "plaintiffs") bring this putative class action against defendants Cigna
Corporation and Cigna Health and Life Insurance Company (collectively, "defendants") for purported wrongful
denial of plaintiffs' claims for benefits and for defendants' use of the automated PxDx algorithm to review plaintiffs'
claims. (Doc. No. 36.) On July 24, 2023, plaintiffs filed this suit. (Doc. No. 1.) Pursuant to various stipulations of the
parties, on June 14, 2024, plaintiffs filed their operative third amended complaint ("TAC"), (Doc. No. 36), in which
they allege as follows.
Plaintiffs are and at all relevant times have been beneficiaries of health insurance [**3] plans, and defendants are
and were the named claims administrators of those plans. (Id. at ¶¶ 16-21.) Plaintiffs Kisting-Leung, Dababneh,
Rentsch, Thornhill, and Abbas had benefit claims wrongfully denied by defendants as not medically necessary. (Id.
at ¶¶ 41, 45, 54, 63, 66, 70, 72, 80, 95-96.) For instance, plaintiff Kisting-Leung's claim for benefits to cover a
transvaginal ultrasound was denied even though "[a]ccording to Cigna's Medical Coverage Policy, a transvaginal
ultrasound is considered 'medically necessary for the evaluation of suspected pelvic pathology or for screening or
surveillance of a woman at increased risk for ovarian or endometrial cancer.'" (Id. at ¶¶ 40-42.) Plaintiff Bredlow had
a claim for benefits wrongfully denied because, according to defendants, "the submitted code for the procedure was
'missing or invalid[.]'" (Id. at ¶ 87.) "Cigna must provide benefits for covered health services and pay all reasonable
and medically necessary expenses incurred by a covered member." (Id. at ¶ 25.)
"Cigna's policies falsely claim that determinations related to medical necessity of health care services would be
made by a medical director, when in reality the medical directors [**4] are not involved in reviewing patients'
claims." (Id. at ¶ 9.) Each of plaintiffs' claims for benefits were in fact reviewed and denied by defendants' PxDx
algorithm. (Id. at ¶ 6.)
"Cigna developed an algorithm known as PXDX that it relies on to enable its doctors to automatically deny
payments in batches of hundreds or thousands at a time for treatments that do not match certain pre-set criteria[.]"
(Id. at ¶ 2.) "Relying on the PXDX system, Cigna's doctors instantly [*996] reject claims on medical grounds
without ever opening patient files, leaving thousands of patients effectively without coverage and with unexpected
bills." (Id. at ¶ 3.) "[O]ver a period of two months in 2022, Cigna doctors denied over 300,000 requests for payment
using this method, spending an average of just 1.2 seconds 'reviewing' each request." (Id.) "The PXDX system
saves Cigna money by allowing it to deny claims it previously paid[.]" (Id. at ¶ 4.)
"Cigna routinely fails to disclose that the PXDX algorithm was the reason for many adverse benefits
determinations." (Id. at ¶ 31.) Plaintiff Rentsch did receive a benefits denial letter indicating that the PxDx algorithm
reviewed his claims. (Id. at ¶ 63.) However, plaintiff [**5] Rentsch only "discovered through an article published by
ProPublica that Defendants had been using the PXDX algorithm to review patients' claims." (Id. at ¶ 73.) "Prior to
that, Mr. Rentsch had no knowledge of this illegal practice by Defendants." (Id.)1
"Defendants' actions constitute an unlawful denial of health insurance benefits under ERISA, as provided in 29
U.S.C. § 1132(a)(1)(B)." (Id. at ¶ 124.) Further, defendants' use of the PxDx algorithm contradicts plan terms
promising medical necessity review by a medical director, which constitutes a breach of fiduciary duty in violation of
29 U.S.C. § 1132(a)(3). (Id. at ¶ 132.) In addition, "[d]efendants' conduct violates the unlawful prong of § 17200
because they violate California's express statutory and regulatory requirements regarding insurance claims
handling pursuant to Cal. Health & Saf. Code §1367.01," and more specifically "[d]efendants violated the unlawful
prong of § 17200 when they allowed the PXDX system to review and deny Plaintiffs and Class members' claims
1 The tension between the allegations of the TAC summarized in this paragraph is of some import as will be made clear below.
Page 3 of 15
Kisting-Leung v. Cigna Corp.
instead of having a licensed physician who is competent to evaluate the specific clinical issues involved in the
health care services requested by the provider to deny or modify requests for authorization of health care services
for an enrollee for reasons [**6] of medical necessity as required by Cal. Health & Saf. Code §1367.01(e)." (Id. at
¶¶ 142-43.)
Plaintiffs assert they are "entitled to recover benefits denied by Defendants, interest, attorneys' fees, and other
penalties as this court deems just, under ERISA § 502(a)(1)(B), 29 U.S.C. § 1132(a)(1)(B)." (Id. at ¶ 125.) In
addition, plaintiffs allege they "are entitled to appropriate equitable relief under 29 U.S.C. § 1132(a)(3)[,]" including
"disgorgement and/or restitution" and "[a]ppropriate declaratory and public injunctive relief enjoining Cigna from
continuing its improper and unlawful claim handling practices as set forth" in the TAC. (Id. at 20, 24.) Finally,
plaintiffs seek an order enjoining defendants from denying benefits owed to insureds through PxDx review, and
restitution of the money wrongfully acquired by defendants. (Id. at ¶¶ 154-55.) Based on these allegations, plaintiffs
bring claims for denial of benefits, 29 U.S.C. § 1132(a)(1)(B), breach of fiduciary duty, 29 U.S.C. § 1132(a)(3), and
violation of California's Unfair Competition Law ("UCL"). (Doc. No. 36.)
On August 23, 2024, defendants filed the pending motion to dismiss plaintiffs' TAC. (Doc. No. 46.) On September
20, 2024, plaintiffs filed their opposition to the motion, and on October 15, 2024, defendants filed their reply thereto.
(Doc. Nos. 59, 50.)
[*997] LEGAL STANDARD
The purpose of a motion to dismiss [**7] pursuant to Rule 12(b)(6) is to test the legal sufficiency of the complaint.
N. Star Int'l v. Ariz. Corp. Comm'n, 720 F.2d 578, 581 (9th Cir. 1983). "Dismissal can be based on the lack of a
cognizable legal theory or the absence of sufficient facts alleged under a cognizable legal theory." Balistreri v.
Pacifica Police Dep't, 901 F.2d 696, 699 (9th Cir. 1988). A plaintiff is required to allege "enough facts to state a
claim to relief that is plausible on its face." Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 570, 127 S. Ct. 1955, 167 L.
Ed. 2d 929 (2007). "A claim has facial plausibility when the plaintiff pleads factual content that allows the court to
draw the reasonable inference that the defendant is liable for the misconduct alleged." Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S.
662, 678, 129 S. Ct. 1937, 173 L. Ed. 2d 868 (2009).
In determining whether a complaint states a claim on which relief may be granted, the court accepts as true the
allegations in the complaint and construes the allegations in the light most favorable to the plaintiff. Hishon v. King &
Spalding, 467 U.S. 69, 73, 104 S. Ct. 2229, 81 L. Ed. 2d 59 (1984). However, the court need not assume the truth
of legal conclusions cast in the form of factual allegations. U.S. ex rel. Chunie v. Ringrose, 788 F.2d 638, 643 n.2
(9th Cir. 1986). While Rule 8(a) does not require detailed factual allegations, "it demands more than an unadorned,
the-defendant-unlawfully-harmed-me accusation." Iqbal, 556 U.S. at 678. A pleading is insufficient if it offers mere
"labels and conclusions" or "a formulaic recitation of the elements of a cause of action." Twombly, 550 U.S. at 555;
see also Iqbal, 556 U.S. at 678 ("Threadbare recitals of the elements of a cause of action, supported by mere [**8]
conclusory statements, do not suffice."). Moreover, it is inappropriate to assume that the plaintiff "can prove facts
that it has not alleged or that the defendants have violated the . . . laws in ways that have not been alleged."
Associated Gen. Contractors of Cal., Inc. v. Cal. State Council of Carpenters, 459 U.S. 519, 526, 103 S. Ct. 897, 74
L. Ed. 2d 723 (1983).
ANALYSIS
A. Standing (Plaintiffs Kisting-Leung, Thornhill, and Bredlow)
"[T]hose who seek to invoke the jurisdiction of the federal courts must satisfy the threshold requirement imposed by
Article III of the Constitution by alleging an actual case or controversy." City of Los Angeles v. Lyons, 461 U.S. 95,
101, 103 S. Ct. 1660, 75 L. Ed. 2d 675 (1983); see also City of Oakland v. Lynch, 798 F.3d 1159, 1163 (9th Cir.
Page 4 of 15
Kisting-Leung v. Cigna Corp.
2015) ("A suit brought by a plaintiff without Article III standing is not a 'case or controversy,' and Article III federal
courts lack subject matter jurisdiction over such suits.") (quoting Cetacean Cmty. v. Bush, 386 F.3d 1169, 1174 (9th
Cir. 2004)). An actual case or controversy will be held to exist when a plaintiff establishes standing. Lujan v. Defs. of
Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555, 560, 112 S. Ct. 2130, 119 L. Ed. 2d 351 (1992). "[S]tanding requires that (1) the plaintiff
suffered an injury in fact, i.e., one that is sufficiently 'concrete and particularized' and 'actual or imminent, not
conjectural or hypothetical,' (2) the injury is 'fairly traceable' to the challenged conduct, and (3) the injury is 'likely' to
be 'redressed by a favorable decision.'" Bates v. United Parcel Serv., Inc., 511 F.3d 974, 985 (9th Cir. 2007) (citing
Lujan, 504 U.S. at 560-61).
In their pending motion, defendants bring a Rule 12(b)(1) factual attack on the standing of plaintiffs Kisting-Leung,
Thornhill, and Bredlow [**9] to bring this action. [*998] (Doc. No. 46 at 10 & n.3.) Defendants furnish an affidavit
from Dr. Julie B. Kessel, a Medical Officer in defendants' Clinical Performance and Quality department, to support
their contention that these three plaintiffs did not have their claims denied through PxDx review, and therefore have
not suffered the alleged injury in fact. (Doc. No. 46-14 at ¶¶ 14, 20, 31.) In their opposition, plaintiffs argue that this
is an issue of fact that is inappropriately raised by defendants by way of motion to dismiss and which cannot be
resolved at this stage of the litigation.
"Rule 12(b)(1) attacks on jurisdiction can be either facial, confining the inquiry to allegations in the complaint, or
factual, permitting the court to look beyond the complaint." Savage v. Glendale Union High Sch., Dist. No. 205,
Maricopa Cnty., 343 F.3d 1036, 1040 n.2 (9th Cir. 2003) (citing White v. Lee, 227 F.3d 1214, 1242 (9th Cir.2000)).
"Once the moving party has converted the motion to dismiss into a factual motion by presenting affidavits or other
evidence properly brought before the court, the party opposing the motion must furnish affidavits or other evidence
necessary to satisfy its burden of establishing subject matter jurisdiction." Id. (citing St. Clair v. City of Chico, 880
F.2d 199, 201 (9th Cir.1989)). "As with a motion for summary judgment, when a court is faced with a factual
attack on standing pursuant [**10] to Rule 12(b)(1), the court must leave the resolution of material factual disputes
to the trier of fact when the issue of standing is intertwined with an element of the merits of the plaintiff's claim."
Bowen v. Energizer Holdings, Inc., 118 F.4th 1134, 1144 (9th Cir. 2024) (citation omitted).
At the outset, the court will assume that plaintiffs' standing relies on their claims of having been subjected to PxDx
review. Accordingly, the court turns to whether that issue is intertwined with the merits of the case. "In making that
assessment, we consider whether the question of standing is dependent on the resolution of factual issues going to
the merits of the action." Id. (citation omitted). Here, plaintiffs' fiduciary duty claim requires that plaintiffs establish
breach, which in turn requires that they allege a violation of plan terms or ERISA. Mathews v. Chevron Corp., 362
F.3d 1172, 1178 (9th Cir. 2004); Mendoza v. Aramark Servs. Inc., No. 15-cv-05142-JSC, 2016 U.S. Dist. LEXIS
18648, 2016 WL 614713, at *3 (N.D. Cal. Feb. 16, 2016). Here, plaintiffs allege that use of PxDx review to process
their claims violated plan terms and provisions of ERISA. (Doc. No. 36 at ¶ 133.) Therefore, whether defendants in
fact used PxDx review to process plaintiffs' claims is intertwined with the merits of plaintiffs' breach of fiduciary duty
claim. In other words, the court concludes that "there is a clear overlap between [plaintiffs'] asserted theory of
Article III [**11] injury and the" breach of fiduciary duty "element" of plaintiffs' fiduciary duty claim. Bowen, 118
F.4th at 1145.
The court will therefore apply the summary judgment standard. In summary judgment practice, the moving party
"initially bears the burden of proving the absence of a genuine issue of material fact." In re Oracle Corp. Sec.
Litig., 627 F.3d 376, 387 (9th Cir. 2010) (citing Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317, 323, 106 S. Ct. 2548, 91 L.
Ed. 2d 265 (1986)). "Where the moving party meets that burden, the burden then shifts to the non-moving party to
designate specific facts demonstrating the existence of genuine issues for trial." Id.
Here, defendants have provided Dr. Kessel's declaration as evidence that plaintiffs Kisting-Leung, Thornhill, and
Bredlow did not have their claims denied through PxDx review. (Doc. No. 46-14.) [*999] Plaintiffs provide no
countervailing evidence, though they do argue defendants' evidence is speculative. (Doc. No. 49.) Specifically,
plaintiffs take issue with Dr. Kessel's use of equivocal terms like "typically" when discussing the remark code used
for denying plaintiffs' claims. (Id. at 10.)
Page 5 of 15
Kisting-Leung v. Cigna Corp.
However, Dr. Kessel asserts without equivocation that "if a claim was denied based on PxDx review, both the
patient and healthcare provider will receive a separate letter detailing the services billed, the diagnosis codes billed,
and [**12] the applicable Cigna clinical coverage policy used in adjudicating that PxDx denial." (Doc. No. 46-14 at ¶
13.) For each of the three plaintiffs at issue, "there were no such PxDx denial letters associated with" their claims.
(Id. at ¶¶ 13, 19, 22.) As a result, Dr. Kessel concludes that the claims of each of the three plaintiffs were not
reviewed using PxDx review. (Id. at ¶¶ 14, 20, 31.) Although it is plaintiffs' theory that "Cigna routinely fails to
disclose that the PXDX algorithm was the reason for many adverse benefits determinations[,]" plaintiffs present no
evidence for this assertion. (Doc. No. 36 at ¶ 31.) Nor do plaintiffs present any other countervailing evidence.
Therefore, based upon the evidence now before it, the court finds that there is no genuine dispute that the claims of
plaintiffs Kisting-Leung, Thornhill, and Bredlow were not subjected to PxDx review.
Finally, plaintiffs argue that because each of their claims for benefits was denied, each plaintiff has standing
regardless of whether the claims were reviewed using the PxDx algorithm. (Doc. No. 49 at 29.) Plaintiffs are correct
that allegedly wrongful denial of benefits can provide one with standing. Bruce M. v. Sutter W. Bay Med. Grp.
Health & Welfare, No. 22-cv-06149-JST, 2023 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 170643, 2023 WL 6277269, at *3 (N.D. Cal. Sept.
25, 2023) ("[C]ourts [**13] have held that an individual suffers a concrete injury when the individual 'was denied
health benefits he was allegedly owed under [a] plan.'") (quoting Springer v. Cleveland Clinic Emp. Health Plan
Total Care, 900 F.3d 284, 288 (6th Cir. 2016)); Davis v. Guam, 785 F.3d 1311, 1316 (9th Cir. 2015) ("[S]tanding
doesn't depend on the merits of the plaintiff's contention that particular conduct is illegal.") (citation omitted, cleaned
up).
Furthermore, defendants' alleged wrongful denial of plaintiffs' claims for benefits does furnish standing for purposes
of plaintiffs' § 1132(a)(1)(B) claim because plaintiffs allege this statute was violated when defendants wrongfully
denied plaintiffs' benefits. 29 U.S.C. § 1132(a)(1)(B) ("A civil action may be brought . . . by a participant or
beneficiary . . . to recover benefits due to him under the terms of his plan . . . ."); (Doc. No. 36 at ¶ 124)
("Defendants' actions constitute an unlawful denial of health insurance benefits under ERISA, as provided in 29
U.S.C. § 1132(a)(1)(B)."). Therefore, all plaintiffs have standing to bring claims under § 1132(a)(1)(B).
However, "a plaintiff must demonstrate standing for each claim he seeks to press." In re Zynga Inc. Secs. Litig., No.
12-cv-04007-JSW, 2014 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 24673, 2014 WL 721948, at *3 (N.D. Cal. Feb. 25, 2014) (citation
omitted). Plaintiffs' remaining claims brought under § 1132(a)(3) and the UCL do not allege that defendants' denial
of plaintiffs' benefits constitutes a violation of these statutes. (Doc. No. 36 at ¶¶ 127-55.) Instead, plaintiffs [**14]
allege defendants violated these statutes by using the PxDx algorithm to review plaintiffs' claims for benefits. (Id.)
Therefore, the court must examine whether the purported injury in fact of denial of benefits is "fairly traceable to
[defendants'] challenged behavior" [*1000] of using the PxDx algorithm.2 Davis v. Fed. Election Comm'n, 554 U.S.
724, 733, 128 S. Ct. 2759, 171 L. Ed. 2d 737 (2008). Because the benefit determinations in response to the claims
submitted by plaintiffs Kisting-Leung, Thornhill, and Bredlow were not made using the PxDx algorithm, denial of
their claims is not fairly traceable to defendants' challenged behavior. See Rombeiro v. Unum Ins. Co. of Am., 761
F. Supp. 2d 862, 873 (N.D. Cal. 2010) ("Plaintiff is correct that wrongful denial of benefits is an injury that could give
him standing to bring some Section 1132(a)(3) claim. But he is wrong that he has standing to obtain relief for those
who did not receive settlement notice when he himself did receive notice."). Therefore, the court concludes that
plaintiffs Kisting-Leung, Thornhill, and Bredlow lack standing to bring their claims under § 1132(a)(3) and the UCL.
B. Timeliness (Plaintiff Rentsch)
Defendants also argue that plaintiff Rentsch's § 1132(a)(1)(B) & (a)(3) claims are time barred. They assert that his
ERISA plan set a limitations period at three years after a claim is submitted for in-network services or three years
after [**15] proof of claim is required under the plan for out-of-network services, and that plaintiff Rentsch's claim
2 Although defendants did not challenge the traceability of plaintiffs' purported injury, "the court has an independent obligation to
assure that standing exists[.]" Summers v. Earth Island Inst., 555 U.S. 488, 499, 129 S. Ct. 1142, 173 L. Ed. 2d 1 (2009).
Page 6 of 15
Kisting-Leung v. Cigna Corp.
for benefits was denied February 27, 2018 - more than five years before the original complaint in this action was
filed on July 24, 2023. (Doc. No. 46 at 16.) Defendants further argue that plaintiff Rentsch's UCL claim is time
barred because a four-year statute of limitations applies. (Id. at 17.) In their opposition, plaintiffs do not dispute the
existence of the contractual limitations period but instead argue that plaintiff Rentsch's claims accrued later than
February 27, 2018 and that a six-year statute of limitations period applies to plaintiff Rentsch's ERISA claims
because he alleges fraud or concealment. (Doc. No. 49 at 11-13.)
1. Timeliness of Plaintiff Rentsch's 29 U.S.C. § 1132(a)(1)(B) Claim
Where the period is not unreasonably short, the Supreme Court has held that contractual limitations periods apply
to "§ 1132(a)(1)(B)" claims. Heimeshoff v. Hartford Life & Acc. Ins. Co., 571 U.S. 99, 109, 134 S. Ct. 604, 187 L.
Ed. 2d 529 (2013) ("We must give effect to the Plan's limitations provision unless we determine either that the
period is unreasonably short, or that a 'controlling statute' prevents the limitations provision from taking effect.").
Further, "[a]bsent a controlling statute to the contrary, a participant [**16] and a plan may agree by contract to a
particular limitations period, even one that starts to run before the cause of action accrues, as long as the period is
reasonable." Id. at 105-06. Because a "3-year limitations provision" is not unreasonably short, the contractual
limitations period applies to plaintiff Rentsch's § 1132(a)(1)(B) claim. Id. at 109. Regardless of when plaintiff
Rentsch's claim accrued or whether it sounds in fraud, the parties' contractual limitations provision provides for a
limitations period of three years after the claim was submitted. (Doc. No. 46 at 16.)
Still, where a contractual limitations period applies, equitable tolling can apply to relieve hardship. Sargent v. S. Cal.
Edison 401(k) Sav. Plan, No. 20-cv-01296-MMA-RBB, 2020 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 190443, 2020 WL 6060411, at *5
(S.D. Cal. Oct. 14, 2020). Even at the motion to dismiss stage, the "litigant seeking [*1001] equitable tolling bears
the burden of establishing two elements: (1) that he has been pursuing his rights diligently, and (2) that some
extraordinary circumstance stood in his way." Id. (quoting Credit Suisse Sec. (USA) LLC v. Simmonds, 566 U.S.
221, 227, 132 S. Ct. 1414, 182 L. Ed. 2d 446 (2012)). "Regarding the second element, 'a garden variety claim of
excusable neglect, such as a simple miscalculation that leads a lawyer to miss a filing deadline, does not warrant
equitable tolling.'" Id. (quoting Kwai Fun Wong v. Beebe, 732 F.3d 1030, 1052 (9th Cir. 2013), aff'd and remanded
sub nom. United States v. Wong, 575 U.S. 402, 135 S. Ct. 1625, 191 L. Ed. 2d 533 (2015)). Rather, "[t]he party
seeking equitable tolling bears [**17] the burden to show that it is appropriate." Id. (citation omitted).
Here, plaintiff Rentsch has not shown extraordinary circumstances justifying equitable tolling. Although he alleges
he did not know that defendants used PxDx to review his claims until he read a 2023 article, in their TAC plaintiffs
admits that he received a benefits denial letter in 2016 in which it was noted that PxDx was used to process his
claim. (Doc. No. 36 at ¶ 63.) Plaintiff Rentsch's alleged lack of knowledge is not therefore attributable to
extraordinary circumstances, but at best to excusable neglect. See Sargent, 2020 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 190443, 2020
WL 6060411, at *5 ("[T]he Court finds that the COVID-19 global pandemic and the surrounding circumstances did
not sufficiently prevent Plaintiff from filing her action."). Because equitable tolling does not apply, plaintiff Rentsch's
§ 1132(a)(1)(B) claim is untimely.
2. Timeliness of Plaintiff Rentsch's 29 U.S.C. § 1132(a)(3) Claim
The timeliness of plaintiff Rentsch's § 1132(a)(3) claim is not as straightforward. In the end, however, the court
agrees with the reasoning of the district court in Sargent that as to that claim a controlling statute, 29 U.S.C. § 1113,
supersedes the plan's contractual limitation period. Sargent, 2020 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 190443, 2020 WL 6060411, at
*7-8. According to this controlling statute:
No action may be commenced under [**18] this subchapter with respect to a fiduciary's breach of any
responsibility, duty, or obligation under this part, or with respect to a violation of this part, after the earlier of—
(1) six years after (A) the date of the last action which constituted a part of the breach or violation, or (B) in
the case of an omission the latest date on which the fiduciary could have cured the breach or violation, or
(2) three years after the earliest date on which the plaintiff had actual knowledge of the breach or violation;
except that in the case of fraud or concealment, such action may be commenced not later than six years after
the date of discovery of such breach or violation.
Page 7 of 15
Kisting-Leung v. Cigna Corp.
29 U.S.C. § 1113. "A plaintiff fails to state a claim, and therefore dismissal is appropriate, where his failure to
comply with the applicable statute of limitations is evident from the allegations of the complaint." Yamauchi v.
Cotterman, 84 F. Supp. 3d 993, 1004 (N.D. Cal. 2015).
It is not clear from the face of the complaint that plaintiff Rentsch had "actual knowledge" of the purported
violation—defendants' use of PxDx to review his claims—until March 25, 2023, when plaintiff Rentsch allegedly
"discovered through an article published by ProPublica that Defendants had been using the PXDX algorithm
to [**19] review patients' claims." (Doc. No. 36 at ¶ 73) ("Prior to that, Mr. Rentsch had no knowledge of this illegal
practice by Defendants."). It is true that [*1002] plaintiff Rentsch may have had constructive knowledge of the use
of PxDx review earlier because at least one "denial letter indicated that the PXDX algorithm reviewed his claim[,]"
but actual knowledge requires more. (Id. at ¶ 63.) The Ninth Circuit has addressed this issue, explaining:
We agree that Intel's evidence demonstrates that Sulyma had sufficient information available to him to know
about the allegedly imprudent investments before October 29, 2012. However, that is insufficient. Because
Sulyma brought a claim under section 1104, he was required to have actual knowledge both that those
investments occurred, and that they were imprudent. But Sulyma declared that he was "unaware that the
monies that [he] had invested through the Intel retirement plans had been invested in hedge funds or private
equity' and that he did 'not recall seeing any documents during [his] employment at Intel that alerted [him] to
the fact that [his] retirement monies were significantly invested in hedge funds or private equity."
Sulyma v. Intel Corp. Inv. Pol'y Comm., 909 F.3d 1069, 1077 (9th Cir. 2018), aff'd, 589 U.S. 178, 140 S. Ct. 768,
206 L. Ed. 2d 103 (2020). Therefore, plaintiff Rentsch's [**20] § 1132(a)(3) claim is not subject to dismissal at this
stage of the litigation as untimely.
3. Timeliness of Plaintiff Rentsch's UCL Claim
Finally, the court turns to the timeliness of plaintiff Rentsch's claim under the UCL. "The statute of limitation for a
UCL violation is four years." Joseph v. Am. Gen. Life Ins. Co., 495 F. Supp. 3d 953, 962 (S.D. Cal. 2020) (citing
Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17208), aff'd, No. 20-56213, 857 Fed. Appx. 297, 2021 WL 3754613 (9th Cir. Aug. 25,
2021). The defendant "bears the initial burden of proving [the plaintiff's] claims are barred by section 17208's fouryear
limitations period." Aryeh v. Canon Bus. Sols., Inc., 55 Cal. 4th 1185, 1197, 151 Cal. Rptr. 3d 827, 292 P.3d
871 (2013). "[T]he UCL statute of limitations is governed by common law accrual rules." Beaver v. Tarsadia Hotels,
816 F.3d 1170, 1178 (9th Cir. 2016) (citation omitted). "Common law rules provide that a cause of action ordinarily
accrues when each of the elements of the cause of action (wrongdoing, causation, and harm) has been satisfied."
Id. Applying this general rule, the court finds defendants have met their initial burden of establishing that plaintiff
Rentsch's UCL claim is untimely.
"Thereafter, the burden shifts to [the plaintiff] to demonstrate his claims survive based on one or more nonstatutory
exceptions to the basic limitations period." Aryeh, 55 Cal. 4th at 1197. "That burden may be imposed even at the
pleading stage." Id.
Plaintiffs argue that the discovery rule applies to delay accrual. (Doc. No. 49 at 12.) "[A] UCL deceptive practices
claim should accrue [**21] only when a reasonable person would have discovered the factual basis for a claim."
Aryeh, 55 Cal. 4th at 1195 (citation omitted). Plaintiffs argue that defendants used "the secret, undisclosed PXDX
algorithm to review and deny claims for benefits." (Doc. No. 49 at 12.) However, once again the court notes that
plaintiffs' own TAC alleges that plaintiff Rentsch received a "denial letter indicat[ing] that the PXDX algorithm
reviewed his claim." (Doc. No. 36 at ¶ 63.) Given this allegation by plaintiffs, plaintiff Rentsch cannot meet his
burden of establishing that the discovery rule renders his UCL claim timely.
Therefore, the court will dismiss plaintiff Rentsch's § 1132(a)(1)(B) and UCL claims as untimely.
[*1003] C. Whether Plaintiffs State a Claim Under 29 U.S.C. § 1132(a)(1)(B) for Wrongful Denial of Benefits
Page 8 of 15
Kisting-Leung v. Cigna Corp.
"To state a claim under [§ 1132(a)(1)(B)], a plaintiff must allege facts that establish the existence of an ERISA plan
as well as the provisions of the plan that entitle it to benefits." Forest Ambulatory Surgical Assocs., L.P. v. United
HealthCare Ins. Co., No. 12-cv-02916-PSG-FFM, 2013 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 190703, 2013 WL 11323600, at *5 (C.D.
Cal. Mar. 12, 2013). A § 1132(a)(1)(B) claim for benefits "stands or falls by 'the terms of the plan.'" Kennedy v. Plan
Adm'r for DuPont Sav. & Inv. Plan, 555 U.S. 285, 300, 129 S. Ct. 865, 172 L. Ed. 2d 662 (2009).
Here, defendants argue plaintiffs have not identified the plan terms that purportedly entitle them to benefits. (Doc.
No. 46 at 18.) In the case of plaintiff Kisting-Leung, she alleges that "[a]ccording to Cigna's [**22] Medical
Coverage Policy, a transvaginal ultrasound is considered 'medically necessary for the evaluation of suspected
pelvic pathology or for screen or surveillance of a woman at increased risk for ovarian or endometrial cancer.'"
(Doc. No. 36 at ¶ 42.) Cigna's "Medical Coverage Policy" is a set of guidelines Cigna uses to adjudicate claims for
benefits. Akhlaghi v. Cigna Corp., No. 19-cv-03754-JST, 2019 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 240174, 2019 WL 13067381, at *1
(N.D. Cal. Oct. 23, 2019) ("Cigna insurance plans exclude from coverage medical services that it considers
'experimental, investigational or unproven.' 'To adjudicate claims for the treatment of lipedema, Cigna uses "Medical
Coverage Policy No. 0531."' This policy classifies '[l]iposuction for the treatment of lipedema' as 'experimental,
investigational or unproven.'"). Cigna's "Medical Coverage Policy" is not the plan itself and does not necessarily
mirror plan terms. Id. Therefore, plaintiff Kisting-Leung has not alleged the plan term or terms that entitle her to

IRAC_summ:
Case Name: Kisting-Leung v. Cigna Corp., 780 F. Supp. 3d 985 (E.D. Cal. 2025).
Court + Jurisdiction: United States District Court, Eastern District of California.
Area of Law: Employment Law—ERISA; Consumer Law—California UCL.
Procedural Posture: Motion to dismiss.
Issue
Whether an insurer’s use of an automated algorithm (PxDx) to deny claims for medical necessity violates ERISA fiduciary duties or California’s Unfair Competition Law (UCL).
Rule
Under ERISA § 1132(a)(1)(B), a plaintiff must establish the existence of a plan and the specific provisions entitling them to benefits [1003]. Under § 1132(a)(3), a fiduciary must act in accordance with plan terms [1004]. ERISA expressly preempts state laws that "relate to" a benefit plan unless they fall under the "saving clause" for laws regulating insurance [1009]. A law regulates insurance if it is directed at the industry and substantially affects the risk-pooling arrangement [1010]. California Health & Safety Code § 1367.01(e) prohibits anyone other than a licensed physician from denying requests for medical necessity [1008].
Application
The court first dismissed the claims of three plaintiffs because evidence showed their claims were not actually processed by the PxDx algorithm [999]. It then dismissed the § 1132(a)(1)(B) claim for all plaintiffs because they failed to plead specific plan language, relying instead on general "Medical Coverage Policies" which are not part of the plan itself [1003].
However, the court allowed the § 1132(a)(3) claim to proceed. The plan required medical necessity determinations to be made by a "Medical Director." The court held that allowing an algorithm to deny claims in 1.2 seconds—with a director merely "pushing a button"—conflicted with the plain language of the plan and constituted an abuse of discretion [1004-1005]. Finally, the court held the UCL claim was not preempted. Although it "related to" the plan, it was saved because § 1367.01(e) regulates insurance by mandating human physician review, which "alters the scope of permissible bargains" and impacts risk pooling [1011].
Conclusion
The court grants the motion to dismiss the § 1132(a)(1)(B) claim but denies it as to the § 1132(a)(3) and UCL claims, granting leave to amend.

case_name: A Local Authority v JB (by his Litigation Friend, the Official Solicitor) [2021] UKSC 52
case:
A Local Authority v JB (by his Litigation Friend, the Official Solicitor) - [2021] All ER (D) 78 (Nov)
A Local Authority v JB (by his Litigation Friend, the Official Solicitor) [2021] 
All ER (D) 78 (Nov)
[2021] UKSC 52
Supreme Court
Lord Briggs, Lady Arden, Lord Burrows, Lord Stephens, Lady Rose
24 November 2021
MENTAL HEALTH – PERSONS WHO LACK CAPACITY – MENTAL CAPACITY
Abstract
The Supreme Court upheld the decision of the Court of Appeal, Civil Division, that in determining capacity to decide 
to engage in sexual relations, the information relevant to the decision to have sexual relations with another person 
inevitably included the fact that any person with whom the person who was the subject of the proceedings engaged 
in sexual activity had to be able to consent to such activity and did, in fact, consent to it. Accordingly, the Supreme 
Court affirmed the Court of Appeal's decision and dismissed the appellant's appeal.
Digest
The judgment is available at: [2021] UKSC 52
  Background     
The proceedings concerned the respondent, JB, a 36-year-old man with a complex diagnosis of autistic spectrum 
disorder combined with impaired cognition. JB had stated in clear terms that he had a strong desire to have a 
girlfriend and engage in sexual relations. The applicant local authority filed an application in the Court of Protection, 
seeking declarations under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 (MCA 2005) as to JB's capacity in various matters, 
including a declaration that JB lacked capacity to consent to sexual relation. A question arose as to whether, in 
assessing JB's capacity to consent to sexual relations, the judge should have regard to whether JB had capacity to 
understand that the other person involved had to give consent, and had in fact given and maintained consent 
throughout the act. 
The judge found that that was not relevant information for the purposes of determining if an individual had capacity 
to consent to sexual relations under MCA 2005. The judge held that, for the purposes of determining the 
fundamental capacity of an individual in relation to sexual relations, the information relevant to the decision for the 
purposes of MCA 2005 s 3(1) did not include information that, absent consent of a sexual partner, attempting 
sexual relations with another person was liable to breach the criminal law. Accordingly, her order included a 
declaration that JB had capacity to consent to sexual relations. The authority appealed against the declaration that 
JB had capacity to consent to sexual relations.
The Court of Appeal, Civil Division, after an extensive analysis of the case law, held that there was no binding 
authority which determined whether the correct formulation of the matter in a case of the present kind was 
'engaging in' rather than 'consenting to' sexual relations. Given that lack of authority, the Court of Appeal 
considered that the correct formulation of the matter related to JB engaging in sexual relations. Accordingly, it 
recast the relevant matter as whether JB had the capacity 'to engage in' rather than 'consent to', sexual relations. 
Page 2 of 4
*A Local Authority v JB (by his Litigation Friend, the Official Solicitor) - [2021] All ER (D) 78 (Nov)
Having recast the decision in those terms, the Court of Appeal held that the information relevant to the decision 
inevitably included the fact that any person with whom JB engaged in sexual activity should be able to consent and 
give and maintain consent. The authority's appeal was therefore allowed. JB, by his Litigation Friend, the Official 
Solicitor, appealed to the Supreme Court. 
 Respond (a charity providing services to children, young people and adults with learning disabilities), and Centre 
for Women's Justice (a charity seeking to combat male violence against women and girls) provided written 
submissions as interveners in the appeal
  Issues and decisions     
(1) Whether it had been wrong to recast the relevant matter as whether JB had capacity to 'engage in' sexual 
relations.
The appellant argued that MCA 2005 s 27(1)(b), which set out those decisions which could not be made on behalf 
of a person, referred to 'consenting to have sexual relations'. The appellant's case was that that section should be 
read as controlling the scope of MCA 2005 s 2(1), which related to whether a person lacked capacity.
It was not accepted that MCA 2005 s 27 governed or controlled MCA 2005 s 2(1) in that way. The function of s 27 
was to identify certain decisions which were so personal to the individual concerned that no one could take them on 
his behalf if he was unable to take them for himself. Section 27 did not speak to, nor did it define, the matter about 
which P potentially lacked capacity to make a decision for himself under MCA 2005 s 2(1). Section 27 only made 
clear that 'where a court finds that a person lacks capacity to consent to sexual relations, then the court does not 
have any jurisdiction to give consent on that person's behalf to any specific sexual encounter'. Co-incidentally, in a 
particular case, a matter in s 27 could also be a matter within s 2(1), but the list in s 27 did not purport to be a 
comprehensive list of the decisions in respect of which issues as to capacity would arise. Accordingly, the 
submission that s 27(1)(b) prescriptively formulated the only matter for decision in s 2(1) would be rejected (see [88] 
of the judgment).
Further, the appellant's argument that his wish to initiate sexual relations was a desire rather than being a decision 
within s 2(1) MCA would be rejected. It was accepted that a wish to initiate sexual relations could be described as a 
desire to do so, but clearly a desire gave rise to a decision as to whether to fulfil that desire. In agreement with the 
Court of Appeal, formulating 'the matter' as engaging in, rather than consenting to, sexual relations better captured 
the nature of the issues in a case such as the present case, where JB wished to initiate relations with others, rather 
than consent to relations proposed by someone else. That formulation was not inconsistent with the authorities (see 
[89], [90] of the judgment).
Furthermore, in agreement with the Court of Appeal, the formulation of engaging in sexual relations was 'how the 
question of capacity with regard to sexual relations (under the MCA) should normally be assessed in most cases' 
(see [91] of the judgment).
X City Council v MB [2006] EWHC 168 (Fam), [2007] 3 FCR 371, [2006] 2 FLR 968, [2006] Fam Law 637 applied
MM, Re; Local Authority X v MM [2007] EWHC 2003 (Fam), [2008] 3 FCR 788, [2009] 1 FLR 443, [2007] Fam Law 
1132 applied
(2) The identification, under section 3(1)(a), of the information relevant to the decision.
The appellant argued that even if 'the matter' for the purposes of s 2 was whether to engage in sexual relations then 
information relevant to JB's decision did not include the fact that the other person had to have the ability to consent 
to the sexual activity and had to in fact consent before and throughout the sexual activity. The appellant contended 
that that inappropriately extended the requisite information in order to protect the other person or members of the 
public. He submitted that that was not the purpose of MCA 2005, which was confined to the protection of P, and did 
not extend to the protection of members of the public. 
Page 3 of 4
*A Local Authority v JB (by his Litigation Friend, the Official Solicitor) - [2021] All ER (D) 78 (Nov)
The appellant's submissions would be rejected. First, it was correct that the Court of Protection should have regard 
to reasonably foreseeable adverse consequences with the aim of protecting members of the public, as well as the 
person who might lack capacity. Second, the test in s 2(1) was decision-specific, not person-specific (see [92]-[96] 
of the judgment).
(3) Whether the Court of Appeal's test for P's capacity to engage in sexual relations created an impermissible 
difference with the criminal law.
The appellant argued that to have regard to whether a person had capacity to understand that the other person 
should be able to consent and should in fact consent before and throughout the sexual relations created an 
impermissible difference between the civil and criminal law. 
No impermissible difference arose, and there were strong policy justifications, including the Court of Protection's 
responsibility to protect persons who might lack capacity as well as to protect others, for any higher standard in the 
civil law test for consent. Further, any differences between the civil law test and the criminal law test should be 
assessed as they arose in individual cases (see [97]-[108] of the judgment).
X City Council v MB [2006] EWHC 168 (Fam), [2007] 3 FCR 371, [2006] 2 FLR 968 considered
A Local Authority v H [2012] EWHC 49 (COP), [2012] 1 FCR 590, [2012] COPLR 305, [2012] All ER (D) 34 (Mar) 
considered
R v Braham [2013] EWCA Crim 3, [2013] 1 Cr App Rep 481, [2014] Crim LR 312, [2013] All ER (D) 24 (Feb) 
considered
R v A (G) [2014] EWCA Crim 299, [2014] 1 WLR 2469, [2014] 2 Cr App Rep 73 considered
(4) Whether the Court of Appeal's test for P's capacity to engage in sexual relations was inconsistent with art 8 of 
the European Convention on Human Rights.
The appellant sought to argue that MCA 2005 should be be construed compatibly with art 8 of the Convention 
which provided for a right to respect for private and family life. That ground had not been raised prior to the appeal 
to the Supreme Court, and permission to raise it would be refused. Nevertheless, the operation of MCA 2005 was 
compatible with art 8 (see [117]-[118] of the judgment).
(5) Whether the Court of Appeal's test for capacity to engage in sexual relations was inconsistent with art 12(2) of 
the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, which provides for recognition that 
persons with disabilities enjoy legal capacity on an equal basis with others in all aspects of life.
The appellant contended that: (a) the fact that the other person should have the ability to consent to the sexual 
activity and had to in fact consent before and throughout the sexual activity created 'a separate standard or test of 
capacity for people with disabilities'; and (b) that treaty obligation should 'preclude the use of a separate standard or 
test of capacity for people with disabilities, for assessing consent to sexual relations.'
That argument would be rejected as there was no separate standard for persons with disabilities. Further, it was 
noted that in R (on the application of SC, CB and 8 children) v Secretary of State for Work and Pensions and 
others[2021] All ER (D) 34 (Jul), the Supreme Court had confirmed that it would not examine whether the UK had 
violated provisions of an international treaty which were unincorporated in domestic law (see [120] of the judgment).
R (on the application of SC, CB and 8 children) v Secretary of State for Work and Pensions and others. [2021] 
UKSC 26, [2021] 3 WLR 428, [2021] All ER (D) 34 (Jul) applied
Decision of Court of Appeal, Civil Division [2021] 1 All ER 1103 Affirmed.
John McKendrick QC, Ian P Brownhill, Helen Law(instructed by Enable Law) for the appellant.
Page 4 of 4
*A Local Authority v JB (by his Litigation Friend, the Official Solicitor) - [2021] All ER (D) 78 (Nov)
Vikram Sachdeva QC, Richard Whittam QC, Alexander Ruck Keene, Fiona Paterson (instructed by Wolferstans 
Solicitors) for the authority.
Aswini Weereratne QC, Sophy Miles, Mary-Rachel McCabeCaragh Nimmo (instructed by Irwin Mitchell) for 
Respond (written submissions only).
Victoria Butler-Cole QC, Tim James-Matthews (instructed by Centre for Women's Justice) for Centre for Women's 
Justice (written submissions only).
 Neneh Munu Barrister

IRAC_summ:
Case Name: A Local Authority v JB (by his Litigation Friend, the Official Solicitor) [2021] UKSC 52
Court + jurisdiction: United Kingdom Supreme Court
Area of law: Mental Capacity Law – Court of Protection
Procedural posture: Appeal from the Court of Appeal, Civil Division.
Issue
Whether, for the purposes of assessing capacity under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, the "relevant information" a person must understand to decide to engage in sexual relations includes the fact that the other person must have the ability to consent and must in fact consent.
Rule
Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 (MCA), capacity is decision-specific. The court must identify the "matter" requiring a decision (s 2(1)) and the "relevant information" pertinent to that decision (s 3(1)). Relevant information includes the reasonably foreseeable consequences of deciding one way or another. Section 27 of the MCA, which prohibits giving substitute consent for sexual relations, does not define the scope of the decision-making capacity for the purposes of section 2.
Application
The Court agreed with the Court of Appeal that the "matter" for decision should be framed as "engaging in" sexual relations rather than merely "consenting to" them. This formulation better reflected the facts, as the respondent (JB) wished to initiate sexual relations with others [89]–[91]. The Court rejected the argument that s 27 of the MCA constrained the definition of the decision under s 2; s 27 merely limits the jurisdiction of the court to act on behalf of a person, not the assessment of that person's capacity [88].
Regarding the "relevant information," the Court held that the necessity of the sexual partner's consent is crucial information. The MCA aims to protect not only the person lacking capacity (P) but also the public. If P engages in non-consensual sex, they face reasonably foreseeable adverse consequences, including criminal prosecution and harm to the victim. Therefore, to have capacity, P must be able to understand that the partner must validly consent [92]–[96].
The Court dismissed the argument that requiring an understanding of consent creates an impermissible divergence between the civil and criminal tests for capacity. The civil law (via the Court of Protection) has a protective function that justifies a potentially higher standard of understanding to prevent harm, distinct from the criminal law’s focus on retrospective liability [97]–[108].
Conclusion
The Court held that the information relevant to the decision to engage in sexual relations includes the fact that the other person must be able to consent and must essentially consent; the appeal was dismissed.

case_name: R v Andrewes [2022] UKSC 24
case:
R v Andrewes - [2022] All ER (D) 63 (Aug)
Page 1 of 4
R v Andrewes [2022] All ER (D) 63 (Aug)
[2022] UKSC 24
Supreme Court
Lord Hodge DP, Lord Kitchin, Lord Hamblen, Lord Burrows and Lord Stephens SCJJ
18 August 2022
CRIMINAL LAW – CONFISCATION ORDER – PROPORTIONALITY
Abstract
The Supreme Court allowed the Crown's appeal against the decision of the Court of Appeal, Criminal Division, that 
the confiscation order made by the Recorder against the respondent in the sum of the recoverable amount 
(£96,737.24) was disproportionate under s 6(5) of Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 (POCA 2002). The respondent had 
pleaded guilty to obtaining a pecuniary advantage by deception in circumstances where his employment had been 
terminated after it had been discovered that his application for the position had contained a number of false and 
misleading statements as to his qualifications and employment history (CV fraud). The Court of Appeal had made 
no confiscation order, but had certified as a point of law of general public importance, a question regarding the 
proportionality of confiscation orders in CV fraud cases. Those cases typically occurred, as in the present case, 
where a defendant had included lies on his or her application form for a job and had performed the agreed services 
satisfactorily and had been paid the agreed salary until the fraud was discovered. The Court held that, among other 
things, where, focusing solely on the performance of services, the fraudster had given full value for the earnings 
received, and putting to one side where the performance of the services had constituted a criminal offence, it would 
normally be disproportionate under the proviso in POCA 2002 s 6(5) to confiscate all the net earnings made. 
However, it would be proportionate to confiscate the difference between the higher earnings made as a result of the 
CV fraud and the lower earnings that the defendant would have made had he or she not committed the CV fraud. In 
the present case, therefore, applying the provision in POCA 2002 s 6(5), confiscating the recoverable amount 
(£96,737.24) was proportionate. Accordingly, although based on different reasoning to that of the Recorder, that 
confiscation order would be restored.
Digest
The judgment is available at: [2022] UKSC 24
  Background     
In October 2004, the respondent (A) had successfully applied for the post of Chief Executive Officer at St 
Margaret's Hospice, Taunton. His application contained a number of false and misleading statements as to his 
qualifications and employment history (CV fraud). Using the same or similar lies, he was also appointed to two 
remunerated roles as a director and then Chair of the Torbay NHS Care Trust and Chair of the Royal Cornwall NHS 
Hospital Trust. In 2015, A's employment came to an end when the truth started to emerge. In January 2017, A 
pleaded guilty to obtaining a pecuniary advantage by deception, under s 16 of the Theft Act 1968 (as regards his 
position at St Margaret's Hospice) and two counts of fraud under s 1 of the Fraud Act 2006 (as regards his 
appointments at the two NHS Trusts). He was sentenced to two years' imprisonment. 
*R v Andrewes - [2022] All ER (D) 63 (Aug)
Page 2 of 4
In subsequent confiscation proceedings in the Crown Court, the Recorder assessed benefit in the sum of 
£643,602.91. That represented the amount of pay (net of Income Tax and National Insurance Contributions) 
received by A in the years of his employment and appointments before his dishonesty was discovered and his 
employment came to an end. The available amount, and therefore the recoverable amount, was assessed in the 
sum of £96,737.24. A confiscation order was made for that sum. 
A successfully appealed to the Court of Appeal, Criminal Division, which held that the confiscation order made was 
disproportionate under s 6(5) of Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 (POCA 2002) because A, by performing the services, 
which it had been lawful for him to carry out, had given full value for the remuneration he had received. The Court of 
Appeal made no confiscation order, but certified as a point of law of general public importance the question: 'Where 
a defendant obtains remuneration as a result of or in connection with an offence of fraud based upon the obtaining 
of employment by false representations or non-disclosure, in what circumstances (if any) will a confiscation order 
based on the wages earned be disproportionate within the terms of POCA 2002 s 6(5), or contrary to art 1 of the 
First Protocol of the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention?'
The Crown appealed to the Supreme Court.
  Issues and decisions     
(1) Whether it would be proportionate under POCA 2002 s 6(5) to make a confiscation order of the full net earnings.
The Crown submitted that, putting to one side the available, and therefore recoverable, amount, A's full net 
earnings during the relevant period should be confiscated (the 'take all' approach).
The 'take all' approach would be rejected (see [41] of the judgment).
If the confiscation order did not reflect a deduction for the value of the services rendered, while requiring the 
defendant to repay the net earnings, the order would constitute double recovery or what could most accurately be 
labelled 'double disgorgement'. Double disgorgement went beyond disgorgement and constituted a penalty. That 
would be disproportionate. In that respect, the reasoning of the Court of Appeal would be accepted (see [41] of the 
judgment).
It was very important to add that cases where the performance of the services was illegal would be put to one side. 
For example, a person was appointed to a job as a surgeon or airline pilot or HGV driver because he or she had 
lied in the job application about having the necessary qualifications or licence to be appointed to that job. In that 
situation, the performance of the services by that person would constitute a criminal offence and it would not be 
disproportionate to confiscate the full net earnings because the performance of those services had no value that the 
law should recognise as valid. There was no lawful market for the performance of those services by that person. 
Confiscation of the full net earnings would not therefore constitute double disgorgement (see [42] of the judgment).
(2) Whether: (i) it would be unsatisfactory to make no confiscation order; and (ii) a 'middle way' approach would be 
proportionate under POCA 2002 s 6(5).
A submitted that, in line with the decision of the Court of Appeal, any confiscation order would be disproportionate 
(the 'take nothing' approach).
The 'take nothing' approach would be rejected (see [44] of the judgment).
A had performed valuable services for the hospice and the two trusts in return for the net earnings and, if the sole 
focus was on his performance of the services (before his fraud had been uncovered), it would be hard to deny that 
the hospice and the two trusts had been receiving full value in exchange for the salary paid. However, the hospice 
and the two trusts had sought to employ or engage in a senior managerial position a person of honesty and integrity 
and A would not have obtained the employment or office, which would have gone to another candidate, if the truth 
about his qualifications had been known. In that sense, the fraudster would be profiting from his crime if no 
confiscation order was made (see [44] of the judgment).
*R v Andrewes - [2022] All ER (D) 63 (Aug)
Page 3 of 4
Where proportionality was being considered, the relevant benefit from the fraud that it was proportionate to disgorge 
was not the full net earnings but rather the difference between the higher earnings that A had obtained and the 
lower earnings that he would have obtained had he not used fraud and hence had not been offered the particular 
job. That was to take away the 'profit' made by the fraud. That approach provided a principled 'middle way' (or 
'halfway house') between the take all or take nothing approaches to confiscation in CV fraud cases (see [45] of the 
judgment).
The principled middle way did not involve plucking a figure out of the air or a discretionary multi-factorial approach. 
On the contrary, it did require some evidential basis for comparing earnings with and without the CV fraud (and, the 
legal burden of proof was on the prosecution). However, a detailed or precise evidential or accounting exercise was 
not needed. That would be inappropriate for confiscation orders where clear rules and a broad-brush approach 
were necessary so as to avoid complicating the administration of justice in the Crown Courts. In many and perhaps 
most situations of CV fraud, it would be appropriate, as a pragmatic approximation of the relevant profit, simply to 
take the difference between the fraudster's initial salary in the new job obtained by fraud and the fraudster's salary 
in his or her prior job (see [48] of the judgment).
The proviso in POCA 2002 s 6(5) instructed the court to address the proportionality question in relation to the 
recoverable amount rather than the benefit obtained. That would sometimes operate to simplify the task of the 
Crown Court judge. That was the position on the facts of the present case. There was no need for much time and 
effort to be expended in assessing, even in a broad-brush way, the difference between the earnings with and 
without the CV fraud if it was clear that, in any event, that difference would exceed the recoverable amount. Where 
that was so, the confiscation order of the recoverable amount should be made (see [50] of the judgment).
Applying the middle way to the facts of the present case, a comparison would be made between A's salary in the 
new job and the salary that he had already been earning. In 2004, he had been earning £54,361 gross. The higher 
initial salary he had obtained by reason of his fraud had been £75,000 gross. The contrast between the two was 
38%. On a broad-brush basis, a proportionate confiscation order (assuming it was not exceeding the recoverable 
amount) would therefore be 38% of £643,602.91 which amounted to £244,569. That was the profit he had made 
from his CV fraud (see [51] of the judgment).
On the facts, as the recoverable amount (£96,737.24) was far lower than £244,569, confiscating £96,737.24 was 
proportionate applying the proviso in POCA 2002 s 6(5). Although based on different reasoning to that of the 
Recorder, the court would restore his confiscation order (see [52] of the judgment).
(3) The court considered the Court of Appeal's certified question.
Although the certified question referred to both POCA s 6(5) and art 1 of the First Protocol to the Convention, it was 
clear that the proviso in s 6(5) embraced art 1 of the First Protocol. They were not laying down two independent 
tests. Therefore, the court could focus simply on the proviso in s 6(5) (see [38] of the judgment).
Although the court was not attempting to deal with all possible circumstances, in CV fraud cases, where, focusing 
solely on the performance of services, the fraudster had given full value for the earnings received, and putting to 
one side where the performance of the services constituted a criminal offence, it would normally be disproportionate 
under the proviso in POCA 2002 s 6(5) to confiscate all the net earnings made. However, it would be proportionate 
to confiscate the difference between the higher earnings made as a result of the CV fraud and the lower earnings 
that the defendant would have made had he or she not committed the CV fraud. In many situations of CV fraud, it 
would be appropriate, as a pragmatic approximation of that profit, simply to base it on the percentage difference 
between the fraudster's initial salary in the new job obtained by fraud and the fraudster's salary in his or her prior 
job. Further, there was no need for much time and effort to be expended in assessing, even in a broad-brush way, 
the difference between the earnings with and without the CV fraud if it was clear that, in any event, that difference 
would exceed the recoverable amount (see [56] of the judgment).

Case Name: R v Andrewes [2022] UKSC 24
Court + jurisdiction: United Kingdom Supreme Court
Area of law: Criminal Law – Confiscation – Fraud – Human Rights
Procedural posture: Appeal from the Court of Appeal, Criminal Division
Issue
Whether a confiscation order based on the full net earnings of a defendant who obtained employment through CV fraud is "disproportionate" under section 6(5) of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002, where the defendant performed the job satisfactorily.
Rule
A confiscation order must not be disproportionate (POCA 2002 s 6(5); A1P1 ECHR). In cases of CV fraud where the defendant performs the role lawfully and satisfactorily, it is generally disproportionate to confiscate the full net earnings ("take all") because this would be double disgorgement (the employer received value). Conversely, making no order ("take nothing") allows the fraudster to profit. The proportionate measure is the "middle way": confiscating the difference between the earnings obtained by fraud and the earnings the defendant would have obtained absent the fraud.
Application
The defendant obtained a CEO position at a hospice by lying about his qualifications. He performed the role for over a decade. The Crown sought to confiscate his full net earnings (£643k), while the Court of Appeal had ordered nothing.
The Supreme Court rejected both extremes. The "take all" approach ignored the value of the services actually rendered by the defendant, amounting to a penalty [41]. The "take nothing" approach ignored the fact that he secured a higher salary than he was qualified for solely through fraud [44]. The Court adopted a "middle way" to disgorge the profit obtained by the fraud. This is calculated as the difference between the defendant's salary in the fraudulent role and the salary he would likely have earned in a job he was actually qualified for (using his previous salary as a proxy) [45], [48].
Applying this, the difference between his fraudulent salary (£75k) and his prior salary (£54k) was 38%. This percentage applied to his total earnings (£643k) yielded a proportionate benefit figure of £244k. Since the recoverable amount (his available assets) was only £96k, confiscating that lower sum was proportionate [51]–[52].
Conclusion
The Court held that in CV fraud cases, a proportionate confiscation order targets the difference between the fraudulent earnings and what the defendant would otherwise have earned; the confiscation order was restored.

partnership to renovate and sell the property. The Bankruptcy Appellate Panel disagreed as to Kate’s culpability, 
holding that §523(a)(2)(A) barred her from discharging the debt only if she knew or had reason to know of David’s

discharge her debt to Buckley. The Bankruptcy Appellate Panel affirmed. The Ninth Circuit reversed in relevant 
part. Invoking Strang v. Bradner, 114 U. S. 555, 5 S. Ct. 1038, 29 L. Ed. 248, the court held that a debtor who is 
liable for her partner’s fraud cannot discharge that debt in bankruptcy, regardless of her own culpability.
Held: Section 523(a)(2)(A) precludes Kate Bartenwerfer from discharging in bankruptcy a debt obtained by fraud, 
regardless of her own culpability. Pp. 3-12.
(a) Kate (hereinafter, Bartenwerfer) disputes a straightforward reading of §523(a)(2)(A)’s text. Bartenwerfer argues 
that an ordinary English speaker would understand that “money obtained by fraud” means money obtained by the 
individual debtor's fraud. This Court disagrees. The passive voice in §523(a)(2)(A) does not hide the relevant  [*70]  
actor in plain sight, as Bartenwerfer suggests—it removes the actor altogether. Congress framed §523(a)(2)(A) 
to [****3]  “focu[s] on an event that occurs without respect to a specific actor, and therefore without respect to any 
actor’s intent or culpability.” Dean v. United States, 556 U. S. 568, 572, 129 S. Ct. 1849, 173 L. Ed. 2d 785. It is true 
that context can confine a passive-voice sentence to a likely set of actors. See, e.g., E. I. du Pont de Nemours & 
Co. v. Train, 430 U. S. 112, 128-129, 97 S. Ct. 965, 51 L. Ed. 2d 204. But the legal context relevant to 
§523(a)(2)(A)—the common law of fraud—has long maintained that fraud liability is not limited to the wrongdoer. 
Understanding §523(a)(2)(A) to reflect “agnosticism” as to the identity of the wrongdoer is consistent with the age
old rule of fraud liability.
Bartenwerfer points out that “‘exceptions to discharge should be confined to those plainly expressed.’” Bullock v. 
BankChampaign, N. A., 569 U. S. 267, 275, 133 S. Ct. 1754, 185 L. Ed. 2d 922. The Court, however, has never 
used this principle to artificially narrow ordinary meaning, invoking it instead to stress that exceptions should not 
extend beyond their stated terms. See, e.g., Gleason v. Thaw, 236 U. S. 558, 559-562, 35 S. Ct. 287, 59 L. Ed. 
717.
Bartenwerfer also seeks support from §523(a)(2)(A)’s neighboring provisions in  [**669]  subparagraphs (B) and 
(C), both of which require some culpable action by the debtor herself. Bartenwerfer claims that these neighboring 
provisions make explicit what is unstated in (A). This argument turns on its head the rule that “‘[w]hen Congress 
includes particular language in one section . . . but omits it in another section of the same Act,’” [****4]  the Court 
generally takes “the choice to be deliberate.” Badgerow v. Walters, 596 U. S. ___, ___, 142 S. Ct. 1310, 212 L. Ed. 
2d 355, 365. If there is an inference to be drawn here, the more likely one is that (A) excludes debtor culpability 
from consideration given that (B) and (C) expressly hinge on it. Bartenwerfer suggests it would defy credulity to 
think that Congress would bar debtors from discharging liability for fraud they did not personally commit under (A) 
while allowing debtors to discharge debt for (potentially more serious) fraudulent statements they did not personally 
make under (B). But the Court offered a possible answer for this disparity in Field v. Mans, 516 U. S. 59, 76-77, 116 
S. Ct. 437, 133 L. Ed. 2d 351. Whatever the rationale, it does not defy credulity to think that Congress established 
differing rules for (A) and (B). Pp. 3-8.
(b) Any remaining doubt about the textual analysis is eliminated by this Court’s precedent and Congress’s response 
to it. In Strang v. Bradner, 114 U. S. 555, 5 S. Ct. 1038, 29 L. Ed. 248, the Court held that the fraud of one partner 
should be imputed to the other partners, who “received and appropriated the fruits of the fraudulent conduct.” Id., at 
561, 5 S. Ct. 1038, 29 L. Ed. 248. The Court so held despite the fact that the relevant 19th-century discharge 
exception for fraud disallowed the discharge of debts “created by the fraud or embezzlement of the bankrupt.” 14 
Stat. 533 (emphasis added). [****5]   [*71]  And when Congress next overhauled bankruptcy law, it deleted the 
Bartenwerfer v. Buckley
Page 6 of 12
phrase “of the bankrupt” from the discharge exception for fraud. The unmistakable implication is that Congress 
embraced Strang’s holding. See Ysleta Del Sur Pueblo v. Texas, 596 U. S. ___, ___, 142 S. Ct. 1929, 213 L. Ed. 
2d 221. Pp. 8-10.
(c) Finally, Bartenwerfer insists that the preclusion of faultless debtors from discharging liabilities run up by their 
associates is inconsistent with bankruptcy law’s “fresh start” policy. But the Bankruptcy Code is not focused on the 
unadulterated pursuit of the debtor’s interest, and instead seeks to balance multiple, often competing interests. 
Bartenwerfer’s fairness-based critiques also miss the fact that §523(a)(2)(A) does not define the scope of one’s 
liability for another’s fraud. Section 523(a)(2)(A) takes the debt as it finds it, so if California did not extend liability to 
honest partners, §523(a)(2)(A) would have no role here. And while Bartenwerfer paints a picture of liability being 
imposed on hapless bystanders, fraud liability generally requires a special relationship to the wrongdoer and, even 
then, defenses to liability are available. Pp. 10-12.
