years, both that rule and its reasoning spread. Circuit after circuit (with just a couple of holdouts) justified adopting a 
prejudice requirement based on the “liberal national policy favoring arbitration.” Carolina Throwing Co. v. S & E 
Novelty Corp., 442 F. 2d 329, 331 (CA4 1971) (per curiam); see, e.g., 
PaineWebber Inc. v. Faragalli, 61 F. 3d 1063, 
1068-1069 (CA3 1995); 
HN4[
Shinto Shipping Co. v. Fibrex & Shipping Co., Inc., 572 F. 2d 1328, 1330 (CA9 1978).
] But the FAA’s “policy favoring arbitration” does not authorize federal courts to invent special, arbitration
preferring procedural rules. Moses H. Cone, 460 U. S., at 24, 103 S. Ct. 927, 74 L. Ed. 2d 765. 
Our frequent use of 
that phrase connotes something different. “Th[e] policy,” we have explained, “is merely an acknowledgment of the 
FAA’s commitment [****11]  to overrule the judiciary’s longstanding refusal to enforce agreements to arbitrate and 
to place such agreements upon the same footing as other contracts.” Granite Rock  [***760]  Co. v. Teamsters, 561 
U. S. 287, 302, 130 S. Ct. 2847, 177 L. Ed. 2d 567 (2010) (internal quotation marks omitted). 
Or in another 
formulation: The policy is to make “arbitration agreements as enforceable as other contracts, but not more so.” 
Prima Paint Corp. v. Flood & Conklin Mfg. Co., 388 U. S. 395, 404, n. 12, 87 S. Ct. 1801, 18 L. Ed. 2d 1270 (1967). 
Accordingly, a court must hold a party to its arbitration contract just as the court would to any other kind. But a court 
may not devise novel rules to favor arbitration over litigation. See Dean Witter Reynolds Inc. v. Byrd, 470 U. S. 213, 
218-221, 105 S. Ct. 1238, 84 L. Ed. 2d 158 (1985). 
If an ordinary procedural rule—whether of waiver or forfeiture or 
what-have-you—would counsel against enforcement of an arbitration contract, then so be it. The federal policy is 
about treating arbitration contracts like all others, not about fostering arbitration. See ibid.; National Foundation for 
Cancer Research v. A. G. Edwards  [**1714]  & Sons, Inc., 821 F. 2d 772, 774, 261 U.S. App. D.C. 284 (CADC 
1987) (“The Supreme Court has made clear” that the FAA’s policy “is based upon the enforcement of contract, 
 [*419]  rather than a preference for arbitration as an alternative dispute resolution mechanism”).
HN5[
] And indeed, the text of the FAA makes clear that courts are not to create arbitration-specific procedural 
rules like the one we address here. Section 6 of the FAA provides that any application under the statute—including 
an application [****12]  to stay litigation or compel arbitration—“shall be made and heard in the manner provided by 
law for the making and hearing of motions” (unless the statute says otherwise). A directive to a federal court to treat 
arbitration applications “in the manner provided by law” for all other motions is simply a command to apply the usual 
federal procedural rules, including any rules relating to a motion’s timeliness. Or put conversely, it is a bar on using 
custom-made rules, to tilt the playing field in favor of (or against) arbitration. As explained above, the usual federal 
rule of waiver does not include a prejudice requirement. So Section 6 instructs that prejudice is not a condition of 
finding that a party, by litigating too long, waived its right to stay litigation or compel arbitration under the FAA.
Morgan v. Sundance, Inc., 596 U.S. 411
Page 7 of 7
Stripped of its prejudice requirement, the Eighth Circuit’s current waiver inquiry would focus on Sundance’s 
conduct. Did Sundance, as the rest of the Eighth Circuit’s test asks, knowingly relinquish the right to arbitrate by 
acting inconsistently with that right? See supra, at 3. On remand, the Court of Appeals may resolve that question, or 
(as indicated above) determine that a different procedural [****13]  framework (such as forfeiture) is appropriate. 
See supra, at 4. Our sole holding today is that it may not make up a new procedural rule based on the FAA’s “policy 
favoring arbitration.”
***
For the reasons stated, we vacate the judgment of the Court of Appeals and remand the case for further 
proceedings consistent with this opinion.
It is so ordered.
End of Document
IRAC_summ:
Case Name: Morgan v. Sundance, Inc. [2022] 596 U.S. 411
Court + jurisdiction: Supreme Court of the United States
Area of law: Civil Procedure – Arbitration – Waiver
Procedural posture: On writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
Issue
Whether federal courts may condition a waiver of the right to arbitrate on a showing that the opposing party was prejudiced by the delay, based on the Federal Arbitration Act's (FAA) "policy favoring arbitration."
Rule
Under the FAA, courts must place arbitration agreements on the same footing as other contracts, but may not devise novel rules to favor arbitration over litigation (Granite Rock Co. v. Teamsters). Section 6 of the FAA requires that applications to compel arbitration be heard "in the manner provided by law" for other motions, necessitating the application of general federal procedural rules. The general federal rule for waiver is the "intentional relinquishment or abandonment of a known right" and does not include a prejudice requirement (United States v. Olano).
Application
The Court rejected the Eighth Circuit's arbitration-specific waiver rule. The lower court had required a showing of prejudice solely because of the "federal policy favoring arbitration" [415]. The Supreme Court clarified that this policy is merely an acknowledgment of the FAA's commitment to overrule judicial hostility toward arbitration and to ensure arbitration agreements are as enforceable as other contracts, "but not more so" [418].
By demanding proof of prejudice—a requirement not present in general federal waiver law—the Eighth Circuit created a "bespoke rule of waiver for arbitration" [417]. This violates Section 6 of the FAA, which instructs courts to apply ordinary procedural rules to arbitration applications [419]. Since the ordinary definition of waiver focuses on the actions of the right-holder (relinquishment) rather than the effects on the opponent (prejudice), the court cannot impose a prejudice requirement to save an arbitration agreement [418]. The Court remanded for the lower court to apply the correct waiver analysis (or forfeiture) without the prejudice prong.
Conclusion
The FAA does not authorize federal courts to create an arbitration-specific prejudice requirement for waiver; the judgment is vacated and remanded.

case_name: G v G [2021] UKSC 9
case:
G v G [2021] All ER (D) 77 (Mar)
Page 1 of 4
[2021] UKSC 9
Supreme Court
G v G [2021] All ER (D) 77 (Mar)
Lord Lloyd-Jones, Lord Hamblen, Lord Leggatt, Lord Burrows and Lord Stephens SCJJ
19 March 2021
Minor – Child Abduction – Asylum proceedings
Abstract
In partially allowing the appellant mother's appeal from a decision of the Court of Appeal, Civil Division, the 
Supreme Court held that a child named as a dependant on her parent's asylum request who could objectively be 
understood to have made a request for international protection had protection from being expelled or returned to a 
country where they could be persecuted, pending the determination of that application so that until then, a return 
order in the 1980 Hague Convention proceedings could not be implemented. The court nevertheless maintained the 
set-aside of a stay and remitted the case to the Family Division for further consideration of the 1980 Hague 
Convention application. 
Digest
The judgment is available at: [2021] UKSC 9
  Background     
An eight-year-old girl, G, who was born in South Africa was wrongfully removed by her mother from South Africa to 
the UK in breach of G's father's rights of custody under South African law. The father commenced proceedings 
under the Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction 1980 (the 1980 Hague Convention) for 
the return of G to South Africa. On her arrival in the UK, the mother applied to the Secretary of State for the Home 
Department for asylum, naming G as a dependant. Accordingly, there was a tension between the objective of the 
1980 Hague Convention proceedings to expeditiously return a wrongfully removed or retained child to his home 
jurisdiction, and the principle of the asylum application that refugees should not be refouled (expelled or returned to 
a country where they could be persecuted). The 1980 Hague Convention proceedings were stayed, but based on 
the misunderstanding that G had made an asylum application in her own right. The Court of Appeal (COA) having 
been informed that there was no separate application by G for asylum but rather that G had been named as a 
dependant on her mother's application, lifted the stay on the basis that where G was named as a dependant on her 
mother's asylum application a return order in respect of G could be both made and implemented in the 1980 Hague 
Convention proceedings prior to the determination by the Secretary of State of the mother's asylum application. If G 
had made her own separate application for asylum, then the COA considered that, whilst a return order could be 
made, it could not be implemented during the pendency of the application. It gave detailed guidance as to the 
discretion to stay the 1980 Hague Convention proceedings in such circumstances stating that as a general 
proposition the High Court should be slow to stay a 1980 Hague Convention. The mother appealed.
  Issues and decisions     
(1) Whether a child named as a dependant on a parent's asylum application (without a separate application in his 
own right) had protection from refoulement pending the determination of that application. 
*G v G [2021] All ER (D) 77 (Mar)
Page 2 of 4
In the UK, the legal procedures for identifying refugees and protecting refugees from refoulement were derived from 
a patchwork of different sources including the 1951 Geneva Convention, EU law, domestic legislation, regulations 
and rules and domestic law incorporating EU and ECHR legal obligations. The principal EU measures were: (i) 
Council Directive 2004/83 (the Qualification Directive); and (ii) Council Directive 2005/85 (the Procedures Directive). 
The Procedures Directive set out the minimum procedural obligations with which a member state needed to comply 
in determining claims for international protection. The transposition of the Directives into domestic law was primarily 
sought to be achieved through amendments to the Immigration Rules (the Rules) (see [77], [78], [83], [90], [96] of 
the judgment). 
Although there was no obligation on the Secretary of State to consider whether an individual was a refugee absent 
any application,  art  2(g) of the Qualification Directive only required there to be a request by a third country national 
or stateless person for protection who could be understood to seek refugee status (or other international protection). 
Also, art 2(b) of the Procedures Directive only required there to be an application made by a third country national 
or stateless person which could be understood as a request for international protection. An omission by a child to 
make an application in their own right could not therefore be regarded as a choice which the child had made (even 
if he or she had legal capacity to make it). Understanding an application for refugee status or which named a child 
as a dependant as including an application by the child accordingly protected the interests of the child by ensuring 
that the child's own status was considered. Such separate consideration was necessary not least because, if the 
principal application was granted, the kind of residence permit for which the child was eligible depended on whether 
or not the child was a refugee or in his or her own right (see [117] of the judgment). 
A child named as a dependant on the parent's asylum application and who had not made a separate request for 
international protection generally could and should be understood to be seeking such protection and therefore 
treated as an applicant (see [121] of the judgment). 
A dependant who could objectively be understood as being an applicant was entitled to rely on art 7 of the 
Procedures Directive which ensured non-refoulement of a refugee who was awaiting a decision so that a return 
order could not be implemented pending determination by the Secretary of State (see [130] of the judgment). 
Such a dependant could also rely on para 329 of the Rules. Paragraph 329 was an emanation of the duty not to 
refoule a refugee under art 7 of the Procedures Directive. Paragraph 329 required that no action would be taken to 
require his or her departure from the UK prior to the determination of the application by the Secretary of State (see 
[131] of the judgment). 
An applicant had protection from refoulement pending the determination of that application, so that until the request 
for international protection was determined by the Secretary of State, a return order in the 1980 Hague Convention 
proceedings could not be implemented. The two Conventions were not independent of each other but rather had to 
operate hand in hand (see [134] of the judgment). 
Saad v Secretary of State for the Home Department, Diriye v Secretary of State for the Home Department, Osorio v 
Secretary of State for the Home Department [2001] EWCA Civ 2008 [2001] All ER (D) 307 (Dec) [2002] INLR 34 
considered; R v Asfaw [2008] All ER (D) 274 (May) [2008] 3 All ER 775 [2008] 1 AC 1061 considered; EN (Serbia) v 
Secretary of State for the Home Department; KC (South Africa) v Secretary of State for the Home Department 
[2009] All ER (D) 289 (Jun) [2009] EWCA Civ 630 [2010] 3 WLR 182 considered; Secretary of State for the Home 
Department v Pankina [2010] All ER (D) 196 (Jun) [2010] EWCA Civ 719 [2011] 1 All ER 1043 considered; R (on 
the application of ST (Eritrea)) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2012] All ER (D) 149 (Mar) [2012] 3 
All ER 1037 [2012] UKSC 12 considered; R (on the application of ST (Eritrea)) v Secretary of State for the Home 
Department [2012] UKSC 12 [2012] 3 All ER 1037 [2012] All ER (D) 149 (Mar) considered; Ali v Secretary of State 
for the Home Department [2016] UKSC 60 [2016] 1 WLR 4799 [2016] All ER (D) 90 (Nov) considered; Secretary of 
State for the Home Department v KN (DRC) [2019] EWCA Civ 1665 [2019] All ER (D) 62 (Oct) considered.
(2) Whether the High Court could determine the 1980 Hague Convention proceedings and make a return order in 
circumstances where there was a pending asylum claim of either the taking parent or the child.
*G v G [2021] All ER (D) 77 (Mar)
Page 3 of 4
The court could consider the merits of the 1980 Hague Convention proceedings even if the factual issues 
overlapped with the asylum claims, so long as the prohibition on determining the claim for international protection 
was not infringed (see [157] of the judgment). 
If, as a result of the decision of the Secretary of State in relation to the asylum process, a reconsideration of the 
1980 Hague Convention proceedings was required, then the court had power in England and Wales under FPR rule 
12.52A or under the inherent jurisdiction to review and set aside a final order under the 1980 Hague Convention 
(see [158] of the judgment).
The COA's clearly reasoned conclusion that 'any bar applies only to implementation' was plainly right (see [157]
[159] of the judgment).
Re B (a child) (abduction: Article 13(b)) [2020] All ER (D) 29 (Aug) [2020] EWCA Civ 1057 [2021] 1 All ER 1138 
applied.
(3) Whether the COA had been wrong to have given guidance to the effect that, in most cases, the High Court 
should proceed to determine the 1980 Hague Convention application rather than stay it pending determination of 
any asylum claim.
The general proposition made by the COA that 'the High Court should be slow to stay an application prior to any 
determination' was entirely consistent with the aims and objectives of the 1980 Hague Convention including the 
obligations of expedition and priority (see [160] of the judgment). 
The matters which the COA had taken into account when determining whether, and, if so, when to grant a stay of 
the 1980 Hague Convention proceedings would be endorsed (see [161], [162] of the judgment). 
(4) Practical points to be considered as to the interplay between the two proceedings.
Under para 328 of the  Rules, the Secretary of State had sole responsibility for both examining and determining 
claims for international protection. Although the 1980 Hague Convention proceedings were separate from the 
asylum process, the same factual background could form the basis for both (see [163], [164] of the judgment). 
 For the Conventions to operate hand in hand, in related claims, there were practical steps which should ordinarily 
be taken, aimed at enhancing decision making in both sets of proceedings.  Proceedings were related once it 
became apparent that an application for asylum had been made by a parent (regardless of whether the child was 
objectively understood to have made an application or been named as a dependant) or by a child (see [165] of the 
judgment). 
With related proceedings, it was desirable that the Secretary of State be requested to intervene in the 1980 Hague 
Convention. The documents in the 1980 Hague Convention proceedings should ordinarily be made available to the 
Secretary of State having regard to any disclosure issues. Also there were other steps that should be taken such as 
joining the child as party to the 1980 Hague Convention proceedings with representation (see [166], [167], [169], 
[170] of the judgment). 
The establishing of a specialist asylum team to which that small group of cases would be assigned as soon as it 
was appreciated that there were related cases was endorsed (see [168] of the Convention). 
Consideration was to be given to the harmonising, in so far as possible, the speed of the decision-making 
processes under the respective Conventions, including the issuing of standard directions in the 1980 Hague 
Convention proceedings where there was a parallel asylum claim. Consideration was also to be given to the 
assignment of cases to a judge with the requisite experience (see [174], [175] of the judgment). 
It was desirable that the High Court should have oversight over and be in a position to co-ordinate both proceedings 
until both have been concluded (see [176] of the judgment). 
*G v G [2021] All ER (D) 77 (Mar)
Page 4 of 4
A child named as a dependant on her parent's asylum request who could objectively be understood to have made a 
request for international protection had protection from refoulement pending the determination of that application so 
that until then a return order in the 1980 Hague Convention proceedings could not be implemented. However, the 
order of the COA setting aside the stay imposed and remitting the case to the Family Division for further 
consideration of the 1980 Hague Convention application would be maintained (see [178]-[180]  of the judgment). 
R v Mc Geough [2015] All ER (D) 180 (Oct) [2015] UKSC 62 [2016] 1 All ER 953 considered; Re H (a child) 
(international abduction: asylum and welfare) [2016] All ER (D) 79 (Oct) [2016] EWCA Civ 988 [2017] 2 FLR 527 
considered; Re H (a child) (disclosure of asylum documents) Secretary of State for the Home Department and 
another v R and another [2021] 1 FLR 586 [2020] EWCA Civ 1001 considered.
Decision of  Court of Appeal, Civil Division  [2020] EWCA Civ 1185 Affirmed In Part.
Henry Setright QC, Michael Gration, Jason Pobjoy and Emmeline Plews (instructed by A & N Care Solicitors 
(Sheffield) for the appellant. 
Edward Devereux QC, Zane Malik QC and William Tyzack (instructed by Dawson Cornwell (London) for the 
respondent.
Alan Payne QC and John Goss (instructed by The Government Legal Department) for the first intervener. 
James Turner QC, Mehvish Chaudhry and Paige Campbell (instructed by Bindmans LLP (London)) for the second 
intervener. 
Richard Harrison QC, Jennifer Perrins and Mark Smith (instructed by Brethertons LLP (Rugby)) for the third 
intervener. 
Alex Verdan QC, Dr S Chelvan and Charlotte Baker (instructed by Goodman Ray LLP (London)) for the fourth 
intervener. 
Raza Husain QC, Malcolm Birdling and Gayatri Sarathy(instructed by Baker & McKenzie LLP (London)) for the fifth 
intervener. 
Mark Twomey QC, Sarah Tyler and Alexander Laing (instructed by Farrer & Co LLP (London)) for the sixth 
intervener.

IRAC_summ:
Case Name: G v G [2021] UKSC 9
Court + jurisdiction: United Kingdom Supreme Court
Area of law: Family Law – Child Abduction – Asylum – Non-Refoulement
Procedural posture: Appeal from the Court of Appeal, Civil Division
Issue
Whether a child named as a dependant on a parent's asylum application has protection from refoulement (return) pending the determination of that application, such that a return order made under the 1980 Hague Convention cannot be implemented until the asylum claim is decided.
Rule
Under the 1951 Refugee Convention and EU Directives (retained in UK law), an asylum applicant is protected from refoulement (return to the country of persecution) until their claim is finally determined. A child named as a dependant on a parent's asylum application is effectively an applicant for international protection. Therefore, a return order under the 1980 Hague Convention on Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction cannot be implemented while the asylum application is pending. However, the Hague Convention proceedings themselves need not be stayed and can proceed to the point of making a return order, subject to the bar on implementation.
Application
The mother wrongfully removed the child (G) from South Africa to the UK and applied for asylum, naming G as a dependant. The father sought G's return under the Hague Convention. The Court of Appeal held the return could be implemented because G had not made a separate asylum application.
The Supreme Court corrected this. It held that naming a child as a dependant constitutes a request for international protection for the child. Consequently, G was an "applicant" protected by the principle of non-refoulement [121], [130]. Implementing a return order before the asylum claim was decided would violate this protection [134].
However, the Court held that the Hague Convention proceedings should not be stayed entirely. The High Court can and should determine the Hague application (including defences under Article 13(b)) concurrently with the asylum process. This avoids delay. If a return order is made, its execution is simply suspended until the asylum claim is rejected [157]–[160]. The Court provided guidance on coordinating the two processes, including inviting the Home Secretary to intervene in the family proceedings [166]–[176].
Conclusion
The Court held that a child named as a dependant on an asylum claim cannot be returned until the claim is determined, but the Hague Convention proceedings should continue to judgment; the appeal was allowed in part.

case:
Page 1 of 6
Davis v. Commonwealth, 2025 Va. App. LEXIS 685

Davis v. Commonwealth
Court of Appeals of Virginia

October 28, 2025, Decided

Record No. 1568-24-1 

Reporter
2025 Va. App. LEXIS 685 *; 2025 LX 443705

MARCUS WARREN DAVIS v. COMMONWEALTH OF VIRGINIA 

Notice: Decision text below is the first available text from the court; it has not been editorially reviewed by 
LexisNexis. Publisher's editorial review, including Headnotes, Case Summary, Shepard's analysis or any 
amendments will be added in accordance with LexisNexis editorial guidelines.

Core Terms

contraband, inside, cocaine, mail, aunt, gun, trial court, guilt, constructive possession, duffle bag, proximity, arrive, 
beyond a reasonable doubt, common area, living room, no evidence, duffel bag, cordon

Opinion

 [*1] FROM THE CIRCUIT COURT OF THE CITY OF PORTSMOUTH

Johnny E. Morrison, Judge

Barrett R. Richardson (Richardson and Rosenberg, LLC, on briefs), for appellant.

Angelique Rogers, Assistant Attorney General (Jason S. Miyares,

Attorney General, on brief), for appellee.

Following a bench trial, the trial court convicted Marcus Warren Davis of possession of cocaine with the intent to 
distribute in violation of Code § 18.2-248. Davis asserts that the evidence is insufficient to support his conviction. 
We agree with Davis and reverse the trial court's judgment.

BACKGROUND

"On appeal, 'we review the evidence in the "light most favorable" to the Commonwealth,' the prevailing party 
below." Diaz v. Commonwealth, 80 Va. App. 286, 295 (2024) (quoting

Clanton v. Commonwealth, 53 Va. App. 561, 564 (2009) (en banc)). "That principle requires us to



Page 2 of 6
Davis v. Commonwealth, 2025 Va. App. LEXIS 685

'discard the evidence of the accused in conflict with that of the Commonwealth, and regard as true all the credible 
evidence favorable to the Commonwealth and all fair inferences that may be drawn therefrom.'" Id. (quoting Kelly v. 
Commonwealth, 41 Va. App. 250, 254 (2003) (en banc)).

* This opinion is not designated for publication. See Code § 17.1-413(A).

A few months before January 25, 2024, Davis was released from jail and his aunt allowed him to stay at her 
residence at 3002 Detroit Street in Portsmouth. On January 25, the police went to the Detroit [*2]  Street address 
with an arrest warrant for Davis and a search warrant 1 for the home. When the police arrived, they found Davis in 
the front yard speaking with another man, approximately ten feet from the house. Davis was arrested, searched, 
and placed in a police car. No drugs or other narcotics were found on his person. When officers cleared the house, 
only Davis's aunt was in the residence.

Upon entry through the front door, officers were inside a living room area. 2 Upon searching that room, the police 
found a .22 caliber handgun on a small end table next to a recliner to the far left. 3 Underneath that table, they 
found a box of sandwich bags on the floor. To the far right of the room, approximately 12 feet away from the end 
table, was a closed red duffle bag on the floor beside a love seat. Inside the duffle bag were 24 individually wrapped 
baggy corners containing a total of 4.31 grams of cocaine and a separate, single "clump," which was 23.5 grams of 
cocaine. 4

On the love seat near the closed duffel bag, the police found a piece of mail addressed to Davis at

1The existence of a search warrant was referred to at trial but no search warrant was provided in discovery and 
none is [*3]  in the record because the trial court sustained defense counsel's motion to exclude admission of a 
copy of the search warrant at trial.

2 The living room area was also referred to by the parties and the trial court as a

"common area."

3The gun was swabbed for DNA but no certificate of analysis was produced at trial nor is there one in the record.

4 Police testified they also found in the living room what they described as "cut"-

"material, normally some sort of powder, that is mixed in with various narcotics in order to -- it weakens the potency 
of it, but it increases the amount that you can distribute"-with empty capsules in a brown bag but "I can't recall 
where that brown bag was." The Commonwealth did not argue at trial or on brief that the presence of "cut" was any 
indicator of knowledge of the substance or dominion and control. It is merely mentioned in a footnote on brief that it 
was depicted in a photograph exhibit admitted at trial.

- 2 -

3002 Detroit Street. There were also two other pieces of opened mail with Davis's name and the

Detroit Street address found elsewhere in the living room. 5

Upon being questioned, Davis denied knowledge of the gun and drugs saying, "he didn't know [*4]  anything about 
that." When the police noted that Davis's aunt was the only other person in the house and asked, "Are you saying 
it's hers?" he replied, "No. I'm not saying that."

The trial court denied Davis's motions to strike and found him guilty of possession of cocaine with the intent to 
distribute. Davis was acquitted of the non-violent felon in possession of a firearm charge in violation of Code § 18.2-
308.2. Davis appeals.

ANALYSIS



Page 3 of 6
Davis v. Commonwealth, 2025 Va. App. LEXIS 685

Davis argues that the evidence is insufficient to support his conviction. "When reviewing the sufficiency of the 
evidence, '[t]he judgment of the trial court is presumed correct and will not be disturbed unless it is plainly wrong or 
without evidence to support it.'" Smith v.

Commonwealth, 296 Va. 450, 460 (2018) (alteration in original) (quoting Commonwealth v. Perkins, 295 Va. 323, 
327 (2018)). "In such cases, '[t]he Court does not ask itself whether it believes that the evidence at the trial 
established guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.'" Secret v.Commonwealth, 296 Va. 204, 228 (2018) (alteration in 
original) (quoting Pijor v.

Commonwealth, 294 Va. 502, 512 (2017)). "Rather, the relevant question is, upon review of the evidence in the 
light most favorable to the prosecution, whether any rational trier of fact could have found the essential elements of 
the crime beyond a reasonable doubt." Id. (quoting Pijor,

294 Va. at 512). "If there is evidentiary [*5]  support for the conviction, 'the reviewing court is not permitted to 
substitute its own judgment, even if its opinion might differ from the conclusions

5 Unsure of where the other pieces of mail were recovered, Detective Barber testified that the photo showing the 
three pieces of mail together was not where those items were actually recovered-"[W]e moved them all to the couch 
to photograph them."

- 3 -

reached by the finder of fact at the trial.'" Chavez v. Commonwealth, 69 Va. App. 149, 161 (2018) (quoting Banks v. 
Commonwealth, 67 Va. App. 273, 288 (2017)).

The Commonwealth relies upon circumstantial evidence to establish Davis's constructive possession of cocaine in 
this case. As such "all necessary circumstances proved must be consistent with guilt and inconsistent with 
innocence and exclude every reasonable hypothesis of innocence." Cordon v. Commonwealth, 280 Va. 691, 694 
(2010). Thus, the Commonwealth was required to establish beyond a reasonable doubt that Davis knew that 
cocaine was inside the duffle bag in the living room of his aunt's house and that bag was subject to his dominion 
and control. Davis asserts that the evidence failed to meet this burden. 6 He argues that "there was no conduct that 
showed that [he] was aware of the presence and character of the cocaine, and there was insufficient evidence the 
cocaine was subject [*6]  to his dominion and control."

"In interpreting the Commonwealth's basic statutes proscribing possession of drugs, . . .

the applicable legal principles are clear: Possession may be actual or constructive." Wright v.Commonwealth, 53 
Va. App. 266, 273 (2009). "Establishing constructive possession requires proof 'that the defendant was aware of 
both the presence and character of the [item] and that it was subject to his dominion and control.'" Watts v. 
Commonwealth, 57 Va. App. 217, 232-33 (2010) (alteration in original) (quoting Powers v. Commonwealth, 227 Va. 
474, 476 (1984)).

"[T]he Commonwealth must present evidence of acts, statements, or conduct by the defendant or other facts and 
circumstances proving that the defendant was aware of the presence and character of the [contraband] and that the 
[contraband was] subject to his dominion and control."

Smallwood v. Commonwealth, 278 Va. 625, 630 (2009) (quoting Bolden v. Commonwealth, 275 Va. 144, 148 
(2008)). To obtain a conviction for possessory offenses, "the Commonwealth must

6 Davis does not argue on appeal that the Commonwealth failed to prove intent to distribute, so we do not address 
it here.

- 4 -

produce evidence sufficient to allow a rational factfinder to conclude beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant 
intentionally and consciously possessed the contraband with knowledge of its nature and character." 



Page 4 of 6
Davis v. Commonwealth, 2025 Va. App. LEXIS 685

Commonwealth v. Garrick, 303 Va. 176, 183 (2024). "Whether evidence is sufficient to prove constructive 
possession [*7]  'is largely a factual' question . . . ." McArthur v.

Commonwealth, 72 Va. App. 352, 368 (2020) (quotingSmallwood, 278 Va. at 630). "Possession need not be actual, 
exclusive, or lengthy in order to support a conviction; instead, the statute criminalizes constructive or joint 
possession of illegal [items] of any duration[,]" regardless of who actually owns them. Wells v. Commonwealth, 32 
Va. App. 775, 781 (2000).

"Although mere proximity to the contraband is insufficient to establish possession, it is a factor that may be 
considered in determining whether a defendant possessed the contraband."

Archer v. Commonwealth, 26 Va. App. 1, 12 (1997). "Some courts have defined dominion and control to mean 'the 
ability to reduce an object to actual possession.'" Hunter v. Commonwealth, 56 Va. App. 50, 60 n.4 (2010). But 
"[s]uspicious circumstances, including proximity to a controlled drug, are insufficient to support a conviction." 
Behrens v. Commonwealth, 3 Va. App. 131, 135 (1986).

At the time the officers arrived, Davis was outside of the home. The record is silent as to how long Davis had been 
outside the home or when he was last inside the home prior to the arrival of the police. Neither the duffle bag nor 
the drugs contained in it could be visible to Davis from outside the home. Nor were the drugs visible or in plain view 
from inside the home. Consequently, Davis's physical proximity to the home's exterior does not equate to physical 
proximity to the drugs discovered [*8]  inside the home. While there was evidence that at the time Davis was 
observed outside the home, he was in a grassy area "10 feet away from the front door," there was no evidence at 
trial touching on the question of whether Davis had any "ability to reduce the [contraband] to his actual possession" 
from where he stood outside the home.

- 5 -

Additionally, the fact that Davis's mail was located in the same room as the drugs found in a closed duffel bag is of 
no moment and does not prove that Davis ever had the ability to actually possess the drugs at any particular time. 
Cordon, 280 Va. at 696 (Personal effects found in the room where drugs were located is insufficient to prove 
beyond a reasonable doubt that Cordon was aware of the presence of the drugs found in a sealed cooler or that he 
had dominion and control.). This is especially true where the duffle bag, like the cooler in Cordon, was a very 
portable item; there were no forensics tying Davis to the drugs; and no evidence of when Davis might have last 
been in the home or when the drugs and gun were placed there.

Proof that drugs are found "in premises . . . owned or occupied by the defendant is insufficient, standing alone, to 
prove constructive possession. [*9]  Such evidence is probative, but it is only 'a circumstance which may be 
considered . . . along with the other evidence.'" Powers, 227 Va. at 476 (second alteration in original) (quoting Gillis 
v. Commonwealth, 215 Va. 298, 301 (1974)); Code § 18.2-250 ("[O]wnership or occupancy of premises or vehicle 
upon or in which a controlled substance was found shall not create a presumption that such person either knowingly 
or intentionally possessed such controlled substance.").

In Powers, the Virginia Supreme Court reversed a conviction for constructive possession of LSD. Police executed a 
search warrant at Powers's home that he rented with his wife.

Powers, 227 Va. at 475. Neither one was present when police arrived. Id. A search of the premises revealed LSD 
hidden in an unfinished attic and Powers was arrested upon returning to the home. Id. at 475-76. The 
Commonwealth could not point to evidence of any acts, conduct or statements of Powers "or other facts or 
circumstances" tending to show he "was aware of both the presence and character of the [LSD] and that [they 
were] subject to his dominion and control." Id. at 476. The fact that Powers and his wife were sole residents of the 
premises,

- 6 -



Page 5 of 6
Davis v. Commonwealth, 2025 Va. App. LEXIS 685

Powers's failure to disclaim guilt, and the street value of the drugs were not sufficient evidence to support a 
conviction for constructive [*10]  possession. Id. at 476-77.

When asked about the contraband, Davis denied it was his and when police suggested that his denial must mean it 
was his aunt's, Davis replied, "I'm not saying that." The Commonwealth argued that this statement "in a roundabout 
way" must mean that the contraband belonged to Davis "if he's saying . . . it's not hers." The trial court flatly rejected 
that argument saying, "I can't make my decision based on a roundabout way and stuff like that. You know that. I 
can't speculate." A trial court is not permitted to infer guilt solely from the fact that an accused makes a statement 
denying knowledge of the drugs. It is true that if a defendant's denial of circumstances relating to an illegal act is 
inconsistent with previous statements or facts, a factfinder may infer guilty knowledge. See Covil v. Commonwealth, 
268 Va. 692, 695-96 (2004). But in this case, Davis's statement was not inconsistent with any other statements 
made by him or with the facts, and the trial court was therefore not entitled to make an inference of guilty knowledge 
and in fact did not do so. See Cordon, 280 Va. at 695.

The Commonwealth argued at trial and on brief that the fact that Davis and his aunt were the only occupants of the 
house and the drugs were in the same room where [*11]  Davis's mail was found was sufficient to prove he had 
knowledge. As noted in Powers, this is not "other evidence" to be considered to show awareness of the presence 
and character of the contraband but rather such evidence "merely tends to reinforce the conclusion that the 
defendant and his wife were the sole residents of the premises; it does not foreclose the possibility that 
the[contraband] was owned and hidden by another." 227 Va. at 476 (emphasis added); see Young v. 
Commonwealth, 275 Va. 587, 592 (2008) ("Countless scenarios can be envisioned in which controlled substances 
may be found in the possession of a person who is entirely unaware of

- 7 -

their nature and character."). Further, there was no testimony that Powers was not surprised when he was charged 
"or that he failed to disclaim his guilt." Powers, 227 Va. at 476.

Here, Davis was outside the residence when the police arrived. No drugs or firearms were found on his person. 
There is no evidence Davis attempted to flee. The drugs and firearm were found in a common area of the home. 
The drugs were not in plain view but inside a sealed duffle bag. None of Davis's mail was found inside the duffel 
bag where the drugs were concealed. While the evidence showed both Davis and his aunt stayed in the home, 
there was no [*12]  evidence about who else may have lived in the home or recently visited. There is no evidence 
as to when Davis was last in the home, when or how his mail came to be in the common area or when the drugs 
and gun were put there. Too, no forensic evidence ties Davis to the gun, the closed duffel bag or the drugs inside 
the duffel bag.

It is well established that "[w]hile a conviction may properly be based upon circumstantial evidence . . . [t]here must 
be an unbroken chain of circumstances 'proving the guilt of the accused to the "exclusion of any other rational 
hypothesis and to a moral certainty."'"

Gordon v. Commonwealth, 212 Va. 298, 300 (1971) (citation omitted). "When proof of constructive possession is 
dependent upon circumstantial evidence, 'all necessary circumstances proved must be consistent with guilt and 
inconsistent with innocence and exclude every reasonable hypothesis of innocence.'" McMillan v. Commonwealth, 
277 Va. 11, 19 (2009) (quoting Garland v. Commonwealth, 225 Va. 182, 184 (1983)).

The Commonwealth's argument for conviction is based on Davis's shared occupancy of the residence with his aunt 
and his refusal to cast blame on her, along with the close proximity of his mail to the closed duffle bag in which the 
cocaine was discovered. Specifically, the Commonwealth argues that because "the drugs and the mail [*13]  and 
the gun are all in the same

- 8 -



Page 6 of 6
Davis v. Commonwealth, 2025 Va. App. LEXIS 685

room, . . . it's all his stuff." However, such evidence does not make a conviction. "[S]uspicion or probability of guilt is 
not enough for a conviction." Model Jury Instrs.-Crim. No. 2.100.

The Commonwealth relies on several cases in support of her argument that there was sufficient evidence of 
constructive possession, but more specifically "this case resembles"

Commonwealth v. Garrick, 303 Va. 176 (2024). Their reliance on Garrick is misplaced. Garrick was found asleep 
behind the wheel of a vehicle parked in a convenience store

parking lot. Id. at 180. He was the only person in the vehicle and was within arm's reach of the drugs and gun found 
in the glovebox. Id. Garrick made statements that he drove the vehicle on a regular basis, and the vehicle 
maintenance receipts in his name were in the same glovebox

"literally intermingled with the firearm and the drugs[.]" Id. at 181 (alteration in original). In affirming Garrick's 
constructive possession conviction, 7 the Virginia Supreme Court found that a reasonable factfinder could conclude 
that the probative value of the fact that he was within arm's reach of the glovebox containing the gun and drugs was 
"increased given that he was the sole occupant of the vehicle." Id. at 184-85. In addition to his close 
proximity, [*14]  Garrick had been in the vehicle a long period of time, fell asleep in the car, was a primary driver of 
the car, and regularly maintained it based on receipts found with the contraband.

Garrick can be distinguished from the facts here. Unlike Garrick, who was the sole occupant of the vehicle 
containing the contraband, Davis was not inside the home when police arrived, and no evidence put him inside the 
home during or after the time the contraband was placed in the common area. On this record, Davis was never 
within close proximity of anything inside the home. The home was easily accessible to others-Davis's aunt not only 
owned the home but was found inside the home when police arrived. While arguably the contraband in

7 The Garrick Court focused on "whether Garrick was aware of the presence of the items." The arguments at trial 
and on appeal did not address dominion and control. Garrick, 303 Va. at 183 n.2.

- 9 -

Garrick was "concealed" in a glovebox, the personal documents with Garrick's name on them were "literally 
intermingled with" the gun and drugs. Not so here, as Davis's personal documents were found loose at various 
locations, some of them unknown, in the common area. There was no temporal evidence as to [*15]  when the mail 
was placed there or when the contraband was placed there.

The evidence here lacks any indicia that Davis knew of the nature and character of the contraband or that he ever 
exercised dominion and control over it. The totality of the circumstances in this case do not support the trial court's 
conclusion that Davis constructively possessed the cocaine.

CONCLUSION

Accordingly, we reverse the trial court's judgment and dismiss Davis's conviction.

Reversed and final judgment.

- 10 -

End of Document
IRAC_summ:
Case Name: Davis v. Commonwealth [2025] Va. App. LEXIS 685
Court and Jurisdiction: Court of Appeals of Virginia
Area of Law: Criminal Law (Possession of Controlled Substances)
Procedural Posture: Appeal from a conviction following a bench trial in the Circuit Court of the City of Portsmouth.
Issue
Whether the evidence was sufficient to prove constructive possession of cocaine found in a closed duffle bag inside a residence, where the defendant was detained outside the home, the residence was jointly occupied, and the only physical link to the contraband was the presence of the defendant's mail in the same room.
Rule
In Cordon, 280 Va. at 696, to establish constructive possession, it must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant was aware of both the presence and character of the contraband and that it was subject to his dominion and control. 
While proximity to contraband and occupancy of the premises are relevant factors, they are insufficient, standing alone, to establish possession (Code § 18.2-250).
 When a conviction relies on circumstantial evidence, the chain of circumstances must be consistent with guilt and exclude every reasonable hypothesis of innocence McMillan v. Commonwealth, 277 Va. 11, 19 (2009).Mere suspicion or probability of guilt is insufficient (Model Jury Instrs Crim. No. 2.100).

Application / Analysis
The court held that the evidence failed to establish the necessary elements of constructive possession. First, regarding proximity, the court noted that the defendant was found outside the residence, ten feet away, while his aunt was inside. There was no evidence regarding when the defendant was last inside the home or if he had the ability to reduce the items to actual possession from his location outside. Unlike cases involving plain view contraband, the drugs here were concealed within a closed duffle bag.
Second, the court addressed the presence of the defendant's mail on a loveseat near the duffle bag. The court distinguished this case from Commonwealth v. Garrick, where a defendant was the sole occupant of a vehicle and his documents were "literally intermingled" with contraband. Here, the mail was merely in the same common area as the closed bag, and not inside it. The court reasoned that personal effects found in a room are insufficient to prove knowledge of the contents of a closed container within that room (at [*14]–[*15]).
Third, the court rejected the Commonwealth's argument that the defendant's refusal to explicitly blame his aunt ("I'm not saying that") constituted an admission of guilt. The statement was not inconsistent with other facts, and based on Covil v. Commonwealth, 268 Va. 692, 695-96 (2004) a factfinder may not infer guilty knowledge solely from a refusal to incriminate another (at [*10]). Finally, because the residence was jointly occupied and accessible to others, and because there was no forensic evidence (DNA or fingerprints) linking the defendant to the bag, the evidence did not exclude the reasonable hypothesis that the contraband belonged to the aunt or another visitor.
Conclusion
The court held that the evidence was insufficient to prove constructive possession, reversed the judgment of the trial court, and dismissed the conviction.

MEMORANDUM OPINION

Relator Michael Schaefer filed a petition for writ of mandamus, requesting that this court compel the trial court to 
rule on a "Motion for Order of Satisfaction," which he alleges remains pending in the underlying proceeding.

Mandamus relief is an extraordinary remedy that is available only when the relator can show both that (1) the trial 
court clearly abused its discretion; and (2) there is no adequate remedy by appeal. In re Academy, Ltd., 625 S.W.3d 
19, 25

(Tex. 2021) (orig. proceeding). As the party seeking relief, relator has the burden of providing this court with a 
sufficient record to establish his claims for mandamus relief. Walker v. Packer, 827 S.W.2d 833, 837 (Tex. 1992) 
(orig. proceeding). "Those seeking the extraordinary remedy of mandamus must follow the applicable procedural 
rules," including "the critical obligation to provide the reviewing court with a complete and adequate record." In re 
Le, 335 S.W.3d 808, 813 (Tex. App.-Houston [14th Dist.] 2011, orig. proceeding).



Page 2 of 2
In re Schaefer, 2025 Tex. App. LEXIS 8266

Relator has failed to establish his entitlement to mandamus relief. Accordingly, we deny relator's petition for writ of

IRAC_summ:
Case Name: In re Schaefer [2025] Tex. App. LEXIS 8266
Court: Court of Appeals of Texas, Fourteenth District
Area of law: Civil Procedure—Mandamus
Procedural posture: Original Proceeding on Petition for Writ of Mandamus
Issue
Whether a relator is entitled to a writ of mandamus compelling a trial court to rule on a pending "Motion for Order of Satisfaction" when the relator fails to provide a sufficient record demonstrating the trial court’s refusal to act. The legal question turns on whether the relator has satisfied his burden of proof to produce a record establishing an abuse of discretion.
Rule
Mandamus is an "extraordinary remedy" that issues only when the relator demonstrates two distinct elements: (1) the trial court clearly abused its discretion; and (2) the relator has no adequate remedy by appeal (In re Academy, Ltd. [25]).
A critical procedural rule governing mandamus relief is the allocation of the burden of proof. The party seeking relief bears the burden of providing the reviewing court with a "sufficient record" to establish his claims (Walker v. Packer [837]). This burden entails a "critical obligation" to provide the appellate court with a "complete and adequate record" that substantiates the allegations of abuse of discretion (In re Le [813]). Without such a record, the appellate court cannot determine if the trial court failed to perform a ministerial duty.
Application
The court applies the burden of proof standard directly to the Relator, Michael Schaefer. Schaefer filed a petition for writ of mandamus seeking to compel the 281st District Court to rule on a "Motion for Order of Satisfaction" that he alleges remains pending in the underlying lawsuit (Cause No. 1994-47202).
The court evaluates whether Schaefer met the threshold requirement of providing a record sufficient to support his claim. The court observes that Schaefer failed to provide the court with a "complete and adequate record" (In re Le [813]). In the context of a request to compel a ruling, a sufficient record typically requires proof that the motion was filed, presented to the trial court, and that the trial court refused to rule within a reasonable time.
Because the Relator failed to submit a record establishing these facts, the court cannot evaluate whether the trial court abused its discretion. The court reasons that the Relator has not met the "critical obligation" required by the procedural rules (In re Le [813]). Consequently, the court determines that the Relator has failed to establish his entitlement to the extraordinary relief requested. The court does not reach the merits of the underlying "Motion for Order of Satisfaction" because the procedural prerequisite regarding the record was not satisfied.
Conclusion
The petition for writ of mandamus is denied because the Relator failed to provide a sufficient record to establish his claim.

Order, Supreme Court, New York County (Althea E.M. Drysdale, J.), entered on or about December 6, 2023, which 
adjudicated defendant a level three sexually violent offender pursuant to the Sex Offender Registration Act 
(Correction Law art 6-C), unanimously affirmed, without costs.

The court providently exercised its discretion in declining a downward departure (see generally People v Gillotti,23 
NY3d 841, 861 [2014]), and we perceive no basis to substitute our discretion and grant a downward departure to a

Guidelines and applies in full regardless of the applicability of an override (see e.g. People v Williams, 238 AD3d

Procedural posture: Appeal from an order adjudicating the defendant a level three sexually violent offender.
Issue
Whether the trial court abused its discretion in denying the defendant's request for a downward departure from his presumptive risk level three status under SORA.
Rule
A court may grant a downward departure from the presumptive risk level if the defendant identifies a mitigating factor that is not adequately taken into account by the risk assessment instrument (People v. Gillotti). The court must then determine if the factor exists by a preponderance of the evidence and whether it warrants a departure as a matter of discretion.
Application
The court affirms the level three adjudication. It finds that the mitigating factors cited by the defendant were already adequately accounted for by the risk assessment instrument. Furthermore, the defendant's participation in sex offender treatment was not so exceptional as to warrant a departure. The court emphasizes the "serious nature" of the crime—a brutal attack on a woman in a nightclub restroom until she lost consciousness—reasoning that the egregiousness of the conduct outweighed any mitigating factors and indicated a high risk of serious harm upon reoffense.
Conclusion
The order adjudicating the defendant a level three sexually violent offender is affirmed.
